gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Samantha, a citizen of the United States of America, can become entitled to the intestate estate of her father Suresh Perera, and to the further shares that came to her on the later intestacies, notwithstanding the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014 as amended by Act No. 21 of 2018.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The Act is deemed to have come into operation with effect from 1 January 2013 (s.1(2)), and the 2018 Amendment Act is deemed to have come into operation on 1 April 2018 (Amendment Act s.1). Section 2(1)(a) prohibits the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka to a foreigner, unless exempted under section 3. Foreigner means a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, and transfer means any sale, donation, gift or any conveyance by or under which title passes to another person (s.25). Section 3(1)(d) exempts from section 2 any land the title of which is transferred by intestacy, gift or testamentary disposition to a next of kin who is a foreigner, in accordance with the applicable law of succession of Sri Lanka, and section 3(1)(e) separately exempts a transfer to a dual citizen. Alienation in contravention of the Act is void (s.18). Section 2 of the 2018 Amendment Act amends section 3(1) by substituting paragraph (b), altering paragraph (h) and adding a new paragraph (i); it leaves paragraph (d) untouched. Who is next of kin on an intestacy is settled by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, under which children take equally per capita (s.24) and, where descendants fail and one parent survives, half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent share in the sibling half (ss.25 and 27).
gold_answer_draft.application: Suresh Perera died intestate on 10 December 1995. The Act operates only from 1 January 2013, so it has no application at all to the vesting of Samantha's one-sixth in 1995; her entitlement from her father is outside the Act on temporal grounds alone. The shares that reached her on Rakitha's death on 2 July 2022 and Muditha's death on 5 June 2023 do fall within the operative period of both the principal Act and the 2018 Amendment. Assuming she holds no Sri Lankan citizenship, Samantha is a foreigner within s.25. Even so, s.2(1) bites only on a transfer of title, and transfer is defined as a sale, donation, gift or conveyance by which title passes, all of which are voluntary dispositions; a devolution by operation of law on an intestacy is not naturally any of them. More directly, s.3(1)(d) expressly exempts land whose title is transferred by intestacy to a next of kin who is a foreigner in accordance with the applicable law of succession of Sri Lanka. Samantha takes as a child of Suresh under s.24 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance and as a half-blood sister of Rakitha and Muditha under ss.25 and 27 of that Ordinance, so she is next of kin taking under Sri Lankan succession law in every instance. The 2018 Amendment does not disturb paragraph (d). Section 18 is therefore not engaged and nothing in her entitlement is void. If Samantha is in fact also a citizen of Sri Lanka, she is not a foreigner at all and s.3(1)(e) would apply independently; the scenario states only her United States citizenship and does not settle the point.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Samantha can become entitled to the intestate estate of Suresh Perera. The Act cannot reach the 1995 devolution because it operates only from 1 January 2013, and the shares that came to her in 2022 and 2023 are within the express intestacy exemption in s.3(1)(d), which the 2018 Amendment left intact. Her entitlement is not an alienation in contravention of the Act and is not void under s.18. One caution should be recorded: s.3(4) provides that where a transfer is effected under s.3 the Act applies to every subsequent transfer of that land, so any later disposition by Samantha would be tested against s.2 in the ordinary way.

The board has resolved to acquire the property and has authorised its managing director, Ms. Ranmali Fernando, to sign on the company's behalf. The property offered to the company is Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2184 dated 12 January 2021 made by K. A. Wijeratne, Licensed Surveyor, in extent one acre two roods and ten perches, situated at Dadalla within the Galle Municipal Council limits and bounded on the south by the sea. The person offering the land as owner is Mr. D. P. Amarasuriya, who now lives in Melbourne and proposes to sign the transfer through his brother, Mr. L. K. Perera, Notary Public, and says the earlier deeds in the chain are with his family and can be produced later. A neighbouring family has fenced off and cultivated the northern portion of the land since 2009 and pays nothing to Mr. Amarasuriya. The price agreed between the parties is Rs 100,000,000, and the deed is to be signed at Galle.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What documents must the notary retained by Sea View Company (Pvt) Ltd examine before the company buys the Galle land: the documents that prove the vendor's title, the documents that show whether the land is encumbered or affected by a claim, the documents that establish the purchasing company's capacity to take title, and the documents needed because the vendor proposes to sign through an attorney.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a) requires the notary, before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land, to search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered, and rule (17)(b)(i) requires him to obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances. Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42 gives the right to search the registry books and take certified copies and extracts. The search matters because under s.7 of that Ordinance an unregistered instrument is void against a later duly registered instrument taken for valuable consideration, because s.11 makes a registered lis pendens bind a purchaser, and because s.32 lets a caveator have a later instrument rectified or cancelled. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33) requires the notary to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property, and rule (16)(a), read with s.13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, requires an accurate description of boundaries, extent and situation, which can only come from the survey plan and the prior deeds. For the purchaser, Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(d) requires the notary to retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and details of the board of directors, and rule (14) requires a copy of the board resolution authorising the signatory to be attached to the protocol; Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2) requires that written board authorisation where the directors cannot attend. Companies Act s.5(3) makes the certificate of incorporation conclusive evidence of incorporation. Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b) prohibits transfer of title to a Sri Lankan company whose direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, s.4(3) requires the company secretary to furnish documentary proof of the foreign shareholding before the Registrar of Lands registers the transfer, and s.18 makes any alienation in contravention void. Where the vendor signs by attorney, Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3(1)(a) requires the power to be registered with the Registrar-General, s.3B(1) requires the notary to examine the relevant volumes and folios in the Registrar-General's department, to be satisfied that the power has not been revoked or cancelled and to say so in the attestation, and to retain identity documents of grantor and attorney, and Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30) requires a true copy of the power to be kept with the protocol and forwarded to the Registrar of Lands. Prescription Ordinance s.3 shows that ten years of possession adverse to the owner can defeat a paper title, so possession must be looked at alongside the deeds.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary should first search the Galle land registry folio for Lot A in Plan No. 2184 and obtain the certified folio extract showing the current ownership and every registered encumbrance, mortgage, lease, lis pendens, seizure notice and caveat. Because Mr. Amarasuriya has produced only Deed of Transfer No. 4712 of 2011, the notary must call for the earlier deeds in the chain and for the title deed itself so that it can be endorsed, and must check that each link is registered, since an unregistered link can be defeated by a later registered instrument. The survey plan of 2021 and the descriptions in the prior deeds must be compared so that the schedule states the boundaries, extent and situation accurately and matches the folio. On the purchaser's side the notary must take a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation PV 00218347, the particulars of the directors and the board resolution authorising Ms. Fernando to sign, and must obtain from the company secretary documentary proof that the Singapore holding of 3,500,000 out of 10,000,000 shares leaves the foreign shareholding below fifty per cent, since the Registrar of Lands will require that proof and a transfer in breach would be void. Because Mr. Amarasuriya will sign through his brother, the notary must see the original power of attorney of 3 March 2024, confirm that it is registered with the Registrar-General, examine the relevant volumes and folios there for any revocation or cancellation, take copies of the identity documents of both grantor and attorney and keep a copy of the power with the protocol. The fenced and cultivated northern portion held by the neighbours since 2009 must be investigated on the ground, because possession adverse to the owner for ten years can defeat the paper title to that portion. Since the company is buying for hotel construction at a price of Rs 100,000,000, the notary should also confirm from the registry entries and the root of title that no State grant or permit condition and no acquisition notice affects the land.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Before the purchase the notary should check, at a minimum: the certified extract of the relevant folio of the Galle land registry showing ownership and registered encumbrances, including any lis pendens, seizure notice or caveat; the vendor's title deed and the earlier deeds forming the chain of title; the survey plan and the descriptions in the prior deeds; the certificate of incorporation, the particulars of directors and the board resolution of the purchasing company together with the company secretary's documentary proof that its foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent; and the registered power of attorney with a Registrar-General's search confirming it has not been revoked, along with the identity documents of grantor and attorney. He should also satisfy himself about possession on the ground and about the absence of any State grant condition or acquisition affecting the land.

answer_claims.claim_text: Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered.
The notary must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry, showing the ownership and the registered encumbrances of the land.
The registry books and indexes may be searched, and certified copies or extracts obtained, by a person interested or by his attorney-at-law or authorised agent.
The search matters because an instrument that is not duly registered is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for valuable consideration.
The search must extend to a registered lis pendens, which binds a purchaser, and to registered caveats, which allow a caveator to have a later instrument rectified or cancelled.
The notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property being transferred.
The deed must embody an accurate and clear description of the land with its boundaries, extent and situation, and registration will be refused if the instrument does not state those particulars.

Where a party is a corporate body the notary must retain a certified copy of its certificate of incorporation and the details of its board of directors, and must attach to the protocol a copy of the board resolution authorising the signatory.
Where the transferee is a corporate body whose board cannot be present, the board must authorise in writing the person who signs the deed on its behalf.
A certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company has been incorporated on the date it specifies and that the incorporation requirements were complied with.

Transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where its direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, and any alienation in contravention of the Act is void.

Where the transferee company has less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof of that shareholding before registering the transfer.
Every power of attorney, whether executed in Sri Lanka or abroad, must be registered with the Registrar-General.

A notary attesting a deed signed under a power of attorney must examine the relevant volumes and folios in the Registrar-General's department, be satisfied that the power has not been revoked or cancelled and state that in his attestation, retain the identity documents of grantor and attorney and a copy of the power, and keep a true copy of the power with his protocol.
Ten years of undisturbed possession adverse to the owner can defeat the paper title, so the deeds alone are not conclusive.

Because the vendor has produced only the 2011 deed, the notary must call for the earlier deeds in the chain and obtain the title deed itself, and must check from the folio extract that each link is registered.
The 2021 survey plan and the prior deed descriptions must be compared so that the schedule of the transfer states the boundaries, extent and situation of Lot A accurately and matches the folio.
The notary must take the purchasing company's certificate of incorporation, the particulars of its directors and the board resolution authorising its managing director to sign.

The notary must obtain from the company secretary documentary proof that the Singapore company's 3,500,000 of 10,000,000 shares leave the foreign shareholding below fifty per cent, because the Registrar of Lands will require it and a transfer in breach would be void.

Because the vendor will sign through his brother, the notary must see the original power of attorney of 3 March 2024, confirm its registration with the Registrar-General, search the volumes and folios there for a revocation, and take copies of the identity documents of grantor and attorney.

The northern portion fenced and cultivated by the neighbours since 2009 must be investigated on the ground, because possession adverse to the owner for ten years can defeat the paper title to that portion.

The notary should check five groups of documents before the company buys: the certified folio extract with all registered encumbrances, lis pendens and caveats; the vendor's title deed and the prior deeds in the chain together with the survey plan; the certificate of incorporation, directors' particulars and board resolution of the purchaser; the company secretary's proof of foreign shareholding; and the registered power of attorney with a revocation search and the identity documents of grantor and attorney.
He should also satisfy himself about possession on the ground and, from the root of title and the registry entries, that no State grant condition or acquisition affects the land.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the proposed mortgage bond is chargeable with stamp duty, on what amount and at what rate the duty is calculated, who must pay it, and where and when payment is made.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged by Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3 on every 'specified instrument' executed in Sri Lanka, at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette; the Act itself fixes no rate. Section 4(g) makes a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money affecting any property a specified instrument. Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 s.16 provides that where the total amount secured is in any way limited, the bond or mortgage is charged as on a bond for the amount so limited, and Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 leaves that measure standing only so far as it is not inconsistent with the 2006 Act. Under s.6(e), in the absence of an agreement to the contrary the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument. Section 8(1) requires payment before or at execution, and s.8(2) provides that duty on a specified instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at execution, or within seven days of execution where earlier payment was impossible, the bank issuing a certificate in the prescribed form which is affixed to the instrument. Section 9 requires stamp duty that is payable to a Provincial Council in respect of instruments in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution to be paid to the Provincial Council within whose limits the instrument was executed or the property is situated. Notaries Ordinance s.31 forbids a notary to attest an instrument without an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided, and requires the notary to pay the duty and to affix the stamps or the original bank receipt to the duplicate.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument Herath proposes to execute is a mortgage bond over land, securing one advance of Rupees Ten Million with no provision for further advances. It is therefore a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum of money affecting property, and a specified instrument. Because the amount secured is limited to Rs. 10,000,000, that is the amount on which the charge is measured. Herath alone executes the bond and there is no agreement putting the duty on the bank, so the duty is his liability, though in practice the notary pays it over and recovers it. The rate to be applied to Rs. 10,000,000 is fixed only by the Ministerial Order published in the Gazette under s.3, and no such Order is in this corpus, so the money figure cannot be stated from the material available. As to place, the bond relates to a mortgage of immovable property, so payment is made to a prescribed bank before or at the time of execution and the bank's certificate is affixed to the instrument; the land is in Anuradhapura and the bond is to be executed there, so both limbs of s.9 point to the Provincial Council for that province where the duty is a devolved one.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The mortgage bond is chargeable with stamp duty, measured on the limited sum of Rs. 10,000,000, and the duty is payable by Herath as the executant in the absence of contrary agreement. Payment is made to a prescribed bank in Anuradhapura prior to or at the time of execution, the bank's certificate or receipt being affixed to the instrument, and where the duty is one payable to a Provincial Council it goes to the Provincial Council within whose limits the bond is executed and the land lies. The rupee amount cannot be calculated on the corpus as frozen, because the Gazette Order under s.3 that fixes the rate for a mortgage bond is not in it. The question is therefore left blocked on that limb pending the rate Order.

The bond is chargeable and the duty is paid to a prescribed bank in Anuradhapura before or at execution, with the certificate or receipt affixed to the instrument.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Herath must obtain the approval of the Divisional Secretary before mortgaging to a licensed commercial bank land that he holds on a grant issued under the Land Development Ordinance.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Land Development Ordinance s.2 defines a 'holding' as land alienated by grant under the Ordinance, defines 'disposition' to include a mortgage, and defines 'licensed commercial bank' by reference to the banking legislation. Section 19(6) requires every grant to contain conditions that the owner shall not dispose of a divided portion or undivided share smaller than the unit of subdivision or the minimum fraction, and shall not dispose of the holding except with the prior approval of the Government Agent. Section 19(7) then provides that notwithstanding paragraph (b) of subsection (6), the approval of the Divisional Secretary shall not be required when mortgaging such holding to a licenced commercial bank, the State Mortgage and Investment Bank, the Development Finance Corporation of Ceylon, the National Development Bank of Sri Lanka, the National Housing Development Authority, the Housing Development Finance Corporation Bank of Sri Lanka, any registered society or other prescribed institution. Section 43(b) independently provides that the owner of a holding shall not mortgage it to any person other than a licensed commercial bank or one of the same listed institutions. The position of a permit-holder is different: by s.46 no permit-holder may effect any disposition of the land alienated on the permit, except that with the written consent of the Government Agent he may mortgage his interest to a registered society of which he is a member, and any other disposition is null and void.
gold_answer_draft.application: Herath is not a permit-holder. He paid the whole purchase amount, complied with the conditions of his permit, and a registered grant of the land was issued to him, so the land is a 'holding' and he is its owner. A mortgage is a disposition, so the condition in his grant that he shall not dispose of the holding except with prior approval is engaged on its face. The proposed mortgagee is a licensed commercial bank, which is both within the class of permissible mortgagees under s.43(b) and within the class that triggers the exemption in s.19(7). That exemption is expressed to displace paragraph (b) of subsection (6), which is precisely the approval condition, and it applies to the whole of the holding, which is what Herath proposes to mortgage rather than a divided portion or an undivided share. Had Herath still been a permit-holder, no approval would have helped him, because a permit-holder may mortgage only to a registered society of which he is a member and then only with the written consent of the Government Agent, and any other disposition would be null and void.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. Herath does not require the approval of the Divisional Secretary to mortgage the land. Because he holds under a grant and the mortgagee is a licensed commercial bank, Land Development Ordinance s.19(7) expressly removes the approval requirement that s.19(6)(b) would otherwise impose, and s.43(b) permits a mortgage to such a bank. The advice should be qualified in two ways: the exemption covers only the approval condition, so the other conditions of the grant, in particular the bar in s.19(6)(a) on disposing of a divided portion or an undivided share below the prescribed unit, continue to apply; and the exemption depends on the bank in fact falling within the definition of a licensed commercial bank, which should be confirmed before the bond is drawn.

answer_claims.claim_text: A 'holding' under the Land Development Ordinance is land alienated by grant under the Ordinance.
A mortgage is a 'disposition' for the purposes of the Ordinance.
Every grant contains a condition that the owner shall not dispose of the holding except with the prior approval of the Government Agent.
Notwithstanding that condition, the approval of the Divisional Secretary is not required when mortgaging the holding to a licensed commercial bank or another listed institution.
The owner of a holding may not mortgage it to any person other than a licensed commercial bank or one of the other listed institutions.
'Licensed commercial bank' bears the meaning given to it by the banking legislation referred to in the Ordinance.
A permit-holder, by contrast, may effect no disposition except a mortgage to a registered society of which he is a member, and then only with the written consent of the Government Agent.
The general bar on seizure and sale of alienated land does not prevent a licensed commercial bank enforcing a mortgage over land alienated on a grant.
Herath holds the land under a registered grant issued after he paid the purchase amount in full, so the land is a holding and he is its owner rather than a permit-holder.
The proposed mortgage is a disposition of the holding, so the approval condition in the grant is engaged on its face.
The intended mortgagee is a licensed commercial bank, so it is a permissible mortgagee and falls within the class that triggers the exemption.
Because the whole holding and not a divided portion or undivided share is being mortgaged, the separate subdivision condition in the grant is not offended.
Herath does not require the approval of the Divisional Secretary to mortgage the land to the bank.
The exemption removes only the approval condition, so the remaining conditions of the grant continue to bind Herath.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary who is instructed by his employer to execute a Deed of Transfer urgently may draw and attest that deed without searching the land registry to ascertain the state of the title, and what follows under the Notaries Ordinance if he does.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 makes it the duty of every notary strictly to observe the rules set out in that section. Rule (17)(a) of s.31 provides that before any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, the notary shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered. Rule (17)(b)(i) requires him to obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing the ownership of and the registered encumbrances on the land. The proviso to rule (17) creates the single exception: if the parties to the transaction authorise the notary in writing to dispense with the search, the search is not compulsory, but he must then write at the head of the deed the reference to the previous registration, if any, before tendering it for registration. Rule (33) adds that on a deed transferring immovable property the notary shall use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed. Breach of rule (17) is an offence: it is not among the rules listed in s.34(1)(a) or (b), so it falls within s.34(1)(c) and carries, on summary trial before a Magistrate, a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability. Section 33 saves an instrument from invalidity only where the notary's non-compliance is in respect of a matter of form; it does not address the notary's own liability.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument is a Deed of Transfer of an allotment of land at Talangama North, so it affects an interest in land and is not a will or codicil, and rule (17)(a) applies to it before the deed is drawn, not merely before it is registered. What the employer has given Saman is a photocopy of the vendor's 2014 deed. That is neither a search of the registers in the land registry nor the certified folio extract required by rule (17)(b)(i), so on these facts nothing has been done to ascertain the state of the title or to discover whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered. The proviso cannot be relied on, because neither the vendor nor the purchaser has authorised Saman in writing to dispense with the search; the employer is not a party to the transaction, and its instruction is in any event oral. The duty under s.31 lies on Saman in his capacity as notary. His employment as a legal officer of the real estate company does not shift that duty to his employer, and the Ordinance recognises no exception for urgency. Whether a deed executed in breach would nonetheless be a valid instrument is a separate question, since s.33 operates only where the omission is a matter of form; that point is open on these facts and does not affect Saman's own position.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. Saman cannot execute the Deed of Transfer without checking the title at the land registry. Rule (17)(a) of s.31 of the Notaries Ordinance obliges him to search or cause to be searched the land registry registers before he draws the deed, and rule (17)(b)(i) obliges him to obtain the certified folio extract. Because neither party has given him written authority to dispense with the search, the proviso to rule (17) does not apply, and his employer's urgency is no answer. If he proceeds he is guilty of an offence under s.34(1)(c), liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability. The proper course is to search the registers and obtain the certified folio extract first or, if the parties are willing, to take their written authority to dispense with the search and then write the reference to the previous registration at the head of the deed before tendering it for registration.

answer_claims.claim_text: Notaries Ordinance s.31 casts on every notary a duty strictly to observe and act in conformity with the rules set out in that section.

Under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a), before any deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting an interest in that land has been registered.

Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(b)(i) requires the notary to obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing the ownership of, and the registered encumbrances on, the land.

The proviso to Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17) makes the search non-compulsory only where the parties to the transaction authorise the notary in writing to dispense with it, and even then the notary must write at the head of the deed the reference to the previous registration, if any, before the deed is tendered for registration.
Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33) separately requires a notary before whom a deed transferring immovable property is executed to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property.

A notary who disregards or neglects to observe rule (17) is guilty of an offence and liable on summary trial before a Magistrate to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability, because rule (17) is not named in Notaries Ordinance s.34(1)(a) or (b) and so falls within the residual paragraph s.34(1)(c).

Notaries Ordinance s.33 protects an instrument from being held invalid only where the notary's non-compliance with a s.31 rule concerns a matter of form, and it does not by its terms relieve the notary of liability for the breach.

The instrument Saman is asked to execute is a deed of transfer of an allotment of land at Talangama North, so it is a deed affecting an interest in land and is not a will or codicil, and rule (17)(a) applies to it.

gold_answer_draft.rule: A notary's warrant entitles him to practise as a notary in the language in which he passed the conveyancing examination and within the judicial zone in which he resides (Notaries Ordinance s.3(1)), and s.9 binds him to keep his office within the area specified in that warrant. Rule (22) of s.31 provides that he shall not authenticate or attest any deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor attest a deed drawn in such another language. The prohibition is expressed in terms of the area in which the notary attests and the language of the instrument; it says nothing about where the land affected by the deed is situated. That the situation of the land is not a bar appears from rule (29) of s.31, which deals expressly with a deed affecting land in a district other than that in which the attesting notary resides and requires him, besides transmitting the duplicate in the ordinary way, to deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy certified by him as correct, with a list in duplicate, on or before the fifteenth day of the month following execution. Rule (30A) of s.31 allows sixty days instead of thirty for submitting for registration a deed required to be registered outside the jurisdiction in which the notary practises, and Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1) requires the instrument to be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land lies. Attesting outside the authorised area is an offence: rule (22) is not among the rules listed in s.34(1)(a) or (b), so a breach attracts s.34(1)(c), a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability. The zone may be changed only by a fresh warrant granted by the Minister under s.11. Employment as a legal officer is not a disqualification; rule (17)(c) of s.31 assumes a notary may be a legal officer of a company and requires him to state the company's registered address on the front page of the deed. The related disqualification is rule (13) of s.31, which bars a notary from attesting a deed to which he is a party.
gold_answer_draft.application: Saman's licence is for the Judicial Zone of Colombo, so by s.3(1) and s.9 his authorised area is Colombo and his office at Hulftsdorp is within it. The deed is to be signed by Mr. Perera and the company's authorised signatory before two witnesses, and attested by Saman, at that Colombo office on 20 April 2026; the attestation therefore takes place inside the area in which he is authorised to practise. The deed is drawn in Sinhala, the language of his warrant. Both limbs of rule (22) of s.31 are thus satisfied. The fact that the land, Kurunduwatta at Malkaduwawa, lies in the Kurunegala District does not put the attestation outside his area, because rule (22) looks to where the notary attests and not to where the land lies, and rule (29) of s.31 proceeds on the footing that a notary may attest a deed affecting land in a district other than his own. Saman is not a party to the deed and holds no shares or directorship in the purchasing company, so rule (13) of s.31 is not engaged; because he is a legal officer of that company, rule (17)(c) of s.31 requires the company's registered address to be stated on the front page of the deed. Because the land is in another district, he must, in addition to the duplicate he transmits to the Registrar of Lands of his own district, deliver or transmit a certified copy of the deed with a list in duplicate to the Registrar of Lands at Kurunegala on or before 15 May 2026, and, since the deed must be registered in the Kurunegala division under s.14(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, he has sixty days from attestation to submit it for registration under rule (30A) of s.31. If instead he yielded to the urgency and travelled to Kurunegala to attest the deed there, he would attest in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, contrary to rule (22) of s.31 and punishable under s.34(1)(c).
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Saman can attest the Deed of Transfer even though the land is situated in Kurunegala, provided he attests it within the Judicial Zone of Colombo, in which his warrant authorises him to practise, and in the language of that warrant. His territorial limitation restricts where he may attest, not where the land the deed affects may be situated. He must then discharge the extra duties that follow from the land lying in another district: a certified copy and list to the Registrar of Lands of Kurunegala by the fifteenth day of the following month under rule (29) of s.31, and submission of the deed for registration at the Kurunegala land registry within sixty days of attestation under rule (30A) of s.31. He cannot attest the deed in Kurunegala itself unless the Minister first grants him a fresh warrant for that zone under s.11 of the Notaries Ordinance.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary's warrant authorises him to practise only in the language in which he passed the conveyancing examination and within the judicial zone in which he resides.

A notary must not authenticate or attest a deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor in a language, or on a deed drawn in a language, other than that in which he is authorised to practise.
The territorial restriction attaches to the place where the notary attests and to the location of his office, not to the situation of the land affected by the deed.

The Ordinance contemplates a notary attesting a deed affecting land in a district other than the one in which he resides, and in that case requires him to deliver or transmit a certified copy of the deed, with a list in duplicate, to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated on or before the fifteenth day of the following month.

Where the deed has to be registered outside the jurisdiction in which the notary practises he has sixty days rather than thirty from attestation to submit it for registration, and the deed is registrable in the division in which the land is situated.

Attesting a deed outside the area in which the notary is authorised to practise is an offence punishable, on summary trial before a Magistrate, by a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability.

Being a legal officer of a company is not a disqualification from attesting; the disqualification is being a party to the deed, and a notary who is a legal officer must state the company's registered address on the front page of the deed.
Saman's authorised area is the Judicial Zone of Colombo and he proposes to have the deed signed and to attest it at his Hulftsdorp office in Colombo, which is inside that zone.
The deed is drawn in Sinhala, the language in which Saman's warrant authorises him to practise, so the language limb of the restriction is also satisfied.

That the land lies at Malkaduwawa in the Kurunegala District does not take the attestation outside Saman's authorised area, because the restriction turns on where he attests and the Ordinance separately regulates deeds affecting land in another district.

Saman is not a party to the deed and holds no shares or directorship in the purchasing company, so the bar on attesting a deed to which the notary is a party does not apply; as its legal officer he must state the company's registered address on the front page of the deed.

Because the land is in the Kurunegala District, Saman must send a certified copy of the deed and a list in duplicate to the Registrar of Lands at Kurunegala by 15 May 2026 and must submit the deed for registration at the Kurunegala land registry within sixty days of attestation.

Saman can attest the Deed of Transfer notwithstanding that the land is in Kurunegala, provided the attestation takes place within the Judicial Zone of Colombo and the deed is in the language of his warrant.
He could not lawfully attest the deed in Kurunegala itself unless the Minister first granted him a fresh warrant authorising practice in that judicial zone.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the Deed of Transfer attested by Saman can be invalidated because he failed to comply with rules set out in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, and whether the answer depends on which rule he broke.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Breach of a rule in section 31 does not of itself destroy the instrument. Notaries Ordinance s.33 provides that no instrument shall be deemed to be invalid by reason only of the failure of any notary to observe any provision of any rule set out in section 31 in respect of any matter of form. The protection is expressly limited by the proviso to s.33, which states that nothing in the section gives validity to any instrument that may be invalid by reason of non-compliance with the provisions of any other written law. Two of the rules in section 31 are engaged here. Rule (17)(c) requires the notary to write on the front page of the deed his name with initials, the number assigned to him, his office address and telephone number, and, if he is a legal officer working in an organisation, the registered address of that organisation; that requirement goes to how the face of the instrument is completed. Rule (12) forbids a notary to attest any deed unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in their presence; the same requirement is imposed independently, and as a condition of the deed having any legal force, by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a), under which no transfer of immovable property shall be in force or avail in law unless the deed is in writing and is signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another and is attested by that notary. Notaries Ordinance s.34(1)(c) makes a breach of a rule in section 31 an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate by a fine, in addition to any civil liability the notary may incur; it says nothing about the validity of the instrument, so the notary's liability and the standing of the deed are separate questions.
gold_answer_draft.application: Saman's omission of his name, notary number, office address and telephone number, and of his employer's registered address, from the front page is a failure to observe rule (17)(c). It concerns the completion of the face of the instrument and not the manner in which the parties bound themselves, and no other written law makes those particulars a condition of a valid transfer. On that default alone the deed would be protected by the main limb of s.33. The second default is of a different character. The executant Nimal Perera and one witness signed at Saman's office, but the second witness signed at his own house on the following day, in the absence of the executant and of the other witness, and Saman attested that all had signed in his presence and in the presence of one another. That is a breach of rule (12); more importantly, it means the deed was not signed by the executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, which the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) makes a condition of a transfer of immovable property being in force or availing in law. Because the deed affects a house and premises at Colombo 05, that Ordinance applies, and the proviso to s.33 withholds from this deed the protection the section would otherwise give. Saman attested at his own office at Colombo 07, within the Judicial Zone of Colombo for which he is licensed, so no separate objection arises under section 31 rule (22) as to the area of attestation. Independently of the fate of the deed, Saman remains exposed to prosecution and a fine under s.34 of the Notaries Ordinance, together with any civil liability towards the parties, and the urgency of his employer's instruction is no answer to either.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Deed can be invalidated, but not simply because rules in section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance were broken. Defaults that are matters of form, such as the omission of the notary's particulars from the front page, do not by themselves affect the instrument, because of Notaries Ordinance s.33. The deed is at risk here because the failure to have the executant and both witnesses sign in Saman's presence and in the presence of one another is also non-compliance with the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a); on the terms of that provision the transfer is not in force and does not avail in law, and by the proviso to s.33 the Notaries Ordinance does not cure it. Saman is in addition liable to be punished under Notaries Ordinance s.34 and to answer civilly to the parties for the loss.

Notaries Ordinance section 31 rule (12) forbids a notary to attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in the presence of the executant and the attesting witnesses.

Under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2(1)(a) a transfer of immovable property is not in force and does not avail in law unless the deed is in writing and signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary.

Notaries Ordinance section 31 rule (17)(c) requires the notary to write on the front page of the deed his name with initials, the number assigned to him, his office address and telephone number, and, where he is a legal officer of an organisation, that organisation's registered address.

Breach of a rule in section 31 is an offence under Notaries Ordinance section 34(1)(c), punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate by a fine in addition to any civil liability the notary may incur, and that section attaches no consequence to the instrument itself.

gold_answer_draft.issue: On the conclusion of the Commissioner of Title Settlement's investigation, which class of title is Kamal eligible to be registered with under the Registration of Title Act, given that his claim to the Homagama parcel rests only on uninterrupted possession since 1980 and he holds no deed, grant or court decree?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under the Registration of Title Act s.13 the Commissioner of Title Settlement investigates the genuineness of claims made in answer to the notice, and s.14 requires him to publish his determination in the Gazette in one of the forms it sets out. Section 14(a) permits a declaration of eligibility for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership only where the Commissioner is of the view that the claimant 'has a title of Absolute Ownership'. Section 14(b) provides that where a claimant does not qualify for a First Class Title but is in bonafide possession of the land parcel, the Commissioner may declare him eligible to be registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership, carrying the right, at the end of ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from the date of registration, to have that title converted into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Prescription Ordinance s.3 shows how prescriptive possession works in statute: undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession for ten years entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour in an action. Registration of Title Act s.31(1) sets out the conversion and adds that no action under s.29 may have been filed against the registration during the ten years, and s.29(1) gives any aggrieved person that ten-year window to move the District Court. Once a parcel is registered with either class of title, s.57 excludes the Prescription Ordinance from it.
gold_answer_draft.application: Kamal's claim rests solely on his occupation since 1980. He holds no deed, grant, permit or other instrument of title, and has never obtained a decree declaring him entitled to the land; no action about the land has ever been filed. Read with Prescription Ordinance s.3, his long possession is a basis on which he could have sought a decree, not an established title of Absolute Ownership that he can put before the Commissioner. He therefore does not satisfy s.14(a). His position does answer to s.14(b): his occupation of Lot 42 has been open, continuous and uninterrupted for more than forty years, he has paid the local authority rates in his own name throughout, he built and lives in a house on the parcel, and no competing claim to Lot 42 was submitted in answer to the Commissioner's notice. On those facts the Commissioner can properly take the view that Kamal is in bonafide possession of the parcel although he does not qualify for a First Class Title.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal is eligible to be declared, in the Commissioner's Gazette determination, eligible for registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership under s.14(b), not with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership under s.14(a). That Second Class Title carries the right, after ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from the date of registration and provided no action under s.29 has been filed in that period, to be converted under s.31 into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership; on registration under either class the Prescription Ordinance ceases to apply to the parcel by s.57. Two qualifications should be stated. Section 14(b) is permissive ('may'), so the declaration rests on the view the Commissioner forms on the investigation, and the Act does not define 'title of Absolute Ownership', so a claimant who could produce a decree or an instrument of title would be assessed under s.14(a) instead.

Under Prescription Ordinance s.3, undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession for ten years entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour in an action; the Ordinance provides for a decree rather than a self-executing documentary title.

A Second Class Title of Ownership carries a right of conversion into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership at the end of ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from registration, provided no action under s.29 was filed in that period.
Once a parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance no longer applies to it.

Kamal holds no deed, grant, permit or other instrument of title and has never obtained a decree declaring him entitled to the land, so he cannot show the Commissioner a title of Absolute Ownership within s.14(a).

Kamal's open, continuous and uninterrupted occupation of Lot 42 since 1980, with rates paid in his own name and no competing claim submitted in answer to the notice, supports the view that he is in bonafide possession of the land parcel.
Kamal is eligible to be declared eligible for registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership, not a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

After ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from that registration, and if no action under s.29 has been filed in the meantime, Kamal becomes eligible for conversion of his registration to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
The declaration under s.14(b) is permissive and depends on the view the Commissioner forms on the investigation, so the class of title is not automatic.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Sureka, a Notary holding no written authority from Kamal, may inspect the title register and the cadastral map maintained under the Registration of Title Act, and whether she is entitled to certified copies of those documents and from whom.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Title Act s.34(1) provides that any person may, on application made in the prescribed form and on payment of the prescribed fee, inspect during office hours any title register and any cadastral map maintained under the Act. Section 34(2) entitles any person, on application made to the relevant Registrar of Title and on payment of the prescribed fee, to receive an extract of the Title Register certified by that Registrar of Title. Section 34(3) entitles any person, on application made to the relevant Superintendent of Surveys and on payment of the prescribed fee, to receive a copy of an extract of the cadastral map used for registration of title, certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General. Section 75 defines 'Registrar of Title' as any person appointed as such under the Act, 'Superintendent of Surveys' as any person performing those functions in the Survey Department, and 'Title Register' as the register under the Act, which fixes who the two custodians are. The forms and fees referred to are those prescribed by regulations made under s.67(2)(g) and (h). By s.35(1) a document purporting to be certified by a Registrar of Title is presumed to have been so certified and is accepted as prima facie evidence of the matter to which it relates without further proof.
gold_answer_draft.application: Section 34 confers each of these rights on 'any person'. It does not require the applicant to be the owner, a claimant, or the agent of one, and it calls for no proof of interest or written authority. Sureka is a person within s.34, so the fact that Kamal has given her no written authority or power of attorney, and that she is not herself a claimant to Lot 42, does not stand in her way; she may apply whether or not she is described as acting for Kamal. What she must do is apply in the prescribed form, pay the prescribed fee and attend during office hours, all of which she is willing to do. For the certified extract of the register relating to Lot 42 she must apply to the relevant Registrar of Title, that is the Registrar at the Homagama Title Registry, who certifies it. For the certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map she must apply not to that Registrar but to the relevant Superintendent of Surveys, here the Superintendent of Surveys for the Colombo District, and the copy is certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes on both counts. Sureka may inspect the title register and the cadastral map under s.34(1) on application in the prescribed form, payment of the prescribed fee and during office hours, and she needs no authority from Kamal because the right belongs to any person. She is also entitled to certified copies, but from two different officers: a certified extract of the Title Register from the relevant Registrar of Title under s.34(2), and a certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map from the relevant Superintendent of Surveys, certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General, under s.34(3). Each is subject to payment of the prescribed fee. A certified document of the first kind is prima facie evidence of what it relates to under s.35. The prescribed forms and the amounts of the fees are set by regulations, which are not reproduced here.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the deed of gift by which Kamal conveyed the Homagama land parcel to Subash must be registered under the Registration of Title Act, and within what period the attesting notary, Sureka, had to forward that instrument to the Registrar of Title.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Once the title to a land parcel is registered under the Registration of Title Act, registration of dealings is compulsory. A person acquiring an interest in such a parcel is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered (s.38), the parcel may not be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the Act and every disposition otherwise effected is void (s.39), and an instrument executed under the Act takes effect only on registration (s.49). An 'instrument' is a document conveying title to or an interest in a land parcel in the prescribed form (s.75); it must be signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public (s.43(2)), the notary attesting it being subject to the identity, capacity and title checks in s.44. An instrument so attested must then be forwarded by the attestor, with the transferor's Certificate of Title, to the Registrar of Title for the area in which the parcel lies, within the period fixed by s.45(1)(a); the heading of that section states seven days and the text expresses the period in working days, but the numeral is missing from the corpus text of the subsection, so the exact period is not confirmable from the corpus and is flagged for the verifier. Failure to forward within the stipulated period is an offence punishable with the prescribed penalty (s.45(1)(b)). The instrument may also be presented by the donee or any person claiming a benefit under it (s.40(1)), and priority runs from the time of presentation (s.41(1)). The thirty day duty in s.31(30A) of the Notaries Ordinance governs the deeds system and is not the period applicable here, the deeds registers being closed to registered parcels (s.28).
gold_answer_draft.application: The Homagama land is a land parcel on the Title Register with Kamal as registered owner holding a Certificate of Title, so the gift to Subash could be effected only under the Act and had to be registered. The deed was drawn in the prescribed form, signed by the parties and two witnesses, and attested by Sureka on 2 January 2026 after she made the s.44 checks; the duty to forward it with Kamal's Certificate of Title therefore fell on her from that date. Eight working days of the Registry had passed by 12 January 2026 and nothing had been sent or presented, so on the seven day reading of s.45(1)(a) the period had run out before she noticed the omission. Until the instrument is registered the gift takes no effect and Subash holds no interest in the parcel, and the gift has no priority position, since priority would date from presentation.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Registration is mandatory: an unregistered gift of a registered land parcel conveys nothing and is void as a disposition outside the Act. The attested instrument had to be forwarded by Sureka, with the Certificate of Title, to the Registrar of Title for the Homagama area within the period in s.45(1)(a), stated in the section heading as seven days and expressed in the section text in working days, and not within the thirty days allowed for deeds under the Notaries Ordinance. She is in breach and exposed to the offence in s.45(1)(b), and the instrument should be presented to the Registrar of Title at once. This answer is withheld from gold status because the numeral in s.45(1)(a) is missing from the corpus text.

answer_claims.claim_text: Where the title to a land parcel is registered under the Registration of Title Act, no person acquiring an interest in that parcel is entitled to the title or interest unless it is registered under the Act (Registration of Title Act s.38).

A registered land parcel or any interest in it may not be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the Act, and every disposition otherwise effected is void (Registration of Title Act s.39).
An instrument pertaining to land executed under the Act takes effect only on registration, so registration is constitutive and not merely evidential (Registration of Title Act s.49).

An 'instrument' for these purposes is a document having the effect of conveying title to or an interest in a land parcel in the prescribed form, and such an instrument must be signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public (Registration of Title Act ss.75 and 43(2)).

An instrument attested in terms of section 44 must be forwarded by the attestor, together with the transferor's Certificate of Title, to the Registrar of Title within whose jurisdiction the land parcel is situated, within the number of working days fixed by section 45(1)(a); the heading of that section in the corpus states seven days, but the numeral is missing from the extracted text of the subsection, so the period cannot be confirmed verbatim from the corpus (Registration of Title Act ss.44 and 45(1)(a)).
Failure to forward the attested instrument within the stipulated period is an offence punishable with the prescribed penalty (Registration of Title Act s.45(1)(b)).

The thirty day period for submitting a deed for registration under the Notaries Ordinance belongs to the deeds registration system and is not the period that governs an instrument affecting a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act (Notaries Ordinance s.31(30A); Registration of Title Act s.28).
The Homagama land is a land parcel whose title is registered under the Act with Kamal as registered owner, so the gift to Subash is a transaction that had to be effected and registered under the Act.

Sureka attested the gift instrument on 2nd January 2026 after carrying out the attestor's checks, so from that date she was the attestor on whom the duty to forward the instrument with Kamal's Certificate of Title lay.

Eight working days had passed by 12th January 2026 and the instrument had still not been sent to the Registrar of Title, so on the seven working day reading of section 45(1)(a) the period had expired and the default was complete.

Because the instrument has not been presented, the gift has not yet taken effect and Subash has acquired no interest in the parcel; the delay also leaves the gift without priority against any instrument presented in the meantime, though Subash may himself present the instrument for registration.

Registration of an instrument affecting a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act is mandatory, and the attesting notary must forward the instrument with the Certificate of Title to the Registrar of Title within the period fixed by section 45(1)(a), which the section heading gives as seven days and which the section text expresses in working days.

Sureka is in breach of that duty and exposed to the offence created by section 45(1)(b); the immediate step is to have the instrument, with the Certificate of Title, presented to the Registrar of Title without further delay.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: Wills Ordinance section 2(2) answers the question in express words: a testator may exclude or disinherit a child without assigning any reason, notwithstanding any contrary law, usage or custom. The conditions on which that power is exercised (age and capacity under section 2(1), form of execution under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 4) are also statutory. No judicial authority or Roman-Dutch doctrine is needed to complete the answer, because the closing words of section 2(2) displace any contrary common law rule.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Martin Perera may execute a last will devising his house to his helper Siripala while leaving nothing to his two adult children, without stating any reason for excluding them, and on what statutory conditions the validity of such a will depends.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Wills Ordinance s.2(1) makes it lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years and is residing within or outside Sri Lanka to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property belonging to him at the time of death which would otherwise devolve on his heirs, in favour of a person not legally incapacitated from taking. Wills Ordinance s.2(2) gives every testator full power to make such testamentary disposition as he feels disposed and, in the exercise of that right, to exclude any child, parent, relative or descendant, or to disinherit or omit to mention any such person, without assigning any reason, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary. The preferential right of children in Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.24 sits in the Part of that Ordinance dealing with inheritance ab intestato and so operates only over property not validly disposed of by will. Freedom of testation must, however, be exercised in the prescribed form: under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 no will containing a devise of immovable property or a bequest of movable property is valid unless it is in writing and the testator signs it and affixes his thumb impression at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time. Under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 a benefit given by the will to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, is null and void so far as concerns that attesting witness, although the will itself remains valid. Wills Ordinance s.9 confirms that landed property in the Ordinance extends to houses and buildings.
gold_answer_draft.application: Martin is seventy-two, of sound mind and under no disability, so he satisfies the age and capacity condition in s.2(1), and he is governed by the general law rather than by Kandyan law, Thesawalamai or Muslim law. The house at No. 47/3, Temple Lane, Nugegoda is his own immovable property, held as sole owner, and it would devolve on Anusha and Dinesh if he did not dispose of it; Siripala, an unrelated domestic helper, is not legally incapacitated from taking it. His decision to leave the children nothing, and to give no explanation for that in the will, falls squarely within the words of s.2(2), and because the children's preferential right in Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.24 applies only on intestacy, they have no statutory claim against a will that disposes of the house. Two conditions must nevertheless be met. The will must be in writing and Martin must sign it and place his thumb impression at the end of it before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time, as Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 requires. The attesting witnesses must not be beneficiaries or the spouses of beneficiaries, which the proposed neighbours are not; had Siripala or his wife attested the will, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 would render the devise of the house to him null and void. Nothing in the facts shows whether the children are in need of support, and no maintenance claim against the estate arises from the provisions relied on here.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Martin Perera may execute the last will leaving the house to Siripala and giving his children nothing, and he need not assign any reason for excluding them, because Wills Ordinance s.2(2) confers that power in terms and notwithstanding any contrary law, usage or custom. The exclusion cannot be attacked merely because no reason is given. The advice is qualified only by the requirement that the will be executed in the manner required by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 and that neither Siripala nor his spouse attest it, failing which the will or the devise to him would fail on grounds unconnected with the absence of reasons.

answer_claims.claim_text: A person who has reached eighteen years and is residing in or outside Sri Lanka may execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property belonging to him at death which would otherwise devolve on his heirs, in favour of a person not legally incapacitated from taking.
Every testator has full power to exclude, disinherit or omit to mention any child without assigning any reason, notwithstanding any law, usage or custom to the contrary.
The preferential right of children to a parent's estate operates in inheritance ab intestato and therefore does not defeat a valid testamentary disposition.

A will containing a devise of immovable property or a bequest of movable property is valid only if it is in writing and the testator signs it and affixes his thumb impression at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time.
A benefit given by a will to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, is null and void so far as concerns that attesting witness.
Martin Perera, aged seventy-two, of sound mind and governed by the general law, satisfies the statutory age and capacity condition for executing a will.

The house at Nugegoda is Martin's own immovable property which would otherwise devolve on his two adult children, and Siripala, an unrelated helper, is not legally incapacitated from taking it under the will.
Because Martin's children take only on intestacy, they acquire no claim to the house against a valid will and cannot attack the exclusion on the ground that the will gives no reason for it.

The proposed execution before a notary public and two disinterested neighbours, with Martin's signature and thumb impression at the end of the will, meets the statutory form, and since neither witness benefits under the will the devise to Siripala is not avoided.

Martin Perera may execute the will leaving his house to Siripala and nothing to his children without assigning any reason, provided the will is executed in the prescribed form and no beneficiary or beneficiary's spouse attests it.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What steps Nihal, as the executor named in Martin Perera's last will and the person who found the original will, is required to take after Martin's death in order to obtain probate and to administer and wind up the estate.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.9 requires that a will be duly proved and recorded after the testator's death in the District Court empowered to grant probate. Civil Procedure Code s.516 requires the person in whose custody the will was, or who finds it after the death, to produce it to the District Court of the district in which he resides or in which the testator died, as soon as reasonably may be, with an affidavit verifying the time and place of death and the nature and value of the property left. Under s.517 the person appointed executor may apply to the District Court of the district in which he resides, in which the testator resided at death, or in which land of the estate is situate, within the time limit and in the manner specified in s.524, to have the will proved and probate granted to him; s.518 shows the process is not optional, since if no application is made the court itself proceeds to grant probate to the named executor or administration to another competent person. Section 524 requires the application to be made within three months of the finding of the will, by petition and affidavit setting out in numbered paragraphs the making of the will, the details and situation of the property, the heirs to the best of the petitioner's knowledge, the grounds of entitlement and the character claimed, with the will annexed or brought into court, evidence proving due execution, and the charges for the notice under s.529. Section 529 requires the Probate Officer to publish notice in Sinhala, Tamil and English calling for written objections supported by affidavit. If no objection is filed, s.531(1)(a)(i) requires the court, on prima facie proof of the due making of the will and the petitioner's character, to declare the will proved, declare the applicant executor and direct the grant of probate; if objections are filed, issues are framed and under s.534 probate is granted if the prima facie proof is not rebutted. Section 539 then requires the executor to take the oath of an executor within fifteen days of the order and to file an inventory and valuation within one month of the oath, whereupon probate issues. By s.542 an unlimited grant carries power over the whole of the deceased's movable and immovable property in Sri Lanka. Section 551 requires a true and final account of the executorship, verified on oath with receipts and vouchers, within twelve months of the issue of probate or such further time as the court allows, and s.552 makes an executor who fails to pay over what is due within a year of the grant personally liable for interest.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nihal found the original will in Martin's safe on 17 February 2026, three days after the death, so he is the finder within the meaning of s.516 and must produce the will to the District Court of Colombo, being both the district in which Martin died and the district in which Nihal resides, as soon as reasonably may be, supporting it with an affidavit of the time and place of death and of the house and bank balance left within that jurisdiction. As the executor named in the will he should then petition the same court under ss.517 and 524 by 17 May 2026, within three months of finding the will, setting out the making of the will of 20 August 2024, the details of the house at No. 47/3 on Lot A in Plan No. 2214 and of the savings account, the heirs Anusha and Dinesh as well as the legatee Siripala, the ground on which he claims and his character as executor, annexing the will and affidavit evidence of the notary and attesting witnesses to prove due execution, and tendering the charges for publication. The Probate Officer will publish the notice under s.529 and the children may file written objections supported by affidavit within the period stated in it. If they do not, the court will declare the will proved and direct that probate issue to Nihal under s.531; if they do object, the matter goes to a final hearing on framed issues and probate follows under s.534 unless the prima facie proof is rebutted. Within fifteen days of that order Nihal must take the executor's oath, and within one month of the oath file the inventory and valuation of the house, the bank balance and the debts under s.539, on which probate will be issued to him. Holding an unlimited grant he may then get in the bank balance, pay the funeral expenses and the hospital bill of about Rs. 350,000, transfer the house at No. 47/3 to Siripala in terms of the will, and file his final account within twelve months of the grant under s.551, remembering that under s.552 delay beyond a year in paying over what is due exposes him to interest out of his own funds. Whether an extension of time will be needed, and what duty is payable on the estate, cannot be settled on the facts given.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Nihal must produce the will to the District Court of Colombo with the prescribed affidavit as soon as reasonably may be after the death, and within three months of finding it petition that court by petition and affidavit to have the will proved and probate granted to him, allow the Probate Officer's notice to be published and any objections to be dealt with, and on the order declaring the will proved take the executor's oath within fifteen days and file the inventory and valuation within a month of the oath. Once probate issues he must administer the estate, pay the debts, give Siripala the house devised to him and file a final account within twelve months, failing which he risks personal liability for interest.

answer_claims.claim_text: After the testator's death the will must be duly proved and recorded in the District Court empowered to grant probate or administration.

The person who held or who finds the will after the death must produce it, as soon as reasonably may be, to the District Court of the district in which he resides or in which the testator died, with an affidavit verifying the time and place of death and the property left.

The executor named in the will may apply to the District Court of the district of his residence, of the testator's residence at death, or where land of the estate lies, in the manner and within the time specified in section 524, to have the will proved and probate granted to him; and if no one applies the court itself proceeds to grant probate to the named executor.

The application must be made within three months of the finding of the will, by petition and affidavit setting out in numbered paragraphs the making of the will, the details and situation of the property, the heirs to the best of the petitioner's knowledge, the grounds of entitlement and the character claimed, with the will produced, proof of due execution and the charges for publication.
Notice of the application is published by the Probate Officer calling on persons with objections to file them in writing supported by affidavit before the date stated in the notice.

Where no objection is filed and the court is satisfied of prima facie proof of the due making of the will and the character of the petitioner, it declares the will proved, declares the applicant executor and directs the grant of probate to him; where objections are filed, probate is granted after the final hearing unless the prima facie proof is rebutted.

The executor in whose favour the order is made must take the executor's oath within fifteen days of the order and file an inventory of the property with a valuation within one month of the oath, whereupon the court grants probate.

An unlimited grant of probate carries power over every portion of the deceased's movable and immovable property in Sri Lanka until the administration is complete, and the executor must file a true and final account verified on oath within twelve months of the grant or such further time as the court allows.
An executor who fails within one year of the grant to pay over the sums due to creditors, heirs or legatees is liable to pay interest out of his own funds unless he shows good and sufficient cause.

Nihal, having found the original will in Martin's safe on 17 February 2026, must produce it with the verifying affidavit to the District Court of Colombo, which is both the district where Martin died and the district where Nihal resides.

As the executor named in the will Nihal must petition that court to have the will proved and probate granted to him by 17 May 2026, within three months of finding the will, naming Anusha and Dinesh as heirs and Siripala as legatee and describing the house and the savings account.
Martin's children may use the published notice to object, in which case the application proceeds to a final hearing on framed issues rather than being allowed on the papers.

On the order declaring the will proved Nihal must take the executor's oath within fifteen days and file within a month of the oath an inventory and valuation covering the house at No. 47/3, the savings account and the debts.

Under the grant Nihal must get in the assets, pay the funeral expenses and the hospital bill, transfer the house to Siripala in terms of the will, and file his final account within twelve months of the grant.

Nihal's required steps are therefore production of the will with an affidavit, a petition within three months for proof of the will and probate, publication and disposal of objections, the executor's oath within fifteen days of the order and the inventory within a month of the oath, then administration of the estate and a final account within twelve months of the grant.

block_reason: The controlling first step, the effect of the prohibition against alienation and the gift over to Subash in Deed of Gift No 515 of 2018, cannot be decided from the corpus. The Abolition of Fideicommissa and Entails Act No. 20 of 1972 is absent, and the Roman-Dutch law of fideicommissum that s 36 of the Ordinance points to is not statute and is not in the corpus. The two available constructions give entirely different owners: Subash alone, or Linda, Sara, Rian and Bimali. A secondary, non-corpus problem is that the background does not say how Prabash's first marriage to Sheela ended, so it does not establish Linda as his lawful surviving spouse for s 22, and it names the same daughter Sunali and then Sonali.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The intestate steps in the chain are pure statute: Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance ss 21 to 27 dispose of the deaths of Prabash in 2019, Brian in 2021 and Sunali in 2023.
