gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s 21(1), and Part III applies to the estate of any person dying after the 1876 proclamation (s 20). A surviving spouse inherits one half (s 22). Subject to that, inheritance runs in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s 23). Children take equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child take by representation (s 24). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, that parent takes half and the full siblings, together with the half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent, take the other half (s 25). Where both parents have died, the estate goes to the siblings of the whole and of the half blood and their issue by representation (s 26). Where half siblings stand on one side only, the full siblings first take one half and then divide the other half with the half siblings (s 27). Persons equally near in degree take per capita (s 30). The Ordinance is silent on the effect of a reserved life interest and of a prohibition against alienation with a gift over; s 36 directs that on any question the Ordinance does not cover, the rules of Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland govern.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Wimala is the purchaser, and therefore the transferee, under a proposed deed of transfer of land at Galle. She cannot be in Sri Lanka when the deed is executed. The issues are whether a transferee must now sign the deed at all, what she must do if she cannot be present, how the instrument by which she authorises another person must be executed abroad and what it must contain, whether that instrument must be registered, and what the attesting notary must satisfy himself of.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) requires that no sale, purchase or transfer of immovable property is in force or avails in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public, all present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary, and unless the thumb impression of every executant is affixed beside the signature on the original, duplicate and protocol in the presence of the notary and the witnesses. Section 2(2), added by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, provides that in relation to a transfer deed both the transferor and the transferee must affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by subsection (1), but that where the transferee is unable to be present and execute the deed she shall authorise in writing any other person to sign on her behalf, that person complying with the requirements of subsection (1). Where such an authorisation is granted for a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3A(1) requires it to be executed subject to s.3A(2) or (3). If it is executed outside Sri Lanka, s.3A(3) requires that it be executed before a person authorised under s.2 of that Ordinance, that it describe the land by metes and bounds and extent, that it refer to the volume and folio of any prior registration, and that it be accompanied by a copy of the bio page of the grantor's passport signed by the grantor and by notarially certified identity documents of the attorney. Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2 defines a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka as one executed before an Ambassador, a High Commissioner, a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer within the meaning of the Consular Functions Act, or a person authorised to attest such an instrument under the law of that country. Section 3 requires every power of attorney to be registered with the Registrar-General, the holder submitting it within three months of execution where it was executed outside Sri Lanka, with a notarially certified copy and the affidavit in Schedule I. Section 3C limits validity to five years from execution unless the instrument states its own period or it is earlier revoked. Section 3B requires the notary attesting the deed to examine the relevant volumes and folios at the Registrar-General's department, to satisfy himself that the power has not been revoked or cancelled and to state that in his attestation. Notaries Ordinance s.31, rule (16)(c), requires the attorney signing a deed to give the notary an affidavit that the power of attorney is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at execution, and rule (30) requires the notary to keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and to forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.

Since the 2024 amendment she cannot simply leave the deed to the vendor: s.2(2)(a) makes her, as transferee, a signatory who must also place a thumb impression, and the vendor Nihal Weerakoon, being in Sri Lanka, can attend and comply for his part. Because her employment prevents her from travelling before March 2026, she is a transferee 'unable to be present and execute the deed' and the proviso to s.2(2)(a) applies: she must authorise her brother Sunil in writing to sign for her, and it will be Sunil who signs, gives his thumb impression and appears before the notary and the two witnesses as s.2(1) requires. That written authority is a power of attorney granted for a s.2 transaction, so s.3A(1) of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance applies, and because she will sign it in Canberra, s.3A(3) governs. Signing at the Sri Lanka High Commission before a consular officer satisfies s.3A(3)(a) read with s.2(b). The instrument must set out Kahatagahawatta by its four boundaries and its extent of eighteen decimal five perches, must refer to Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry as the prior registration, and must be accompanied by the bio page of her passport signed by her and by a notarially certified copy of Sunil's identity document. Once executed on 12 November 2025 it must be lodged by Sunil with the Registrar-General within three months, that is by 12 February 2026, together with a certified true copy and the Schedule I affidavit; since the deed is to be executed in the first week of December 2025 the authority should in practice be registered before then, because the notary must be able to examine the volumes and folios and certify under s.3B that it has not been revoked. The authority will still be current at that date, being well within the five-year period allowed by s.3C. At execution Sunil must give the notary the affidavit required by Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(c) confirming that the power is genuine and in force and that Wimala is alive, and the notary will keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and send a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands under rule (30). Wimala being a citizen of Sri Lanka, nothing in Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) stands in the way of the transfer.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Wimala can complete the purchase without travelling. She should execute, before a consular officer at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra, a written power of attorney appointing her brother Sunil to sign the deed of transfer for her, drawn so as to describe the Galle land by metes and bounds and extent and to refer to Volume 214 Folio 85, and accompanied by her signed passport bio page and Sunil's certified identity document. Sunil must register it with the Registrar-General within three months of execution, and in practice before the deed is executed, and must then sign the deed, affix his thumb impression and appear with the two witnesses before the notary, giving the notary the affidavit that the power is genuine, in force and that Wimala is alive. A deed executed in that way is in force and avails in law under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 as amended by Act No. 4 of 2024. If instead she simply stays away and lets the vendor alone sign, the deed will not satisfy s.2(2)(a) and will not avail in law. The precise date of operation of the 2024 amendment should be confirmed before the advice is acted on.

answer_claims.claim_text: A purchase or transfer of immovable property is not in force and does not avail in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by a person duly authorised by the executant and by the witnesses before a licensed notary all present together, attested by that notary, and bearing the thumb impression of every executant on the original, duplicate and protocol.

Since the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024, section 2(2)(a) requires both the transferor and the transferee of a transfer deed to affix their signatures and thumb impressions as required by section 2(1).

Where the transferee is unable to be present and execute the deed, she must authorise another person in writing to sign on her behalf, and that person must comply with the requirements of section 2(1).

A power of attorney granted for a transaction within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance must be executed subject to section 3A(2) or (3) of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, according to whether it is executed in or outside Sri Lanka.

A power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka must be executed before an Ambassador, High Commissioner, Diplomatic Officer or Consular Officer, or a person authorised to attest it under the law of that country.

Such a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka must describe the land by metes and bounds and extent, refer to the volume and folio of any prior registration, and be accompanied by the grantor's signed passport bio page and notarially certified identity documents of the attorney.

Every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar-General, and one executed outside Sri Lanka must be submitted for registration within three months of execution with a notarially certified copy and the affidavit in Schedule I.

The notary attesting the deed must examine the relevant volumes and folios at the Registrar-General's department, satisfy himself that the power of attorney has not been revoked or cancelled, and state that in his attestation.

An attorney signing a deed must give the notary an affidavit that the power of attorney is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at execution, and the notary must keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
A power of attorney is valid for only five years from execution unless it states its own period or is earlier revoked or cancelled.
Wimala's purchase of the Galle land is a purchase and transfer of immovable property within section 2(1), so the section 2 formalities govern her deed.

As transferee Wimala is now required to sign and place her thumb impression on the deed, and because her employment prevents her from travelling before March 2026 she is a transferee unable to be present within the proviso to section 2(2)(a).
Wimala must therefore authorise her brother Sunil in writing to sign the deed for her, and it is Sunil who must sign, give his thumb impression and appear before the notary and the two witnesses.

Signing the instrument at the Sri Lanka High Commission in Canberra before a consular officer satisfies the requirement of execution before an authorised person for a power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka.

The instrument must set out Kahatagahawatta by its four boundaries and its extent of eighteen decimal five perches and refer to Volume 214 Folio 85 of the Galle Land Registry, and be accompanied by Wimala's signed passport bio page and a certified copy of Sunil's identity document.

Executed on 12 November 2025, the instrument must be lodged with the Registrar-General by 12 February 2026, and in practice before the deed is executed in the first week of December 2025 so that the notary can examine the volumes and folios and certify that it is unrevoked; it remains within the five-year validity period at that date.
Wimala being a citizen of Sri Lanka, the prohibition on transfers of land to a foreigner does not apply to this purchase.

A deed of transfer signed by Sunil under a power of attorney executed and registered as described, with the affidavit given to the notary, is in force and avails in law under section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance as amended by Act No. 4 of 2024.
If Wimala neither attends nor authorises anyone in writing and the vendor alone signs, the deed will not satisfy section 2(2)(a) and will not avail in law.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary licensed to practise in Colombo do before he drafts a deed of transfer when the subject is a divided portion of a registered coconut estate lying in the Kurunegala district: what has to be searched, described, valued, consented to and checked, and whether he may act at all given his area of authority.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A notary must, before any deed affecting an interest in land is drawn by him, search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered, and must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (Notaries Ordinance s.31, rules (17)(a) and (17)(b)(i)). The search matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a party who takes for valuable consideration under a later registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)); a purchaser may protect the interval by registering a priority notice before execution (s.30(1)). The deed may not be attested unless it embodies, in the body or in a schedule, an accurate and clear description of the land with its boundaries, extent and situation specifying the district (Notaries Ordinance s.31, rule (16)(a)), and where a divided share is sold that share must be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent (rule (16)(b)); registration law requires the same and the Registrar must refuse to register an instrument that does not comply (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(2) and (5)). For an estate planted in coconut, the transfer of ownership of the estate or of any portion of it by sale is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has been previously obtained by the transferor and the transfer follows any conditions of that consent (Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1), read with the definitions in s.25 and with s.3(1)(c) of Act No. 20 of 2005, which substitutes the words 'tea, rubber or coconut estates' throughout); a coconut estate for this purpose is one of not less than four hectares registered under the Coconut Development Act, and 'transfer of ownership' expressly covers a portion of the estate (s.25). The certificate is issued by the Secretary of the Board (s.14), must be attached to the deed, and its number and date must be stated in the attestation (s.3(4)). A coconut estate is agricultural land, and a person who becomes the owner of agricultural land beyond the ceiling of fifty acres holds the excess as vested in the Land Reform Commission (Land Reform Law s.3(1) and s.5(1)). The notary must also ascertain the true legal nature of the transaction and explain it (Notaries Ordinance s.38A(1)), ascertain and set out the true and full consideration (s.38(1)), have an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided (s.31, rule (6)), and establish the identity of the executants by national identity card, passport or driving licence (rule (9)). His warrant specifies the area and language in which he may act (s.2) and his office must be within that area (s.9); he may not attest in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (s.31, rule (22)). Where the land lies in a district other than that in which he resides, he must in addition transmit a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated (rule (29)). Behind all of this, a sale of land has no force in law unless the deed is signed before and attested by a licensed notary (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)).
gold_answer_draft.application: The subject is a divided two acre portion of Polwatta, a twelve hectare coconut estate at Wariyapola in the Kurunegala district that is registered with the Coconut Cultivation Board, and Piyasena is shown on the folio as sole owner. Before drafting, the notary must search the registers of the Kurunegala Land Registry and take a certified folio extract to confirm Piyasena's title and the registered encumbrances, since any earlier unregistered dealing would rank behind a later registered one and the purchaser is buying on the faith of the register; a priority notice may be lodged to hold the position until registration. Because the portion has never been surveyed and no plan of it exists, the boundaries and extent needed for the schedule do not yet exist, so the notary must have the portion surveyed and a plan prepared before he can draft a schedule that satisfies rule (16)(a) and (b) and that the Registrar will accept. The estate exceeds four hectares and is registered, and the sale of a portion is a transfer of ownership within the definition, so the notary must require Piyasena to produce a certificate of consent of the Board obtained before the transfer, to be attached to the deed and recited in the attestation; without it the transfer would be null and void. As Sarath owns no other agricultural land, two acres does not carry him past the fifty acre ceiling, but the notary should make and record that check. He must take instructions establishing that an outright sale, and not some other arrangement, is intended, put the true price of six million rupees in the deed, satisfy himself that the stamp duty on that value will be provided, and see the parties' identity documents. Being licensed for Colombo, he may draw and attest this deed for Kurunegala land provided the parties execute it at his Colombo office and in his authorised language, which they are willing to do; the situation of the land does not disqualify him, but after execution he must send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the Kurunegala district.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary may act, but only if the deed is executed within his Colombo area of authority. Before drafting he should: search the Kurunegala Land Registry and obtain the certified folio extract for the estate; examine the vendor's title deeds and identify the parties by their identity documents; have the portion surveyed and a plan prepared so that the schedule can define it by its own boundaries and extent; require the vendor to produce the certificate of consent of the Fragmentation Board for the transfer of a portion of a registered coconut estate; check the purchaser's agricultural holdings against the land reform ceiling; ascertain the true nature of the transaction and the true consideration; and arrange for the stamp duty to be provided. He should also plan for lodging a priority notice and, after execution, for transmitting a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies.

answer_claims.claim_text: Before a deed affecting an interest in land is drawn, the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered.
He must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio showing the ownership of and registered encumbrances on the land.

An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later duly registered instrument, which is what the search guards against.
A purchaser may, before execution of the instrument by the transferor and with his written consent, register a priority notice of his intention to register the instrument.
The deed may not be attested unless it embodies, in the body or a schedule, an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation specifying the district.

Where a divided share is transferred, that share must be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent, registration law requires the same of a divided portion, and the Registrar must refuse to register an instrument that does not state those particulars.

The transfer of ownership of a coconut estate, or of any portion of it by sale, is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has previously been obtained by the transferor and the transfer conforms to the conditions of that consent.
A coconut estate for this purpose is one of not less than four hectares in extent that is or is deemed to be registered under the Coconut Development Act, No. 46 of 1971.
The certificate of consent is prepared and issued by the Secretary of the Board, must be attached to the deed, and its number and date must be stated in the notary's attestation.

A person who becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling, which is fifty acres for land that is not exclusively paddy, holds the excess as land deemed to vest in the Land Reform Commission under a statutory lease.
The notary must ascertain the true legal nature of the transaction and explain it to the executants, and must ascertain and set out the true and full consideration.

He must have an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided and must establish the identity of the executants by inspecting a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence unless they are known to him.

A notary's warrant specifies the area and language in which he may practise, his office must be within that area, and he may not attest a deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Where the deed affects land in a district other than that in which the attesting notary resides, he must deliver or transmit a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated.

A sale of land is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by the executants and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary and attested by him, which is why the transaction must be cast as a notarial deed.

The notary must therefore search the Kurunegala Land Registry and take a certified folio extract to confirm that Piyasena is the registered owner and to see the registered encumbrances before he drafts anything.

Because the two acre portion has never been separately surveyed and no plan of it exists, the notary must have it surveyed and a plan prepared so that the schedule can define the portion by its own boundaries and extent.

Since Polwatta is twelve hectares, planted in coconut and registered with the Coconut Cultivation Board, and Sarath is buying a portion of it, the sale falls within the fragmentation control and the notary must require the vendor's certificate of consent before drafting.
As Sarath owns no other agricultural land, a purchase of about two acres does not take him past the fifty acre ceiling, so the ceiling is no obstacle here although the notary should verify it.
The notary must record the true price of six million rupees as the consideration, satisfy himself that the stamp duty on that value will be provided, and inspect the parties' identity documents.

Being authorised for Colombo, the notary may draw and attest a deed relating to Kurunegala land so long as the parties execute it at his office in Colombo, which they are willing to do, because his authority is limited by the area of attestation and the language, not by where the land lies.
After execution he must transmit a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands of the Kurunegala district, because the land lies outside the district in which he resides.

The steps to be taken before drafting are therefore the registry search and certified folio extract, examination of the vendor's title deeds and identification of the parties, a survey and plan of the portion, production of the Board's certificate of consent, the land reform ceiling check, ascertaining the true nature of the transaction and the true consideration, and arranging the stamp duty; and the deed must be set down for execution within the notary's Colombo area.

PROV-M014-020 is therefore unresolved and a lawyer must decide whether the consent requirement bites before this can be gold. The notarial steps in the answer are separately verified.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Romani, the owner of a Battaramulla land who is leaving for New Zealand, may present a caveat for registration in respect of that land, and who is entitled to file a caveat under the Registration of Documents Ordinance as amended by Act No. 32 of 2022.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 32 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance (Chapter 117) provides for caveats. Its subsection (1) was repealed and substituted by section 2(1) of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022. Before that amendment section 32(1) allowed any person to present a caveat for registration. Under the substituted section 32(1)(a) a person who has, or who claims to have, a right, title or interest to a land, an undivided land, a land parcel or a condominium parcel may present for registration a caveat substantially in Form VIII of the Second Schedule, requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting that land. Section 32(1)(c)(i) extends the term caveator to a body of persons, a beneficiary under any trust affecting a land, the lawful guardian or next friend of a minor or of a person of unsound mind or mentally deficient person, an attorney of a person, a judgement creditor, an executor or administrator of the estate of a deceased, a legal heir, and an intended purchaser who has entered into an agreement with the owner or a developer of a land. Section 32(1)(c)(iii) extends the term interest to interests arising from an unregistered deed incapable of immediate registration, a trust, testate or intestate inheritance, instruments relating to a mortgage or an agreement to sell, co-ownership, condominium ownership and the estate of a minor or of a person of unsound mind. Land itself is defined in section 3 of the Ordinance to include things attached to the earth and any estate or interest in land. Standing is not sufficient on its own: section 32(1)(b)(i) requires the caveat to be in duplicate with an affidavit of the caveator and a certificate of an Attorney-at-law substantiating the right, title or interest; section 32(1)(b)(iii) requires a certified copy of a duly registered power of attorney where the caveator is an attorney; and section 32(1)(b)(iv) requires the caveat to contain the caveator's name, signature, identity card, passport or driving licence number, an address of the caveator in Sri Lanka for service, the right, title or interest claimed, the grounds of the claim and the description of the land. Section 32(2) obliges the Registrar to register a caveat received and to retain it, and section 32(3) as substituted by section 2(3) of the 2022 Act limits a caveat to a maximum of two years. Section 2(5) of the 2022 Act substituted sixty days for thirty days in section 32(5), so a caveator served with notice of a competing instrument has sixty days from posting of the notice to sue. A power of attorney relied on must be registered with the Registrar-General under section 3 of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, and by section 26(1)(d) of the Ordinance a notary may present an instrument for registration on behalf of an entitled person. Section 33(1)(a), inserted by section 3(2) of the 2022 Act, allows the caveator or an attorney to withdraw the caveat in writing.

As owner holding title under a registered deed she has a right, title and interest to the land and so falls squarely within section 32(1)(a) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance as substituted by section 2(1) of Act No. 32 of 2022, provided she lodges it in Form VIII in duplicate with her affidavit and an attorney-at-law's certificate under section 32(1)(b)(i) and gives an address in Sri Lanka for service under section 32(1)(b)(iv). answer_claims.claim_text: Under section 32(1)(a) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance as substituted by section 2(1) of Act No. 32 of 2022, a person who has, or claims to have, a right, title or interest to a land, undivided land, land parcel or condominium parcel may present a caveat for registration in Form VIII of the Second Schedule.
Before that substitution section 32(1) permitted any person to present a caveat, so the amendment narrowed standing to persons with, or claiming, a right, title or interest.

Section 32(1)(c)(i) extends the term caveator to a body of persons, a beneficiary under a trust affecting land, the lawful guardian or next friend of a minor or of a person of unsound mind or mentally deficient person, an attorney of a person, a judgement creditor, an executor or administrator of a deceased's estate, a legal heir, and an intended purchaser who has entered into an agreement with the owner or a developer.

Section 32(1)(c)(iii) extends the term interest to interests under an unregistered deed incapable of immediate registration, a trust, testate or intestate inheritance, mortgage or agreement-to-sell instruments, co-ownership, condominium ownership and the estate of a minor or person of unsound mind.
A caveat must be lodged in duplicate with an affidavit of the caveator and a certificate of an Attorney-at-law substantiating the right, title or interest claimed.

The caveat must contain the caveator's name, signature, identity card, passport or driving licence number and an address of the caveator in Sri Lanka at which notices relating to the caveat are to be served, together with the interest claimed, the grounds and the description of the land.

Where the caveator is the holder of a power of attorney, a certified copy of the power of attorney duly registered with the Registrar-General or the relevant Registrar must accompany the caveat, and every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar-General.

A caveat is in force for a maximum period of two years, the Registrar must register and retain a caveat received, and a caveator served with notice of a competing instrument must commence action in a competent court within sixty days of the posting of that notice.

Romani holds title to the Battaramulla allotment under a registered deed of transfer, so she has a right, title and interest to land and meets the standing test in section 32(1)(a); the allotment and the house on it are land under section 3 of the Ordinance.
Because she is ready to lodge in duplicate with her affidavit and her attorney-at-law's certificate of title, she can satisfy section 32(1)(b)(i).
Her departure for New Zealand does not disqualify her, but she must give an address in Sri Lanka for service; her sister's Rajagiriya address satisfies section 32(1)(b)(iv).

As she is the owner, she need not rely on the extended classes of caveator or the extended meaning of interest, and the notices to other owners required where the caveator is not the owner do not arise.

The notary consulted by Romani may present the caveat papers for registration on her behalf, and her brother, once his power of attorney is registered, may act for her as an attorney in relation to the caveat.
Since the caveat expires after two years and her absence is expected to last about three, it will have to be renewed during that period.

Romani can file a caveat in respect of her Battaramulla property, provided the caveat is in the prescribed form with the affidavit, the attorney-at-law's certificate and an address in Sri Lanka for service.

Under the Ordinance as amended a caveat may be filed only by a person who has or claims to have a right, title or interest in the land, including the classes listed in the inclusive definition of caveator, and no longer by any person at large.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Under section 32(5) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, where an instrument affecting the land described in a caveat is presented for registration while the caveat is in force, the caveator's remedy is an action commenced in a competent court within the period fixed by that subsection, running from the posting of the notice required by section 32(4). Section 32(4) is the notice given to the caveator when an instrument affecting the same land is subsequently presented, sent by registered letter to the address given in the caveat; the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(4) recast it as a notice in Form XI of the Second Schedule. As originally enacted section 32(5) allowed thirty days, but s.2(5) of the same 2022 Act substituted 'a competent court within sixty days' for 'a competent court within thirty days'. In that action the caveator must prove that the instrument presented is or was void or voidable by her, or fraudulent as against her, or in derogation of her lawful rights, and the court may then order it to be rectified or cancelled and the register corrected. A caveat itself lasts a maximum of two years under section 32(3) as substituted by s.2(3) of the 2022 Act.

gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Romani must commence her action in a competent court within sixty days from the posting of the Registrar's notice, that is by about 11 August 2025 on a notice posted on 12 June 2025. gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 s.3(1) charges stamp duty on every "specified instrument" executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka, at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette. Section 4(i) makes "a lease or hire of any property" a specified instrument. Section 6(c) makes the duty on a lease payable by the lessee unless the parties agree otherwise. Section 8(2) allows the duty on a lease of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution, with the bank's certificate affixed to the instrument. Section 13 makes the imposition provisions of the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 inoperative so far as they are inconsistent with the 2006 Act, so the rate for a post-2006 lease must be found in an Order under s.3(1) of the 2006 Act and not in the 1982 Act.

Unless the agreement provides otherwise, s.6(c) puts the burden on Sheela as lessee, and s.8(2) allows payment to a prescribed bank at or before execution. The base for the charge would be the rental consideration secured by the lease, on these facts Rs. 100,000 a month for twenty-four months, that is Rs. 2,400,000. Two further points affect the base: the Rs. 600,000 advance is a prepayment of part of the first year's rental rather than an addition to it, and the Rs. 300,000 deposit is refundable and so arguably not consideration at all. Both the rate and the treatment of the deposit are matters for the Ministerial Order under s.3(1), and no such Order is in the frozen corpus. The Act supplies no percentage, no slab and no minimum, so no figure can be computed from the statutory text alone.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) excludes only a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month from the requirement of a notarially executed writing, so a two-year lease of a house must be in writing, signed before a licensed notary public and the witnesses and attested by that notary, or it will not avail in law. Beyond that requirement of form, the corpus prescribes no content for lease covenants; the reciprocal duties of lessor and lessee come from the Roman-Dutch common law of lease and from conveyancing practice. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.6(c) is relevant to one covenant only, in that it makes the duty payable by the lessee unless the lease agrees otherwise, so the parties may allocate it expressly.
gold_answer_draft.application: Working from the facts, the covenants that need drafting are: a covenant to pay rent of Rs. 100,000 per month on the 20th day of each month of the two-year term; a covenant recording the Rs. 600,000 advance and the manner in which it is set off against the first year's rental, so that the sum actually payable each month in year one is unambiguous; a covenant on the Rs. 300,000 refundable deposit, stating that it is held as security, is not to be treated as rent, and is repayable at the end of the term subject to deductions for arrears or damage; a covenant restricting Sheela to use of the premises as a private dwelling house and prohibiting sub-letting or assignment without Mala's written consent; and a covenant on maintenance and repair, allocating interior upkeep and utility charges to Sheela and structural repair to Mala, coupled with a right of re-entry on default in rent and a covenant for quiet enjoyment while the rent is paid. Because Mala is in Kurunegala and the house is in Colombo, a covenant on notices and on inspection upon reasonable notice is worth adding, as is an express covenant on who bears the stamp duty, since without one the duty falls on Sheela as lessee. Which five a marker expects, and the exact wording, is a drafting judgment shaped by practice rather than by statute.

enrichment.original_background:
Mala is living with her daughter in Kurunegala. She intends to lease out her own house in Colombo for a monthly rental of Rs. 100,000/ for two years to Sheela. The rentals of the house have to be paid on the 20th day of each month commencing from 2020. Mala obtained a refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000/ from Sheela. She also obtained an advance payment of Rs. 600,000/ and intends it to be set off against the 1st year's monthly rental.

Mala intends to visit her son in Australia. Mala has given a Special Power of Attorney to her daughter Visaka to sell the said house in Colombo in 2017.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Two questions arise. First, whether Visaka can execute the two-year lease to Sheela on Mala's behalf under a Special Power of Attorney granted in 2017 that authorises her to sell the Colombo house. Second, what Mala must do so that the lease can validly be executed while she is in Australia.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property for two years is an agreement establishing an interest affecting immovable property and so falls within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, the only leases excepted being a lease at will or one for a period not exceeding one month. Such an instrument is of no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant, signed together with the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary all present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary. A person is duly authorised by a power of attorney within the definition in section 2 of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, that is a written authority to represent the grantor or do the acts specified, executed in Sri Lanka before two witnesses and attested by a notary, or executed outside Sri Lanka before an Ambassador, High Commissioner, Diplomatic or Consular Officer, or a person authorised to attest such a power under the law of that country. Because a lease falls within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2, section 3A of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance requires the power itself to describe the land by metes and bounds and extent, to give the volume and folio of any prior registration, to carry the grantor's thumb impression beside the signature, and to be accompanied by certified copies of the identity documents of grantor and attorney. Section 3 requires every power of attorney to be registered with the Registrar General, the attorney submitting it within one month of execution in Sri Lanka or three months if executed abroad, with a notary-certified copy and the Schedule I affidavit. Section 3C limits a private power to five years from the date of execution unless the instrument specifies its own period of validity or it is earlier revoked under section 4. Where a deed is signed by an attorney, rule (16)(c) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance requires the attorney to give the notary an affidavit that the power is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at execution, section 3B of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance requires the notary to examine the Registrar General's volumes and folios and to state in the attestation that the power has not been revoked or cancelled, and rule (30) of section 31 requires the notary to keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and to send a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands. What none of these provisions supplies is the rule that fixes how far an attorney's mandate extends; the scope of a special power is a matter of the general law of mandate and of judicial authority, outside the statutory corpus.

Mala herself need not sign if the deed is signed by a person duly authorised by her, so execution in her absence is possible in principle. The difficulty is the instrument she has. The 2017 grant is a Special Power of Attorney authorising Visaka to sell the house. A sale alienates the property; a lease for a term does not, and a special power is confined to the acts it names. On the statutory material alone one cannot conclude that a power to sell carries a power to lease, and Visaka could not honestly swear the affidavit required by Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(c) that the power is in force for a transaction it does not cover. There are two further difficulties even if scope were not in issue. The instrument was executed in 2017 and, unless it specifies its own period of validity, s.3C would put its life at five years from execution, which would have expired well before October 2025; and under s.8 of the Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022 a pre-2022 power survives only if it was registered, an unregistered one having had to be submitted within six months of commencement on pain of being deemed null and void. The scenario does not say whether the 2017 power specified a period or was ever registered, so neither point can be resolved on the facts given. As to what Mala should do, the safe course is a fresh power of attorney expressly authorising Visaka to lease the Colombo house and to sign the lease. If Mala grants it before she leaves it must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary under s.2(a); if she has already gone, she may execute it in Australia before the Sri Lankan High Commission or a consular officer, or before a person authorised to attest such a power under Australian law, under s.2(b). Because the lease falls within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, the power must satisfy s.3A, describing the Colombo house by metes and bounds and extent with the volume and folio of prior registration and carrying Mala's thumb impression and the certified identity documents. Visaka must then register it with the Registrar General under s.3, within one month if executed here or three months if executed in Australia, and should give the power its own stated period so that it is not cut short by s.3C. At execution of the lease Visaka signs as attorney, gives the notary the s.31 rule (16)(c) affidavit, the notary checks the Registrar General's folios under s.3B and says so in the attestation, and keeps and forwards copies of the power under rule (30). The alternative, if Mala is still in the country, is simply for her to sign the lease deed herself before the notary and witnesses before she travels.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for two years falls within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, because the only leases excepted are a lease at will and a lease for a period not exceeding one month.

An instrument within section 2 has no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by the executant together with the witnesses, in the presence of a licensed notary and of one another, and attested by that notary.

A person is duly authorised to sign for another by a power of attorney, that is a written authority to represent the grantor or do the acts specified, executed in Sri Lanka before two witnesses and attested by a notary public.

A power of attorney executed outside Sri Lanka must be executed before an Ambassador, a High Commissioner, a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer within the meaning of the Consular Functions Act, or a person authorised to attest such a power under the law of that country.

A power of attorney granted for use in a transaction falling within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance must additionally comply with section 3A of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, including a description of the land by metes and bounds and extent, the volume and folio of prior registration, the grantor's thumb impression, and certified copies of the identity documents of grantor and attorney.

Every power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar General, and the attorney must submit it for registration within one month if executed in Sri Lanka or three months if executed outside Sri Lanka.

A power of attorney other than one executed by a State institution is valid only for five years from the date of execution unless the instrument specifies its own period of validity or it is earlier revoked or cancelled under section 4.

A power of attorney executed before the 2022 amendment and already registered continues to be valid and effectual until revoked or cancelled, while an unregistered one had to be submitted for registration within six months of commencement and is otherwise deemed null and void.

Where a deed is signed by an attorney, the attorney must give the notary an affidavit affirming that the power of attorney is genuine and in force and that the grantor is alive at the time of execution, and the notary must satisfy himself from the Registrar General's volumes and folios that the power has not been revoked or cancelled and state that in the attestation.
A notary attesting a deed executed by means of an attorney must keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
The proposed lease to Sheela, being for two years at Rs. 100,000 a month, is well outside the one-month exception and must therefore be executed as a notarially attested deed.
Execution in Mala's absence is possible in principle, because the deed may be signed by a person duly authorised by her rather than by Mala herself.

The instrument Visaka holds is a Special Power of Attorney to sell the house, and whether an authority to sell extends to granting a lease is not answered by any provision of the statutory corpus, so this limb cannot be resolved on statute alone.

If the power does not cover a lease, Visaka could not truthfully give the notary the affidavit that the power of attorney is in force for this transaction, so the notary should decline to attest a lease signed by her under it.

Independently of scope, the 2017 instrument's continued validity at the October 2025 reference date is doubtful: unless it specifies a period of validity the five-year limit would have run out, and if it was never registered the transitional rule would have rendered it null and void, and the scenario states neither fact.

The course open to Mala is to sign the lease deed herself before a notary and two witnesses before she travels, or to grant a fresh power of attorney expressly authorising Visaka to lease the Colombo house, executed before two witnesses and a notary in Sri Lanka or before a High Commission or consular officer or other authorised person in Australia.

That fresh power must comply with section 3A, be registered with the Registrar General within one month of execution in Sri Lanka or three months if executed in Australia, and should state its own period of validity so that it is not cut short by the five-year limit.
Visaka cannot safely execute the lease under the 2017 Special Power of Attorney to sell, and a definitive answer on the scope of that power needs authority outside the statutory corpus.

The lease can validly be executed in Mala's absence if she grants a fresh, properly executed and registered power of attorney that expressly authorises the leasing of the Colombo house, whereupon Visaka may sign the notarially attested lease deed on her behalf.

gold_answer_draft.rule: A deed of partition affects immovable property, so Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) governs its form: it must be in writing and signed by every executant, or by any person duly authorised by such executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12) states the same requirement as a duty of the notary. A notary's warrant runs only within the judicial zone in which he resides (Notaries Ordinance s.3(1), extended from division to zone by s.4A), and by s.31 rule (22) he shall not attest any deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise; a breach is an offence carrying a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees besides civil liability (s.34(1)(c)), and s.33 does not save a breach of another written law. The Ordinance nevertheless allows a deed to be completed piecemeal. Section 32(2) applies where a deed to be executed by two or more parties is not signed by all of them at the same time and place, and s.31 rule (25) governs a deed executed or acknowledged before more than one notary: the notary who first attests complies with the whole of rule (20) and keeps the protocol, every other attesting notary complies with paragraphs (a) to (e) of rule (20), numbers the deed under rule (23) and keeps a certified copy as his protocol. By rule (28) the duplicate is transmitted by the notary who first attests, and by rule (29), the land lying in another district, a certified copy must also go to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated. Rule (27)(c)(ii) means the deed should be completed within three months of the first signature. As an alternative, s.2(1)(a) of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance permits signature by a person duly authorised by the executant. Such authority must be a power of attorney within Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2, executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary; because it is granted for a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance it must also satisfy s.3A(2), namely notarial attestation in accordance with the Notaries Ordinance and the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, a description of the land with metes and bounds and extent, the volume and folio of prior registration, the grantor's thumb impression and copies of identity documents. It must be registered with the Registrar-General within one month of execution (s.3), the attesting notary must satisfy himself that it has not been revoked or cancelled and say so in the attestation (s.3B(1)(b)), the attorney must give the notary an affidavit that the power is genuine, in force and the grantor alive (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (15A)(c)), and the notary must keep a true copy with his protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate (rule (30)). A third route lies outside the Notaries Ordinance: by s.2 of the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance a deed which s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance would otherwise require to be notarially executed is valid if signed by the party, or by a person lawfully authorised by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, before the District Judge for the district in which that party resides, and certified by that officer, subject to the conditions in s.4 and the duplicate and registration requirements of s.3.

Ranjan, Malini and Suranga are in Colombo and can attend Mr. Jayasuriya's office; they and two witnesses sign there in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he attests under s.31 rule (20), which satisfies Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) and s.31 rule (12) as to those three executants. Kanthi cannot come to Colombo and, being bedridden on medical advice for six months, cannot be waited for. Mr. Jayasuriya cannot go to her, because his warrant is confined to the Colombo judicial zone and Tangalle is outside it, so attesting there would breach s.31 rule (22) and expose him to the penalty in s.34(1)(c). Three lawful courses remain. First, the same deed may be taken to Tangalle and Kanthi's signature obtained at her residence before Mr. Kumarasiri, whose warrant covers that zone, with two witnesses signing in his presence and in the presence of one another; s.32(2) accommodates the different time and place, and s.31 rule (25) tells each notary what to do, Mr. Jayasuriya as the first attesting notary complying with the whole of rule (20) and keeping the protocol and Mr. Kumarasiri complying with paragraphs (a) to (e), numbering the deed in his own series and keeping a certified copy as his protocol. Mr. Jayasuriya then transmits the duplicate under rule (28), and because the land is in the Hambantota District a certified copy goes to that district's Registrar of Lands under rule (29). Second, Kanthi may grant her nephew Nuwan a power of attorney answering Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2 and s.3A(2), which itself must be attested by a notary and can be attested where she is by a notary authorised for that area, register it with the Registrar-General within one month under s.3, whereupon Nuwan signs the partition deed in Colombo before Mr. Jayasuriya, who must verify under s.3B(1)(b) that the power stands unrevoked and state that in his attestation, take the attorney's affidavit under s.31 rule (15A)(c), and keep and forward copies of the power under rule (30). Third, Kanthi may execute the deed before the District Judge for the district in which she resides under s.2 of the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance, with two witnesses present at the same time and the deed read over and explained and the other conditions of s.4 met, the duplicate then being transmitted for registration under s.3. On any of the three courses the parties should complete all signatures well within three months of the first, as rule (27)(c)(ii) contemplates, and they intend to finish within October 2025.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: All four parties can sign the deed of partition without the Colombo notary leaving his zone and without the Tangalle party travelling. answer_claims.claim_text: A deed of partition affects immovable property, so it is of no force in law unless it is in writing and signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary.
The notary may not attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he signed in their presence.

A notary's warrant authorises him to practise only within the judicial zone in which he resides, and a warrant expressed for a judicial division is deemed to authorise practice in the corresponding judicial zone.

A notary must not authenticate or attest any deed in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, and a breach of that rule is an offence punishable by a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees in addition to any civil liability.

The Notaries Ordinance expressly contemplates a deed to be executed by two or more parties who do not all sign at the same time and place, and a deed executed or acknowledged before more than one notary, prescribing how the first attesting notary and every other attesting notary must attest, number and keep a protocol.

Where a deed is executed by two or more parties before more than one notary, the duplicate is transmitted by the notary who first attests, and where the land lies in a district other than that of the transmitting notary a certified copy must also be sent to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated.

Where a deed is not signed by all parties within three months of the date on which it was first signed, the notary may be called on to deliver the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands, so staggered signing should be completed within that period.

A person duly authorised to sign for an executant must hold a power of attorney, which if executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary, and which, being granted for a transaction within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, must also be attested in accordance with the Notaries Ordinance and the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and carry the prescribed land description, registration reference, thumb impression and identity copies.

A power of attorney must be submitted for registration with the Registrar-General within one month of execution where it is executed in Sri Lanka, the notary attesting the deed must satisfy himself that it has not been revoked or cancelled and state that in his attestation, the attorney must give the notary an affidavit that the power is genuine and in force and the grantor alive, and the notary must keep a true copy with his protocol and forward a like copy with the duplicate.

A deed which section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance would otherwise require to be notarially executed is also valid if signed by the party, or by a person lawfully authorised by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, before the District Judge for the district in which that party resides and certified by that officer, subject to the reading over, stamping and legibility conditions and to execution in duplicate for transmission to the Registrar of Lands.

The three parties resident in Colombo can sign the engrossed deed with two witnesses at the Colombo notary's office, all present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and he can attest their signatures there.

The Colombo notary cannot travel to Tangalle to take the fourth party's signature, because Tangalle is outside the judicial zone covered by his warrant and attesting there would be a breach of the territorial rule.
Because the fourth party is bedridden for at least six months, the parties cannot simply postpone her signature until she can travel to Colombo, so an alternative mode of execution is necessary.

The same deed can be taken to Tangalle and signed there by the fourth party and two witnesses before a notary whose warrant covers that zone, the difference in time and place being provided for, with the Colombo notary as first attesting notary complying with the whole of the attestation rule and keeping the protocol and the Tangalle notary complying with paragraphs (a) to (e), numbering the deed in his own series and keeping a certified copy as his protocol.

On that course the Colombo notary transmits the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of his own district and sends a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands for the district in which the Tangalle land is situated.

Alternatively the fourth party may grant a notarially attested power of attorney to her nephew in Colombo, taken at her residence by a notary authorised for that area and registered with the Registrar-General within one month, after which the nephew signs the deed in Colombo before the Colombo notary, who verifies that the power is unrevoked, takes the attorney's affidavit and keeps and forwards copies of the power.

As a further alternative the fourth party may execute the deed before the District Judge for the district in which she resides, with two witnesses present at the same time and the deed read over and explained, the duplicate then being transmitted for registration.

All four parties can therefore sign the same deed of partition, the three in Colombo before the Colombo notary and the fourth at Tangalle before a notary authorised for that zone, the deed being executed before two notaries at different times and places and completed within three months of the first signature.

If a second notary is not used, the fourth party may sign through an attorney under a power of attorney meeting the statutory conditions, or execute before the District Judge for her district, each of which produces a validly executed deed.

What the parties cannot lawfully do is have the Colombo notary attest the fourth party's signature at Tangalle, or have her sign away from an attesting notary and witnesses, and the saving for defects of form gives no protection where the form required by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance is not met.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Two issues arise. First, what is the minimum age for executing a last will under the Wills Ordinance as most recently amended, and whether Sunil, who is 20, meets it. Second, what procedure Sunil must follow to execute a valid last will, given that he is seriously ill and wishes to dispose of both a house and a fixed deposit.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The latest amendment to the Wills Ordinance is the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022. Section 2 of that Act repealed section 2 of the Ordinance and substituted a new section under which it is lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years, residing within or outside Sri Lanka, to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property (Wills Ordinance s.2(1)). Section 3 of the amending Act repealed section 3 of the Ordinance, the provision that had invalidated wills made below the prescribed age and that had earlier been amended by Act No. 5 of 1993 to replace twenty-one years for males and eighteen years for females with a uniform eighteen years. The age limit is therefore eighteen completed years. The word will in the Ordinance extends to a testament, a codicil and any other testamentary disposition (Wills Ordinance s.9). As to form, no will is valid unless it is in writing and executed as prescribed, and the testator must sign and affix his left or right thumb impression at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are present at the same time; if the thumb impression cannot be obtained, another finger impression or the toe impression is to be affixed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(1) and (2), as amended by Act No. 30 of 2022). The notary must not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters (Notaries Ordinance s.31(8)) and unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, he himself signing in their presence (Notaries Ordinance s.31(12)). In the case of a will the notary must set out in the attestation that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will, and must enter in his deed register the number assigned to the will, its date and the name of the testator (Notaries Ordinance s.31(20)(h)). For a will the notary must also affix to the protocol a sealed passport size photograph of the signatory and keep a copy of his identity document with the protocol (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(b)(iii)). A will is excepted from the requirement that notarial instruments be executed in triplicate (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.16). A benefit given by the will to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void so far as that witness is concerned, though the witness remains competent to prove the will (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11). A will duly executed needs no other publication; it is proved in the District Court after the testator's death (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.9).
gold_answer_draft.application: Sunil was born on 14 March 2005 and is 20 years old at the intended date of execution, so he has reached the age of eighteen years and is competent under Wills Ordinance s.2(1) as substituted in 2022. His estate consists of an immovable property held on a deed of gift and a fixed deposit, both of which fall within the movable and immovable property that s.2(1) permits him to dispose of, and s.9 of the Ordinance means the same rule would govern any codicil he later makes. His illness does not by itself affect competence under the Ordinance; his physician's record that he remains lucid and able to sign and place a thumb impression means the notary can properly make the statement of good and sound mind that Notaries Ordinance s.31(20)(h) requires, and that the signature and thumb impression required by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(2) can be obtained. Had the thumb impression been unobtainable, the proviso permitting another finger impression or a toe impression would apply. The procedure he should follow is therefore to have the notary draw the will in writing; to assemble the notary and his two neighbours as witnesses at his residence at the one time; to sign and affix his thumb impression at the foot or end of the will in the presence of all of them, with the two witnesses subscribing their signatures in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, and the notary signing in their presence, as s.4(2) and Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) and (12) require; and to allow the notary to complete the attestation stating the sound mind of the testator, to make the deed register entry, and to attach the photograph and the copy of the identity document to the protocol. Because his chosen witnesses take no benefit under the will, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 does not cut down any of the gifts. Only one instrument need be executed, s.16 excepting wills from the triplicate rule, and no publication is needed during his lifetime, the will being proved in the District Court after his death under s.9.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The age limit for executing a last will is eighteen years, fixed by Wills Ordinance s.2(1) as substituted by the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022, the former section 3 having been repealed by the same Act. Sunil, at 20, is competent to make a will disposing of both his house and his fixed deposit. To make it valid he must execute it in writing and sign it, together with his thumb impression, at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses all present at the same time, the notary attesting it, stating in the attestation that Sunil was of good and sound mind, entering the will in his deed register and attaching Sunil's photograph and a copy of his identity document to the protocol. His illness is no bar so long as he is of sound mind at execution, and if his thumb impression cannot be taken another finger impression or a toe impression may be used instead.

answer_claims.claim_text: The most recent amendment to the Wills Ordinance is the Wills Ordinance (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2022, which repealed and substituted section 2 of the Ordinance.

Under the substituted section 2(1) it is lawful for any person who has reached the age of eighteen years, residing within or outside Sri Lanka, to execute a will disposing of movable and immovable property, so the age limit is eighteen completed years.

Section 3 of the Wills Ordinance, which formerly invalidated wills made below the prescribed age and had been amended in 1993 to set a uniform age of eighteen years for males and females, was repealed by the 2022 amending Act, so the age question is now answered solely by section 2.
The word will in the Wills Ordinance extends to a testament, a codicil and any other testamentary disposition.

A will is not valid unless it is in writing and the testator signs and affixes his left or right thumb impression at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are present at the same time, another finger impression or the toe impression being permitted where the thumb impression cannot be obtained.

The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters and unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, the notary signing in their presence.

In the case of a will the notary must state in the attestation that the testator was in good and sound mind to execute the will and must enter the number assigned to the will, its date and the testator's name in his deed register.

For a will the notary must also affix to the protocol a sealed passport size photograph of the signatory and keep a copy of his national identity card, passport or driving licence attached to the protocol.
A benefit given by the will to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void so far as that witness is concerned, although the witness remains competent to prove the will.

A will is excepted from the rule that notarially attested instruments be executed in triplicate, and once duly executed it needs no other publication, being proved in the District Court after the testator's death.
Sunil, born on 14 March 2005 and aged 20 at the intended date of execution, has reached the age of eighteen years and is competent to execute a will.
The house held on the deed of gift and the fixed deposit are respectively immovable and movable property within what section 2(1) permits a testator to dispose of.

Sunil's chronic illness does not affect his competence under the Ordinance, and because he remains lucid and able to sign and place a thumb impression, the notary can properly certify his good and sound mind and the signature and thumb impression required at execution can be obtained.

The steps Sunil should follow are to have the will drawn in writing, to sign it and affix his thumb impression at its foot or end before the notary and his two witnesses all present at the same time, with the witnesses subscribing in letters in the presence of each other and of the notary, and to let the notary complete the attestation, the deed register entry and the protocol requirements.
Because the two proposed witnesses and their spouses take no benefit under the will, no gift in the will is cut down on account of the attestation.
Only one instrument need be executed and no publication is required during Sunil's lifetime.
The age limit is eighteen years and Sunil, at 20, may lawfully execute a last will disposing of his house and his fixed deposit.

To be valid the will must be in writing and signed by Sunil, with his thumb impression, at the foot or end before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time, the notary attesting it, stating his good and sound mind, entering it in the deed register and attaching his photograph and a copy of his identity document to the protocol.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary who attested the will may tell the testator's children, during the testator's lifetime and without his permission, that he has executed a will and what it contains; and what the notary is exposed to if she does.
gold_answer_draft.rule: It is the duty of every notary, under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1), not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office. Rule (1) allows only two exceptions: the express permission of his employer, or a case where he is required to divulge by law. The Ordinance treats a will as confidential in its own record-keeping rules as well: under s.31 rule (24) the notary preserves the protocol of the will but enters only the number and date of the instrument in his register, and under s.31 rule (27)(a)(i) the duplicate of a will is not delivered to the Registrar of Lands and only the number and date of the document go into the monthly list. A notary who acts in violation of rule (1) is guilty of an offence under s.34(1)(a) and is liable, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that the will exists, and learned its contents, because the testator instructed her to draw it and executed it before her; that is information of which she became possessed in the execution of her office, and it is exactly the kind of information the Ordinance keeps out of her register and out of the monthly list. The employer for the purposes of rule (1) is the testator, who engaged her, and he is alive and has given no permission of any kind. His children are not her employers and cannot waive a secrecy owed to their father; while he lives they have no vested interest in his estate, only an expectation. Nor is she required by law to answer: no court order, summons or lawful demand by a public officer has been served on her, and an informal enquiry at her office is not legal compulsion. Neither exception in rule (1) is therefore satisfied, so the prohibition applies in full, and it applies to the bare fact that a will was executed as much as to its contents, since confirming the fact would itself divulge a secret.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. She should decline to say whether a will was executed before her or what it provides, and direct the children to their father, who alone can authorise disclosure while he lives. She may answer only if the testator gives express permission or if she is required by law to do so, for example under a court order. If she divulges without either, she commits an offence under s.34(1)(a) and is liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, and the breach may also be treated as misconduct in her office as a notary.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21(1)), which applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation (s.20). A surviving spouse first takes one-half of the intestate's property (s.22). Subject to that, inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23), children taking equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes (s.24). If descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with half-brothers and sisters related through the deceased parent, take the other half (s.25). If both parents have failed, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26); where all the half-siblings are related on one side only they take the whole, unless an ascendant on the other side survives (s.29). Heirs equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). The word 'unmarried' means not having a husband or wife living (s.3).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kapila held the entirety of Lot 1 under Deed of Gift No 925 once his father's reserved life interest ended on Mahesh's death on 24 April 2008. On Kapila's intestate death on 24 January 2011 his widow Champa took one-half (s.22) and his four surviving children Anusha, Prema, Rupa and Seetha took the remaining half equally per capita under s.24, that is 1/8 each. Anusha died on 15 June 2012 issueless, leaving her husband Hasitha Perera, who took one-half of her 1/8, that is 1/16 (s.22). Her descendants having failed and both her parents Kapila and Sandya having predeceased her, the balance 1/16 passed to her siblings under s.26; her only siblings were the three half-sisters Prema, Rupa and Seetha, all related to her on her father's side alone, and no ascendant on her mother's side is shown to survive, so under s.29 they took the whole 1/16, per capita under s.30, that is 1/48 each. Prema died on 4 September 2015 unmarried (s.3) and issueless, so no spouse's half is deducted under s.22 and no descendant takes under s.24. Her father Kapila had predeceased her and her mother Champa survived, so under s.25 Champa took half of 7/48, that is 7/96, and the other 7/96 went to her sisters. Her only surviving siblings were her full sisters Rupa and Seetha, Anusha having already died issueless, so they took 7/192 each under s.25 read with s.30. Section 27 does not alter Anusha's devolution because she left no full siblings, so the half-blood division there is governed by s.29.

A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the spouse's half, children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation.
Where descendants fail and both parents have predeceased the intestate, the estate passes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood, and their issue by representation.
Where all the surviving half-siblings are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole inheritance unless a grandparent or higher ascendant related on the other side survives.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with half-siblings related through the deceased parent, take the other half.
Heirs who are equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes.
A person who dies unmarried leaves no husband or wife living, so no spouse's half falls to be deducted from that estate.
On Kapila's intestate death on 24 January 2011 his widow Champa took one-half of Lot 1 and his four surviving children Anusha, Prema, Rupa and Seetha took 1/8 each.
Anusha's husband Hasitha Perera took one-half of her 1/8 share, that is 1/16.

The balance 1/16 of Anusha's share passed to her three half-sisters Prema, Rupa and Seetha, who took 1/48 each, both her parents having predeceased her and all her siblings being related to her on her father's side only.
After Anusha's death each of Prema, Rupa and Seetha held 7/48 of Lot 1.
On Prema's death unmarried and issueless on 4 September 2015 her surviving mother Champa took half of her 7/48, that is 7/96, and her full sisters Rupa and Seetha took 7/192 each.
The present shares are Champa 55/96, Rupa 35/192, Seetha 35/192 and Hasitha Perera 1/16.
Malani and Mithila hold no share in Lot 1, because Mahesh had gifted the entirety to Kapila before his death.
