gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month is within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, because the only leases excluded are a lease at will and a lease for a period not exceeding one month. Such an instrument has no force in law unless it is in writing and signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12) casts the same requirement on the notary as a duty, and rule (22) forbids her from attesting in any area other than that in which she is authorised to practise; s.4A treats the warrant as authorising practice in the judicial zone in which she resides. Notaries Ordinance s.32(2) deals expressly with a deed executed by two or more parties who do not sign it at the same time and place, and s.31 rule (25) governs attestation where an instrument is executed before more than one notary, the notary who first attests complying with the whole of rule (20) and every other notary with paragraphs (a) to (e). Rule (27)(c)(ii) contemplates completion within three months of the first signature. Alternatively, s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance allows the instrument to be signed by a person duly authorised by the executant. That authority is a power of attorney within Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2, which if executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and notarially attested, must satisfy s.3A because the lease is a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and must be registered with the Registrar General under s.3; Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30) then requires the attesting notary to keep a true copy of the power with her protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.
gold_answer_draft.application: The proposed lease runs for two years at Rs 150,000 a month, so it is well outside the one-month exclusion and must be executed notarially. The parties cannot cure Rupa Perera's absence by exchanging the document through the post and signing it apart, because both s.2 and rule (12) require signature in the presence of the notary and of the witnesses, all present together. Malani Silva practises in Colombo, and rule (22) with s.4A stops her from attesting a signature taken in Galle, so she cannot solve the problem by travelling to the lessor. Two routes remain. First, the one instrument may be executed in parts: Rupa Perera signs in Galle with two witnesses before a notary authorised to practise in that zone, and Gamini Sirisene signs in Colombo before Malani Silva, each notary attesting the signatures taken before her. That is the situation s.32(2) addresses, and rule (25) then allocates the attestation, numbering and protocol duties between the two notaries, the notary who first attests complying with the whole of rule (20). Rule (27)(c)(ii) shows the execution is expected to be completed within three months of the first signature. Second, Rupa Perera may grant a power of attorney to a person able to attend in Colombo. Because the lease is a transaction within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, that power must be notarially attested and comply with s.3A of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, and must be registered with the Registrar General under s.3; the attorney then signs the lease before Malani Silva, who keeps a copy of the power with her protocol under rule (30). The facts do not say whether Rupa Perera is willing to appoint an attorney or whether a notary is readily available in the Galle zone, so the choice between the two routes is practical rather than legal.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month falls within section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, because the only leases excluded are a lease at will and a lease for a period not exceeding one month.

An instrument within section 2 has no force in law unless it is in writing and signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and is attested by that notary.

A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise, that area being the judicial zone in which she resides.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21(1)), which applies to the estate of any person dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance (s.20) and does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22); subject to that, inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children and remoter descendants are preferent to all others and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation (s.24). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to both parents if both are alive; if only one parent is alive, that parent takes half and the other half goes to the brothers and sisters of the full blood, the issue of deceased full-blood siblings by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent (s.25). A person is "unmarried" for the purposes of the Ordinance when he has no husband or wife living (s.3). Where those who succeed are equally near in degree they take per capita (s.30). Dispositions of immovable property must be by notarially attested writing (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2), and on an intestacy the District Court identifies the heirs and their shares in a testamentary proceeding (Civil Procedure Code s.531) and discharges the administrator once the estate has been duly administered and distributed (Civil Procedure Code s.724B).
gold_answer_draft.application: Gamini Jayasinghe held the entirety under the final decree of 25 October 2010 in Partition Case No. 582/P. By Deed of Transfer No.2778 of 10 March 2011 he conveyed the entirety to Kamala Silva, and by Deed of Gift No.5634 of 18 April 2011 Kamala gifted the entirety to her only son Kasun. Kamala therefore held no interest in this land when she died on 7 July 2011, and nothing in it passed to her surviving husband Namal Silva or to her children Sarathi and Amal at that point. Kasun died on 3 May 2013 intestate and unmarried, that is without a spouse living within the meaning of s.3, and without issue, so no half share arises under s.22 and the descendant class in s.23 is empty. Under s.25 his mother Kamala had predeceased him and his father Thilak survived: Thilak took one-half, and the other half went to the brothers and sisters of the half-blood related to Kasun by the side of his deceased parent, namely his mother's other children Sarathi and Amal, who being equally near in degree took that half per capita under s.30, one-quarter each. Sunil and Lalith, Thilak's children by Sumana, are half-blood siblings on the side of the surviving parent and so take nothing out of Kasun's estate. That devolution was carried into effect in Testamentary Proceeding No.1589/2013/T, in which the heirs and their shares were determined (Civil Procedure Code s.531), and by the notarially attested Administrator's Conveyance No.6231 of 21 March 2014 executed by Thilak as administrator on the termination of the proceeding (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2; Civil Procedure Code s.724B). Sarathi died intestate and issueless on 8 August 2018 leaving her husband Sena. Under s.22 Sena took one-half of her one-quarter share. Subject to the surviving spouse's one-half under s.22, the right of inheritance is divided in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals.

Where a person dies intestate leaving no descendants and only one parent alive, that surviving parent takes one-half and the other half goes to the full-blood brothers and sisters and to the half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent.
A person is unmarried for the purposes of the Ordinance when he has no husband or wife living, so an intestate who dies unmarried leaves no spouse to take a half share under s.22.
Children and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of a parent and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation.
Persons equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What documents should the purchaser's lawyer call for to examine title before Tea Exports (Private) Limited buys the ten perch property with the office building in Colombo, and what is the reason for each. Three groups arise: documents proving the seller's title and the extent of the land, documents disclosing encumbrances and claims, and documents dealing with the corporate capacity of the two companies and with the local authority and planning position of the building.
gold_answer_draft.rule: No sale or transfer of immovable property avails in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by the executants and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary and attested by him, and where the transferee is a corporate body whose board cannot attend, the board must authorise a signatory in writing (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) and s.2(2)(a)). An unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7), registration counts only if made in the proper folio or a folio opened in continuation of it (s.14), a lis pendens does not bind a purchaser until registered (s.11), and any person interested, or his attorney-at-law, may search the books and obtain certified copies and extracts (s.42). Paper title is not conclusive, because ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession founds a title (Prescription Ordinance s.3). An instrument that is not duly stamped may not be registered or acted upon (Western Province Financial Statute s.60), and a plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared or certified as the Survey Act s.13 requires. Where a company creates a charge on land it must deliver the instrument to the Registrar for registration (Companies Act s.102), and registration is notice of the particulars of the charge to all persons (s.105). A certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence of incorporation (s.5), and a company may not enter into a major transaction, which includes acquiring assets worth more than half the value of its assets before the acquisition, except by special resolution, unanimous written shareholder consent or express authority in its articles (s.185). Transfer of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, unless an exemption in s.3 applies (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2). A building in a Municipality may not be occupied until the Council certifies conformity (Municipal Councils Ordinance s.127), council expenses of the kind described are a first charge on the premises payable by successors in title (s.152), development activity in a declared development area requires a permit (Urban Development Authority Law s.8J), and land may be under notice of intended acquisition given to the owner (Land Acquisition Act s.4). Where land lies in an area declared under the Registration of Title Act s.1, the Certificate of Title under s.37 replaces the deed chain, and a registered power of attorney is required for a deed signed by an attorney (Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3).
gold_answer_draft.application: Since the land is on a deeds folio in Colombo and not in a declared title registration area, the deed chain governs. The seller has produced only three instruments, the latest being Deed of Transfer No. 3128 of 2012 and the earliest Deed of Gift No. 812 of 1986; earlier deeds, or their registered duplicates or certified registry copies, must be called for so that the chain runs back well beyond any period in which a possessory title could have been perfected, and each deed must be inspected for the notarial attestation and for the stamp or endorsement of payment. A certified extract of the land registry folio and of every folio connected to it by cross reference must be called for, because that alone will show the mortgage bond of 2019, any other registered instrument taking priority, and any registered lis pendens. Because Deed No. 1476 of 1994 was signed by an attorney, the power of attorney, its registration particulars and evidence that it was unrevoked at that date must be produced. Plan No. 4372 of 2011 and a certified copy must be called for and, since the boundaries have not been checked on the ground, a fresh survey by a registered licensed surveyor is prudent to confirm that the ten perches match the description in the deeds and that the building stands within the boundaries. Possession must be proved independently of the deeds by rates and assessment receipts, utility bills and the tenancy or lease records for the office building. Because the seller is a company, certified copies of its certificate of incorporation, articles, directors' particulars and the resolution authorising the sale must be called for, a search made of the Registrar's register of charges, and the certificate of registration of the 2019 charge, the mortgage bond and the bank's letter agreeing to release the mortgage on payment obtained. On the purchaser's side, the certificate of incorporation, the articles, the share register and the latest annual return must be produced to show that direct and indirect foreign shareholding stands at thirty-five per cent and so below the prohibited level, and since the price of Rs. 480 million exceeds half the value of the company's assets, the special resolution or written consent of all shareholders approving the acquisition, together with the written board authority for the signatory to the transfer, must be in hand before execution. As the building was put up in 2013 within the Municipality and a declared development area, the approved building plan, the development permit and the certificate of conformity must be called for, along with a council statement of rates and other charges, which will disclose the unpaid drainage works expenses and the gap in rates receipts after 2021, and confirmation about street lines and building limits. Confirmation must also be obtained that no notice of intended acquisition affects the land, since none has been produced.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The purchaser's lawyer should call for, and give the following reasons for: the seller's deed and the prior deeds or their registered duplicates and certified registry copies, going back far enough to exclude a possessory claim, because only a notarially executed and duly registered chain gives priority; a certified extract of the land registry folio and connected folios, covering registered instruments and lis pendens, because registration decides priority and a registered pending action binds a purchaser; the power of attorney for the 1994 deed; the survey plan, a certified copy and if necessary a fresh survey, because only a properly certified plan is receivable in evidence and the extent must match the deeds; possessory documents, being rates receipts, utility bills and tenancy records, because ten years of adverse possession can defeat a paper title; stamp endorsements and receipts on every deed, because an unstamped instrument cannot be registered or acted upon; the seller company's certificate of incorporation, articles, directors' particulars and authorising resolution, a search of the Registrar's register of charges and the release of the registered mortgage, because registration of a charge is notice to all persons; the purchaser company's certificate of incorporation, articles, share register and annual return, because a transfer to a company with fifty per cent or more foreign shareholding is prohibited, together with the special resolution or unanimous written shareholder consent for what is a major transaction and the written board authority for the signatory; and the approved building plan, development permit, certificate of conformity, council rates and charges statement, street line and building limit confirmation, and confirmation that no acquisition proceeding affects the land. Title should not be accepted until the outstanding council expenses are settled or retained from the price and the mortgage is released on completion.

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale or transfer of immovable property does not avail in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary and attested by him, so every link in the chain produced must be a notarially executed deed.

An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a subsequent instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered, so the deeds must be checked against what is actually registered on the folio.

A person interested in the land, or his attorney-at-law, may search the registry books and indexes and obtain certified copies and extracts, which is the authority for calling for a certified folio extract and for certified copies of registered duplicates of missing deeds.

Registration is effective only in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the land was registered or in a folio opened in continuation of it with cross references, so the extract called for must cover every connected folio.
A registered lis pendens binds a purchaser for valuable consideration, so the search must extend to registered pending actions and particulars of any disclosed action must be called for.
Ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted possession adverse to the paper owner founds a title, so documents evidencing possession must be called for in addition to the deeds.

An instrument chargeable with stamp duty may not be registered or acted upon unless duly stamped, so each deed must carry the stamp or the endorsement of payment and the receipts must be produced with it.

A plan or map is receivable in evidence only if prepared or certified by the Surveyor-General, an authorised registered surveyor or a registered licensed surveyor, so the plan called for must satisfy that requirement.

A charge on land created by a company must be delivered to the Registrar for registration, and registration is notice to all persons of the particulars of the charge, so a search of the register of charges is required where the seller is a company.

A certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company was incorporated and that the incorporation requirements were met, which is why it and the articles and current directors' particulars are called for from each company.

A company may not enter into a major transaction, which includes acquiring assets worth more than half the value of its assets before the acquisition, unless it is approved by special resolution, consented to in writing by all shareholders or expressly authorised by its articles.
Transfer of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, unless one of the statutory exemptions applies.
Where the transferee is a corporate body whose board cannot attend to execute the deed, the board must authorise a signatory in writing, so that written authority must be obtained before execution.

A building in a Municipality may not be occupied until the Council certifies that it conforms to the Ordinance and the by-laws, and development activity in a declared development area requires a permit, so the approved plan, permit and certificate of conformity are called for.

Council expenses of the kind described rank with the rates as a first charge on the premises and are payable by the owner and his successors in title, so a council statement of rates and charges must be called for.
A power of attorney must be registered with the Registrar-General, so where a deed in the chain was signed by an attorney the power and its registration particulars must be produced.
Land may be under a notice of intended acquisition given to the owner, so the purchaser must call for any such notice and for confirmation that no acquisition proceeding affects the land.

Title registration applies only to areas declared by Order, and in a declared area the Certificate of Title is the document to be called for; since this land remains on a deeds folio, the deed chain and folio extract govern.

Because the seller has produced only the 2012, 1994 and 1986 instruments, the earlier deeds or their registered duplicates or certified registry copies must be called for so that the chain runs back beyond any period in which a possessory title could have matured.

A certified extract of the Colombo land registry folio and of every folio connected to it must be called for, since that is what will disclose the 2019 mortgage bond, any competing registered instrument and any registered lis pendens.
Because the 1994 deed was signed by an attorney, the power of attorney, its registration particulars and evidence that it was unrevoked at that date must be produced before that link is accepted.

Plan No. 4372 of 2011 and a certified copy must be called for, and because the boundaries have not been checked on the ground a fresh survey by a registered licensed surveyor should be obtained to confirm that the ten perches and the building match the description in the deeds.

Since the seller is a company that filed particulars of the 2019 mortgage with the Registrar of Companies, its certificate of incorporation, articles, directors' particulars and authorising resolution must be called for, a search made of the register of charges, and the bank's release of the mortgage obtained on completion.

The purchaser's share register and latest annual return must be produced to establish that direct and indirect foreign shareholding stands at thirty-five per cent, below the level at which a transfer to the company would be prohibited.

Because the price of Rs. 480 million exceeds half the value of the purchaser's assets before the acquisition, a certified special resolution or the written consent of all its shareholders, together with the articles and the written board authority for the signatory, must be in hand before the transfer is executed.

As the building was put up in 2013 within the Municipality and a declared development area, the approved building plan, the development permit and the certificate of conformity must be called for, and the council statement will disclose the unpaid drainage works expenses and the gap in rates receipts after 2021.
Since nothing has been produced about any intended State acquisition, confirmation must be obtained from the acquiring officer that no acquisition proceeding affects the land.

The documents to be called for are the chain of notarially executed deeds with their registration and stamp endorsements, a certified folio extract covering registered instruments and lis pendens, the power of attorney for the 1994 deed, the survey plan and if necessary a fresh survey, possessory documents such as rates receipts, utility bills and tenancy records, the corporate documents and charge search for the seller company with the release of the mortgage, the purchaser company's incorporation, shareholding and resolution documents with the written board authority, and the building plan, development permit, certificate of conformity, council rates and charges statement, street line confirmation and confirmation that no acquisition affects the land.

Title should not be accepted, and the price should not be paid over, until the outstanding council expenses are settled or retained and the registered mortgage is released on completion, because both would otherwise bind the company as successor in title.

enrichment.original_background: Kanthi Peiris is a Notary practicing in Colombo. Shantha Ratnayake is her brother-in-law and is the owner of an apartment in Negambo. Shantha wishes to lease out his apartment for 3 years at a monthly rental of Rs.120,000/= to one Ananda Gamage who is willing to take on lease in accordance with the said terms. However, Shantha who lives in Negambo is unable to come to Colombo to sign the Agreement.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How a three-year lease of a Negombo apartment at Rs.120,000 a month can be signed by a lessor who cannot come to Colombo and by a lessee who can, and what a Colombo notary must then do to register the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month is of no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant, or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a)). The notary may not attest unless the executant and the witnesses signed in her presence and in the presence of one another (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12)), and she may not attest in any area other than the area in which she is authorised to practise (s.31 rule (22)). The Ordinance nevertheless contemplates a deed executed or acknowledged before more than one notary and divides the attestation duties between the first attesting notary and every other attesting notary (s.31 rule (25)), and s.32(2) provides for parties who do not sign at the same time and place, deeming the instrument executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed. Alternatively the lessor may authorise an attorney: a power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary (Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2), must meet the additional requirements of s.3A where the transaction falls within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, must be submitted for registration with the Registrar-General within one month (s.3(1)(b)), and the attesting notary must check the Registrar-General's volumes and folios and state in her attestation that it has not been revoked (s.3B), keep a true copy with her protocol and forward a copy with the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30)), and take the attorney's affidavit that the power is genuine, in force and the grantor alive. As to registration, an instrument creating an interest in land is deemed to affect land and so is registrable (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)), an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for value (s.7(1)), registration must be effected in the book allotted to the division in which the land is situated (s.14(1)), and the notary acting for a party may present it (s.26(1)(d)). The notary must submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation, or sixty days where it is to be registered outside the jurisdiction in which she practises (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30A)), send the duplicate and Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month (rule (26)), send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies (rule (29)), and use due diligence in registering where she has instructions and funds (s.37).
gold_answer_draft.application: The lease is for three years, well outside the one-month exclusion, so notarial execution is compulsory and Shantha cannot simply sign at home and send the paper to Colombo. Kanthi practises in Colombo and the apartment and Shantha are in Negombo, so rule (22) prevents her attesting Shantha's signature outside the area she is authorised for. Two lawful routes remain. First, execution before more than one notary under rule (25): Ananda Gamage signs the agreement before Kanthi in Colombo with two witnesses, and Shantha signs the same instrument before a notary authorised to practise where he is, each notary attesting the signatures taken before her or him, each numbering the instrument in his or her own protocol register, and s.32(2) accommodating the fact that the parties sign at different times and places. Second, Shantha grants a power of attorney, attested by a notary before two witnesses and complying with s.3A because the lease falls within s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, registers it with the Registrar-General within one month, and his attorney then signs before Kanthi in Colombo along with Ananda; Kanthi must satisfy herself from the Registrar-General's volumes and folios that the power stands unrevoked and say so in her attestation, take the attorney's affidavit, and keep and forward copies of the power. Either way she must have an assurance that the stamp duty is provided before attesting. On registration, the lease creates an interest in land and is registrable; it must go to the land registry for the division in which the Negombo apartment is situated, not Colombo. Because that registration is outside the jurisdiction in which Kanthi practises, she has sixty days from attestation to submit it, she must transmit the duplicate and Form F1 list to the Registrar of Lands of her own district by the fifteenth of the following month, and she must send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the apartment lies. gold_answer_draft.rule: The certificate that a person is a notary duly authorised to practise is issued yearly by the Registrar of the High Court; it must be applied for and granted on or before 1 April in every year and is in force for one year and no longer (Notaries Ordinance s.27(2)). Where the certificate was not applied for within that time, the High Court Judge may, if satisfied that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, direct the Registrar to issue it notwithstanding the delay (s.27(2), proviso). A person who acts as a notary without having obtained such a certificate is guilty of an offence for or in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him while he was without it, and is liable to a fine of not less than five thousand rupees and not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees (s.30). The Registrar-General may, instead of prosecuting, accept from the notary such sum as he considers proper in composition of a section 30 offence (s.35(1)). Separately, on a High Court Judge's report of an offence or of misconduct, the Minister may cancel the notary's warrant or suspend her from office for such period as appears just (s.21(2)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Kanthi attested the lease agreement in a year for which she had not obtained the yearly certificate, so at the moment of attestation she was acting as a notary without the certificate required by s.27. That engages s.30 directly, and because the offence is framed 'for or in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him', her exposure is counted per deed: the lease agreement is one such deed, and any other deed she attested while uncertificated attracts its own fine of between Rs.5,000 and Rs.25,000. The Registrar-General may take the matter administratively and accept a composition sum instead of prosecuting her. Beyond the fine, a conviction or a finding of misconduct reported by the High Court Judge exposes her to cancellation of her warrant or to suspension. She should apply at once for the certificate and, since the 1 April date has passed, ask the High Court Judge to direct the Registrar to issue it on the ground that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, but that relief operates on the issue of the certificate and does not erase the attestation already made without one. Whether the lease agreement itself is invalid is not settled by these provisions: s.33 saves an instrument only from a notary's failure in a matter of form under a s.31 rule and expressly does not validate an instrument invalid under any other written law, and s.30 is not a s.31 rule.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette (Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1)). A lease or hire of any property is a specified instrument (s.4(i)). Unless the parties agree otherwise, the duty on a lease is payable by the lessee (s.6(c)). Duty on an instrument relating to a lease of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at the time of execution, or within seven days of execution where it could not be paid earlier for reasons beyond the payer's control, and the bank's certificate is affixed to the instrument (s.8(2)). A notary must not attest a deed unless she has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6)), and the stamp duty required on a deed executed under any written law is to be paid by the notary (s.31 rule (7)(a)).

enrichment.original_background: In 1995 Shantha Silva purchased a land in extent of 10 perches situated in Kalutara for Rs.700,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs.2,000,000/-. He wishes to gift this house and land to his daughter Sumana and he instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift in this regard. gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is chargeable on a deed of gift by which a father gifts to his daughter a 10-perch land at Kalutara that he bought in 1995 for Rs.700,000 and on which he built a house at a cost of Rs.2,000,000, the present market value being Rs.10,400,000; on what value is the duty computed, who pays it, and what is the procedure for payment and attestation.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Kalutara is in the Western Province, so stamp duty on an instrument relating to a transfer of this land is charged by the Financial Statute of the Western Province, No. 6 of 1990. Section 37 charges duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Province, and s.106 defines "transfer" to include a gift and "gift" as a voluntary transfer without consideration in money or money's worth. Section 48(1) requires the duty to be calculated on the value of the property conveyed. For immovable property that is gifted and that the donor acquired after 31 March 1977, s.106 defines "value" as the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the gift, and (ii) the price it would fetch in the open market at the date of the instrument of gift. The rate applied to that value is a prescribed rate, that is a rate fixed by regulation of the provincial Minister published in the Gazette under s.77(1)(a). By s.51(a) the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee. Section 40(1) requires payment before or at the time of execution; s.40(2) allows payment for a transfer of immovable property to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate of payment that is affixed to the instrument, and permits payment within seven days of execution where earlier payment was impossible for reasons beyond the payer's control. Section 9 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 directs the duty to the Provincial Council within whose limits the property is situated, and to a bank prescribed by the Commissioner-General while the Council stands dissolved. Section 78(1) requires the deed to set out the parties, the consideration and all facts affecting chargeability together with the amount of duty, and s.78(2) requires the attesting notary to satisfy himself that the value stamped represents the value of the property. Under the Notaries Ordinance, s.31 rule (6) the notary may not attest a deed unless he has an assurance that the required duty is provided, and rule (7A) requires the notary to pay the duty, to affix the original bank receipt to the duplicate and copies of it to the original and the protocol. Section 39 of the Statute exempts certain instruments, none of which covers a gift between private persons, and by s.60 an instrument that is not duly stamped cannot be registered, authenticated or acted upon except on payment of the deficit and a penalty. Section 62 allows the proper duty to be adjudicated in advance by an Assessor on payment of a fee of two hundred and fifty rupees.

The first measure is the open-market price at acquisition, for which the Rs.700,000 paid in 1995 is the figure on the facts, increased by the Rs.2,000,000 spent on constructing the house, which is an addition made after acquisition and before the gift: Rs.700,000 + Rs.2,000,000 = Rs.2,700,000. The second measure is the open-market price at the date of the deed, Rs.10,400,000. The Statute takes the lower, so the deed is chargeable on Rs.2,700,000 and not on Rs.10,400,000. The duty is then the prescribed rate applied to Rs.2,700,000. Two qualifications should be noted. The Rs.700,000 is the price actually paid in 1995, whereas the Statute speaks of the price the property would have fetched in the open market at that date in the opinion of the Assessor, so the Assessor may substitute a different figure. And the rate to be applied is fixed by a Gazette regulation which is not part of this corpus, so the money figure cannot be stated from the materials available here. The deed falls within no exemption in s.39.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The deed of gift is chargeable with Western Province stamp duty on a value of Rs.2,700,000, being the Rs.700,000 acquisition price plus the Rs.2,000,000 cost of construction, that being lower than the Rs.10,400,000 present market value. The duty payable is the prescribed rate applied to Rs.2,700,000; the rate regulation is outside this corpus, so the figure is left open rather than stated. The duty falls on the donee unless the deed provides otherwise. In practice the notary computes the duty, pays it to the prescribed bank before or at the time of execution, affixes the original receipt to the duplicate and copies to the original and the protocol, sets out in the deed the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty, and attests only once satisfied that the duty has been provided and that the value stamped is the value of the property. gold_answer_draft.issue: On what grounds, and by what route, may a father revoke a gift he has made to his son by a deed of gift that reserves no power of revocation, where the son has since assaulted him and refused to maintain him?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Where a deed of gift is irrevocable, the donor cannot simply take the gift back. Under the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017 s.2, an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, and only on an order of a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee. Section 3 bars the court from entertaining such an action unless it is filed both within ten years of the execution of the deed and within two years of the date on which the cause of action arose; both limbs must be satisfied. Section 5 makes the action an ordinary civil action regulated by the Civil Procedure Code, so the ground must be pleaded and proved at trial. Section 4(1) requires the plaintiff to file, with the plaint, an application to register the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered or, if it is not registered, in which the land lies; the point of that step appears from the Registration of Documents Ordinance s.11(1), under which a lis pendens does not bind a purchaser until it is registered. The Act itself does not say what conduct amounts to gross ingratitude: its interpretation section, s.6, defines only 'Registrar of Lands' and 'land'. The content of the ground therefore comes from the Roman-Dutch common law of donation and from judicial authority, neither of which is in this statutory corpus, and this part of the answer is left open for a lawyer to complete. Where a deed of gift does reserve a power of revocation to the donor, the 2017 Act is not the governing route at all, and the donor's rights depend on the terms of the deed and on the general law.
gold_answer_draft.application: Deed No. 4821 of 12 March 2019 reserved no power of revocation and is expressed to be irrevocable, so the father cannot revoke it by his own act; his only route is an action under s.2 of the 2017 Act, filed by him as donor against his son as donee, and the deed can be set aside only if the court so orders. The conduct relied on, namely the assault causing a fractured wrist, the expulsion from the house on the gifted land, and the continuing refusal of food, shelter and medical care to a father who has no other income, is what he must prove as gross ingratitude; whether it meets that threshold is a question the Act does not answer on its own text. On timing he is within both limbs of s.3: the action would be filed in October 2024, about five and a half years after the deed was executed in March 2019, and roughly eight months after the cause of action arose in February 2024. Because the deed was registered in the Kalutara land registry, the s.4(1)(a) lis pendens application must be addressed to the Registrar of Lands of that district and filed with the plaint; although the son has not yet sold the land, registering the action is what would protect the father against a purchaser for value under s.11(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance. The action proceeds under the Civil Procedure Code by force of s.5.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The father has no self-help remedy. On these facts the single ground open to him is gross ingratitude under s.2 of Act No. 5 of 2017, pursued by a civil action against his son in the District Court, filed in time under s.3 and accompanied by the s.4(1) lis pendens application; the deed stands unless and until the court orders its revocation. Whether the son's assault and refusal of maintenance in fact constitute gross ingratitude cannot be settled from the statutory text alone, and that step needs common-law and judicial authority outside this corpus, so the answer is reserved rather than offered as complete.

The court cannot entertain such an action unless it is filed both within ten years of the execution of the deed and within two years of the date the cause of action arose.
The revocation action is an ordinary civil action regulated by the Civil Procedure Code, so the donor must plead and prove the ground at trial.
The plaintiff must file an application to register the action as a lis pendens together with the plaint.
Registration matters because a lis pendens does not bind a purchaser until it is duly registered.

An action filed in October 2024 is within ten years of the execution of the deed on 12 March 2019 and within two years of the cause of action arising in February 2024, so it is not time-barred.

The only ground on which the father can obtain revocation of this deed under the statutory corpus is gross ingratitude, and only by a court order obtained in a timely action against his son.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether an Attorney-at-Law and Notary may lawfully draw and attest a deed transferring the freehold title of a private allotment of bare land in Dehiwala to a Swedish citizen who intends to develop and run an apartment business on it; if not, what consequences follow for such a deed and what lawful routes remain open to the client at October 2024.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 2(1) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, No. 38 of 2014 prohibits the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka to a foreigner, to a Sri Lankan company in which direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above, or to a foreign company, unless exempted under section 3. Section 25 defines a foreigner as a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, defines land to include State and private land and any interest in it, and defines transfer as any sale or conveyance by which title passes. Section 3(1) lists the exemptions, of which the only one relevant to an apartment business is section 3(1)(b), a condominium parcel specified under the Apartment Ownership Law where the entire value is paid upfront by inward foreign remittance before the deed is executed; section 3(2) allows the Minister, with prior Cabinet approval, to exempt a foreign entity in listed sectors engaged in a Strategic Development Project. Under section 9(4) of the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 a condominium parcel may be held and dealt with as land only after a Condominium Plan is registered. Section 18 of the 2014 Act makes any alienation in contravention of the Act void, and section 4(1) forbids the Registrar of Lands to register such a transfer. The lawful alternatives are a lease under section 5(1), which may not exceed ninety-nine years and on which, by section 5A, no Land Lease Tax is charged for an indenture executed on or after 1 January 2016, or acquisition through a company incorporated in Sri Lanka with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, which by section 2(2)(a) must stay below fifty per cent for twenty consecutive years. Section 11(1) bars mortgaging or pledging such land to a licensed bank for five years from execution of the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: Mr. Holmqvist is not a citizen of Sri Lanka and has no dual citizenship, so he is a foreigner within section 25 and the prohibition in section 2(1)(a) applies to him. The subject matter is a 38.5 perch allotment of private land at Hill Street, Dehiwala, which is land within section 25, and the proposed deed of transfer for Rs. 240,000,000 is a transfer within that section. None of the section 3(1) exemptions is available on these facts: he is not a diplomatic mission or an international organisation, not a dual citizen, not the next of kin of the owner, not a bank or a finance leasing institution, and the land is bare land over which no condominium plan has been registered, so there is no condominium parcel he could buy under section 3(1)(b). His willingness to remit the whole price from Stockholm does not assist, because that condition attaches only to the condominium exemption. He holds no Ministerial Order under section 3(2) and his venture has not been identified as a Strategic Development Project. A deed executed in October 2024 in his own name would therefore be void under section 18, and the Registrar of Lands would be bound by section 4(1) to refuse registration, so he would part with the price and acquire nothing. Because he is willing to restructure, two routes remain: a lease of the land to him for a term not exceeding ninety-nine years under section 5(1), on which no Land Lease Tax is payable because the indenture would be executed after 1 January 2016; or incorporation of a Sri Lankan company in which his shareholding stays below fifty per cent, subject to the twenty-year holding condition in section 2(2)(a), breach of which would render the transfer void. On his question about construction finance, section 11(1) prevents the land from being mortgaged or pledged to a licensed bank for five years from the execution of the transfer or lease. If instead his object is to own completed apartments rather than to develop the site, he could buy condominium parcels in a project whose Condominium Plan is already registered, paying the entire value upfront by inward foreign remittance before execution.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: He must be advised that he cannot buy this land in his own name: a deed of transfer to him would be void under section 18 of Act, No. 38 of 2014 and would not be registered. As his Notary you should decline to draw or attest such a deed. He should be advised instead to take a lease of the land for a term not exceeding ninety-nine years, on which no Land Lease Tax is now chargeable, or to acquire through a company incorporated in Sri Lanka whose foreign shareholding is and remains below fifty per cent for twenty years, or, if what he wants is completed apartments, to purchase registered condominium parcels with the entire value remitted from abroad before execution. He should also be warned that the land cannot be mortgaged to a licensed bank for five years, which affects his construction funding.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 2(1)(a) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, No. 38 of 2014 prohibits the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka to a foreigner, unless exempted under section 3.
For the purposes of that Act a foreigner is a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka.
Land includes private as well as State land and any interest in it, and transfer means any sale or conveyance by which title passes to another person.

The exemptions from section 2 are those set out in section 3(1), which include a condominium parcel specified under the Apartment Ownership Law where the entire value is paid upfront by inward foreign remittance before the deed of transfer is executed.

A condominium parcel may be held and dealt with in the same manner as land only after a Condominium Plan or Semi Condominium Plan has been registered under the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973.
The Minister may, with prior Cabinet approval and by Order published in the Gazette, exempt a foreign entity in the listed sectors engaged in a project identified as a Strategic Development Project.
Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the Act is void and of no effect in law.
The Registrar of Lands must refuse to register an instrument effecting a transfer referred to in section 2 unless satisfied that it complies with the Act.
A land may lawfully be leased to a foreigner, subject to the Land Lease Tax under section 6, for a maximum tenure of ninety-nine years.
No Land Lease Tax is charged, levied or collected on a lease to a foreigner under an indenture of lease executed on or after 1 January 2016.

Where land is transferred to a Sri Lankan company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, that shareholding must remain below fifty per cent for twenty consecutive years from the date of transfer for the transfer to remain valid.
Land transferred or leased to a person or company referred to in section 2(1) or 5(1) may not be mortgaged or pledged to a licensed bank for five years from execution of the instrument.
Mr. Holmqvist, being a Swedish citizen who has never been a citizen of Sri Lanka and holds no dual citizenship, is a foreigner for the purposes of the Act.

The proposed acquisition of a 38.5 perch allotment of private land at Hill Street, Dehiwala by deed of transfer for Rs. 240,000,000 is a transfer of title of land situated in Sri Lanka and so falls within section 2(1)(a).

No section 3(1) exemption is available to him: he is not a diplomatic mission or international organisation, not a dual citizen, not the next of kin of the owner, and not a bank or finance leasing institution, and the subject land is bare land over which no condominium plan has been registered, so there is no condominium parcel for him to purchase.

His proposal to remit the entire price of Rs. 240,000,000 from Stockholm before execution does not save the transaction, because the inward remittance condition attaches only to the condominium parcel exemption and not to a purchase of bare land.
He cannot rely on the Ministerial exemption either, because he holds no Order made with Cabinet approval and his private apartment venture has not been identified as a Strategic Development Project.
A deed of transfer to him executed in October 2024 would therefore be void, and the Registrar of Lands would be bound to refuse its registration, leaving him with no title for the price he pays.

Since he is willing to restructure, a lease of the land to him for a term not exceeding ninety-nine years is lawful, and because the indenture would be executed well after 1 January 2016 no Land Lease Tax would be chargeable on it.

Alternatively he may acquire through a company incorporated in Sri Lanka in which his foreign shareholding is less than fifty per cent, provided he is warned that it must stay below that level for twenty consecutive years or the transfer becomes void.
On his question about construction finance, whichever of those routes he takes, the land cannot be mortgaged or pledged to a licensed bank for five years from execution of the instrument.
He must be advised that he cannot purchase this land in his own name, that a deed of transfer to him would be void and unregistrable, and that as his Notary you should decline to draw or attest it.

He should be advised to proceed instead by a lease not exceeding ninety-nine years, or through a Sri Lankan company with foreign shareholding kept below fifty per cent for twenty years, or, if his object is completed apartments, by purchasing registered condominium parcels with the entire value remitted from abroad before execution.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What steps the notary retained by the intending purchaser of a thirty-acre coconut estate with a bungalow in Kurunegala must take before, at and after the execution of the conveyance.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A sale of land is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing and signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary who attests it (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a)). A notary may act only in the area and language for which he is authorised (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule 22). Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land he must search the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (s.31 rule 17(a)) and must obtain from the Registrar the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (s.31 rule 17(b)(i)); the registry books may be searched and certified extracts obtained by a person interested or his agent (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42). The search matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming adversely for value under a later duly registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)), and a transferee for value may lodge a priority notice which holds for six weeks and back-dates registration (s.30(5)). On a transfer the notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed and endorse the new deed's particulars on it (s.31 rule 33). The deed must carry an accurate description of the land by boundaries, extent and situation with the district, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and Grama Niladhari Division (s.31 rule 16(a)), and the true and full consideration must be ascertained and set out (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)). The notary may not attest without an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided (s.31 rule 6), duty being payable by him (s.31 rule 7A(a)) and charged on every specified instrument (Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1)). He must identify the executants from personal knowledge or their identity documents (s.31 rule 9), attest without delay under his signature and seal recording execution, identification, date, place, reading over, consideration paid in his presence and stamps (s.31 rule 20), and submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation (s.31 rule 30A). Two statutory restrictions must be excluded: agricultural land other than paddy may not be owned above fifty acres (Land Reform Law s.3(1)(b)), and land held on a state grant cannot be disposed of without the prior approval of the Government Agent (Land Development Ordinance s.19(6)); a consent certificate of the Board is required only for tea or rubber estates (Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1)).
gold_answer_draft.application: The estate lies at Wariyapola in the Kurunegala District and the notary is authorised to practise in Sinhala in that district, so he may accept the retainer and attest the deed. He should take full instructions, call for and examine the vendor's prior deeds, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 1032 of 1998 and tracing back through the 1979 partition decree, and search the Kurunegala land registry folio in which that deed is registered, taking a certified folio extract. That extract should disclose Bond No. 2210 of 2021 in favour of the bank, and the notary must arrange for a registered discharge, or for the bank's release to be executed and registered simultaneously with the conveyance out of the purchase money; otherwise the client would take subject to that earlier registered interest. Because execution is not to take place until 20 May 2024, a priority notice should be considered so that no instrument executed by the vendor in the interval gains priority. The thirty-acre extent and the boundaries of Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 must be checked on the ground against the folio description and reproduced in the schedule with the village, Divisional Secretary's Division and district, the bungalow being described with the land. The whole thirty acres is coconut and the client owns no other agricultural land, so the purchase leaves him below the fifty-acre ceiling; coconut is neither tea nor rubber, so no consent certificate is needed; and as the chain shows private freehold with no state permit or grant, no approval of the Government Agent is called for. The full price of Rs. 42,000,000, including the Rs. 4,200,000 advance paid under the agreement of 10 January 2024, must be set out as the consideration, and the balance paid at execution recorded in the attestation with the details of any cheque or draft. Stamp duty on that value must be provided for and paid before attestation. At execution the notary must identify both parties from their national identity cards, have two witnesses of good repute sign, read over and explain the deed, then attest, sign and seal it without delay, endorse the particulars on the vendor's title deed, and lodge the deed for registration by 19 June 2024.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary's steps are, in sequence: confirm his competence for the area and take instructions; call for and examine the vendor's title deeds; search the Kurunegala land registry and obtain a certified folio extract; deal with the disclosed mortgage and consider a priority notice; verify extent and boundaries against the survey plan; satisfy himself that no ceiling or consent regime bars the purchase; draw the deed with an accurate schedule and the true and full consideration; provide for and pay stamp duty; execute and attest the deed with identified parties and two witnesses; and submit it for registration within thirty days of attestation. On these facts nothing in the statutory material bars the purchase, provided the bond is discharged and the deed is properly drawn, attested and registered in time.

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale of land has no force in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary who attests it, so the transaction has to be carried through by a notary.
A notary may only attest a deed in the area and language in which he is authorised to practise.

Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search, or cause to be searched, the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.

The notary must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing the ownership of and the registered encumbrances on the land.
The registry duplicates, books and indexes may be searched by a person interested or by his agent duly authorised in writing, and certified extracts obtained.

An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later instrument that is duly registered, so priority depends on registration.

A person acquiring an interest in land for valuable consideration may lodge a priority notice, which remains in force for six weeks and back-dates the registration of the instrument to the date of the notice.
The notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed on a transfer and endorse on it the number and date of the new deed and the nature of the transaction.

The deed must embody, in itself or in an annexed schedule, an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division and Grama Niladhari Division.
The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed.

The notary may not attest unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided, and stamp duty on the instrument is payable by the notary, duty being charged on every specified instrument at the rate the Minister determines.
The notary must establish the identity of the executants, either by personal knowledge or by inspecting the national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence.

The notary must without delay attest the deed and sign and seal an attestation recording, among other things, execution in his presence and in the presence of one another, how the executants were identified, the date and place, the reading over, the consideration actually paid in his presence and the stamps.
The attested deed must be submitted for registration within thirty days of attestation.
A person may not own more than fifty acres of agricultural land where the land is not exclusively paddy, and land owned in excess of that ceiling vests in the Commission.
Land alienated on a state grant may not be disposed of except with the prior approval of the Government Agent, and not in portions below the minimum specified in the grant.
Prior consent of the Board, evidenced by a certificate attached to the deed, is required only for the transfer of a tea or rubber estate.

The notary should also satisfy himself that an out-and-out purchase is the transaction the parties actually intend and explain the deed to them before signature, although this express duty was introduced by an amendment of 2024 whose commencement relative to April 2024 is not established on the corpus.
Because the estate lies at Wariyapola in the Kurunegala District and the notary is authorised to practise in Sinhala in that district, he may accept the retainer and attest the deed himself.

The vendor's assertion that he owns on Deed of Transfer No. 1032 of 1998, traced back to the 1979 partition decree, must be tested by searching the Kurunegala land registry folio in which that deed is registered and by obtaining the certified folio extract, and the notary should call for and examine the prior deeds themselves.

The search and folio extract should disclose Bond No. 2210 of 2021 in favour of the bank, so the notary must arrange for a registered discharge or for the release to be executed and registered together with the conveyance, since otherwise the buyer takes subject to that earlier registered interest.

Because the bond is outstanding and execution is not to take place until 20 May 2024, the notary should consider lodging a priority notice so that an instrument executed by the vendor in the interval cannot gain priority over the client's conveyance.

The schedule to the deed must reproduce the thirty-acre extent and the boundaries of Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 4127 with the village, Divisional Secretary's Division and district, and the notary should have the plan checked on the ground against the folio description before drawing the deed.

Since the whole thirty acres is coconut land and the client owns no other agricultural land, the purchase leaves his holding well below the fifty-acre ceiling, but the notary should record that check.
Coconut is neither tea nor rubber, so no consent certificate of the Board needs to be obtained or attached to this deed.
The chain shows private freehold and no state permit or grant, so no prior approval of the Government Agent has to be obtained before the vendor conveys.

The full price of Rs. 42,000,000, including the Rs. 4,200,000 advance already paid under the agreement of 10 January 2024, must be set out in the deed as the consideration, and the balance paid at execution must be recorded in the attestation with the details of any cheque or bank draft.
Stamp duty on that consideration must be worked out, provided for and paid by the notary before he attests, and the receipt or stamps dealt with as the rules require.

At execution the notary must identify Mr. Ranasinghe and the vendor from their national identity cards, have two witnesses of good repute sign, read over and explain the deed, and then attest, sign and seal it without delay.

If the deed is executed on 20 May 2024 it must be lodged for registration in the Kurunegala land registry by 19 June 2024, and the notary should also endorse the particulars of the new deed on the vendor's title deed.

The notary's steps therefore run in sequence: confirm his own competence for the area, call for and examine the vendor's title deeds, search the land registry and take a certified folio extract, deal with the disclosed mortgage and consider a priority notice, verify the extent and boundaries against the survey plan, check that no statutory ceiling or consent regime bites, draw the deed with an accurate schedule and the true consideration, provide for stamp duty, execute and attest it with identified parties and two witnesses, and lodge it for registration within thirty days.
On the enriched facts nothing in the frozen statutory material bars the purchase, provided the bank's bond is discharged and the deed is properly drawn, attested and registered in time.

gold_answer_draft.issue: On what value, and at whose charge, is stamp duty payable on the deed of gift of the business premises at Assessment No.78, Maradana Road, Borella, and can the amount of duty be computed from the statutory material available.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and s.106 defines "Transfer" to include a gift, so a deed of gift of Borella premises is chargeable under that Statute. Section 13 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside the 2006 regime, and s.9 of that Act directs such duty to the Provincial Council within whose limits the property is situated. Section 48(1) requires the duty to be calculated on the value of the property conveyed. For immovable property which is gifted, s.106 defines "value" artificially: where the donor acquired it on or before 31 March 1977, the open market price on 31 March 1977 increased by the cost of improvements made afterwards, or the open market price at the date of the deed, whichever is lower; where he acquired it after that date, the open market price at acquisition increased by the cost of improvements, or the price at the date of the deed, whichever is lower. Section 51(a) makes the duty on an instrument of transfer payable by the grantee unless the parties agree otherwise, and the exemptions in s.39 do not cover a family gift. The rate itself is only prescribed, that is, fixed by regulation or order made under the Statute.
gold_answer_draft.application: The property is at Maradana Road, Borella, within the Western Province, and the intended instrument is a gift, so s.37 read with the definition of "Transfer" charges it. The donor acquired the property in 1977 and spent about Rs.1,000,000 on renovations afterwards; the present market value is Rs.100,000,000. On either limb of the definition of "value" the two competing figures are the acquisition-date open market price increased by the cost of improvements, which on the facts given is of the order of Rs.100,000 plus Rs.1,000,000, that is about Rs.1,100,000, and the present open market price of Rs.100,000,000. The lower of the two is about Rs.1,100,000, so that and not Rs.100,000,000 is the chargeable value. The scenario does not say whether the 1977 purchase was before or after 31 March 1977, but both limbs produce the same comparison here. Two cautions: the Statute takes the Assessor's opinion of the open market price at the relevant date, for which the actual 1977 purchase price of Rs.100,000 is only a proxy, and the renovation figure is given as an approximation. The duty falls on the donee, Sarathi Perera, under s.51(a) unless the deed provides otherwise, and no exemption in s.39 applies. The final step, multiplying the chargeable value by the prescribed rate, cannot be taken: s.37 leaves the rate to subordinate legislation and no rate order or schedule for the Western Province is in the corpus.

Kamal was previously married to Senani and had a child, namely Ravi. On June 04, 2013, Akash met with an accident and died intestate, issueless, leaving his wife Seena. gold_answer_draft.issue: Trace the devolution of title to the land and premises bearing Assessment No. 3, Alwis Road, Nugegoda (Lot A in Plan No. 135) from Kanthi Perera, in whom title was allotted by the final decree of 5 September 2005 in Partition Case No. 371/P, down to the persons who own it today, identifying at each intestate death which heirs took and on what statutory footing.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21(1)), which applies to the estates of persons dying after its proclamation (s.20) and to persons not governed by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Tesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse takes one-half (s.22); subject to that, inheritance runs in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children are preferent and take equally per capita, issue of a deceased child taking by representation (s.24). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, that parent takes half and the other half goes to full-blood brothers and sisters together with half-blood brothers and sisters related through the deceased parent (s.25). Where both parents are dead the collateral share goes to brothers and sisters of the whole and half blood (s.26). Section 27 fixes how full and half blood divide: the fund is halved, the full siblings sharing one half with the father's-side half siblings and the other half with the mother's-side half siblings, but where half siblings of one side only qualify the full siblings take one-half in the first place and divide the remainder with them. Those equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). An administrator's power extends to the deceased's immovable property (Civil Procedure Code s.542), and deeds affecting immovable property require notarial execution (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The Ordinance is silent on the effect of a reserved life interest and on its extinction at the death of the life holder, and by s.36 those questions fall to Roman-Dutch law, which is outside the material available here.
gold_answer_draft.application: Kanthi Perera became sole owner under the final decree of 5 September 2005. By Deed of Gift No. 1663 of 20 January 2006 she gifted the property absolutely and irrevocably to Suneth, reserving life interests to herself and to Kamal, so Suneth held the ownership from that date burdened by the two life interests. On Kanthi's death on 18 August 2006 her life interest determined and no ownership interest in this land passed from her, so her children Salinga, Suneth, Lalani and Akash took nothing from her here. Suneth died on 1 July 2008 intestate, unmarried and without issue, owning the property subject to Kamal's surviving life interest. Descendants failing and his mother having predeceased him, s.25 gives his father Kamal one-half and gives the other half to the full-blood siblings Lalani and Akash together with Salinga, the half-sister related through the deceased parent Kanthi; Ravi, related only through the surviving parent Kamal, is excluded by the words of s.25. Applying the one-side proviso in s.27 to that sibling half, Lalani and Akash take one-half of it in the first place, one-eighth each of the whole, and divide the remaining quarter with Salinga per capita under s.30, one-twelfth each. Suneth's estate having been administered in Testamentary Case No. 1231/2008/T, Administrator's Conveyance No. 2635 of 22 December 2008, executed by Kamal under the power described in Civil Procedure Code s.542 and notarially attested as Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 requires, formalised that vesting. Kamal then held twelve twenty-fourths, Lalani five twenty-fourths, Akash five twenty-fourths and Salinga two twenty-fourths. Kamal died on 2 January 2012 intestate; his life interest determined and his one-half passed under s.24 to his surviving children Ravi, Lalani and Akash equally per capita, Suneth having predeceased him leaving no issue to represent him, so each took one-sixth. The holdings then stood at Lalani nine twenty-fourths, Akash nine twenty-fourths, Ravi four twenty-fourths and Salinga two twenty-fourths. Akash died on 4 June 2013 intestate and issueless leaving his wife Seena. Under s.22 Seena took one-half of his nine twenty-fourths. Both his parents being dead, the remaining half fell to his collaterals under s.26, divided by the two-part rule in s.27: one half of it shared by his full sister Lalani with his father's-side half-brother Ravi, and the other half shared by Lalani with his mother's-side half-brother Salinga.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs from Kanthi Perera, by Deed of Gift No. 1663, to Suneth Perera subject to two life interests; from Suneth on his intestacy in 2008 to Kamal as to one-half and to Lalani, Akash and Salinga as to the other half, confirmed by Administrator's Conveyance No. 2635; from Kamal on his intestacy in 2012 to Ravi, Lalani and Akash; and from Akash on his intestacy in 2013 to his widow Seena as to one-half and to Lalani, Ravi and Salinga as to the other. The present owners are therefore Lalani, Ravi, Salinga and Seena, both life interests having determined. This is a proposed statutory map only: the steps that depend on the nature and extinction of the reserved life interests, and the effect of the partition final decree, rest on authority outside the statutes available here.

gold_answer_draft.rule: The fractions follow from the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance. Section 22 gives a surviving spouse one-half; s.23 orders the remainder among descendants, ascendants and collaterals; s.24 gives children equal per capita shares with representation for the issue of a deceased child; s.25 gives a sole surviving parent one-half and gives the other half to full-blood siblings and to half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent; s.26 sends the collateral share to brothers and sisters of the whole and half blood where both parents are dead; s.27 halves that share between the father's side and the mother's side, with a proviso that where qualifying half siblings are on one side only the full siblings take one-half in the first place and divide the rest with them; and s.30 makes the division within each class per capita.

Kamal's death in 2012 divided his ninety-six parts equally under s.24 among Ravi, Lalani and Akash, thirty-two parts each, leaving Lalani seventy-two, Akash seventy-two, Ravi thirty-two and Salinga sixteen. All five are citizens of Sri Lanka resident in Galle, no share is held directly or indirectly by any person or body outside Sri Lanka, and none of the five owns any other land that is used or is capable of being used for agriculture.
