gold_answer_draft.issue: The company has retained you on a purchase of a 41-acre rubber-planted estate in Galle. The question is what steps you must take, before the deed is drawn, at execution and after execution, so that the company acquires a title that is valid, unencumbered and registrable, and so that no statutory prohibition or consent requirement is overlooked.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Several statutes bear on a purchase of this kind. First, the transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has previously been obtained by the transferor and the transfer complies with any conditions of that consent (Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1)), but the Act bites only where the land answers the definition of 'rubber estate', which requires both a minimum extent and registration as an estate under the rubber control legislation (s.25). Secondly, rubber land is agricultural land (Land Reform Law s.66); the ceiling on non-paddy agricultural land is fifty acres per person (s.3(1)(b)); where agricultural land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it for the purpose of the ceiling in proportion to their shareholdings (s.8); and where a person becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling after the commencement of the Law, the excess vests in the Commission and is held on a statutory lease (s.5(1)). Thirdly, a transfer of title to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where foreign shareholding in it, direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)); an alienation in contravention of the Act is void (s.18); and the Registrar of Lands must satisfy himself on this point by requiring documentary proof from the company secretary (s.4(3)). Fourthly, the company cannot enter into a major transaction, which includes an acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of its assets before the acquisition, unless it is approved by special resolution, made contingent on one, consented to in writing by all shareholders, or expressly authorised by the original articles (Companies Act s.185(1) and (2)); and an obligation which a natural person would have to execute notarially is entered into by the company in writing signed under its name by two directors (s.19(1)(a)). Fifthly, no sale, purchase or transfer of immovable property avails in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant and attested by a notary before two witnesses present at the same time, with the prescribed thumb impressions (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, in the form substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2). Sixthly, before drawing the deed the notary must search the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a)) and must obtain the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (s.31(17)(b)(i)); where a company is a party he must retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and the details of the board (s.31(17)(d)); where a corporate body executes he must obtain the seal and the signatures of the board or of a person authorised by board resolution (s.31(14)); the deed must contain an accurate description showing boundaries, extent and situation (s.31(16)(a)); attestation requires an assurance that stamp duty is provided (s.31(6)); and the deed must be submitted for registration within thirty days of attestation (s.31(30A)). Finally, an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)), and the registry books may be searched and certified extracts obtained by an intending purchaser's attorney-at-law (s.42).
gold_answer_draft.application: Take the statutory checks in order. The estate is 16.6 hectares and has never been registered as an estate in the statutory register of rubber estates, so it does not answer the definition in s.25 and the prohibition in s.3(1) is not engaged; you should nonetheless obtain written confirmation of the registration position, because if the land were a rubber estate as defined the vendor would first have to obtain the Board's certificate of consent and a transfer without it would be null and void. The estate is planted with rubber and is therefore agricultural land within s.66. Because the purchaser is a private company, s.8 attributes the estate to the five shareholders in proportion to their shares, so each is deemed to acquire one fifth of 41 acres, that is 8.2 acres; since none of them owns any other agricultural land, no shareholder comes near the fifty-acre ceiling in s.3(1)(b) and the vesting sanction in s.5(1) will not operate. Had any shareholder been near the ceiling, the excess created by the purchase would have vested in the Commission, so the shareholders' existing agricultural holdings must be verified in writing before you advise the company to commit. All five shareholders are citizens of Sri Lanka and no share is held directly or indirectly by a foreigner, so the transfer is not prohibited by s.2(1)(b) and s.18 does not avoid it; but you should have the company secretary prepare the documentary proof of the shareholding that the Registrar of Lands will require under s.4(3), and advise the company of the continuing obligation to report on its foreign shareholding after registration. On the company's authority, the assets to be acquired are worth Rs. 41,000,000 against an asset base of Rs. 60,000,000, so the acquisition is greater than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition and is a major transaction within s.185(2)(a); as the original articles contain no express authorisation, a special resolution under s.185(1), or the written consent of all five shareholders, must be obtained before the company binds itself, and any agreement to sell must be signed under the company's name by two directors and notarially executed as required by s.19(1)(a) read with s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. On title, exercise the right of search under s.42, examine the Galle Land Registry folio E 214/86 as required by s.31(17)(a) and obtain the certified folio extract under s.31(17)(b)(i); call for the original of Deed No. 1420 of 1998 and the earlier deeds in the chain, since a photocopy proves nothing and only notarially executed instruments pass title under s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. The 2019 mortgage bond is registered in the folio, so by force of the priority rule in s.7(1) the company's later deed would take subject to it; you must therefore arrange for the bank's discharge to be executed and registered, or for the redemption amount to be paid out of the purchase money at completion against delivery of the discharge. Furnish the notary with a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and the details of the directors under s.31(17)(d), and with the board resolution and seal if the company is to execute anything under s.31(14); settle a schedule with an accurate description of boundaries, extent and situation as s.31(16)(a) requires, if necessary on a fresh survey; provide funds for stamp duty so that the notary has the assurance s.31(6) requires; and see that the executed transfer is submitted for registration within thirty days of attestation under s.31(30A), which is what secures the company's priority under s.7(1).
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: You should advise the company that the purchase can proceed, but only after the following steps. Verify in writing that the estate is not registered as an estate for the purposes of the fragmentation legislation, and if it is, require the vendor to obtain the Board's certificate of consent first. Verify the existing agricultural holdings of all five shareholders so that no one is taken over the fifty-acre ceiling by the deemed proportionate ownership. Confirm and document that there is no direct or indirect foreign shareholding, and have the secretary ready to prove it to the Registrar of Lands. Obtain a special resolution, or the written consent of all shareholders, before the company commits itself, since the acquisition is a major transaction. Search the Galle Land Registry, take the certified folio extract, call for the originals of the chain of notarially executed deeds and satisfy yourself on the vendor's title and possession. Have the registered mortgage discharged, or redeemed out of the purchase money at completion. Furnish the notary with the certificate of incorporation, the details of the board and any board resolution, settle an accurate schedule of the land, provide for stamp duty, have the deed executed by the vendor before a notary and two witnesses in the form then required, and see that it is lodged for registration within thirty days of attestation.

answer_claims.claim_text: A transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless the transferor has previously obtained a certificate of consent of the Board and the transfer complies with any conditions of that consent.

That prohibition applies only where the land answers the statutory definition of a rubber estate, which requires both a minimum extent and registration as an estate under the rubber control legislation.

Because the estate is 16.6 hectares and has never been registered as an estate in the statutory register of rubber estates, it falls outside the definition, so no certificate of consent is required; the registration position should still be confirmed in writing.

Land planted with rubber is agricultural land, the ceiling on non-paddy agricultural land is fifty acres per person, and where agricultural land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it for the purposes of the ceiling in proportion to their shareholdings.

Where a person becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling after the commencement of the Law, the excess is deemed to vest in the Commission and to be held by that person on a statutory lease.

Each of the five shareholders is deemed to acquire one fifth of the 41 acres, that is 8.2 acres, and since none owns other agricultural land no shareholder exceeds the fifty-acre ceiling, so no part of the estate would vest in the Commission on this purchase.

A transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where foreign shareholding in that company, direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above, and an alienation in contravention of the Act is void.

Since all five shareholders are citizens of Sri Lanka and no share is held directly or indirectly by any person or body outside Sri Lanka, the transfer is not prohibited, but the company secretary must be ready to give the Registrar of Lands documentary proof that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent.

A company may not enter into a major transaction, which includes the acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition, unless it is approved by special resolution, made contingent on one, consented to in writing by all shareholders, or expressly authorised by a provision in the articles included at incorporation.

An acquisition of Rs. 41,000,000 against an asset base of Rs. 60,000,000 is greater than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition, so it is a major transaction and, the original articles containing no express authority, a special resolution or the written consent of all five shareholders must be obtained before the company commits itself.

No sale, purchase or transfer of immovable property, and no agreement for such a purpose, avails in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant and attested by a notary before two witnesses present at the same time, with the prescribed thumb impressions; and an obligation of that kind is entered into on behalf of a company in writing signed under the company's name by two directors.

Before the deed is drawn the notary must search the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered, and must obtain the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances; an intending purchaser's attorney-at-law may himself search the registry books and take certified extracts.

You must therefore search folio E 214/86 of the Galle Land Registry, take the certified extract, and call for the original of Deed No. 1420 of 1998 and the earlier deeds in the chain rather than accept the photocopy the vendor has produced.

Because the 2019 mortgage bond is registered in the folio, the priority rule protecting a subsequent registered instrument taken for valuable consideration cannot be used to defeat it, so a registered discharge must be obtained, or the redemption amount paid out of the purchase money at completion against delivery of the discharge.

The notary must be furnished with a certified copy of the company's certificate of incorporation and the details of its board, and with the seal and board resolution if the company is itself to execute; the deed must carry an accurate description showing boundaries, extent and situation; funds must be provided so that the notary has an assurance that stamp duty is met.
The executed transfer must be submitted for registration within thirty days of attestation, and prompt registration is what protects the company against a competing instrument registered earlier.

The purchase may proceed once the registration position of the estate, the shareholders' agricultural holdings and the absence of foreign shareholding have been verified, a special resolution or unanimous written consent obtained, the title investigated and the registered mortgage cleared, the deed notarially executed by the vendor and lodged for registration within thirty days.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The question asks which documents must be called for and why. Each document in the gold answer is called for because a statute makes it necessary: the certified folio extract and the registry search are the notary's express duties; the priority rule, the lis pendens rule and the caveat rule explain what the folio must be read for; only notarially executed instruments pass title, which is why the originals of the chain of deeds must be produced; the description requirement is why a survey plan is needed; the corporate-party rule is why the certificate of incorporation and board details are needed; and where a parcel is under title registration, the Certificate of Title replaces the chain of deeds. Possession has to be investigated because of the statutory prescriptive period. No case law is required to identify the documents or the reasons. Documents that a practitioner would also call for but which rest on legislation outside the corpus (local-authority rates receipts, street line and non-vesting certificates, approved building plans) are excluded and recorded as corpus gaps.

legal_issues.issue: Which registration system governs the parcel, and therefore whether the documents to be called for are a chain of deeds and folio extracts or a Certificate of Title.
What documentary evidence of the vendor's paper title must be produced, and in what form, for the purchaser to be satisfied that title can pass.
What registry material must be obtained to disclose prior registered instruments, encumbrances, pending actions and caveats affecting the parcel.
What evidence of identity of the parcel and of possession must be called for, given that adverse possession can defeat a paper title.
What documents are required because the intending purchaser is a company.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps: (1) the notary's search duty (PROV-M036-015) leads to the specific document, the certified folio extract (PROV-M036-016); (2) that document matters because of the registration priority rule (PROV-M036-022), which is also what makes registered encumbrances, a registered lis pendens (PROV-M036-024) and a caveat (PROV-M036-025) relevant; (3) the deeds themselves must be produced in original because only notarially executed instruments avail in law (PROV-M036-013 with PROV-M036-014), and the chain must be traced far enough back and tested against possession because of the prescriptive period (PROV-M036-026). Verifier: the hop count of 3 is confirmed. PROV-M036-903 (the notary's duty to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed) reinforces step (3) and PROV-M036-904 supplies the caveat text in force at the matter date behind PROV-M036-025, so neither adds an independent reasoning edge. The Prevention of Frauds reasoning edge was reversed for the same reason as in M036-Q01.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The company has instructed you to examine the title to a forty-perch residential premises adjoining the rubber estate. The question is which documents you must call for in order to carry out that examination, and what makes each of them necessary.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The starting point is that only a notarially executed instrument passes title to immovable property: no sale, purchase or transfer of land avails in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant and attested by a notary before two witnesses present at the same time (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, in the form substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2). Next, before any deed affecting an interest in land is drawn, the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a)), and he must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry the certified extract of the folio containing the last entry, showing the ownership and the registered encumbrances (s.31(17)(b)(i)). An intending purchaser's attorney-at-law may himself search the registry books and indexes and take certified copies and extracts (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42). What the folio must be read for is fixed by the priority rule: an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument (s.7(1)); a lis pendens does not bind a purchaser unless registered (s.11(1)); and a caveat registered by a third party requires notice to be given to him of any instrument presented for registration (s.32(1)). A deed cannot be drawn unless it embodies an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a)), which is why a plan is needed. Where a party to the deed is a corporate body, the notary must retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation or other instrument establishing it, and the details of the board (s.31(17)(d)). Documentary title is not conclusive: undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by rent or service, for ten years founds a prescriptive claim (Prescription Ordinance s.3). Finally, where a parcel has been registered under the title registration scheme the owner may obtain a Certificate of Title which is conclusive evidence of that interest (Registration of Title Act s.37), so the first question is which system governs the parcel.
gold_answer_draft.application: Since the parcel is not within any declared title registration area, the Certificate of Title route under s.37 is unavailable and the title has to be proved by the deeds and the deeds register, which fixes the documents you must call for. First, call for the original of Deed of Transfer No. 3120 of 8 July 2004 and the originals, or certified copies from the notarial protocols or the Registrar's duplicates, of the 1985 and 1972 deeds and of every other instrument in the chain, together with any instrument by which title devolved otherwise than by deed. The photocopy the vendor has produced proves nothing, and by force of s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance an instrument that was not notarially executed in the required form did not pass title at all, so each link has to be inspected and its attestation checked. Trace the chain back far enough to be safe against the ten-year prescriptive period in s.3 of the Prescription Ordinance and to see that no link is missing. Secondly, call for the certified extract of the relevant folio of the Galle Land Registry, which s.31(17)(b)(i) requires the notary to obtain and which s.42 entitles you to take: it will show the registered ownership and the registered encumbrances, and it is the only way to find out whether some instrument registered earlier would, under s.7(1), prevail over the company's deed. Thirdly, read the folio for the two matters the vendor has already hinted at: the security given for the 2016 loan, for which you must call for the instrument creating it and, before completion, an executed and registrable discharge; and the document lodged by the relative in 2022, which if it is a caveat under s.32(1) means that notice of any instrument presented for registration will go to the caveator, and if it is a registered lis pendens under s.11(1) means the company would take subject to the pending action, so the pleadings and the state of that action must be called for. Fourthly, call for Plan No. 2456 of 3 March 1996 and, since the parcel is to be conveyed to a company that has never seen it, a current figure of survey superimposed on the earlier plan, because s.31(16)(a) requires the deed to carry an accurate description showing boundaries, extent and situation, and because the occupied strip must be located on the ground. Fifthly, because a neighbour has occupied the shed and well since about 2010 without paying rent or rendering service, call for whatever documents the vendor has to rebut a prescriptive claim to that strip, such as a written permission, a tenancy or licence agreement, receipts for rent or acknowledgment of the vendor's title, and evidence of the vendor's own possession such as assessment and rates receipts. Sixthly, since the purchaser is a corporate body, the company's certified certificate of incorporation and the details of its board must be produced for the notary under s.31(17)(d), together with the board resolution authorising the purchase. You should also call for the local authority certificates and receipts that a purchaser of built-up residential property would ordinarily require, although these arise under legislation outside the statutes considered here.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Call for the originals or certified copies of the whole chain of notarially executed deeds beginning with Deed No. 3120 of 2004 and running back through the 1985 and 1972 deeds; the certified extract of the relevant Galle Land Registry folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances, together with a search of the registers for prior instruments, pending actions and caveats; the instrument securing the 2016 loan and a registrable discharge of it; the document lodged in 2022 and, if it evidences a pending action, the record of that action; Plan No. 2456 of 1996 with a current figure of survey; documents evidencing the vendor's possession and any permission given to the occupier of the shed and well; and the company's certificate of incorporation, details of its board and the resolution authorising the purchase. Each of these is called for because title passes only by notarially executed deeds, because priority depends on registration, because a registered pending action or caveat binds or warns a purchaser, because the deed must describe the land accurately, because ten years of adverse possession can defeat the paper title, and because the notary must have the corporate documents of a company that is a party.

answer_claims.claim_text: No sale, purchase or transfer of immovable property avails in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant and attested by a notary before two witnesses present at the same time, so only notarially executed instruments can pass title in the chain.

Before a deed affecting an interest in land is drawn, the registers in the land registry must be searched to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered, and the certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances must be obtained from the Registrar.
An intending purchaser's attorney-at-law may search the registry duplicates, books and indexes and obtain certified copies or extracts.

An unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument, which is why the folio has to be examined before the purchase.
A registered lis pendens binds a purchaser, and a registered caveat requires notice to be given to the caveator of any instrument presented for registration, so the folio must be read for both.

Undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by rent or service, for ten years founds a prescriptive claim, so an examination of title cannot stop at the deeds.

A deed cannot be drawn unless it embodies an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation, and where a party is a corporate body the notary must retain a certified copy of its certificate of incorporation and the details of its board.
Because the parcel is not within any declared title registration area, no Certificate of Title is available and title must be proved by the chain of deeds and the deeds register.

You must call for the original of Deed of Transfer No. 3120 of 2004 and the originals or certified copies of the 1985 and 1972 deeds and every other link in the chain, because the photocopy produced proves nothing and each link must be shown to have been notarially executed.

You must call for the certified extract of the relevant Galle Land Registry folio, since it is the only way to establish the registered ownership and the registered encumbrances and to find any earlier registered instrument that would prevail over the company's deed.

You must call for the instrument securing the 2016 loan and a registrable discharge of it, and for the document lodged by the relative in 2022 together with the record of any action it evidences, because a registered security binds a later purchaser and a registered pending action or caveat affects any dealing.

You must call for Plan No. 2456 of 1996 and a current figure of survey, because the deed must carry an accurate description showing boundaries, extent and situation and because the occupied strip has to be located on the ground.

You must call for whatever documents rebut a prescriptive claim to the strip occupied since about 2010, such as a written permission, a tenancy or licence, receipts for rent or an acknowledgment of the vendor's title, together with evidence of the vendor's own possession.

You must call for the purchasing company's certified certificate of incorporation, the details of its board and the resolution authorising the purchase, because the notary must retain those documents where a party to the deed is a corporate body and because a corporate executant signs through its board or an authorised person.

The documents to be called for are therefore the whole chain of notarially executed deeds, the certified folio extract and a registry search, the security instrument and its discharge, the document lodged in 2022 and any related record, the survey plan and a current figure of survey, evidence of possession and of any permission given to the occupier, and the company's corporate documents.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a deed of gift of land and a house at Kadawatha is an instrument chargeable with stamp duty, and under which enactment.
On what amount the duty is calculated: the 1980 purchase price plus the cost of the house, or the present market value of Rs. 5,400,000.
What rate applies to that value and therefore what sum is payable.
Who must pay the duty, and by what procedure it is paid, evidenced and attested before and at execution.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Four necessary linked steps: section 37 charges duty on an instrument transferring immovable property in the Western Province; the section 106 definition of Transfer brings a gift within that charge; section 48(1) directs that duty be calculated on the value of the property conveyed; and the section 106 definition of value, paragraph (c) with its lower-of limb, fixes that value for immovable property gifted by a donor who acquired it after March 31, 1977. The payment provisions (sections 51 and 40) are a parallel required step for the procedure limb of the question, not a fifth hop.

enrichment.original_background: In 1980 February Dayani Perera had purchased a land in extent of 15 perches situated in Kadawatha for Rs. 400,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs. 3,100,000/-. She wishes to gift this house and land to her son Saranga and she instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift. The present market value of the house and property is Rs. 5,400,000/-.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the proposed deed of gift of the Kadawatha land and house from Dayani Perera to her son Saranga is chargeable with stamp duty, on what amount that duty is calculated, at what rate, by whom it is payable and by what procedure it must be paid and attested.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The land is at Kadawatha, in the Gampaha District of the Western Province, so stamp duty on an instrument transferring it is a provincial charge under the Financial Statute of the Western Province No. 06 of 1990. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside that Act's scheme. Financial Statute s.37 charges duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and s.106 defines Transfer to include a gift, a gift itself being a voluntary transfer without consideration in money or money's worth. No exemption in s.39 covers a gift between private persons. By s.48(1) the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed. Where the property gifted is immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, s.106 defines value as the open market price at the date the donor acquired it increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the gift, or the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, whichever is the lower. The rate to be applied to that value is not fixed by the Statute; s.37 leaves it to be prescribed. Duty is payable by the grantee under s.51(a) unless the parties agree otherwise. Under s.40(1) it must be paid before or at the time of execution and shown on the instrument by adhesive or impressed stamps or a certificate of payment; under s.40(2) duty on an instrument transferring immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate of payment to be affixed to the instrument. Stamp duty on transfers of immovable property was not brought within the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006, which expressly excludes such instruments from the displacement of the earlier stamp duty law.

Transfer in the Financial Statute includes a gift, so a deed of gift of land is an instrument relating to a transfer for the purposes of section 37; a gift is a voluntary transfer without consideration in money or money's worth.
None of the exemptions in section 39 covers a gift of land between private individuals.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed.

For immovable property gifted by a donor who acquired it after March 31, 1977, value means the open market price at the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made before the gift, or the open market price at the date of the deed of gift, whichever is the lower.

Because the donor acquired the Kadawatha land in February 1980, paragraph (c) of the definition of value applies rather than paragraph (b), which is confined to property acquired on or before March 31, 1977.
The acquisition-plus-improvements figure is Rs. 400,000 plus Rs. 3,100,000, that is Rs. 3,500,000.
Rs. 3,500,000 is lower than the Rs. 5,400,000 open market value at the date of the gift, so the chargeable value is Rs. 3,500,000 and not the present market value.
The duty on the deed of gift is payable by the donee Saranga as grantee, unless the deed provides otherwise.

The duty must be paid before or at the time of execution and evidenced on the deed by stamps or a certificate of payment; for a transfer of immovable property it may be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues the certificate to be affixed to the instrument.

The attesting notary must satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, deal with and recite any adhesive stamps, and where payment was made to a bank certify that the bank's certificate of payment has been affixed to the duplicate.

Because the chargeable value depends on the Assessor's opinion of open market prices, the deed may be submitted for adjudication to an Assessor on payment of the prescribed fee for a written determination of the duty chargeable.

enrichment.enriched_background: Wimalasena Perera, aged 74, a retired schoolmaster of Panadura, gifted the land called Kahatagahawatta, thirty-two perches in extent with the house standing on it, at Panadura in the District of Kalutara, to his nephew Chaminda Perera. gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a deed of gift which states on its face that it is absolute and irrevocable can nevertheless be revoked, and if so on what ground, by whom and in what manner; and whether the donor here is within the time allowed for seeking revocation of the 2019 deed after the donee's conduct in June 2023.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The words "absolute and irrevocable" in the deed do not put the gift beyond recall. Section 2 of the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017 provides that an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, only on an order made by a competent court, in an action filed by the donor against the donee. Three limits follow from the section itself: gross ingratitude is the only ground; an order of a competent court is the only mode, so the donor cannot revoke by his own act or by executing a deed of revocation; and the action lies at the suit of the donor against the donee. Section 3 adds that the court shall not entertain such an action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose, and both limits must be satisfied. Under section 4(1) the plaintiff must file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered or, where it is unregistered, in which the land lies. Under section 5 the action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code. The Act does not define gross ingratitude, so whether particular conduct amounts to it is for the court to decide on the evidence.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed of gift of Kahatagahawatta was executed on 12 March 2019 and declares the gift absolute and irrevocable. That wording is no answer to a claim under section 2. The donor, Wimalasena Perera, is the proper plaintiff and the donee, his nephew Chaminda Perera, the proper defendant. The conduct relied on is the assault in June 2023 and the donor's eviction from the annexe of the very house he gave away, neither of which the donee denies; that is the material the donor would place before the court as gross ingratitude, though the finding is for the court and cannot be assumed. On the dates, an action filed in or shortly after October 2023 is within ten years of 12 March 2019 and within two years of the June 2023 conduct, so section 3 does not shut the donor out. Because the land is registered in the Kalutara land registry, the lis pendens application under section 4(1) goes to the Registrar of Lands of that district and must be filed with the plaint, and the action proceeds under the Civil Procedure Code. What the donor cannot do is execute a deed cancelling the gift and treat the property as his own again; nothing short of a court order will undo the gift.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes, it could be revoked, but only in one way. Despite the recital that it is absolute and irrevocable, the deed can be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude by order of a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee under section 2 of Act No. 5 of 2017, and on these dates such an action is within both the ten-year and the two-year limits in section 3. The donor should be advised to sue promptly, filing the lis pendens application with the plaint; whether the donee's conduct amounts to gross ingratitude is a matter for the court on the evidence, and the donor has no power to revoke the deed himself.

answer_claims.claim_text: A recital that a deed of gift is absolute and irrevocable does not prevent its revocation; an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude.
Revocation may be effected only on an order made by a competent court, in an action filed by the donor against the donee, so the donor cannot revoke the gift by his own act or deed.
Gross ingratitude is the only ground on which such an action may be founded, and the Act does not define the term, so whether given conduct amounts to gross ingratitude is for the court to decide.
The court shall not entertain the action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose.
The plaintiff must file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered.
The revocation action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code.
The donor is the proper plaintiff and the donee, his nephew, the proper defendant in the revocation action.

The assault in June 2023 and the eviction of the donor from the annexe, neither of which the donee denies, are the matters the donor would place before the court as gross ingratitude; the finding remains for the court.

An action filed in or shortly after October 2023 is within ten years of the execution of the deed on 12 March 2019 and within two years of the June 2023 cause of action, so the time limits do not bar the donor.
Because the land is registered in the Kalutara land registry, the lis pendens application is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of that district and must be filed with the plaint.

The deed can be revoked, but only by order of a competent court on the ground of gross ingratitude in an action by the donor against the donee, and on these dates such an action is within both statutory time limits.
The donor cannot undo the gift by executing a deed of revocation himself; without a court order the gift stands.

enrichment.original_background: By a final decree dated 21/05/2000, entered in Partition Case bearing No.7268/P of District Court of Nugegoda Kamal Gunatilleke was allotted all that allotment of land marked Lot 1 depicted in Partition Plan No.2372 dated 15/06/1998 made by.A.W. Silva Licensed Surveyor of land called Kandawatta bearing Assessment No.15, Kandawatta Road, Nugegoda containing in extent 14 Perches. He was married to Thilaka Gunatilleke and had 3 children namely Pethum, Kalum and Shanthi. Kamal Gunatilleke upon Deed of Gift No.232 dated 02/08/2002 attested by A.C. Sisira Notary Public gifted said Lot 1 depicted in the said Plan No.2372 unto to the eldest son Pethum as an absolute and irrevocable gift subject to life interest of him and his wife Thilaka. Kamal Gunatilleke died on 07/07/2005. Kamal had two children named Sadun and Nadun by his first wife Kanthi. Pethum died intestate and issueless on 08/06/2010 leaving his wife Sadana. Sadun married to Roshini and died intestate on 02/08/2011 leaving one child named Rohan. Rohan met with an accident and died on 03/10/2018 unmarried and issueless.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the devolution of title to the land and premises bearing Assessment No.15, Kandawatta Road, Nugegoda can be traced from Kamal Gunatilleke to the persons who presently own it, and who holds the outstanding life interest.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), 'immovable property' being defined in s.3 to include any interest in land; Part III applies to the estate of anyone dying after the Ordinance was proclaimed (s.20), save that it does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22). Subject to that half, the residue goes to descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals (s.23). Children are preferent and take per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes (s.24). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the other half goes to the full brothers and sisters and to the half-brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent (s.25). Where the half-blood are all on one side, s.27 gives the full blood a preference: the full brothers and sisters take one-half of that portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-blood. Within each group those equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Where descendants fail and no brother or sister is alive, the surviving parent takes the whole (s.25). Where the Ordinance is silent the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland applies (s.36); the Ordinance says nothing about the operation of a deed of gift or of a reserved life interest.
gold_answer_draft.application: Kamal Gunatilleke took Lot 1 under the final decree of 21/05/2000 in Partition Case No.7268/P. By Deed of Gift No.232 of 02/08/2002 he gifted Lot 1 absolutely and irrevocably to Pethum, reserving a life interest to himself and to Thilaka. The dominium therefore passed to Pethum in 2002, burdened by the two life interests, and Lot 1 formed no part of Kamal's estate when he died on 07/07/2005; Kamal's own life interest fell in on that date, leaving Thilaka's life interest running. Those two steps rest on the common law of donation and of life interests, to which s.36 refers, and not on any provision of the Ordinance. Pethum died intestate and issueless on 08/06/2010. Under s.22 his widow Sadana took one-half. The descendant class being empty (s.24), s.25 applies: his father Kamal had died in 2005 and his mother Thilaka survived, so Thilaka took half of the remaining half, that is 1/4 of Lot 1, and the other 1/4 formed the sibling portion. That portion is shared by his full brother and sister Kalum and Shanthi and by Sadun and Nadun, who are half-blood siblings related to Pethum by the side of the deceased parent Kamal. The half-blood are all on the father's side, so under s.27 Kalum and Shanthi first take one-half of the sibling portion, that is 1/8 shared equally at 1/16 each, and the remaining 1/8 is divided among all four of them per capita under s.30 at 1/32 each. Kalum and Shanthi therefore hold 3/32 each and Sadun and Nadun 1/32 each. Sadun died intestate on 02/08/2011 holding 1/32. Under s.22 his widow Roshini took 1/64 and under s.24 his only child Rohan took the other 1/64. Rohan died on 03/10/2018 unmarried, issueless and with no brother or sister; his father Sadun had predeceased him, so under the closing limb of s.25 his surviving mother Roshini took the whole 1/64, bringing Roshini to 1/32.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Kamal Gunatilleke (title under the final decree of 21/05/2000) gifts Lot 1 to Pethum by Deed of Gift No.232 of 02/08/2002, subject to the life interests of Kamal and Thilaka; Kamal dies 07/07/2005 and his life interest falls in; Pethum dies intestate and issueless on 08/06/2010, his interest passing to Sadana as widow, to Thilaka as surviving mother, and to Kalum, Shanthi, Sadun and Nadun as siblings; Sadun dies intestate on 02/08/2011, his interest passing to Roshini as widow and to Rohan as his only child; Rohan dies unmarried and issueless on 03/10/2018, his interest passing wholly to his mother Roshini. The present owners of Lot 1 are therefore Sadana, Thilaka, Kalum, Shanthi, Nadun and Roshini, the whole land remaining subject to the life interest of Thilaka reserved by Deed of Gift No.232. This devolution is proposed and unverified; the effect of the deed of gift and of the reserved life interest is not covered by any provision in the corpus.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to immovable property situated in Sri Lanka, including any undivided interest in Lot 1, is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance.
Part III of the Ordinance applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation, and the Ordinance does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property.

Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the inheritance passes first to descendants, then to ascendants, then to collaterals, children taking per capita and the issue of a deceased child by representation.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the other half goes to the full siblings and to the half-siblings related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent.

Where the half-blood siblings are all on one side, the full siblings take one-half of the sibling portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-blood, those equally near in degree taking per capita.
Where descendants fail and no brother or sister is alive at the death, the surviving parent inherits the whole.

Where the Ordinance is silent on a question of intestate distribution, the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland governs, and the Ordinance is silent on the effect of a deed of gift and of a reserved life interest.

Deed of Gift No.232 of 02/08/2002 passed the dominium in Lot 1 to Pethum subject to the life interests reserved to Kamal and Thilaka, so that Lot 1 did not form part of Kamal's intestate estate when he died on 07/07/2005, and Kamal's life interest fell in on that date while Thilaka's continued.
On Pethum's intestate death on 08/06/2010 his widow Sadana took one-half of his interest.

Pethum left no descendants, so the residue passed under the ascendant and collateral rules; his father Kamal had died in 2005 and his mother Thilaka survived, so Thilaka took 1/4 of Lot 1 and the remaining 1/4 formed the sibling portion.

Sadun and Nadun are half-blood siblings of Pethum on the side of his deceased father Kamal and there are no half-blood siblings on the mother's side, so Kalum and Shanthi take 1/16 each out of the first half of the sibling portion and all four take 1/32 each out of the second half, giving Kalum 3/32, Shanthi 3/32, Sadun 1/32 and Nadun 1/32.
On Sadun's intestate death on 02/08/2011 his widow Roshini took 1/64 and his only child Rohan took 1/64.

On Rohan's death on 03/10/2018 unmarried, issueless and without any brother or sister, his father having predeceased him, his surviving mother Roshini took his whole 1/64, so that Roshini holds 1/32 in all.

The present owners of Lot 1 are Sadana, Thilaka, Kalum, Shanthi, Nadun and Roshini, the land remaining subject to Thilaka's reserved life interest; the chain of devolution runs Kamal to Pethum by Deed of Gift No.232, then Pethum's intestacy in 2010, Sadun's intestacy in 2011 and Rohan's intestacy in 2018.

enrichment.original_background: By a final decree dated 21/05/2000, entered in Partition Case bearing No.7268/P of District Court of Nugegoda Kamal Gunatilleke was allotted all that allotment of land marked Lot 1 depicted in Partition Plan No.2372 dated 15/06/1998 made by.A.W. Silva Licensed Surveyor of land called Kandawatta bearing Assessment No.15, Kandawatta Road, Nugegoda containing in extent 14 Perches. He was married to Thilaka Gunatilleke and had 3 children namely Pethum, Kalum and Shanthi. Kamal Gunatilleke upon Deed of Gift No.232 dated 02/08/2002 attested by A.C. Sisira Notary Public gifted said Lot 1 depicted in the said Plan No.2372 unto to the eldest son Pethum as an absolute and irrevocable gift subject to life interest of him and his wife Thilaka. Kamal Gunatilleke died on 07/07/2005. Kamal had two children named Sadun and Nadun by his first wife Kanthi. Pethum died intestate and issueless on 08/06/2010 leaving his wife Sadana. Sadun married to Roshini and died intestate on 02/08/2011 leaving one child named Rohan. Rohan met with an accident and died on 03/10/2018 unmarried and issueless.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What undivided share in Lot 1 each surviving heir presently owns, after the three intestacies of Pethum, Sadun and Rohan, and subject to the life interest reserved by Deed of Gift No.232.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), 'immovable property' being defined in s.3 to include any interest in land; Part III applies to the estate of anyone dying after the Ordinance was proclaimed (s.20), save that it does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai (s.2). A surviving spouse inherits one-half (s.22). Subject to that half, the residue goes to descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals (s.23). Children are preferent and take per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes (s.24). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the other half goes to the full brothers and sisters and to the half-brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent (s.25). Where the half-blood are all on one side, s.27 gives the full blood a preference: the full brothers and sisters take one-half of that portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-blood. Within each group those equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Where descendants fail and no brother or sister is alive, the surviving parent takes the whole (s.25). Where the Ordinance is silent the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland applies (s.36); the Ordinance says nothing about the operation of a deed of gift or of a reserved life interest.
gold_answer_draft.application: Kamal Gunatilleke took Lot 1 under the final decree of 21/05/2000 in Partition Case No.7268/P. By Deed of Gift No.232 of 02/08/2002 he gifted Lot 1 absolutely and irrevocably to Pethum, reserving a life interest to himself and to Thilaka. The dominium therefore passed to Pethum in 2002, burdened by the two life interests, and Lot 1 formed no part of Kamal's estate when he died on 07/07/2005; Kamal's own life interest fell in on that date, leaving Thilaka's life interest running. Those two steps rest on the common law of donation and of life interests, to which s.36 refers, and not on any provision of the Ordinance. Pethum died intestate and issueless on 08/06/2010. Under s.22 his widow Sadana took one-half. The descendant class being empty (s.24), s.25 applies: his father Kamal had died in 2005 and his mother Thilaka survived, so Thilaka took half of the remaining half, that is 1/4 of Lot 1, and the other 1/4 formed the sibling portion. That portion is shared by his full brother and sister Kalum and Shanthi and by Sadun and Nadun, who are half-blood siblings related to Pethum by the side of the deceased parent Kamal. The half-blood are all on the father's side, so under s.27 Kalum and Shanthi first take one-half of the sibling portion, that is 1/8 shared equally at 1/16 each, and the remaining 1/8 is divided among all four of them per capita under s.30 at 1/32 each. Kalum and Shanthi therefore hold 3/32 each and Sadun and Nadun 1/32 each. Sadun died intestate on 02/08/2011 holding 1/32. Under s.22 his widow Roshini took 1/64 and under s.24 his only child Rohan took the other 1/64. Rohan died on 03/10/2018 unmarried, issueless and with no brother or sister; his father Sadun had predeceased him, so under the closing limb of s.25 his surviving mother Roshini took the whole 1/64, bringing Roshini to 1/32.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Subject to Thilaka's reserved life interest over the whole land, the shares presently owned in Lot 1 are: Sadana 1/2; Thilaka 1/4; Kalum 3/32; Shanthi 3/32; Nadun 1/32; and Roshini 1/32, being 1/64 as Sadun's widow and 1/64 inherited from Rohan. These add to unity. On the 14 perches that is 7 perches to Sadana, 3.5 perches to Thilaka, 1.3125 perches each to Kalum and Shanthi and 0.4375 perches each to Nadun and Roshini. The figures are proposed and unverified. If s.27 were held not to reach the sibling portion arising under s.25, the four siblings would instead share it per capita and the shares would be Kalum, Shanthi, Nadun and Roshini 1/16 each.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to immovable property situated in Sri Lanka, including any undivided interest in Lot 1, is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance.
Part III of the Ordinance applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation, and the Ordinance does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils subject to the Tesawalamai.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property.

Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the inheritance passes first to descendants, then to ascendants, then to collaterals, children taking per capita and the issue of a deceased child by representation.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the other half goes to the full siblings and to the half-siblings related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent.

Where the half-blood siblings are all on one side, the full siblings take one-half of the sibling portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-blood, those equally near in degree taking per capita.
Where descendants fail and no brother or sister is alive at the death, the surviving parent inherits the whole.

Where the Ordinance is silent on a question of intestate distribution, the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland governs, and the Ordinance is silent on the effect of a deed of gift and of a reserved life interest.

Deed of Gift No.232 of 02/08/2002 passed the dominium in Lot 1 to Pethum subject to the life interests reserved to Kamal and Thilaka, so that Lot 1 did not form part of Kamal's intestate estate when he died on 07/07/2005, and Kamal's life interest fell in on that date while Thilaka's continued.
On Pethum's intestate death on 08/06/2010 his widow Sadana took one-half of his interest.

Pethum left no descendants, so the residue passed under the ascendant and collateral rules; his father Kamal had died in 2005 and his mother Thilaka survived, so Thilaka took 1/4 of Lot 1 and the remaining 1/4 formed the sibling portion.

Sadun and Nadun are half-blood siblings of Pethum on the side of his deceased father Kamal and there are no half-blood siblings on the mother's side, so Kalum and Shanthi take 1/16 each out of the first half of the sibling portion and all four take 1/32 each out of the second half, giving Kalum 3/32, Shanthi 3/32, Sadun 1/32 and Nadun 1/32.
On Sadun's intestate death on 02/08/2011 his widow Roshini took 1/64 and his only child Rohan took 1/64.

On Rohan's death on 03/10/2018 unmarried, issueless and without any brother or sister, his father having predeceased him, his surviving mother Roshini took his whole 1/64, so that Roshini holds 1/32 in all.
Subject to Thilaka's life interest over the whole, the present shares are Sadana 1/2, Thilaka 1/4, Kalum 3/32, Shanthi 3/32, Nadun 1/32 and Roshini 1/32.

Every step in the answer is imposed by a statutory rule in the corpus: the notarial rules in section 31 and section 38 of the Notaries Ordinance, the writing and attestation requirement in the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, the registration priority rule in the Registration of Documents Ordinance, the corporate execution and major transaction provisions of the Companies Act, the foreign shareholding restriction in the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, and the agricultural land ceiling in the Land Reform Law. Whether the purchase is a major transaction requiring shareholder approval by special resolution.
Whether the restriction on transfer of land to a company with foreign shareholding of fifty per cent or above bars the transfer, and what proof the notary must have for the Registrar of Lands.

What the notary must do about consideration, stamp duty, attestation and registration of the completed deed.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Longer than three necessary linked steps, and it runs across enactments. The chain is: the purchase must be by notarially attested deed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2), which triggers the pre-drafting search and folio extract duties (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rules (17)(a) and (17)(b)(i)); the purchaser being a company brings in the corporate execution route (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)) together with the notarial corporate rules (s.31 rules (14) and (17)(d)); the value of the acquisition brings in the major transaction rule (Companies Act s.185) which in turn requires a special resolution (s.92(1)(b)); and the agricultural character of the estate brings in the ceiling (Land Reform Law s.3(1)(b)) which can only be applied through the attribution rule for private companies (s.8). Independently, the corporate purchaser brings in the foreign shareholding prohibition (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)).

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary instructed by Sales Plus (Private) Limited do, step by step, before, at and after executing a deed transferring a fifteen-acre planted coconut estate at Kuliyapitiya to the company?
gold_answer_draft.rule: A purchase of immovable property is of no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). Before drawing such a deed the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a)), and must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio showing ownership and registered encumbrances (rule (17)(b)(i)); the search matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a later duly registered instrument taken for value (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7). He must use his best endeavours to obtain the vendor's title deed and endorse the transaction on it (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)), and must embody in the deed or its schedule an accurate description of the land showing boundaries, extent and administrative situation (rule (16)(a)). Where a party is a corporate body he must retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and the details of the board of directors (rule (17)(d)); at execution he must cause the seal of the corporate body to be affixed and obtain the signatures of the board or of a person authorised by board resolution (rule (14)), and attach a copy of that resolution to the protocol (rule (14), final sentence). A company enters a notarially attested obligation by a writing signed under the name of the company by two directors, by a sole director, by a class authorised by the articles, or by an appointed attorney, and notarially executed (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)). The acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets is a major transaction which the company may not enter into without approval (Companies Act s.185(1) and (2)(a)), and that approval is exercised by special resolution (Companies Act s.92(1)(b)). Transfer of title to a Sri Lankan company in which direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above is prohibited (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)); the Registrar of Lands must be satisfied by documentary proof from the company secretary that foreign shareholding is below that level (s.4(3)), and an alienation in contravention of that Act is void (s.18). Agricultural land, meaning land used or capable of being used for agriculture (Land Reform Law s.66), is subject to a ceiling of fifty acres where it is not exclusively paddy (s.3(1)(b)); land owned by a private company is deemed owned by its shareholders in proportion to their shares (s.8), and land acquired in excess of the ceiling vests in the Land Reform Commission (s.5(1)). The notary must ascertain and set out the true and full consideration (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)), must not attest until assured that the required stamp duty, charged on specified instruments under the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1), is provided (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6)), must state in the attestation whether the money was paid in his presence and the details of any bank draft (rule (20)(e)), and must submit the deed for registration within thirty days of attestation (rule (30A)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the company is buying immovable property the transaction has to be by notarially attested deed, so the notary is engaged from the outset. His first step is the land registry search against the vendor's chain: Mr. Piyadasa claims on Deed No. 4172 of 2009 and holds the earlier deeds back to 1985, and the certified folio extract for Delgahawatta discloses Mortgage Bond No. 2201 of 2018 in favour of a bank with no discharge entered, so the notary must require the bond to be discharged or a release executed and registered before or at the transfer rather than treat the title as clear. He must call for the vendor's title deeds and endorse the new transfer on them, and must take Plan No. 1123 and the locality particulars of Ihala Gomugomuwa village, Grama Niladhari Division 615, Kuliyapitiya East Divisional Secretary's Division, Kurunegala District, so that the schedule describes the fifteen acres accurately. On the purchaser's side he must call for and retain a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation of Sales Plus (Private) Limited, registration number PV 128654, and the particulars of its two directors. Since the price of Rupees Sixty Two Million exceeds half of the company's Rupees Ninety Five Million of assets, the acquisition is a major transaction and the notary must call for a special resolution of the shareholders as well as the board resolution authorising Ms. Ranatunga and Mr. Wickramasinghe to sign; a copy of the board resolution goes on the protocol, and the deed is signed under the name of the company by those two directors with the company seal affixed and is notarially executed. Because the purchaser is a Sri Lankan company the notary must establish its shareholding: both shareholders are Sri Lankan citizens and there is no foreign holding, so the prohibition is not attracted, but he should still obtain the secretary's documentary proof of that for the Registrar of Lands. The estate is planted with bearing coconut and so is agricultural land; treating the company's fifteen acres as belonging to the two shareholders in their equal shares gives each a further seven and a half acres, which added to Ms. Ranatunga's twenty acres and Mr. Wickramasinghe's twelve acres leaves both well under fifty acres of non-paddy agricultural land, so nothing vests in the Land Reform Commission. He must then set out the true consideration of Rupees Sixty Two Million, satisfy himself that the stamp duty on the transfer is provided, record in the attestation that payment was made in his presence together with the particulars of the bank draft, and lodge the deed for registration at the Kuliyapitiya Land Registry within thirty days of attestation. Two things remain open on the facts: whether the bank will in fact release the mortgage on payment, and whether the vendor's earlier chain of deeds is unbroken, and the notary cannot advise the company to complete until both are resolved.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should, in order: search the registers and obtain the certified folio extract for the estate; examine the vendor's chain of deeds and require the subsisting mortgage bond to be discharged or released; obtain the survey plan and locality particulars for the schedule; call for and retain the company's certificate of incorporation and board details; obtain the special resolution approving the major transaction and the board resolution authorising the two directors to sign; draw the deed with an accurate description and the true consideration; see that the stamp duty is provided; attest the deed with the company seal affixed and the directors' signatures under the company's name, recording the bank draft payment in the attestation and attaching the board resolution to the protocol; endorse the transfer on the vendor's title deed; and submit the deed for registration within thirty days. On the facts as enriched no shareholding bar and no ceiling on agricultural land stands in the way, so the notary may complete the transaction once the mortgage is cleared and the special resolution is in hand.

answer_claims.claim_text: A sale or purchase of immovable property is of no force in law unless it is in writing and attested by a notary, so the company's purchase must be effected by notarial deed.

The notary must obtain from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry showing ownership and the registered encumbrances.
An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later duly registered instrument.
The notary must use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property transferred and endorse on it the number and date of the new deed and the nature of the transaction.
The deed or its schedule must carry an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and administrative situation.
Where a party to the deed is a corporate body the notary must retain a certified copy of its certificate of incorporation and the details of its board of directors.

Where the executant is a corporate body the notary must cause the seal of the corporate body to be affixed and obtain the signatures of the board of directors or of a person authorised by board resolution, and must attach a copy of that resolution to the protocol.

A company enters into a notarially attested obligation by a writing signed under the name of the company by two directors, by a sole director, by a class of persons authorised by the articles, or by an appointed attorney, and notarially executed.

An acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of a company's assets is a major transaction which the company may not enter into unless it is approved, and that shareholder approval must be given by special resolution.

Transfer of title to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka in which direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above is prohibited, the Registrar of Lands must be satisfied by documentary proof from the company secretary that the foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent, and an alienation in contravention of that Act is void.

Agricultural land means land used or capable of being used for agriculture, the ceiling on agricultural land that is not exclusively paddy is fifty acres, agricultural land owned by a private company is deemed owned by its shareholders in proportion to their shares, and land acquired above the ceiling vests in the Land Reform Commission.

The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed, must not attest until assured that the required stamp duty, which is charged on specified instruments, is provided, and must state in the attestation whether the money was paid in his presence and the details of any bank draft.
The notary must submit the attested deed for registration within thirty days of the date of attestation.

gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month is within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, so it has no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary and attested by him; by s.16 of the same Ordinance it must be executed in triplicate. The Notaries Ordinance prescribes some of what the instrument must contain. Section 31 rule (18) requires the notary to insert in letters the day, month and year on which and the place where the deed is executed. Section 31 rule (17)(a) requires an accurate and clear description of the property, showing its boundaries, extent and situation, either in the deed or in a schedule annexed to it. Section 38(1) requires the notary to ascertain the true and full consideration and to set it forth in the deed, which for a lease means the rent actually agreed. Section 31 rule (6) forbids attestation unless the notary has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided. Beyond these fragments the corpus contains no provision that divides a deed of lease into parts or fixes the content of any part; the conventional structure of introduction and parties, recitals, operative or granting words, habendum, reddendum, covenants and conditions, and testimonium rests on the Roman-Dutch law of letting and hiring and on conveyancing precedent, which are outside the corpus.

The recitals would set out the lessor's title on Deed of Transfer No. 4127 and his agreement to lease. The operative part would demise the premises more fully described in the schedule, the description itself satisfying s.31 rule (17)(a). The habendum would fix the five-year term from 1 June 2023 and the reddendum the rent of Rs.50,000 a month payable in advance, which is the true consideration the notary must set out under s.38(1). gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on the lease agreement between Shantha Silva and Asela Pathirana, and by whom?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 s.3(1) charges stamp duty at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka. Section 4(i) makes a lease or hire of any property a specified instrument. Section 6(c) makes the duty on a lease payable by the lessee, otherwise than where there is an agreement to the contrary. Section 8(1) requires the duty to be paid by affixing adhesive stamps of the required value prior to or at the time of execution, and s.8(2) allows the duty on an instrument relating to a lease of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate to be affixed to the instrument. Section 13 leaves the imposition and exemption provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 without operation so far as inconsistent, save for transfers of immovable property, motor vehicle transfers and documents filed in court, none of which covers a lease. Section 5 leaves exemptions to be specified by Order in the Gazette. The Act itself fixes no rate.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument is a lease of the shop premises, so it is a specified instrument under s.4(i), and it is to be executed in Sri Lanka on 20 May 2023, so it falls within s.3(1)(a). The rent reserved for the five-year term is Rs.3,000,000 with no premium or other capital payment, so that is the consideration by reference to which duty would be computed. There being no agreement to the contrary, s.6(c) places the duty on the lessee, Asela Pathirana. Payment must be made by adhesive stamps before or at execution under s.8(1), or to a prescribed bank under s.8(2), and the notary may not attest the deed until he has an assurance under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) that the duty is provided. The 1982 Act supplies no alternative rate for a lease, because s.13 of the 2006 Act displaces it. The rate itself is fixed only by an Order made by the Minister under s.3, and no such Order is in the corpus, so the rupee amount cannot be computed here.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The lease agreement is chargeable with stamp duty as a specified instrument, and the duty falls on the lessee, Asela Pathirana, to be paid before or at execution.
