gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, s.21(1), which applies to the estate of anyone dying after its proclamation, s.20. Subject to the surviving spouse's one-half under s.22, the order of succession is descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals, s.23. Children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita, with the issue of a deceased child taking per stirpes, s.24. Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, that parent takes half and the other half goes to the full brothers and sisters and to the half-brothers and sisters related to the intestate through the deceased parent, s.25; those siblings being equally near in degree take that half per capita, s.30. Where both parents fail, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters, whole or half-blood, s.26, and where the half-blood is on one side only the full siblings take the first half and share the remaining half with the half-blood, s.27. 'Unmarried' means not having a husband or wife living, s.3, so no s.22 share arises out of the estate of a person who dies unmarried. Where the Ordinance is silent the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland governs, s.36; that is the source of the rules on a donation reserving a life interest, which the statutes do not address.
gold_answer_draft.application: The final decree of 07.09.1999 vested Lot 5 in Nihal Gamage. By Deed of Gift No. 663 of 21.11.2002 he gifted the lot to his son Piyal absolutely and irrevocably, reserving life interests to himself and to his wife Kanthi. The dominium therefore passed to Piyal in 2002; what Nihal kept was a life interest, which is not an inheritable interest and fell in on his death on 28.04.2003. Nihal's intestacy in 2003 accordingly passes nothing in Lot 5, and his heirs take in this land only through the later intestacies. Kanthi's life interest continued after 2003 and burdened Piyal's dominium. Piyal died intestate on 02.08.2006 unmarried and issueless. Having no spouse (s.3, s.22) and no descendants (s.24), s.25 applies: his father Nihal had predeceased him, his mother Kanthi survived, so Kanthi takes half of the dominium and the other half goes to his full sisters Aruna and Leela and to his paternal half-sisters Nikitha and Rikitha, who are related to him through the deceased parent, in equal per capita shares under s.30. The letters of administration issued to Kanthi in District Court of Kaduwela Case No. 1052/2006/T, terminated on 27.11.2007, administered that estate but did not alter the devolution, Civil Procedure Code s.526. Kanthi died intestate on 17.03.2010; her life interest was extinguished on that date and the land became unencumbered, and the half she had inherited from Piyal passed under s.24 to her surviving children Aruna and Leela, Piyal having died before her without issue to represent him. Nikitha and Rikitha are not Kanthi's children and take nothing out of her estate. Rikitha married Sanatha and died intestate on 02.08.2016 without children. Her husband takes one-half of her share under s.22. The background does not say that Anusha survived; proceeding on the footing that neither parent survived Rikitha, the other half of her share goes under s.26 to her sister Nikitha and her paternal half-sisters Aruna and Leela, divided in the s.27 proportions because the half-blood is on the father's side only: Nikitha takes the first half of that collateral portion and shares the remainder with Aruna and Leela.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Nihal Gamage under the final decree of 07.09.1999; Deed of Gift No. 663 of 21.11.2002 to Piyal Gamage subject to the life interests of Nihal and Kanthi, so that Nihal's death on 28.04.2003 carried nothing in Lot 5; Piyal's intestate death on 02.08.2006 dividing his dominium as to one-half to his mother Kanthi and one-half equally among Aruna, Leela, Nikitha and Rikitha; Kanthi's intestate death on 17.03.2010 extinguishing her life interest and passing her half equally to Aruna and Leela; and Rikitha's intestate death on 02.08.2016 passing one-half of her share to her husband Sanatha and the other half to Nikitha, Aruna and Leela. The present owners are therefore Aruna, Leela, Nikitha and Sanatha. Two points remain open: whether Anusha survived Rikitha, and whether the sibling half under s.25 is divided per capita under s.30 or in the s.27 proportions.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to Lot 5, being immovable property in Sri Lanka, is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, which applies to the estate of any person dying after its proclamation.
Subject to the surviving spouse's one-half, the right of inheritance devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals.
Where the Ordinance is silent on a question of distribution, the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland governs; the corpus contains no provision on the effect of a donation reserving a life interest.

Under Deed of Gift No. 663 the dominium of Lot 5 passed to Piyal Gamage in 2002 and Nihal retained only a life interest, so Nihal's intestate death on 28.04.2003 devolved no interest in Lot 5 on his heirs.
Piyal died unmarried within the meaning of the Ordinance and left no descendants, so neither the surviving spouse's half nor the preferential right of children arises out of his estate.
Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full siblings together with the half-siblings related through the deceased parent take the other half.
Siblings who are all equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes.
On Piyal's death Kanthi took one-half of his dominium as surviving parent, and Aruna, Leela, Nikitha and Rikitha took the other half in equal per capita shares.
The grant of letters of administration to Kanthi in the testamentary case did not alter who succeeded to Piyal's estate.
Children are preferent to all others in the estate of a parent and take equally per capita, the issue of a deceased child taking by representation.

On Kanthi's death her life interest was extinguished and the half she had inherited from Piyal passed equally to her surviving children Aruna and Leela, Piyal having predeceased her without issue and Nikitha and Rikitha not being her children.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person dying intestate, so Sanatha took one-half of Rikitha's share.

Both parents failing, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the whole or half-blood, and where the half-blood is on one side only the full siblings take the first half and share the remainder with the half-blood.

On the footing that neither of Rikitha's parents survived her, the other half of her share passed to her full sister Nikitha and her paternal half-sisters Aruna and Leela in the proportions fixed by section 27.
The pedigree therefore ends with Aruna, Leela, Nikitha and Sanatha as the present owners of Lot 5, the land being free of both reserved life interests since 17.03.2010.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What fraction of Lot 5, 30 perches in extent, is presently owned by each heir, given that Nihal parted with the dominium by Deed of Gift No. 663 in 2002 and that Piyal, Kanthi and Rikitha each died intestate thereafter.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The same Part III rules govern each computation. Inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is regulated by the Ordinance, s.21(1), for estates of persons dying after its proclamation, s.20. A surviving spouse takes one-half, s.22; 'unmarried' means not having a husband or wife living, s.3. Subject to that half the order is descendants, ascendants, collaterals, s.23. Children take equally per capita, issue of a deceased child by representation, s.24. Descendants failing and one parent surviving, that parent takes half and the full siblings and the half-siblings related through the deceased parent take the other half, s.25, which they take per capita being equally near in degree, s.30. Both parents failing, the siblings of whole and half-blood take, s.26; the half-blood being on one side only, the full siblings take the first half and divide the remainder with the half-blood, s.27. Where the Ordinance is silent the Roman-Dutch law of North Holland applies, s.36, which is what governs the reserved life interests.
gold_answer_draft.application: Take the whole of Lot 5 as 1. Piyal held the entire dominium from 21.11.2002, subject to the life interests. On his death on 02.08.2006 without spouse or descendants (s.3, s.22, s.24), s.25 gives Kanthi as surviving parent 1/2, and the remaining 1/2 is shared per capita under s.30 by Aruna, Leela, Nikitha and Rikitha, so each of the four takes 1/8. On Kanthi's death on 17.03.2010 her life interest ended and her 1/2 passed under s.24 to her surviving children Aruna and Leela, 1/4 each; Nikitha and Rikitha take nothing out of her estate. Holdings then stood at Aruna 3/8, Leela 3/8, Nikitha 1/8 and Rikitha 1/8. On Rikitha's death on 02.08.2016 her husband Sanatha took 1/2 of her 1/8, that is 1/16, under s.22. On the footing that neither of her parents survived her, the other 1/16 passed under s.26 to her full sister Nikitha and her paternal half-sisters Aruna and Leela, divided under s.27: Nikitha takes the first half of it, 1/32, and the remaining 1/32 is divided among Nikitha, Aruna and Leela, 1/96 each. Nikitha therefore adds 1/32 plus 1/96, which is 1/24, and Aruna and Leela add 1/96 each.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: On the reading adopted, Aruna owns 37/96, Leela owns 37/96, Nikitha owns 1/6 or 16/96, and Sanatha owns 1/16 or 6/96, of Lot 5; the four fractions total 96/96. Against the 30 perch extent that is 11.5625 perches each to Aruna and Leela, 5 perches to Nikitha and 1.875 perches to Sanatha, and the land is free of both life interests since 17.03.2010. Two alternatives must be resolved before these figures are treated as settled: if the sibling half of Piyal's estate is divided in the section 27 proportions rather than per capita under section 30, every figure changes; and if Anusha survived Rikitha, section 25 applies to Rikitha's estate and Anusha takes 1/32 with Nikitha, Aruna and Leela taking 1/96 each.

Where the value of a condominium parcel is recorded, how the share value entered on the registered Condominium Plan is fixed, and what that share value governs.
What documents and searches a prospective purchaser can use before contracting to satisfy herself about the value of the parcel, including registered encumbrances and the municipal assessment.
Whether the value at which the transfer is stamped operates as an independent check on the figure the parties agree, and what machinery exists for having that value determined officially.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. First, what passes on a sale of a parcel: section 11 deems the undivided share in the common elements to be conveyed with the parcel. Second, the size of that share: section 20A makes the share value shown on the plan the measure of the undivided share, the voting rights and the contributions, and section 9(3) ties the share value to the user of the parcel. Third, where the figure is found: section 5(1)(m) requires the plan to enter the share value in compliance with section 20A, and the section 26 definition of 'share parcel' places it in the Schedule endorsed on the registered plan. Only these indispensable links are counted; the stamp duty provisions add a parallel check rather than a further step in the chain.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How a prospective purchaser of a condominium parcel in Colombo can ascertain the value of the property she proposes to buy, and what the statutory scheme fixes for her as against what she must obtain from valuation evidence outside the statutes.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A condominium parcel cannot be valued as an apartment standing alone. Apartment Ownership Law s.11 deems any alienation of a condominium parcel also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to it, and s.9(4) allows the parcel together with those common elements to be held and dealt with in the same manner and form as any land. The measure of that undivided share is the share value. Under s.20A(1) the share value of each parcel shown in the plan lodged for registration is taken as share parcels, and by s.20A(2) the share parcels determine the voting rights of the owners, the quantum of the undivided share of each owner in the common elements, and the proportion of the contributions levied by the management corporation under s.20H; no share value is allotted to an accessory parcel. By s.9(3) share value is given according to the user of the parcel, whether commercial or residential. The figure is a matter of record: s.5(1)(m) requires the Condominium Plan to enter the share value of each parcel in compliance with s.20A, s.5(1)(h) requires it to specify the approximate floor area of each parcel, and the s.26 definition of 'share parcel' places the share parcels in the Schedule endorsed on the Condominium Plan. Ownership taken under a registered plan is, by s.7A(2), subject to encumbrances registered or notified in the relevant register. On the conveyance itself, for a Colombo property, Western Province Financial Statute s.48(1) charges stamp duty on the value of the property conveyed rather than on the sum the parties recite, s.78(2) obliges the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.62 allows a person bringing an instrument to an Assessor to obtain his determination of the duty chargeable. Under Municipal Councils Ordinance s.235 the Council keeps an assessment book of annual values, but inspection as of right is confined to the owner or occupier or his authorised agent.
gold_answer_draft.application: Neela Kumari should begin with the registered Condominium Plan No. 4127 and the Schedule endorsed on it. The plan gives her the approximate floor area of parcel C/07/03, 132 square metres, under s.5(1)(h), and enters its share value as 96 under s.5(1)(m) read with the s.26 definition of 'share parcel'. Applying s.20A(2), a share value of 96 out of an aggregate entitlement of 3,600 fixes her undivided share in the common elements and the proportion of management corporation contributions she will carry, so the price should be tested against that proportion and not against floor area alone. Because s.9(3) ties share value to user, the residential user recorded for the parcel explains the figure entered. The car park bay A/12 is an accessory parcel, and s.20A(1) allots no share value to an accessory parcel, so it adds convenience but no share of the common elements and should not be priced as though it did. Section 11 confirms that the undivided share passes with the parcel whether or not the deed mentions it, so the whole of that share is part of what she is paying for. A search of the relevant register is the next step: the bank mortgage registered against parcel C/07/03 binds her under s.7A(2), and the sum required to redeem it has to be set against the Rs. 46,000,000 quoted. She can ask Suranga Jayalath, as the owner in whose name the assessment stands, to produce the Colombo Municipal Council assessment under s.235, although the annual value entered there is a rating figure and not the capital value of the parcel. Since no agreement for sale has been signed and no deed drawn, the value on which the transfer will be stamped is still open: s.48(1) requires duty to be computed on the value of the property conveyed, her notary must under s.78(2) satisfy himself that the value stamped represents that value, and the instrument can be taken to an Assessor for a determination under s.62. What none of these provisions gives her is the open market price of the parcel; that has to come from valuation evidence, and the statutes are silent on how it is produced.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Neela Kumari can fix the statutory measure of the property's value from the registered Condominium Plan: the floor area under s.5(1)(h) and, decisively, the share value of 96 out of 3,600 entered under s.5(1)(m) and shown in the endorsed Schedule under the s.26 definition, which by s.20A(2) fixes her undivided share in the common elements and her contribution proportion, is given by reference to the residential user under s.9(3), and passes to her with the parcel under s.11. She should read that against a search of the relevant register for the registered mortgage under s.7A(2) and, through the vendor, the municipal assessment under s.235, and should treat the accessory car park bay as carrying no share value under s.20A(1). Before the transfer is stamped the value must in any event be one that represents the value of the property conveyed under Western Province Financial Statute s.48(1) and s.78(2), and it may be put to an Assessor on adjudication under s.62. The open market price at which she should buy is not fixed by any of these provisions and must be established by valuation evidence outside the statutes.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the purchase had been at an undervalue between related parties, the open market price at acquisition would have to be assessed separately and the first limb would exceed Rs.250,000/- plus improvements.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What value should be stated in the Deed of Gift by which Rohan Perera gifts his Maharagama house and land to his son Wasantha, for the purpose of stamp duty, given that he bought the property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, improved it at a cost of Rs.800,000/- and it is now worth Rs.6,500,000/-.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute s.37), and Transfer is defined by s.106 of that Statute to mean a sale and to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable although nothing is paid for it. Section 48(1) provides that where property is conveyed by an instrument, the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, so the operative figure is a statutory value and not the consideration. For gifted immovable property, value is defined in s.106. Where the donor acquired the property after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of that definition applies: value means the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the price it would fetch in the open market on the date of that instrument. The national Act states the same rule for gifted land in Stamp Duty Act s.71, which continues to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property because Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 excepts such instruments from the displacement of the 1982 Act. Section 78(2) of the Western Province Financial Statute requires the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.78(1) requires the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty to be set out in the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The land is at Maharagama in the Western Province and the instrument is a Deed of Gift, so s.37 read with the definition of Transfer in s.106 brings it into charge; no exemption in s.39 covers a gift from a father to his son. Duty is therefore calculated under s.48(1) on the value of the property conveyed. Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value applies and paragraph (b), which is pegged to a 31 March 1977 open market price, does not. The first limb is the open market price on the date he acquired the property, which on the facts given is the Rs.250,000/- he paid at arm's length in December 1977, increased by the Rs.800,000/- spent on the upper floor, garage and boundary wall, all of which were built after he acquired the property and before the proposed deed. That limb comes to Rs.1,050,000/-. The second limb is the open market price on the date of the instrument, which the valuation as at October 2022 puts at Rs.6,500,000/-. Paragraph (c) directs that whichever price is the lower is the value, and Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, being the Rs.250,000/- open market price at which Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977 together with the Rs.800,000/- cost of improvements made before the gift, that sum being lower than the present open market value of Rs.6,500,000/-. The attesting notary should satisfy himself that this figure represents the statutory value and set it out in the deed, and the figure remains open to the Assessor's own opinion of the open market prices at the two relevant dates.

answer_claims.claim_text: A Deed of Gift of immovable property situated in the Western Province is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property and is chargeable with stamp duty.
Transfer is defined to mean a sale and to include a gift, so the absence of consideration does not take a Deed of Gift out of the charge.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on any consideration recited.

For immovable property that is gifted and was acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, value means the lower of (i) the open market price on the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the open market price on the date of that instrument.

The valuation rules of the Stamp Duty Act of 1982 continue to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property, because those instruments are excepted from the displacement of that Act by the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act.
No exemption covers a gift of land between a father and his son, so the deed is not exempt.
The property is at Maharagama in the Western Province, so the provincial charging and valuation provisions apply to the proposed deed.
Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value governs and paragraph (b) does not.
The first limb is Rs.250,000/- as the open market price at acquisition plus Rs.800,000/- for improvements made after acquisition and before the deed, that is Rs.1,050,000/-.
The second limb is Rs.6,500,000/-, the open market price of the property at the date of the deed.
Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two limbs and is therefore the statutory value of the property gifted.

The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, and the attesting notary must take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that this figure represents the value of the property conveyed and must set out in the deed the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty.

block_reason: The rate of duty is prescribed by an Order or regulation made under Western Province Financial Statute s.37 (and, for the national Act, under Stamp Duty Act s.2), and no such rate instrument, schedule or Gazette Order is in the corpus. Grep over the corpus for rate language returns only the words at the prescribed rate. The base is established at Rs.1,050,000/-, but supplying a percentage would mean quoting a rates schedule that was never extracted.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The quantum of stamp duty on a deed of gift of land is a purely statutory question: the charging section imposes duty at the prescribed rate and the rate itself is fixed by subordinate legislation made under that Statute. No judicial authority or common law doctrine is needed. The difficulty is not the kind of authority required but that the rate instrument is absent from the corpus.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What amount of stamp duty is payable on the Deed of Gift by which Rohan Perera gifts his Maharagama house and land to his son Wasantha, and on what base and by whom it is payable.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Province, and permits different rates for different classes of instruments; Transfer is defined in s.106 to include a gift. Section 48(1) directs that the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and s.106 defines value for gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977 as the lower of the open market price at acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made before the gift, and the open market price at the date of the instrument. Section 51(a) makes the duty payable by the grantee unless the parties agree otherwise, and s.40(1) requires it to be paid before or at the time of execution. The rate itself is not fixed by the Statute; it is prescribed by subordinate legislation made under it, and that instrument is not in this corpus.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876, s.21(1), and 'immovable property' under s.3 of that Ordinance includes land and things attached to the earth, so Lot A and the building on it are covered. Part III applies to the estate of any person dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance, s.20, and does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, s.2. Where an intestate leaves a surviving spouse, the spouse inherits one half, s.22, and the residue devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals, s.23. Descendants are preferent and the issue of a deceased child take by representation, s.24. Where the descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the other half goes to the full-blood brothers and sisters together with the half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate through the deceased parent, s.25. Persons equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes unless the Ordinance expressly provides otherwise, s.30. Where the Ordinance is silent the rules of Roman-Dutch law govern, s.36. The Ordinance does not itself govern the effect of a life interest reserved by a donor on a deed of gift.
gold_answer_draft.application: By the final decree of 25.03.2002 in DC Colombo case 102/P, Nishantha Jayakodi became sole owner of Lot A, and the commercial building he erected on the land forms part of that immovable property, s.3. By Deed of Gift No. 1012 dated 12.08.2002 he gifted Lot A to his youngest son Lalantha absolutely and irrevocably, reserving a life interest to himself, so that from that date Lalantha held the ownership burdened by the donor's life interest. On the donor's death on 13.09.2007 the life interest determined and Lalantha held Lot A free of it. Nishantha's own intestacy of 2007 does not touch this land, because he had already parted with the ownership in 2002 and retained only a life interest that ended with him, so his widow Kanthi and his children take nothing in Lot A through his estate. Lalantha died intestate and issueless on 04.10.2009 leaving his wife Nishi Fernando, his mother Kanthi, his full brother Harsha, his full sister Dushani and his half-sister Minoli through his father. Nishi takes one half under s.22. The residue of one half devolves under s.23, and since Lalantha left no descendants s.24 is exhausted, so s.25 applies: his father had predeceased him and his mother survived, so Kanthi takes half of that residue, a quarter of the whole, and the other quarter goes to Harsha and Dushani as full-blood siblings together with Minoli, a half-blood sister related through the deceased father. Those three are equally near in degree and, on the reading taken here, share that quarter per capita under s.30, one twelfth each. gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Nimal, a stranger in undisturbed and uninterrupted possession for more than ten years of a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 in another person's name with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, can claim prescriptive title to that parcel.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prescriptive title to land rests on Prescription Ordinance s.3, which entitles a person to a decree on proof of ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted possession by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce or by any act from which an acknowledgment of another's right would fairly be inferred. That Ordinance is withdrawn from land brought on to the Title Register: Registration of Title Act s.57 provides that the Prescription Ordinance shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under that Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership, and s.14 shows that these are the classes with which a claimant is declared eligible to be registered on initial compilation. Registration of Title Act s.73 gives that Act effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other written law, so the Prescription Ordinance cannot survive s.57 in this field. Alongside the exclusion, Registration of Title Act s.33(1) makes entries in the Title Register conclusive evidence of the ownership recorded and provides that they shall not be questioned in a court of law except as the Act provides, and s.38 denies entitlement to any title or interest in a registered land parcel unless that title or interest is itself registered. The only route by which ten years' possession improves a position under the Act is s.31(1), and it belongs to a person already registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership, who becomes eligible at the end of ten years from registration, absent an action under s.29, for conversion to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
gold_answer_draft.application: The parcel Nimal occupies lies in a declared area and is registered under the Registration of Title Act, with Somapala entered in the Title Register as owner with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership since March 2009. Nimal's occupation from January 2011 to October 2021 is continuous, unaccompanied by rent or produce and free of any act of acknowledgment, so on its own terms it would answer the description in Prescription Ordinance s.3 and exceed the ten-year term. That does not assist him, because the parcel is land registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership and Registration of Title Act s.57 makes the Prescription Ordinance inapplicable to it; the rule he would invoke is simply not available for this land. Nor can he reach the same result by another statutory route. He is not named in the Title Register in any capacity, so under s.38 he is not entitled to any title or interest in the parcel, and under s.33(1) Somapala's registered ownership is conclusive and cannot be questioned in court except as the Act allows, which does not extend to a claim founded on adverse possession. The conversion right in s.31(1) is closed to him as well, since it presupposes registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership and Nimal has no registration at all.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. Nimal cannot claim prescriptive title. Because the parcel is registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, s.57 puts the Prescription Ordinance out of play, so no period of adverse possession, however long or however undisturbed, can ripen into title to it, and s.38 leaves him without entitlement while he remains off the register. This assumes the parcel was on the Title Register throughout the period relied on; if part of that possession ran before the land was brought under the Act, the position for that earlier period would need separate consideration.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance entitles a person to a decree on proof of ten years' undisturbed and uninterrupted possession of land by a title adverse to or independent of the owner's, unaccompanied by rent, produce, service or any act from which an acknowledgment of another's right would fairly be inferred.

On initial compilation under the Registration of Title Act a claimant is declared eligible for registration either with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or, where he does not so qualify but is in bonafide possession, with a Second Class Title of Ownership.

Registration of Title Act s.57 provides that the Prescription Ordinance shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under that Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership.
The Registration of Title Act has effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other written law, so the Prescription Ordinance cannot operate against s.57.
Entries in the Title Register are conclusive evidence of the ownership specified in them and shall not be questioned in a court of law except as provided for in the Registration of Title Act.
No person acquiring an interest in a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act is entitled to that title or interest unless it is itself registered under the Act.

A person registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership becomes eligible, at the end of ten years from that registration and absent an action under s.29, for conversion of his registration to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

Nimal's occupation from January 2011 to October 2021 was continuous, without payment of rent or produce and without any act of acknowledgment, so it would answer the description of adverse possession in Prescription Ordinance s.3 and exceed the ten-year term.

The parcel is land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership in Somapala's name, so it falls within the exclusion in s.57 and the Prescription Ordinance does not apply to it.

Because Nimal is not named in the Title Register in any capacity, he is not entitled to any title or interest in the parcel, and Somapala's registered ownership is conclusive and not open to challenge in court on a ground the Act does not provide for.
The ten-year conversion right is not open to Nimal, because it presupposes an existing registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership and he holds no registration at all.

Nimal cannot claim prescriptive title to the parcel; no length of adverse possession of land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership can ripen into title, and he remains without entitlement while he is off the register.

The conclusion assumes the parcel was on the Title Register throughout the period of possession relied on; possession running before the land was brought under the Act would need separate consideration.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The notary is asked to attest a deed of transfer executed by a man he does not know, in circumstances where he knows one of the two attesting witnesses. The issue is whether, and on what conditions, the rules to be observed by notaries permit him to attest a deed when the executant is a stranger to him.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9), in the form in force in October 2021, provided that a notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto. The statutory test therefore looks to the notary's knowledge of the executant, and failing that to the knowledge which at least two attesting witnesses have of the executant; the notary's acquaintance with a witness is not itself a substitute. Where the notary relies on the witnesses, the same rule requires that he satisfy himself, before accepting them as witnesses, that they are persons of good repute and that they are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation, and residence, and that the witnesses sign a declaration at the foot of the deed to that effect. Section 31 rule (8) forbids attestation of a deed to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and rule (12) forbids attestation unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, the notary signing before them. Rule (20) then requires the attestation to state whether the executants are known to the notary or whether the witnesses are known to him, and in the latter case to specify which executant is known to which witness. Notarial attestation of this kind is what the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 makes a condition of a valid transfer of immovable property.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary does not know Mr. Dharmasena, so the first branch of rule (9) is unavailable and he cannot attest on the strength of his own knowledge. That he has known Mr. Silva for years does not cure this: rule (9) asks whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses, not whether a witness is known to the notary. Here the second branch is satisfied, because both Mr. Silva and Mr. Fernando have been acquainted with the executant for more than twenty years and know his proper name, occupation and residence, so the executant is known to at least two of the attesting witnesses even though one of them is a stranger to the notary. Before accepting them the notary must satisfy himself that they are of good repute and that their acquaintance with the executant is real; on the facts both are of settled reputation in the executant's village and both are willing to sign the declaration at the foot of the deed, which the rule requires them to sign. Two witnesses will subscribe their signatures in letters, as rule (8) requires, and executant and witnesses can sign together before the notary as rule (12) requires. Having attested on the strength of the witnesses rather than his own knowledge, the notary must say so in his attestation and specify which of the witnesses knows the executant.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary may attest the deed, but only in these circumstances: the executant, though unknown to him, must be known to at least two of the attesting witnesses; the notary must first satisfy himself that those witnesses are persons of good repute and are well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence; the witnesses must sign the declaration to that effect at the foot of the deed; at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters, and executant, witnesses and notary must sign in one another's presence; and the attestation must record that the executant was not known to the notary and specify which witness knows him. Knowing one witness is not enough on its own. This states the position under section 31 as it stood at the October 2021 examination session; the rule was recast in 2022 to allow identity to be established by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, which was not an available route at that date.

answer_claims.claim_text: In October 2021 a notary could not authenticate or attest a deed unless the person executing it was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses.

Where the notary relies on the witnesses' knowledge, he must satisfy himself before accepting them that they are persons of good repute and well acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and the witnesses must sign a declaration to that effect at the foot of the deed.
A deed may not be attested unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters.
The executant and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign before them.
The attestation must state whether the executants are known to the notary or whether the witnesses are known to him, and in the latter case specify which executant is known to which witness.

Because the notary does not know the executant, he cannot attest on the first branch of the rule, and his acquaintance with one witness does not supply the missing knowledge, since the test is whether the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses.
The second branch is satisfied on these facts, because both attesting witnesses have long been acquainted with the executant and know his proper name, occupation and residence.
The witnesses may be accepted because they are of good repute and are willing to sign the required declaration at the foot of the deed.
Two witnesses will subscribe their signatures and executant, witnesses and notary can sign together, so the remaining execution formalities are met.

The notary may attest the deed, but only where the executant is known to at least two attesting witnesses whom he has satisfied himself are of good repute and well acquainted with the executant, who sign the declaration at the foot of the deed, with at least two witnesses subscribing and all signing in one another's presence, and with the position recorded in the attestation.
The notary's acquaintance with one witness alone does not entitle him to attest the deed.

This states the position as at October 2021; the identification rule was recast in 2022 to allow identity to be established by inspection of a national identity card, passport bio-page or driving licence, which was not available at the matter date.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Alfred Perera purchased a property in Pannipitiya in January 1978 for Rs.160,000/-. He constructed a house on the property spending Rs.900,000/- and now the property is valued at Rs.9,000,000/-. He intends to gift this property to his daughter Himall.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How an Assessor of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council arrives at the value of the Pannipitiya property for stamp duty on the proposed Deed of Gift, where the donor bought the land in January 1978 for Rs.160,000, spent Rs.900,000 building a house on it, and the property is now worth Rs.9,000,000.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990 s.37(a)), and 'transfer' is defined in s.106 to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable. Section 48(1) provides that where property is conveyed by an instrument the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed. 'Value' is neither the consideration nor simply today's market price: under the definition in s.106, where the property gifted is immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, value means the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched, in the opinion of the Assessor, if sold in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the deed, and (ii) the price it would have fetched, in the opinion of the Assessor, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument of gift. Had the donor acquired the property on or before March 31, 1977, the first figure would instead be built on the open-market price on March 31, 1977. To obtain the determination the deed, with a copy, is brought to the Assessor under s.62 with the prescribed fee of Rs.250; the Assessor determines the duty in his opinion chargeable and notifies it in writing, and under s.63 he may require the applicant to produce documents and other evidence proving the facts relevant to chargeability and amount. Under s.78(2) the attesting notary must separately take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
gold_answer_draft.application: The gift is of immovable property at Pannipitiya, which lies in the Western Province, so s.37(a) applies and the valuing officer is the Provincial Assessor of Revenue. Mr. Perera acquired the property in January 1978, after March 31, 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' governs and the March 31, 1977 valuation date in paragraph (b) is irrelevant. The Assessor therefore builds two figures. For the first, he forms an opinion of the open-market price of the property as at January 1978; the Rs.160,000 paid on that purchase is evidence of that price, and he may call for the 1978 deed under s.63, though the statutory test is his opinion of the open-market price at that date rather than the price recited in the deed. To that he adds the cost of the improvements made after acquisition and before the deed of gift, which on the facts is the Rs.900,000 spent on constructing the house, supported by plans, bills and receipts he may call for. That gives Rs.160,000 + Rs.900,000 = Rs.1,060,000. For the second, he forms an opinion of the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the facts as stated is Rs.9,000,000. He then takes the lower of the two. Nothing is deducted because the donee is the donor's daughter, and no exemption in s.39 covers a family gift. If the gift were made subject to a reservation in favour of the donor, s.48(3) would require the value to be taken as if no reservation had been made; no reservation appears on these facts.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Assessor takes the lower of Rs.1,060,000 (open-market price at acquisition in January 1978, evidenced by the Rs.160,000 purchase price, plus the Rs.900,000 cost of the house built afterwards) and Rs.9,000,000 (open-market price at the date of the deed), and so arrives at a value of Rs.1,060,000 for the purpose of stamp duty on this Deed of Gift. Both amounts remain the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at each date under s.106, so the figures given in the scenario are evidence of value rather than binding on him, and the amounts actually adopted turn on the evidence produced under s.63.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, at the prescribed rate.
A gift is a transfer for the purposes of the Statute, so a Deed of Gift is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration.

For immovable property that is gifted and was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, 'value' means the lower of the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made before the deed, and his opinion of the open-market price at the date of the deed of gift.

On an application under section 62 with a copy of the instrument and a fee of two hundred and fifty rupees, the Assessor determines the duty chargeable in his opinion and notifies the determination in writing, and may require production of documents and other evidence proving the facts relevant to the amount.
The attesting notary must take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.

Because the donor acquired the Pannipitiya property in January 1978, that is after March 31, 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' applies rather than the March 31, 1977 comparison in paragraph (b).

The first comparison figure is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price of the property in January 1978, for which the Rs.160,000 purchase price is evidence, increased by the Rs.900,000 cost of constructing the house after acquisition and before the deed, giving Rs.1,060,000.
The second comparison figure is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the facts as given is Rs.9,000,000.
Taking the lower of Rs.1,060,000 and Rs.9,000,000, the Assessor arrives at a value of Rs.1,060,000 for the purpose of stamp duty on this Deed of Gift.
The value so arrived at remains the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at each date, so the figures in the scenario are evidence of value rather than binding on him.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Alfred Perera purchased a property in Pannipitiya in January 1978 for Rs.160,000/-. He constructed a house on the property spending Rs.900,000/- and now the property is valued at Rs.9,000,000/-. He intends to gift this property to his daughter Himall.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on the proposed Deed of Gift of the Pannipitiya property, and how that duty is calculated.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under s.37(a) of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, stamp duty at the prescribed rate is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and 'transfer' in s.106 includes a gift. Section 48(1) directs that the duty be calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and the definition of 'value' in s.106 fixes that value, for gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, as the lower of the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at acquisition plus the cost of later improvements made before the deed, and his opinion of the open-market price at the date of the deed. Section 39 exempts certain instruments, but nothing in that list covers a gift between family members. The rate is not stated in the Statute: s.37 charges duty 'at the prescribed rate' and allows different rates for different classes of instrument, and s.77(1)(a) empowers regulations to prescribe what the Statute requires to be prescribed, such regulations operating from publication in the Gazette. The duty is payable by the grantee under s.51(a) unless the deed provides otherwise, and under s.40(1) must be paid before or at the time of execution by adhesive or impressed stamps or by a certificate of payment issued by a prescribed bank and affixed to the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The chargeable value is settled first. The donor acquired the property in January 1978, so the comparison is between Rs.160,000 as the open-market price at acquisition plus the Rs.900,000 spent on the house built afterwards, which is Rs.1,060,000, and Rs.9,000,000 as the open-market price at the date of the deed; the lower, Rs.1,060,000, is the chargeable value. No exemption applies. The duty is then that chargeable value multiplied by the prescribed rate, applied band by band if the Gazette Order in force in October 2021 prescribes different rates for successive slabs of value, so that the mode of calculation is: duty = (rate for the first slab x that part of Rs.1,060,000) + (rate for the next slab x the balance), continuing until the whole of Rs.1,060,000 is exhausted. The Order that would supply those percentages and slab thresholds is not part of the frozen corpus, so the money amount cannot be stated here without assuming a rate. Whatever the figure, it falls on the daughter as grantee unless the deed provides otherwise, and must be met before or at execution in one of the modes allowed by s.40.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The mode of calculation is to identify the chargeable value under s.48(1) read with the definition of 'value' in s.106, which is Rs.1,060,000, and then apply to it the rate prescribed by Order under s.37, slab by slab if the Order is banded. The money amount of duty cannot be stated on the material available, because the Western Province rate Order in force in October 2021 is not in the corpus. The question is therefore left blocked for want of that subsidiary legislation rather than answered with an assumed percentage.

answer_claims.claim_text: A Deed of Gift of immovable property in the Western Province is chargeable with stamp duty at the prescribed rate, because 'transfer' in the Statute includes a gift.

The duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, which for gifted immovable property acquired after March 31, 1977 is the lower of the open-market price at acquisition plus the cost of later improvements and the open-market price at the date of the deed.
No exemption in the Statute covers a gift of land between family members.

The duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and must be paid before or at the time of execution by stamps or by a bank certificate of payment affixed to the instrument.

The chargeable value on these facts is Rs.1,060,000, being Rs.160,000 as the price at acquisition in January 1978 plus Rs.900,000 spent on constructing the house, that sum being lower than the Rs.9,000,000 value at the date of the deed.
The duty is that chargeable value multiplied by the rate prescribed by Order, applied slab by slab where the Order prescribes different rates for successive bands of value.
The money amount of duty cannot be stated from the corpus, because the rate is left to be prescribed under section 37 and no Western Province rate Order in force in October 2021 is in the corpus.
Whatever the rate, the duty falls on the donee as grantee unless the deed provides otherwise, and must be met before or at execution of the Deed of Gift.

legal_map.block_reason: The rate of stamp duty is not in the corpus. Section 37 charges duty 'at the prescribed rate' and section 77(1)(a) leaves the rate to regulations published in the Gazette; no Western Province rate Order or regulation is in the frozen corpus, so the money amount of duty on a chargeable value of Rs.1,060,000 cannot be computed without inventing a percentage. The chargeable value and the mode of calculation are settled; only the rate is missing. Verified: the corpus holds no rate for this charge - s 37 charges 'at the prescribed rate', s 77(1)(a) leaves it to Gazette regulations, s 76 covers only the description of stamps and reciprocal exemptions, and a grep for 'per centum' and 'prescribed rate' across the corpus returns no stamp-duty rate for the Western Province. The verifier also notes that s 37 authorises different rates for different classes or categories of instruments, not for successive bands of value, so the banded mode of calculation in the draft is an assumption about the missing Order (claim CL-M051-Q02-006 marked disputed).

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: Each document in the list is required by, or is the direct means of discharging, a duty imposed by a statute in the corpus: the registry search and the title deed by the Notaries Ordinance, the certified folio extract and the priority rule by the Registration of Documents Ordinance, the notarial form of title documents by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, the stamp position by the Stamp Duty Act, the possession inquiry by the Prescription Ordinance, the consent certificate and the extent threshold by the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act, the landholding declarations by the Land Reform Law, and the corporate and shareholding documents by the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act and the Companies Act. Conveyancing practice adds further items, such as a thirty-year search convention, local-authority and street line certificates and non-vesting certificates, which are not traceable to this corpus; they are recorded in corpus_gaps rather than asserted in the gold answer, which is drawn only from the provisions above.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What documents an attorney-at-law and notary must call for in order to examine the title of a twenty-acre rubber estate in Kalutara that a Sri Lankan private limited company proposes to buy, and which statutory duties fix that list.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a)). The registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42), so the search is reduced to a certified extract of the relevant folio. That extract governs the purchaser's position because an unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7). The notary must also use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)), and only notarially executed and attested writings can operate as dispositions of land at all (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The deed and the registered instruments must describe the land by boundaries, extent and situation (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(a); Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1)), which requires the survey plan and the schedules of the earlier deeds. An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered or acted upon unless duly stamped (Stamp Duty Act s.33). Paper title is not conclusive: ten years of undisturbed adverse possession entitles the possessor to a decree (Prescription Ordinance s.3). Where the property is a rubber estate within the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act, a transfer of ownership is null and void without a previously obtained certificate of consent of the Board, which must be attached to the deed (s.3(1) and s.3(4)); but a rubber estate for that Act means one of not less than one hundred acres registered under the Rubber Control Act (s.25). Agricultural land above fifty acres is subject to the ceiling (Land Reform Law s.3), and where such land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares (s.8). Transfer of title of land to a Sri Lankan company with direct or indirect foreign shareholding of fifty per cent or above is prohibited (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)), and where the transferee is a Sri Lankan company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof of that fact (s.4(3)); the certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and register of charges are records the company must keep available for inspection (Companies Act s.120).
gold_answer_draft.application: Applying these rules to the estate at Bombuwala, the following must be called for. First, the vendor's chain of notarial deeds, namely Deed of Transfer No. 4562 of 2003, Deed of Gift No. 1120 of 1979 and the earlier deeds behind them, together with any testamentary or partition proceedings through which the land devolved, since only notarially attested writings can pass title (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2) and the notary is bound to obtain the title deed (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)). Second, a certified extract of the folio of the Kalutara Land Registry in which the land is registered, together with certified copies of every instrument noted on it, obtained under s.42 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance in performance of the search duty under s.31 rule (17)(a); this is what discloses Mortgage Bond No. 987 of 2016, and because of s.7 of that Ordinance the purchaser's protection depends on the state of the register rather than on the vendor's assurance. Third, the instrument of discharge or a formal release of Bond No. 987, since the vendor's statement that the loan is settled is not itself a document of title. Fourth, Plan No. 2143 of 1998 and a current survey plan and report, so that the description by boundaries and extent required by s.31 rule (16)(a) and by s.13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance can be checked against the ground; the two acres fenced by the neighbour for fifteen years must be identified on that survey, because under s.3 of the Prescription Ordinance such possession may already have displaced the paper title to that portion, so evidence of possession and of the neighbour's claim must be called for as well. Fifth, proof that stamp duty was duly paid on the deeds in the chain, since s.33 of the Stamp Duty Act denies effect to an instrument that is not duly stamped. Sixth, the extent and registration status of the estate: the property is twenty acres, so it is below the one hundred acres required by s.25 of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act, and the certificate of consent contemplated by s.3(1) and s.3(4) of that Act is not called for, but the extent and registration must be documented before that conclusion can be drawn. Seventh, a declaration of the vendor's agricultural landholdings, and of the holdings of the purchaser's shareholders, to test the fifty-acre ceiling in s.3 of the Land Reform Law read with the deeming provision in s.8. Eighth, the purchaser's own corporate documents, namely the certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and a board resolution authorising the purchase, and, because thirty per cent of its shares are held by a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, a certificate of the company secretary with the share register behind it showing that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent, which s.4(3) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act requires the Registrar of Lands to call for and without which registration will be refused.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The documents to be called for are: the vendor's original chain of notarial title deeds and any testamentary or partition proceedings in the chain; a certified extract of the relevant folio of the Kalutara Land Registry with certified copies of the registered instruments noted on it; the discharge of the registered mortgage bond; the survey plan and a current survey report with evidence of possession, including the position of the neighbour occupying two acres; proof of payment of stamp duty on the deeds in the chain; documents establishing the extent and registration status of the estate, which on these facts show that no certificate of consent of the fragmentation Board is required because the estate is twenty acres and not one hundred; declarations of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the purchaser's shareholders; and the purchaser's certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries, board resolution and a company secretary's certificate of foreign shareholding below fifty per cent. The examination is not complete on the papers alone: possession must be verified on the ground, and the undischarged bond and the encroached two acres must be resolved before the transfer is drawn.

answer_claims.claim_text: Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.
The registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained.
An unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument affecting the same land that was taken for valuable consideration and duly registered.
The notary attesting a transfer of immovable property must use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of that property.
Only a writing executed before and attested by a notary can operate as a sale, transfer or mortgage of immovable property.
The deed and every registrable instrument must describe the land by its boundaries, extent and situation, in the body or in an annexed schedule.
An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered, authenticated or acted upon unless it is duly stamped.
Ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted possession adverse to the paper owner entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour.

A transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has been previously obtained, and that certificate must be attached to the deed and recited in the attestation.
For that Act a rubber estate means an estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which is or is deemed to be registered under the Rubber Control Act.

The maximum extent of agricultural land that may be owned by any person is fifty acres where the land is not exclusively paddy, and where such land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares.
Transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding in that company is fifty per cent or above.

Where the transferee is a company incorporated in Sri Lanka with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent.
A company must keep its certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and register of charges available for inspection.

The vendor's chain of notarial deeds, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 4562 of 2003 and Deed of Gift No. 1120 of 1979, together with any testamentary or partition proceedings behind them, must be called for.

A certified extract of the folio of the Kalutara Land Registry, with certified copies of the instruments noted on it, must be called for; it is what discloses the registered mortgage bond and it governs priority between the purchaser and earlier claimants.
The discharge or release of Mortgage Bond No. 987 of 2016 must be called for, because the vendor's statement that the loan has been settled does not remove the entry from the register.
Plan No. 2143 of 1998 and a current survey plan and report must be called for so that the boundaries and extent stated in the deeds can be checked against the ground.

Evidence of possession must be called for, and the two acres fenced by the neighbour for fifteen years must be identified on the survey, because possession of that length may have displaced the paper title to that portion.
Proof that stamp duty was duly paid on each deed in the chain must be called for.

Documents establishing the extent and the registration status of the estate must be called for; the estate is twenty acres, which is below the hundred-acre threshold, so a certificate of consent of the fragmentation Board is not required for this transfer.
Declarations of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the shareholders of the purchaser company must be called for, so that the fifty-acre ceiling can be tested against both.
The purchaser's certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and a board resolution authorising the purchase must be called for.

Because thirty per cent of the purchaser's shares are held by a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, a company secretary's certificate supported by the share register, showing foreign shareholding below fifty per cent, must be called for, failing which the Registrar of Lands will refuse registration.

The documents to be called for are the chain of notarial title deeds, a certified folio extract with certified copies of the registered instruments, the discharge of the registered bond, the survey plan and a current survey with possession evidence, proof of stamp duty on the chain, proof of the extent and registration status of the estate, declarations of agricultural landholdings, and the purchaser's corporate records including a secretary's certificate of foreign shareholding.
Examination on the papers alone is not sufficient here: the undischarged bond and the two acres held adversely must be resolved before the transfer is drawn.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 governs the question on its own face. Section 39 makes the Act the exclusive channel for dealings with a registered land parcel, section 46 expressly permits a conveyance subject to a life interest, section 48 expressly voids an instrument of ownership in favour of two or more persons in common, and sections 47 and 36 supply the sub-division route. Section 73 displaces any competing written law. No judicial authority or Roman-Dutch doctrine is needed for a complete answer; the remaining open points are matters of regulation and of fact, not of case law.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a gift of a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act may reserve a life interest to the donor and still be registrable.
Whether one registered land parcel may be gifted by a single instrument to two donees in common.
Whether the donor may instead gift a divided portion of the parcel to each daughter, and what he must do first.
What form the gift must take and when it takes effect.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. One: section 39 makes the Act the exclusive and mandatory channel for any dealing with this registered parcel, read with the section 75 definitions of 'instrument' and 'interest in land parcel'. Two: applying section 46 (the proviso saves the life interest) and section 48 (which voids a gift to two donees in common) to the proposed single deed. Three: section 47 read with section 36, which requires a registered sub-division before any divided portion can be gifted. Counting only these indispensable dependencies gives a hop count of 3.

enrichment.original_background: Nimal Siriwardhana wishes to gift his property registered under the Registration Title Act No.21 of 1998 to his two daughters subject to life interest of him.
enrichment.enriched_background: Nimal Siriwardhana wishes to gift his property registered under the Registration Title Act No.21 of 1998 to his two daughters subject to life interest of him. The property is a single land parcel of about forty perches at Meegoda, in the Homagama Divisional Secretary's Division of the Colombo District, separately delineated as Parcel No. 214 on the cadastral map for that area and entered in the Title Register kept at the Homagama Title Registry, where Nimal is recorded as the sole owner with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership and no encumbrance stands registered against the parcel. His daughters, Kanchana Siriwardhana and Dilini Siriwardhana, are both over eighteen years of age. Nimal wants the two of them to take the whole parcel together, in undivided equal half shares, under one deed of gift, and he intends to keep for himself, for the rest of his life, the right to live on the land and to take its produce. The parcel has never been sub-divided; no sub-division plan of it has been surveyed or registered, and Nimal has made no application to the Registrar of Title to sub-divide it. He proposes to have the deed drawn and attested by a notary public in October 2021.

Whether it is one parcel or several, and whether the title is a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, decides whether the co-ownership bar and the part-parcel bar bite at all. Naming the parcel and the registry also settles the property identity the classification flagged as missing.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the property were already two separate registered parcels he could simply gift one parcel to each daughter subject to his life interest and the co-ownership bar would never be engaged. If it were not registered under this Act at all, the question would fall to be answered under the general law of gifts instead.

added_facts.reason: Supplies the property location the classification flagged as missing and gives the parcel an extent, so the sub-division route can be discussed as a realistic option rather than in the abstract.

added_facts.reason: Supplies the party identity the classification flagged as missing and removes any minority or capacity side-issue, so the answer turns on the registration rules alone.

added_facts.fact: Nimal wants both daughters to take the whole parcel together in undivided equal half shares under one deed of gift; the parcel has never been sub-divided, no sub-division plan has been surveyed or registered, and he has made no application to the Registrar of Title to sub-divide it.
added_facts.reason: The question does not say whether the daughters are to take jointly in undivided shares or a divided portion each. That is the fact the answer turns on, and the absence of any sub-division is what makes the divided-portion alternative unavailable as things stand.
