gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary retained by Exotic Tea Trading (Private) Limited do, before, at and after execution, to carry through the purchase of a twenty acre planted property at Bandarawela from Mrs. Dias, given that the buyer is a private company and the land is under tea?
gold_answer_draft.rule: The transaction can take effect only through a writing executed before a notary and attested by him (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). Before drawing such a deed the notary must search, or cause to be searched, the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a)); registration matters because an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)). The deed must carry an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent, situation, district, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division and village (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(a)), and the notary must ascertain and set forth the true and full consideration (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)), be assured that the required stamp duty is provided (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6)), attest without delay and sign and seal the attestation (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (20)), and, having instructions and funds, use due diligence in registering the deed (Notaries Ordinance s.37). Where the buyer is a company, an obligation that a natural person would have to make in a notarially attested writing may be entered into on behalf of the company by two directors, by a sole director, by a person allowed by the articles or by an attorney appointed by the company, signing under the company's name and notarially executed (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)); the company may not enter into a major transaction unless it is approved by special resolution, made contingent on one, consented to in writing by all shareholders, or expressly authorised by articles adopted at incorporation (Companies Act s.185(1)), a major transaction including the acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition (Companies Act s.185(2)(a)); and objects stated in the articles operate as a restriction on the company's business (Companies Act s.17(1)). Land that is used or capable of being used for agriculture is agricultural land (Land Reform Law s.66), the ceiling on non-paddy agricultural land owned by any person is fifty acres (Land Reform Law s.3(1)(b)), the shareholders of a private company are deemed to own the company's agricultural land in proportion to their shares (Land Reform Law s.8), and land acquired in excess of the ceiling after the commencement of that Law vests in the Land Reform Commission and is held under a statutory lease (Land Reform Law s.5(1)). A transfer of ownership of a tea estate without a prior certificate of consent of the Board is null and void (Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1)), but a tea estate for that purpose is one of not less than one hundred acres registered or deemed registered under the Tea Control Act (s.25). Finally, transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)), a foreigner being a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka (s.25); an alienation in contravention of that Act is void (s.18); the foreign shareholding must be kept below half for twenty years from the transfer (s.2(2)(a)); and the Registrar of Lands must satisfy himself of the shareholding on documentary proof from the company secretary (s.4(3)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Take the steps in that order. First, obtain from the company its certificate of incorporation, its articles and the register of shareholders, and establish that all four shareholders are citizens, so that foreign shareholding is nil and s.2(1)(b) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act does not prohibit the transfer; keep the company secretary's documentary proof of shareholding for the Registrar under s.4(3), and warn the board that under s.2(2)(a) foreign shareholding must stay below half for twenty years or the transfer becomes void. Second, apply the ceiling. The twenty acres under mature tea is agricultural land within Land Reform Law s.66, and because the buyer is a private company s.8 deems each shareholder to own it in proportion to his shares, so Mr. Perera, holding sixty per cent, will be deemed to own twelve of the twenty acres; added to his existing eighteen acres at Yatiyantota that is thirty acres, below the fifty acre ceiling in s.3(1)(b), and no part of the land will vest under s.5(1). Confirm the same for the other three shareholders. Third, on fragmentation, the property is twenty acres and is not part of any larger planted property, so it is not a tea estate of not less than one hundred acres within s.25, and no certificate of consent under s.3(1) is required; had it been a divided part of a larger estate, consent would have had to be obtained first. Fourth, search the land registry folio for the land yourself rather than relying on the photocopy of Deed No. 2104 produced by the seller, trace the seller's title and any mortgages, leases, life interests or other encumbrances, and check the plan and the survey against the folio. Fifth, before execution obtain from the board a resolution authorising the purchase and authorising named directors to sign; because the price of Rs. 96,000,000 exceeds half the Rs. 150,000,000 value of the company's assets before the acquisition, the purchase is a major transaction under s.185(2)(a), and the articles adopted at incorporation give no express authority, so a special resolution of shareholders, or written consent of all of them, must be obtained and retained under s.185(1). Sixth, draw the deed with a schedule giving the name, boundaries, extent, plan number, village, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, Urban Council limits and District as required by rule (16)(a), state the true price of Rs. 96,000,000 as required by s.38(1), see that stamp duty is provided, and have the deed signed under the company's name by two of the three directors in the manner allowed by s.19(1)(a) and by the seller, before you and two witnesses. Seventh, attest without delay, sign and seal the attestation, and then, having been instructed and put in funds, register the deed promptly in the Bandarawela land registry so that the company takes priority under s.7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance and you do not fall foul of s.37.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should investigate the shareholding of the purchasing company and confirm that no foreign shareholding brings the transfer within the prohibition, apply the fifty acre agricultural ceiling through the shareholders of the private company and satisfy himself that no shareholder's deemed holding exceeds it, satisfy himself that a twenty acre property is not a tea estate needing a fragmentation certificate, search the land registry and investigate the seller's title and encumbrances before drawing the deed, obtain the board resolution and, this being a major transaction, the special resolution or unanimous written consent of shareholders, draw the deed with a proper schedule and the true consideration, see to stamp duty, have it executed under the company's name by two directors before himself and two witnesses, attest it without delay and register it promptly. On the facts as stated none of the statutory prohibitions bars this purchase, so the notary may proceed once those checks and authorities are in hand.

answer_claims.claim_text: A purchase of immovable property is of no force in law unless it is made by a writing executed in the presence of a notary and two witnesses and attested by the notary.

Before drawing a deed affecting any interest in land the notary must search, or cause to be searched, the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.
An instrument that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later instrument that is duly registered.

The deed must embody, in itself or in an annexed schedule, an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation, specifying the district, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladhari Division and village.
The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the deed and set it forth in the deed.
The notary must not attest the deed unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided, and he must attest without delay and sign and seal the attestation.
A notary who has instructions to register a deed he attested and a sufficient sum to meet the expense must use due diligence in effecting registration.

An obligation that a natural person would have to enter into by notarially attested writing may be entered into for a company by two directors, a sole director, a person allowed by the articles, or an attorney appointed by the company, signing under the company's name, and must be notarially executed.

A company may not enter into a major transaction unless it is approved by special resolution, contingent on such approval, consented to in writing by all shareholders, or expressly authorised by a provision included in its articles at incorporation; an acquisition of assets worth more than half the value of the company's assets before the acquisition is a major transaction.

Land used or capable of being used for agriculture is agricultural land, the ceiling on agricultural land that is not exclusively paddy is fifty acres for any person, and the shareholders of a private company are deemed to own the company's agricultural land in proportion to their shares.

Where a person becomes owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling after the commencement of the Land Reform Law, the excess vests in the Land Reform Commission and is held by that person under a statutory lease.

A transfer of ownership of a tea estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board was previously obtained by the transferor, and a tea estate for this purpose is one of not less than one hundred acres in extent registered or deemed registered under the Tea Control Act.

Transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding in it is fifty per cent or above, a foreigner being a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, and an alienation in contravention of that Act is void.

Where title passes to a company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, that shareholding must remain below half for twenty years from the transfer, and the Registrar of Lands must confirm the position on documentary proof furnished by the company secretary.

The notary must first call for the company's certificate of incorporation, articles and share register; here all four shareholders are citizens of Sri Lanka and no share is held directly or indirectly by a person who is not a citizen, so the transfer of title to the company is not prohibited.

The notary should keep the company secretary's documentary proof of shareholding for production at registration and warn the board that foreign shareholding must be kept below half for twenty years from the transfer.

The twenty acres under mature tea is agricultural land, and since the buyer is a private company the ceiling is tested against each shareholder: Mr. Perera's sixty per cent shareholding makes him the deemed owner of twelve of the twenty acres, which with his existing eighteen acres comes to thirty acres, below the fifty acre ceiling, so no part of the land vests in the Commission.

The property is twenty acres and is not part of any larger planted property, so it is not a tea estate of not less than one hundred acres and no certificate of consent of the Fragmentation Board is needed for the transfer.

The notary must search the land registry folio himself rather than rely on the photocopy of Deed No. 2104 produced by the seller, and must trace the seller's title and any registered encumbrances before the deed is drawn.

At Rs. 96,000,000 the price exceeds half of the Rs. 150,000,000 value of the company's assets before the acquisition, so the purchase is a major transaction, and since the articles adopted at incorporation give no express authority the notary must see a special resolution or the written consent of all the shareholders in addition to the board resolution authorising the signatories.

The deed should be drawn with a schedule giving the name of the land, its boundaries, extent, plan number, village, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, Urban Council limits and District, and should state the true price of Rs. 96,000,000.

The deed should be signed under the company's name by two of the three directors, together with the seller, in the presence of the notary and two witnesses, and the notary must then attest it without delay and sign and seal the attestation.
Having been instructed to register and placed in funds, the notary must register the deed promptly in the Bandarawela land registry to secure the company's priority.

On the facts stated none of the statutory prohibitions bars the purchase, so the notary may proceed once the shareholding check, the ceiling check, the title search and the company authorities are in hand, and must then draw, execute, attest and register the deed in the manner required.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The Notaries Ordinance states the duty and its exhaustive exceptions in one rule: a notary shall not divulge secrets acquired in the execution of his office unless the employer expressly permits it or the law requires it. On the enriched facts (testator alive, no permission given, no legal compulsion) the rule disposes of the question without needing judicial authority or common-law doctrine. Professional conduct rules for attorneys-at-law would say the same thing but add nothing the statute does not already decide.

legal_issues.issue: Whether knowledge that a notary attested a particular will, and knowledge of its contents, is a secret which he became possessed of in the execution of his office.
Who the notary's "employer" is for the purposes of the duty of secrecy where a will was drawn and attested on the testator's instructions, and whether express permission to disclose has been given.
Whether disclosure to the testator's son is "required to do so by law" so as to fall within the second exception.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: One directly applicable provision. enrichment.original_background: A client asks whether you have attested his father's will.
enrichment.enriched_background: Ranjith Perera, a businessman of Nugegoda, calls at your office and tells you that he believes his father made a will some years ago. You did in fact draw and attest that will as a notary public on 12 October 2018, and the protocol of it remains in your custody. His father, Sarath Perera, aged 78, is alive, lives on his own and is of sound mind. When he gave you his instructions he asked you to keep the will and its contents to yourself, and he has since neither withdrawn that instruction nor given you permission, in writing or otherwise, to speak about the will to anyone. Ranjith is not an executant of that will and is not named in it as an executor. No court, and no officer acting under any written law, has called on you to produce the will or to disclose what it contains. Ranjith now asks you to confirm whether you attested his father's will and to tell him what it says.

added_facts.fact: You yourself drew and attested the will as a notary public on 12 October 2018 and the protocol remains in your custody.
added_facts.reason: The duty of secrecy bites only on what the notary came to know "in the execution of his office". The original background implies but does not state that the notary acted; making it explicit fixes the source of the knowledge.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the notary had never attested the will and knew nothing of it, there would be no secret acquired in the execution of his office and rule (1) would not engage; he could simply say he has no knowledge of the matter.

added_facts.fact: The father, Sarath Perera, aged 78, is alive and of sound mind.
added_facts.reason: Identifies a living principal who can still give or refuse the express permission that the first exception requires, and keeps the question inside the statute rather than raising the untreated problem of a notary's duty after the testator's death.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the father were dead, the availability of his express permission would fall away and the position of an heir or executor seeking the will would raise questions the corpus does not answer; the question would then be blocked for missing authority rather than answerable on the statute alone.

added_facts.fact: The father instructed you to keep the will and its contents to yourself and has never given you permission, in writing or otherwise, to disclose them to anyone.
added_facts.reason: Closes the first statutory exception, which turns on the express permission of the employer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the father had expressly authorised you to tell his son about the will, the exception would apply and disclosure within the terms of that permission would be lawful.

added_facts.fact: No court and no officer acting under any written law has required you to produce the will or to disclose its contents.
added_facts.reason: Closes the second statutory exception, which turns on disclosure being required by law.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a court had ordered production of the will or of your protocol, disclosure to that extent would be required by law and the duty of secrecy would yield to it.

added_facts.fact: The client, Ranjith Perera, is the testator's son; he is not an executant of the will and is not named in it as an executor.
added_facts.reason: Fixes the identity of the enquirer and his relationship to the instrument. It does not change the outcome, because the rule looks to the employer's permission rather than to the enquirer's status.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Even if the client had been an executant of the will, disclosure would still require the employer's express permission or a legal requirement, so the conclusion would not change on this fact alone.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary may confirm to the son of a living testator that he attested the father's will, and tell him what the will contains, when the father has given no permission to disclose and no law requires disclosure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) makes it the duty of every notary not to divulge the secrets confided to him, or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The duty covers everything learned by reason of the office, and the two exceptions are the only gateways to disclosure. Breach of the rule is treated seriously by the Ordinance: it is made a punishable offence, in addition to any civil liability (s.34, the text of which in the corpus is the version substituted in 2022), and gross misconduct in the discharge of the office or repeated breaches of the rules can lead to an inquiry and to suspension or cancellation of the warrant (s.21(1)(b) and (c)).

Your employer for this purpose is the testator, the father, on whose instructions the will was drawn and executed, not his son. The father is alive, of sound mind, has asked you to keep the matter to yourself and has given no express permission for disclosure, so the first exception is not open. No court or officer has called for the will or its contents, so nothing requires disclosure by law and the second exception is not open either. The son's relationship to the testator does not put him in the place of the employer, and he is neither an executant nor a named executor of the instrument; confirming even that a will exists and that you attested it would divulge part of what the rule protects. If the son wants to know about the will, the proper course is for him to ask his father, or for the father to authorise you expressly.

You should decline politely, explain that a notary is bound to keep secret what he learns in the execution of his office, and tell him that you can speak about the will only if his father expressly permits it or if the law requires you to do so.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
That duty admits only two exceptions: the express permission of the notary's employer, or a legal requirement to disclose.

Breach of the duty of secrecy exposes the notary to a criminal penalty in addition to civil liability, and gross or repeated breach of the notarial rules can ground an inquiry leading to suspension or cancellation of his warrant.
The fact that you attested the father's will and the contents of that will are secrets you became possessed of in the execution of your office.

The employer whose express permission could release you is the testator, the father on whose instructions the will was drawn and executed, and he is alive, of sound mind and has given no such permission.
Nothing requires you by law to disclose the will or its contents to the son, because no court or officer acting under any written law has called for them.

Being the testator's son does not put the client in the position of the employer, and he is neither an executant nor a named executor of the will, so his relationship gives him no claim on the information.
You should not tell the client about the will, and you should not confirm or deny that you attested it; you may speak about it only if the father expressly permits it or the law requires it.

A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22)), and may not attest unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in their presence (rule (12)), with at least two witnesses subscribing their signatures in letters (rule (8)). The Ordinance nevertheless allows one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary: the notary who attests first must comply with all of rule (20), every other attesting notary must comply with paragraphs (a) to (e) of rule (20) and with paragraph (g) as to erasures in the signatures he attests and in his serial number, each notary numbers the deed in his own series under rule (23), the first notary keeps the protocol under rule (24) and every other notary keeps a certified copy as his protocol (s.31 rule (25)). Where the parties do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed (s.32(2)(i)). The duplicate goes to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the first attesting notary resides, and the other notary need not send one (rule (28)). A notary may not attest a deed drawn by another person unless a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed (rule (2)). A company enters an obligation that must be notarially attested by signing under the company's name by two directors, or by its sole director, or by a person authorised by its articles, or by an attorney appointed by it, and being notarially executed (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Neither notary can take both signatures, because rule (22) confines Anil Fernando to Colombo and Ruwan Perera to Galle, and rule (12) forbids either of them from attesting a signature not made in his presence. Ruwan Perera drafts the lease in Galle and endorses on it his certificate under rule (2) that he drew it, which is what allows Anil Fernando to attest it later. Russel Perera signs in Galle before Ruwan Perera in the presence of two witnesses who also sign; Ruwan Perera attests there and then as the first notary and, as first notary, must satisfy the whole of rule (20). answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month must be in writing and notarially attested to be of force in law.
A notary may not authenticate or attest any deed in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

A notary may not attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence, and at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters.

One deed may be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary, the first attesting notary complying with the whole of rule (20) and every other attesting notary with paragraphs (a) to (e) and, as to erasures in the signatures he attested and his serial number, paragraph (g).
Where the parties to a deed do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed by a party.

Each attesting notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series, the first notary preserves the protocol and every other notary supplies himself with a certified copy that is deemed to be his protocol.
A notary may not attest a deed drawn by another person unless a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed.

A company enters an obligation that the law requires to be notarially attested by signing under the name of the company by two directors, or by its sole director, or by a person authorised by its articles, or by an attorney appointed by it, and by the deed being notarially executed.
Because Anil Fernando is authorised to practise in Colombo and Ruwan Perera in Galle, neither of them can attest both parties' signatures unless one party travels to the other's area.
Ruwan Perera should draft the lease in Galle and endorse on it his certificate that he drew it, so that Anil Fernando may lawfully attest the same deed in Colombo.

Russel Perera signs in Galle before Ruwan Perera and two witnesses, who sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and Ruwan Perera attests as the first notary in compliance with the whole of rule (20).

The company then signs the same deed in Colombo under the name of the company in the manner allowed by Companies Act section 19(1)(a), before Anil Fernando and two witnesses, and Anil Fernando attests as the second notary with the lighter duties rule (25)(a) imposes on him.
Ruwan Perera, as the notary who first attests, transmits the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, and Anil Fernando need not transmit one.

The lease can therefore be executed as a single deed signed at different times and places before two notaries, Ruwan Perera attesting in Galle and Anil Fernando attesting in Colombo, so that Russel Perera need not travel to Colombo.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on the Deed of Transfer of the shop at Assessment No. 2, Galle Road, Kollupitiya for a consideration of Rs. 30,000,000, on what amount is it computed, and who must pay it.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty on an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province is charged by the Western Province Financial Statute s.37, at the rate prescribed; the Statute itself fixes no rate and s.77(1)(a) leaves it to regulations published in the Gazette. Duty on a conveyance is calculated on the value of the property conveyed: s.48(1). 'Value', for property other than immovable property which is gifted, means the price the property would have fetched in the open market on that date in the opinion of the Assessor: s.106. Unless there is agreement to the contrary the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee: s.51(a). It must be paid before or at the time of execution and evidenced by stamps or by a bank certificate of payment affixed to the instrument: s.40. The instrument itself must state the consideration and the amount of duty chargeable: s.78(1). The notary may not attest the deed unless he has an assurance that the required duty is provided: Notaries Ordinance s.31(6). The national regime does not apply: the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 excludes instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property (s.13), and its list of specified instruments in s.4 contains no conveyance of land.
gold_answer_draft.application: The shop at Galle Road, Kollupitiya is immovable property situated in the Western Province, so the Deed of Transfer is an instrument chargeable under s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute and not under the 2006 Act. The duty is computed under s.48(1) on the value of the premises conveyed, and since this is a sale and not a gift the relevant value under s.106 is the open-market price in the opinion of the Assessor; on the facts given, the consideration of Rs. 30,000,000 is the figure to be used unless the Assessor puts a higher open-market value on the premises. The purchaser Amara Perera is the grantee and therefore bears the duty under s.51(a), no contrary agreement being mentioned. Payment falls due before or at the time of execution under s.40 and, in practice, is made to a prescribed bank whose certificate is affixed to the deed. The rate to be applied to Rs. 30,000,000 is the one prescribed by regulation under s.77; that regulation is not in the corpus, so the multiplication cannot be carried out here and no figure is offered.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Deed of Transfer is chargeable with provincial stamp duty under the Western Province Financial Statute s.37, computed on the value of the premises conveyed, which on these facts is Rs. 30,000,000, and payable by the purchaser Amara Perera before or at the time of execution. gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the father of a minor landowner may, by virtue of fatherhood alone, sell his child's immovable property, and if a sale is possible at all, what steps are required to make it effective in law.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A person under eighteen cannot bind himself by a conveyance of his own land; the Civil Procedure Code treats eighteen as full age (s.502). The Code confers no power of sale on a father as such. What it provides is a curatorship route: a person claiming charge of a minor's property by nearness of kin may apply for a certificate of curatorship (s.582), the application being by petition in the way of summary procedure (s.583); the court may grant the certificate to a near relative who is willing and fit (s.585(2)) and may appoint a guardian of the person unless the father has already appointed one (s.585(3)), or, failing a fit relative, to any fit person (s.586). Where a certificate has been granted the court may fix an allowance for the minor's maintenance and education and, if satisfied that it is in the minor's interest, direct that allowance to be raised out of the corpus of the estate by sale (s.587(4)). The curator files an inventory and half-yearly accounts (s.588(2)) and may be required to give security (s.752). Any sale that is sanctioned must be by a written deed signed before and attested by a notary public (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)) and should be registered, since an unregistered instrument is void against a later registered instrument taken for value (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)). By contrast, the Code says expressly of a person of unsound mind that the manager may not sell without a prior District Court order (s.571); it contains no such express words about a minor, and the corresponding restriction on a father or curator of a minor rests on the common law rather than on any provision in this corpus.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nimal is fourteen and so is a minor; he cannot execute a valid transfer himself. His father, Sunil, has not been appointed by any will, deed or court order, so on the statutory material he has no recorded authority to convey the land, and a deed of transfer signed by him simply as father would not carry the boy's title. Because nobody is entitled under the grandmother's will or a deed, the father is a near relative who may apply under s.582 by petition in the way of summary procedure under s.583, and the court may certify him under s.585(2) if it is satisfied he is willing and fit and has no adverse interest, which on these facts he does not. The land is worth about Rs. 6,500,000, far above the twenty thousand rupee figure in the proviso to s.582, so the relaxation in that proviso is of no help. The father's stated purpose, the boy's maintenance and education, is the purpose s.587(3) and (4) address, so the court could fix an allowance and direct that it be raised out of the corpus by sale if satisfied that this is in the boy's interest. Once sanctioned, the transfer to Mr. Silva must be executed as a notarial deed under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) and registered in the Gampaha land registry to be safe against a later registered purchaser under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1). Whether the father may act at all short of that sanction, and on what footing he holds the boy's property in the meantime, are questions the statutes in this corpus do not answer.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: On the statutes available, the father cannot sell the land on his own authority as father. A sale is possible only through the court: a petition by way of summary procedure for a certificate of curatorship over the boy's property, an order of court sanctioning the realisation of the corpus in the boy's interest, execution of a notarial deed of transfer, registration of that deed, and accounting to the court for the proceeds. The answer is incomplete as a statement of Sri Lankan law, because the father's position as natural guardian, and the rule that a natural guardian cannot alienate a minor's immovable property without the sanction of the court as upper guardian, come from Roman-Dutch common law and decided cases and not from any provision in this corpus; section 584 of the Code, which sits inside the very chapter relied on, is also missing from the corpus edition.

answer_claims.claim_text: A person who has not attained eighteen years is a minor for the purposes of the Code's provisions on minors and cannot give a valid conveyance by his own act.
The statutes in this corpus confer no power on a father, simply as father, to sell his minor child's immovable property.

A person claiming charge of a minor's property by nearness of kin may apply for a certificate of curatorship, and until a certificate is obtained he cannot institute or defend an action connected with the minor's estate.
The application is made by petition in the way of summary procedure, asking the court to appoint a fit person to take charge of the minor's property or person or both.

Where nobody is entitled under a will or deed, the court may grant the certificate to a near relative of the minor who is willing and fit to be entrusted with charge of the property, and may otherwise grant it to any fit person it appoints.

Where a certificate has been granted the court may fix an allowance for the minor's maintenance and education and, if satisfied that it is in the minor's interest, direct that allowance to be raised out of the corpus of the estate by sale or other realisation.

A curator who does not derive title under a will or deed must file an inventory of the minor's property within a time fixed by the court and file accounts twice a year, and the District Court may require him to give security for the due administration of the estate.
A sale of immovable property has no force in law unless it is effected by a written deed signed by the executant and the witnesses in the presence of a notary public and attested by that notary.

An unregistered instrument affecting land is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later duly registered instrument, so the deed of transfer should be registered.
Nimal, being fourteen, cannot execute a valid deed of transfer of Delgahawatta himself.

Because no person is entitled under the grandmother's will or any deed and no court appointment has been made, the father is a near relative who may petition for a certificate of curatorship over the boy's property.
The land being worth about Rs. 6,500,000, the proviso to section 582 for property below twenty thousand rupees does not assist the father.

Since the father wants the proceeds applied to the boy's maintenance and education, the court could fix an allowance for that purpose and direct it to be raised out of the corpus by a sale, if satisfied the sale is in the boy's interest.
Any transfer to Mr. Silva that the court sanctions must be executed as a notarially attested deed and then registered in the Gampaha land registry.

The father cannot sell the land on his own authority as father; a sale is possible only with the sanction of the court, obtained on a summary-procedure petition, followed by a notarial deed of transfer, registration of that deed and accounting for the proceeds.

The statutory material alone does not settle the father's status as natural guardian or the precise sanction he must obtain before alienating the minor's land, so the answer is not complete on statute alone.

The Original Land was allotted to one Alfred Almeida by Final Decree in the District Court of Colombo Partition case No. 1256/P and subsequently by Survey Plan 1125 made by Anil Silva Licensed surveyor sub-divided the said Lot 1 into 4 allotments of land marked A,B,C.and R. and by Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23rd March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva Notary Public sold Lot B together with undivided 1/3rd share of the Road Reservation marked Lot R to Sunil Peiris. 2. Sunil Peiris had died Intestate without children on 6th December 2016 leaving behind his widow Kusum Peiris. His estate was duly Administered in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T and proceedings terminated on 7th May 2018.On examining the Testamentary Case it was observed that the father of Sunil Peiris one Charles Peiris had pre-deceased him leaving behind 2 children named Upul and Wimal by his 1st marriage to Kamala Peiris and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by his 2nd marriage to Pushpa Peiris. Pushpa Peiris was alive and she too had a child by her 1st marriage to Lal Perera named Keerthi Perera and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by her 2nd marriage to Charles Peiris.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What share of Lot B, and of the undivided one-third share of the road reservation Lot R, does each surviving heir of Sunil Peiris hold, he having died intestate and childless on 6 December 2016 leaving a widow, a surviving mother, two full sisters, two paternal half-brothers and one maternal half-brother?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21). The surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (s.22), and subject to that right inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23), descendants being preferent to all others (s.24). Where children and remoter descendants fail and only one parent is alive, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters of the deceased, together with the half-brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, take the other half (s.25). Where the qualifying half-siblings are all of one side, the full siblings first take one-half of that portion and divide the remaining half with the half-siblings (s.27), those equally near in degree taking per capita (s.30).
gold_answer_draft.application: Sunil Peiris died intestate on 6 December 2016 leaving no children, so the descendant class fails. His widow Kusum Peiris takes one-half of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R under s.22. His father Charles Peiris had predeceased him and his mother Pushpa Peiris was alive, so under s.25 Pushpa takes half of the remaining half, that is one-fourth. The other one-fourth goes to the full sisters Kanthi and Manel, both children of Charles and Pushpa, together with Upul and Wimal, who are half-brothers related to Sunil by the side of the deceased parent Charles. Keerthi Perera is the child of Pushpa by her earlier marriage to Lal Perera and is therefore related to Sunil only through the surviving parent, so s.25 does not admit him. Because the qualifying half-siblings are all on the father's side, s.27 gives Kanthi and Manel one-half of that one-fourth, that is one-eighth or one-sixteenth each, and the remaining one-eighth is divided per capita under s.30 among Kanthi, Manel, Upul and Wimal, that is one thirty-second each.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The present heirs hold Lot B, and the undivided one-third share of Lot R, as follows: Kusum Peiris, the widow, one-half; Pushpa Peiris, the mother, one-fourth; Kanthi three thirty-seconds; Manel three thirty-seconds; Upul one thirty-second; Wimal one thirty-second. Keerthi Perera takes no share. The six shares exhaust the whole, so all six must join in any conveyance of the entirety of Lot B to the purchaser.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, whatever the deceased's domicile.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person dying intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, inheritance devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals, descendants being preferent to all others.
Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full siblings together with the half-siblings related through the deceased parent take the other half.
Half-siblings related to the intestate only through the surviving parent are not admitted to the collateral half under section 25.

Where the qualifying half-siblings are all of one side, the full siblings take one-half of the collateral portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-siblings, those equally near in degree taking per capita.
Sunil Peiris left no children, so the descendant class fails and his widow Kusum Peiris takes one-half of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R.
Because Charles Peiris predeceased Sunil and Pushpa Peiris survived him, Pushpa takes one-fourth of the estate as the surviving parent.

Kanthi and Manel are Sunil's full sisters and Upul and Wimal are half-brothers by the side of the deceased father Charles, so those four share the remaining one-fourth, while Keerthi Perera, related only through the surviving mother, is excluded.
Applying section 27 to that one-fourth, Kanthi and Manel take one-eighth between them and the other one-eighth is divided per capita among Kanthi, Manel, Upul and Wimal.

The shares are Kusum Peiris one-half, Pushpa Peiris one-fourth, Kanthi three thirty-seconds, Manel three thirty-seconds, Upul one thirty-second and Wimal one thirty-second, and Keerthi Perera nothing.
All six heirs must join in a conveyance if the purchaser is to obtain the entirety of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Which four classes of documentation should the purchaser Anura Perera obtain from the present owners and from the Land Registry in order to establish a clear chain of title to Lot B, together with the undivided one-third share of the road reservation Lot R?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Duplicates, copies, books and indexes kept under the Registration of Documents Ordinance may be searched by an interested person or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42); such a certified copy or extract is admissible without proof of the Registrar's signature and is prima facie evidence of the contents of the folio (s.43). Registration matters, because an unregistered instrument is void against a later duly registered instrument taken for value (s.7), and an instrument must describe a divided allotment by its own boundaries and an undivided share by the proportion it bears to the whole (s.13). Every transfer of immovable property must be by a notarially attested deed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, executed in triplicate under s.16), and the notary who is to draw the purchaser's conveyance must himself search the land registry to ascertain the state of the title (Notaries Ordinance s.31). Where a link is a court record, the decree or a certified copy of it is the sole primary evidence of what the court decided (Civil Procedure Code s.206), certified copies of the judgment, decree or proceedings are obtainable from the Registrar of the court (s.205), a certificate of heirship is sufficient proof of the true heirs and of each heir's share on an intestacy (s.531), and a sealed duplicate or certified copy of letters of administration has the same effect as the original (s.554X). A plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared and certified as the Survey Act requires (s.13).
gold_answer_draft.application: First, certified extracts of the relevant Colombo Land Registry folios: the folio for the original land, Lot 1 in Partition Plan No. 567, and the folio opened for Lot B and Lot R after the sub-division, showing the ownership and every registered encumbrance, lis pendens, caveat, mortgage or seizure down to the date of the search. These come under s.42 and carry the evidentiary weight given by s.43, and they are what shows whether Deed No. 234 was duly registered and so protected by s.7. Second, certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, taken either from the registered duplicate in the Land Registry under s.42 or from the attesting notary's protocol, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23 March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva, Notary Public, and including any later deed by which an heir has dealt with a share; each must satisfy s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and must describe Lot B by its own boundaries and the share of Lot R as an undivided one-third under s.13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance. Third, certified copies of the court records that carry the title over the two links that are not deeds: the final decree and the partition plan filed in District Court of Colombo Partition Case No. 1256/P, obtained under s.205 and constituting under s.206 the primary evidence of the allotment of Lot 1 to Alfred Almeida; and the order, the letters of administration or certificate of heirship and the final proceedings in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T, obtained under s.205 and s.554X, the certificate of heirship being sufficient proof under s.531 of who the heirs of Sunil Peiris are and what share each takes. Fourth, a current survey plan with a superimposition, prepared and certified by a registered licensed surveyor, identifying Lot B and Lot R on the ground and tying Survey Plan No. 1125 dated 2 January 2000 back to Lot 1 of Partition Plan No. 567; a plan not so certified would not be receivable in evidence under s.13 of the Survey Act, and it is this document that shows whether the thirty perches recited in the deed match what is on the ground.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The purchaser should obtain, first, certified extracts of the relevant Colombo Land Registry folios; second, certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, starting with Deed of Transfer No. 234 of 2015; third, certified copies of the final decree and plan in Partition Case No. 1256/P and of the order, letters of administration or certificate of heirship and final proceedings in Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T; and fourth, a current plan and superimposition certified by a registered licensed surveyor. Taken together these establish the chain from the partition decree to the persons who now hold Lot B and disclose any registered encumbrance. Nothing short of all four will show that Kusum Peiris cannot convey the entirety by herself.

answer_claims.claim_text: An interested person or his attorney-at-law may search the duplicates, copies, books and indexes kept under the Registration of Documents Ordinance and obtain certified copies of or extracts from them.
A copy or extract certified under the hand of a Registrar is admissible without proof of his signature or appointment and is prima facie evidence of the contents of the folio.
An unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument duly registered and taken for valuable consideration, which is why the registered state of the folio has to be checked.

A transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless made by a deed in writing signed by the executants and witnesses before a notary and attested by him, and such deeds are executed in triplicate.
A notary must search the land registry before drawing an instrument affecting an interest in land, to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered.

A decree or a certified copy of it is the sole primary evidence of the decision of the court, and certified copies of the judgment, decree or proceedings may be obtained from the Registrar of the court.

A certificate of heirship is sufficient proof of the true heirs of the deceased and of the share each is entitled to receive on an intestacy, and a sealed duplicate or certified copy of letters of administration has the same effect as the original.

A plan is receivable in evidence only if it has been prepared and certified as the Survey Act requires, and an instrument must describe a divided allotment by its own boundaries and an undivided share by the proportion it bears to the whole.

The purchaser should obtain certified extracts of the Colombo Land Registry folios for the original land and for Lot B and Lot R, showing ownership and every registered encumbrance down to the date of the search.

The purchaser should obtain certified copies of every notarially attested deed in the chain, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23 March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva, Notary Public, taken from the registered duplicate or from the notary's protocol.

The purchaser should obtain certified copies of the final decree and plan in District Court of Colombo Partition Case No. 1256/P and of the order, letters of administration or certificate of heirship and final proceedings in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T.

The purchaser should obtain a current survey plan and superimposition certified by a registered licensed surveyor, identifying Lot B and Lot R on the ground and tying Survey Plan No. 1125 back to Lot 1 of Partition Plan No. 567.
These four classes of document, taken together, establish the chain of title from the partition decree to the persons who now hold Lot B and disclose any registered encumbrance affecting it.

enrichment.original_background: Gamini Perera intends to purchase a house and property situated in Ratmalana bearing Assessment No. 23, 1st Lane, Ratmalana. He applied for a loan from the Mortgage Bank and the Bank approved his Loan and informed him to get a certain Notice registered in the Land Registry and submit together with the folio in order to release the Loan on the simultaneous execution of the Transfer Deed and the Mortgage Bond without awaiting the completion of registration formalities.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How is the notice the Bank asked for to be drawn up and presented to the Land Registry? The notice is the priority notice under section 30 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and the question is what its parties, recitals, schedule and formal parts must be so that the transfer deed and the mortgage bond, when executed, are deemed registered as at the date the notice was registered.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A person acquiring or proposing to acquire an interest in land for valuable consideration (the transferee) may present for registration a notice of his intention to register the instrument, which the Ordinance calls a priority notice; if the notice is lodged before the transferor executes the instrument it must carry the transferor's written consent, and if lodged afterwards it need not (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.30(1)). While the notice is in force, an instrument by which the transferee acquires the interest described in it is deemed to have been registered at the time the notice was registered (s.30(2)). The Registrar registers the notice in the same manner as other instruments and retains it (s.30(4)), so the notice must contain, embodied in it or in a schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land with its boundaries, extent and situation, the district and division and, the land being in a town, the street (s.13(1)), and it must carry at its head, typewritten or in ink, a reference to the volume and folio in which an earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered (s.13(7)). It may be signed and presented by the transferee, by any person claiming an interest or benefit under the instrument, or by a notary or attorney-at-law acting for him (s.26(1)); it should be tendered in duplicate, because the Registrar retains the original (s.30(4)) and his endorsement on the duplicate is prima facie evidence of registration (s.43(2)). The notice remains in force for six weeks from the date of its registration and may be renewed once for a further six weeks (s.30(5)). By s.50 the form contained in the Second Schedule to the Ordinance is to be used, with such variations as circumstances may require.
gold_answer_draft.application: Gamini Perera is a person proposing to acquire for valuable consideration an interest in the house and premises bearing Assessment No. 23, 1st Lane, Ratmalana, so he is a transferee within s.30(1) and his vendor is the transferor. Because the Bank wants the loan released on simultaneous execution of the transfer deed and the mortgage bond without awaiting completion of registration, the notice has to be lodged before those deeds are executed, and it must therefore carry the vendor's written consent (s.30(1)). The instrument whose intended registration is notified is the deed of transfer to be executed by the vendor in his favour; the Bank's own security is covered by a corresponding notice in which the Bank is the transferee and Gamini Perera the transferor in respect of the mortgage bond. The premises being in a town, the schedule must give the street, the boundaries and the extent as well as the assessment number (s.13(1)), and the folio the Bank asked him to submit gives the volume and folio reference to be written at the head of the notice (s.13(7)). A draft on these lines reads: at the head, 'Registered in Volume ...... Folio ...... of the ...... Land Registry'; then 'PRIORITY NOTICE UNDER SECTION 30 OF THE REGISTRATION OF DOCUMENTS ORDINANCE. To the Registrar of Lands, ...... Land Registry. Take notice that I, Gamini Perera of ......, propose to acquire for valuable consideration from ...... of ...... the land and premises described in the Schedule hereto, and that I intend to register the deed of transfer to be executed by the said ...... in my favour in respect of the said premises. I present this notice before the execution of the said instrument, with the written consent of the said transferor endorsed below. Dated this ...... day of ...... . [Signature of transferee, or of the notary or attorney-at-law presenting it under s.26(1)]. I, ......, the transferor above named, consent in writing to the registration of this notice. The notice is tendered in duplicate so that the Registrar, who retains the original, endorses registration on the duplicate for the Bank (ss.30(4), 43(2)), and it must be acted on within the six weeks it remains in force (s.30(5)).

A priority notice lodged before the transferor executes the instrument must carry the transferor's written consent; one lodged after execution need not.

Because the Registrar registers a priority notice in the same manner as other instruments and retains it, the notice must be drawn with a schedule giving an accurate and clear description of the land with its boundaries, extent, situation, district and division and, the land being in a town, the street.
A reference to the volume and folio in which an earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered must be typewritten or written in ink at the head of the notice.

The notice may be signed and presented by the transferee, by a person claiming an interest or benefit under the instrument, or by a notary or attorney-at-law acting for him, and should be tendered in duplicate so that the Registrar's endorsement of registration is available as evidence.

The notice carries a date and is effective for six weeks from its registration, renewable once for a further six weeks, so the transfer deed and bond must be executed and registered within that period.
The form to be used is the form contained in the Second Schedule to the Ordinance, with such variations as circumstances may require.

enrichment.original_background:
Gamini Perera intends to purchase a house and property situated in Ratmalana bearing Assessment No. 23, 1st Lane, Ratmalana. He applied for a loan from the Mortgage Bank and the Bank approved his Loan and informed him to get a certain Notice registered in the Land Registry and submit together with the folio in order to release the Loan on the simultaneous execution of the Transfer Deed and the Mortgage Bond without awaiting the completion of registration formalities.

Gamini Perera is hoping to obtain a loan of Rupees 3 Million from the Bank.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the mortgage bond Gamini Perera is to execute in favour of the Bank over the Ratmalana property to secure a loan of Rs. 3,000,000 attracts stamp duty, who must bear it, on what amount it is computed, and what sum is payable in April 2020.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 3(1) of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 charges stamp duty on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka, at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette; section 3(2) permits different rates for different classes of instrument. Section 4(g) makes a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property a specified instrument. Section 6 allocates the burden: otherwise than where there is an agreement to the contrary, in cases not falling within paragraphs (a) to (ddd) the duty is payable under section 6(e) by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument. Section 13 provides that the imposition provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, other than those on transfers of immovable property, motor vehicle transfers and documents filed in court, have no operation in so far as they are inconsistent with the 2006 Act. Section 16 of the 1982 Act, so far as it still operates, charges a bond or mortgage for money to be lent with the duty appropriate to the limited sum secured. Section 8(2) of the 2006 Act allows the duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution, with the bank's certificate affixed to the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument Gamini Perera will execute is a mortgage bond over the house and premises at Assessment No. 23, 1st Lane, Ratmalana, securing a definite and certain sum, the Rs. 3,000,000 loan approved by the Bank. It is therefore a specified instrument under section 4(g) and is charged with stamp duty under section 3(1). It is a mortgage, not a transfer of immovable property, a motor vehicle transfer or a court document, so by section 13 the 2006 Act governs the imposition. As mortgagor he is the person executing the bond and no paragraph of section 6 other than (e) covers a mortgage, so in the absence of an agreement to the contrary the duty is payable by him rather than by the Bank. The sum secured is limited to Rs. 3,000,000, so that is the base on which the ad valorem duty is computed. The rate, however, is not fixed by the Act: section 3(1) leaves it to the Minister's Order published in the Gazette, and no such Order is available in the corpus consulted. The duty can therefore be identified and its base stated, but the multiplication the question calls for cannot be carried out on the material available, and no figure is proposed. Payment would in practice be made to a prescribed bank under section 8(2) at or before execution, which fits the Bank's requirement that the transfer and the bond be executed simultaneously.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The mortgage bond is chargeable with stamp duty under section 3(1) read with section 4(g) of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006, the duty is payable by Gamini Perera as the person executing it under section 6(e), and it is computed ad valorem on the Rs. 3,000,000 secured. The actual amount depends on the rate determined by the Minister by Order under section 3(1) and in force in April 2020; that Order is not in the corpus, so no figure is stated here and the numerical part of the answer is left open pending the rate instrument.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette.
A bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property is a specified instrument for the purposes of the charging provision.
Where no specific paragraph applies and there is no agreement to the contrary, stamp duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument.

Imposition of stamp duty on an instrument that is not a transfer of immovable property, a motor vehicle transfer or a document filed in court is governed by the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 where the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 is inconsistent with it.
A bond or mortgage for money to be lent, where the total amount secured is limited, is charged with the duty applicable to the amount so limited.
Stamp duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution.

The bond Gamini Perera will execute over the Ratmalana premises to secure the approved loan is a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum affecting property, and so is a specified instrument chargeable with stamp duty.
Because a mortgage bond is neither a transfer of immovable property nor a motor vehicle transfer nor a court document, the 2006 Act and not the 1982 Act governs the imposition of duty on it.
Gamini Perera, as the mortgagor executing the bond, is the person by whom the duty is payable in the absence of an agreement to the contrary with the Bank.
The sum secured being limited to Rs. 3,000,000, that amount is the base on which the ad valorem duty is computed.
The rate applicable to a bond or mortgage in April 2020 is fixed by Ministerial Order under section 3(1) and that Order is not available in the corpus, so the arithmetic cannot be completed.

The mortgage bond is chargeable with stamp duty payable by Gamini Perera, computed ad valorem on Rs. 3,000,000 at the rate determined by the Minister's Gazette Order in force in April 2020; no figure is stated because that Order is outside the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Colombo notary may attest a partition deed in respect of a signature placed in Kandy before a different notary, given the requirement that the executant and witnesses sign in the attesting notary's presence.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. enrichment.original_background: Nimal Perera is a Notary practicing in Colombo. Waruna Liyanage a client of his said that his father who is very sick and bed ridden living in Kandy wishes to execute a Partition Deed by himself together with his two brothers and wanted Nimal Perera to attest it. A Notary in Kandy is willing to visit the bed ridden father and get it executed by him. The other two brothers are willing to come to Colombo to execute it before Nimal Perera.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What does the Notaries Ordinance require where one partition deed is to be signed by a bedridden executant in Kandy before a Kandy notary and by his two brothers in Colombo before Nimal Perera, and may Nimal Perera attest the whole deed?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance rule 31(12) forbids a notary to authenticate or attest any deed unless the person executing it and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence, so a notary can attest only the execution that took place before him; rule 31(8) requires at least two witnesses to subscribe their signatures in letters. Rule 31(22), read with s.9 and s.4A, forbids a notary to attest in any area other than the area in which he is authorised to practise. Rule 31(25) expressly allows one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary: under 31(25)(a) the notary who first attests must comply with the whole of rule 31(20) and every other attesting notary with paragraphs (a) to (e) of that rule and with paragraph (g) for erasures in the signatures he attested; under 31(25)(b), read with rule 31(23), each notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series; under 31(25)(c) the first attesting notary preserves the protocol required by rule 31(24) and the other notary supplies himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol; and under 31(25)(d) every attesting notary must, as far as possible, comply with the other provisions of s.31. Section 32(2) governs a deed executed by two or more parties who do not sign at the same time and place: for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) it is deemed executed when first signed, and for rules (18) and (20) it is deemed executed whenever it is signed, while rule (19), which forbids erasure, alteration or interpolation after signature, applies from the first signing. Rule 31(18) requires each notary to insert in letters the day, month, year and place of the execution before him, and rule 31(20)(a) and (c) require each attestation to state that the party and witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and to give the date, the place and the attesting witnesses. Rule 31(28) puts the duty to transmit the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands on the notary who first attests and relieves the other notary of it; rule 31(29) adds a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies if that is a different district. Rule 31(26)(c) requires a part-executed deed to be included in the monthly list and allows the Registrar of Lands to call for the duplicate, and if the deed is not signed by all parties within three months of the first signature the notary may be required to deliver the duplicate to the registrar. Section 33 saves an instrument from invalidity for a failure in a matter of form only, and s.34(1)(c) makes breach of a s.31 rule an offence triable summarily, in addition to civil liability.
gold_answer_draft.application: The father cannot come to Colombo and the brothers will sign before Nimal Perera in Colombo, so the three executants will not sign at the same time and place. Rule 31(12) means Nimal Perera cannot attest the father's signature, which will be made in Kandy before another notary and outside his sight, and he cannot sign the attestation in the father's presence. He also cannot travel to Kandy and attest there, because rule 31(22) confines him to the area in which he is authorised to practise, and s.9 and s.4A tie that area to his warrant and to the judicial zone in which he resides. The lawful course is the one the facts already suggest: the Kandy notary attests the father's execution in Kandy, with two witnesses who sign in that notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and Nimal Perera attests the two brothers' execution in Colombo with two witnesses signing before him. Rule 31(25) then divides the duties. Whichever of the two attests first must comply with the whole of rule 31(20), keep the protocol under rules 31(24) and 31(25)(c) and transmit the duplicate under rule 31(28); the other confines his attestation to paragraphs (a) to (e) of rule 31(20) and keeps a certified copy as his protocol. Each numbers the deed in his own series under rules 31(23) and 31(25)(b), and each states the true date and place of the execution before him under rules 31(18) and 31(20)(c). Section 32(2) makes the two dates workable: the deed counts as executed at the first signing for numbering and for the multi-notary rule, and as executed on each occasion for the dating and attestation rules, and nothing may be altered after the first signature. Because the executions may fall in different months, rule 31(26)(c) requires the part-executed deed to be listed, and the execution should be completed within three months of the first signature. The facts do not say where the land subject to the partition lies or which notary will attest first, so rule 31(29) and the allocation of the first-attesting notary's duties can only be stated conditionally.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Nimal Perera may not attest the whole partition deed, and may not go to Kandy to attest the father's execution. Under the Notaries Ordinance the deed may lawfully be executed before two notaries: the Kandy notary attesting the bedridden father's execution in Kandy and Nimal Perera attesting the two brothers' execution in Colombo, each with two witnesses signing in his presence, each dating and numbering his own execution and each attesting only what he witnessed, with the notary who attests first holding the protocol and transmitting the duplicate under rules 31(25), 31(24) and 31(28), and s.32(2) supplying the timing rules. If Nimal Perera instead attested the father's signature he would breach rule 31(12) and commit an offence under s.34.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary may not authenticate or attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence.
At least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters to a deed the notary attests.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which he is authorised to practise, that area being fixed by his warrant and extending to the judicial zone in which he resides.
The Ordinance permits one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary, and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who first attests and every other attesting notary.

Each attesting notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series, the first attesting notary keeps the protocol and the other notary supplies himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol, and every attesting notary must otherwise comply with section 31 as far as possible.

Where two or more parties do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed at the first signing for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25), is deemed executed on each occasion of signing for rules (18) and (20), and the bar on erasure, alteration or interpolation applies from the first signing.

Each notary must insert in letters the day, month and year and the place of the execution before him, and must state in his attestation that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, together with the date, the place and the attesting witnesses.

Where a deed is executed by two or more parties before more than one notary the duplicate is transmitted to the Registrar of Lands by the notary who first attests it and the other notary need not transmit one, and a certified copy must also go to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land lies if that is a different district.

A deed signed by only some of the parties must still be included in the notary's monthly list and produced if the Registrar of Lands calls for it, and if all parties have not signed within three months of the first signature the notary may be required to deliver the duplicate to the registrar.
Nimal Perera cannot attest the bedridden father's signature, because that signature will be placed in Kandy before another notary and not in Nimal Perera's presence.
Nimal Perera cannot cure this by travelling to Kandy himself, because he practises in Colombo and may not attest outside the area in which he is authorised to practise.

The deed may be attested by the Kandy notary as to the father's execution in Kandy and by Nimal Perera as to the two brothers' execution in Colombo, each with two witnesses signing in the presence of the attesting notary and of one another.

Because the three executants will sign at different times and places, each notary dates and attests only the execution before him, each numbers the deed in his own series, the notary attesting first keeps the protocol and transmits the duplicate, and nothing may be altered after the first signature.
The execution should be completed within three months of the first signature, failing which the notary who holds the duplicate may be called on to deliver it to the Registrar of Lands.

The facts do not state where the partitioned land lies or which notary will attest first, so the destination of the certified copy and the allocation of the first-attesting notary's duties can only be stated conditionally.

Nimal Perera may not attest the whole partition deed and may not attest in Kandy; the deed may lawfully be executed before the two notaries, each attesting only the execution that took place before him.

If Nimal Perera attested the father's signature without the father having signed before him he would breach rule 31(12) and commit an offence punishable on summary trial in addition to any civil liability, and section 33 would not save the position because the breach is not a matter of form.

Does the area specified in a notary's warrant limit where he may attest a deed, and does it also limit the location of the land the deed affects?
In which of the available methods may Gayan Alwis, whose warrant covers the Galle judicial zone, attest the deed of transfer himself?
