enrichment.original_background: Gayan Alwis is a Notary licensed to practice within the High Court Jurisdiction of Galle. His client Anura Fernando wishes to purchase a property in Ratnapura from a person living there who is unable to travel to Galle due to ill health to execute the Deed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How can a valid deed transferring the Ratnapura property be executed when the vendor is too ill to travel to Galle, and in which of those methods may Gayan Alwis, whose warrant authorises him to practise only within the Galle judicial zone, attest the deed himself?
gold_answer_draft.rule: A transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by a person duly authorised by the executant, together with the witnesses, in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The person who signs need not be the vendor: the authorisation contemplated by that section takes the form of a power of attorney, that is, a written authority given by one person to another to represent him and do any act on his behalf, which if executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary public (Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.2) and must be registered with the Registrar-General (Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3). The Notaries Ordinance in terms allows a notary to attest a deed executed before him by means of an attorney, requiring him to preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with his protocol and to forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands (s.31 rule (30)). A notary's competence is territorial: his warrant specifies the area within which he is authorised to practise (Notaries Ordinance s.2), a warrant for the judicial division of residence being deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone of residence (s.4A), and he shall not attest any deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (s.31 rule (22)), breach of which is an offence punishable summarily (s.34). That limit is on the place of attestation only, not on the situation of the land: where the deed affects land in another district the notary must in addition transmit a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land lies (s.31 rule (29)). Independently of the notarial route, a deed that Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 would otherwise govern is valid if signed by the party or by a person lawfully authorised by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, before the District Judge, or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace, for the district in which that party resides, and certified by that officer (Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance s.2).
gold_answer_draft.application: The vendor lives in Ratnapura and cannot travel; Gayan Alwis's warrant covers only the Galle High Court jurisdiction. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22) therefore stops him from going to Ratnapura and attesting the deed at the vendor's bedside, and s.34 makes doing so an offence. It does not stop him from acting on a Ratnapura property, since s.31 rule (29) expressly assumes that a notary may attest a deed affecting land in another district and merely adds a filing duty. The first method open to Anura Fernando is therefore to have the vendor grant a power of attorney in Ratnapura, executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary who is authorised to practise in the judicial zone in which Ratnapura lies, appointing an attorney who can travel; that power is registered with the Registrar-General, and the attorney then signs the deed of transfer in Galle, with the witnesses, in the presence of Gayan Alwis. Because the signature of a duly authorised person satisfies Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 and the attestation takes place inside his own area, Gayan Alwis may attest that deed, keeping a true copy of the power with his protocol under rule (30) and sending a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands for the Ratnapura district under rule (29). The second method is to have the deed attested in Ratnapura itself, either by a notary who holds a warrant for that zone, who may attend on the vendor at home, or, without any notary, by execution before the District Judge or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace for the district in which the vendor resides under Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance s.2. In that second method the attesting officer must be the local notary or the public officer, and rule (22) prevents Gayan Alwis from taking that role.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Gayan Alwis can advise two methods. First, the vendor grants a notarially attested power of attorney in Ratnapura and the attorney executes the deed of transfer in Galle. Second, the deed is executed in Ratnapura, either before a notary authorised to practise in that zone or before the District Judge or an authorised Justice of the Peace for that district under the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance. Only in the first method can Gayan Alwis himself attest the deed of transfer, because the execution then takes place within the area specified in his warrant; if he does, he must keep a copy of the power of attorney with his protocol and send a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies. How far the vendor is willing to entrust an attorney with the sale, and whether a suitable attorney is available, are matters of fact on which the papers say nothing.

answer_claims.claim_text: A transfer of immovable property is of no force in law unless the deed is in writing, signed by every executant or by a person duly authorised by the executant, and by the witnesses, in the presence of a licensed notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and attested by that notary.

The authorisation by which someone other than the executant may sign takes the form of a power of attorney, a written authority given by one person to another to represent him and do any act on his behalf, which if executed in Sri Lanka must be executed before two witnesses and attested by a notary public.
A power of attorney executed in Sri Lanka is to be registered with the Registrar-General.

A notary may attest a deed executed before him by means of an attorney, and must then preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with his protocol and forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands.

A notary's warrant specifies the area within which he is authorised to practise, and a warrant for the judicial division in which he resides is deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which he resides.

A notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise, and breach of that rule is an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate.

The territorial limit bears on where the deed is attested, not on where the land lies; a notary who attests a deed affecting land in another district must transmit a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated.

A deed otherwise governed by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance is also valid if signed by the party or a person lawfully authorised by him, and by two or more witnesses present at the same time, before the District Judge or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace for the district in which that party resides, and certified by that officer.
Because Gayan Alwis is authorised to practise only within the Galle High Court jurisdiction and the vendor is in Ratnapura, he cannot lawfully travel to the vendor and attest the deed there.

The first method is for the vendor to grant a power of attorney in Ratnapura, before two witnesses and attested by a notary authorised for that area, so that the attorney can sign the deed of transfer in Galle in the presence of Gayan Alwis and the witnesses.

The second method is to have the deed executed in Ratnapura itself, either before a notary who holds a warrant for that judicial zone or before the District Judge or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace for that district.

Gayan Alwis may himself attest the deed of transfer only in the power-of-attorney method, because the deed is then signed before him inside the area specified in his warrant by a person duly authorised by the vendor.

If Gayan Alwis attests the deed on a power of attorney, he must keep a true copy of the power with his protocol and, because the land is in Ratnapura, send a certified copy of the deed to the Registrar of Lands of that district.

The notary's own duties as to witnesses are in the Notaries Ordinance s.31. No judicial authority or Roman-Dutch common law rule is needed for a complete answer on these facts.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a will is invalid because one of its two attesting witnesses is a beneficiary named in it.
Whether the beneficial devise and legacy given by the will to the attesting witness, and to the attesting witness's spouse, remain effective.
Whether a debt owed by the testator to the proposed witness and charged on the estate, and the witness's appointment as executor with a commission, are affected by his attesting the will.
What the attesting notary should accordingly advise the testator about the choice of attesting witnesses.

Section 12 was demoted because the charge-for-debt exception is written into section 11 itself and section 12 only confirms the attesting creditor's competence; removing section 12, like removing sections 13 and 31, would not change the conclusion.

enrichment.original_background: The testator of a Will wants one of the beneficiaries in his Will to sign as an attesting witness of the Will.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The testator wishes his nephew, who takes a devise of a house under the will and whose wife takes a legacy under it, to sign the will as one of the two attesting witnesses. The notary must advise the client on the effect of that course on the validity of the will, on what the nephew and his wife would take, on the debt charged in the nephew's favour and on his office as executor, and on what the testator should do instead.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 provides that where a person attests the execution of a will and any beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition or appointment of movable or immovable property is thereby given to that attesting witness or to that witness's wife or husband, the gift is utterly null and void so far as concerns the attesting witness, the spouse and any person claiming under either, while the attesting witness is still admitted as a witness to prove the execution or the validity of the will. Charges and directions for the payment of debts are expressly excepted from that avoidance, and Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.12 confirms that a creditor whose debt is so charged is admitted as a witness notwithstanding the charge. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.10 provides that a will is not invalid merely because an attesting witness is, at the execution or afterwards, incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove it. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.13 provides that attesting does not make an executor incompetent as a witness and does not forfeit the recompense or commission payable for his trouble. Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) forbids the notary to attest an instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and Notaries Ordinance s.31(12) requires the executant and the witnesses to sign in the presence of the notary and of one another.
gold_answer_draft.application: The nephew is a person to whom a beneficial devise of immovable property, the house and premises at Kalutara, is given by the very will he is asked to attest, so under s.11 that devise would be utterly null and void so far as concerns him and anyone claiming under him. The legacy of Rs. 500,000 to his wife falls within the same provision, which reaches a gift to the wife or husband of the attesting witness, and would equally be void. The will would not itself fail: s.10 keeps the will valid despite any incompetency in an attesting witness, and s.11 in terms admits the attesting witness to prove the execution and validity of the will, so the second witness and the notary's attestation would still carry it. The direction that the estate be charged with and pay the Rs. 400,000 owed to the nephew on the promissory note is a charge and a direction for the payment of a debt, which s.11 expressly excepts from the avoidance, and s.12 confirms that he is admitted as a witness notwithstanding that charge, so that entitlement would survive. His appointment as executor and the commission for his trouble are preserved by s.13 and would not be forfeited by his attesting. On these facts the nephew would therefore keep only the charged debt and the executorship and would lose the house, and his wife would lose her legacy, for no gain; and since Notaries Ordinance s.31(8) requires two subscribing witnesses in any event and the testator is willing to call in another person, a disinterested witness to sign alongside the neighbour is readily available.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should advise the testator not to have the nephew sign as an attesting witness. If he does so the will remains valid and the notary may still attest it, but the devise of the house to the nephew and the legacy to the nephew's wife would be utterly null and void so far as they are concerned, while the charged debt of Rs. 400,000 and the executorship with its commission would survive. The safe course, which the notary should press on the client, is to have the will attested by two witnesses who take no benefit under it, such as the neighbour and one other disinterested person of good repute, so that every disposition the testator intends takes effect. Who is in fact available to sign is a matter the notary must satisfy himself about at the execution.

answer_claims.claim_text: Where a person attests the execution of a will, a beneficial devise, legacy, estate, interest, gift, disposition or appointment of movable or immovable property given by that will to the attesting witness is utterly null and void so far as concerns that witness and any person claiming under him.
The same avoidance applies to a gift given by the will to the wife or husband of the attesting witness.

The will itself is not invalidated by the fact that an attesting witness is or becomes incompetent to be admitted a witness to prove its execution, and the attesting witness remains admissible to prove the execution or the validity of the will.
Charges and directions for the payment of debts are excepted from that avoidance, and a creditor whose debt is so charged is admitted as a witness notwithstanding the charge.
An executor is not rendered incompetent as a witness by attesting the will, and does not thereby forfeit the recompense or commission payable for his trouble.

The notary may not attest an instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters, and the executant and the witnesses must sign in the presence of the notary and of one another.
If the nephew attests the will, the devise to him of the house and premises at Kalutara is avoided so far as concerns him and anyone claiming under him.
The legacy of Rs. 500,000 to the nephew's wife is likewise avoided if the nephew attests the will, because she is the wife of the attesting witness.
The will would still be valid and the notary could still attest it, with the neighbour as the second subscribing witness.
The direction charging the estate with the Rs. 400,000 owed to the nephew on the promissory note survives his attestation, and he remains a competent witness notwithstanding that charge.
The nephew's appointment as executor and the commission for his trouble are not lost by his attesting the will.

The notary should advise the testator that the nephew should not sign as an attesting witness, and that the will should be attested by two witnesses who take no benefit under it, so that the devise to the nephew and the legacy to his wife take effect.

If the testator nevertheless insists, the notary may attest the will, which remains valid, but the nephew and his wife lose the devise and the legacy while the charged debt and the executorship with its commission survive.

The corpus supplies every formal and procedural step of the alternative (notarial execution, description and title-search duties, registration and priority), but it does not contain the Partition Act, No. 21 of 1977 or the Roman-Dutch common law of co-ownership from which a co-owner's right to partition, and the right of co-owners to partition amicably by agreement instead of by action, are derived. The effect of the voluntary partition on the Bank's existing mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share is likewise not resolved by any corpus provision. The answer therefore requires authority beyond the statutory corpus and is reserved rather than proposed as gold.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The steps of the alternative route are statutory and can be sourced entirely to the corpus: notarial execution (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2), the description and title-search duties of the notary (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rules (16) and (17)), the description and priority rules on registration (Registration of Documents Ordinance ss.7, 8 and 13) and the notary's duty to register (s.37). The identification of the alternative itself is not. The Partition Act, No. 21 of 1977, the comparator the question is framed against, is also absent from the corpus, so the corpus cannot show what a partition action requires or that a deed of partition is a lawful substitute for one. The corpus statutes only presuppose the instrument (see PROV-M075-010). A complete answer therefore needs authority outside the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the three brothers, who hold equal undivided shares in a single divided allotment of 45 perches, can obtain divided and defined blocks otherwise than by instituting a partition action - that is, by a voluntary partition effected by a deed of partition executed by all the co-owners.

What formal and procedural steps a deed of partition requires: survey and blocking out of the 45 perches into three defined lots, search of title at the Land Registry, drawing of the deed with a schedule describing each lot by boundaries and extent, notarial execution by all three co-owners, and registration.

What the Bank's registered mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share means for the alternative route - whether the mortgage must be discharged or the Bank joined in or made to concur in the deed before the shares are converted into divided lots.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps across three enactments. Step one: the instrument must be a notarially attested deed to have force in law (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). Step two: the notary may not attest it unless it describes the land and defines each divided share by boundaries and extent (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rules (16)(a) and (16)(b)), which is what makes the survey necessary. Step three: the deed, being an instrument affecting land, must be registered or it is void against a later registered instrument for value (Registration of Documents Ordinance ss.8 and 7). Only these dependencies are counted.

enrichment.original_background: Anuk de Silva, Pramuk de Silva and Dinuk de Silva are three brothers and they own equal undivided shares of a divided portion of a land in extent of 45 perches as per a Partition Decree in the District Court of Ratnapura in case No. 345/P. Anuk wishes to sell his entitlement of the land. Pramuk wishes to construct a house on his share of the land having mortgaged it to a Bank. Dinuk wants to Lease his share of land to a Company for a commercial purpose. The Bank informed Pramuk that he should have a divided and defined block of land in order to enable them to grant him a loan. Therefore, he informs his brothers that they should file a Partition Action for the division of the property. Anuk has approached you for Legal advice.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Anuk asks whether the brothers must file a partition action to give each of them a divided and defined block of the 45-perch allotment they hold in equal undivided shares under the decree in D.C. Ratnapura case No. 345/P, or whether there is an alternative, and what that alternative requires. The issues are whether a voluntary partition effected by a deed of partition executed by all three co-owners is available, what steps it involves, and how the Bank's mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share affects it.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A deed of partition among co-owners is an instrument affecting land. It has no force in law unless it is in writing and attested by a notary in the presence of witnesses (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The notary may not attest a deed affecting land unless the deed itself, or a schedule annexed to it, carries an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(a)), and where the property is a share the deed must state whether the share is divided or undivided, state the fraction it bears to the whole, and, if it is a divided share, define it clearly and accurately by its particular boundaries and extent (Notaries Ordinance s.31(16)(b)). Before drawing such a deed the notary must search the Land Registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a)). An instrument that purports or operates to create, declare, transfer, release or extinguish any interest in land is an instrument affecting land for registration purposes (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)); a divided portion presented for registration must be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent, failing which the Registrar must refuse registration (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(2) and (5)); and an unregistered instrument is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later registered instrument (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1)). Once instructed and put in funds, the notary must use due diligence to register the deed (Notaries Ordinance s.37). A plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared and certified as the Survey Act s.13 requires, which is why the blocking-out survey should be entrusted to a registered licensed surveyor. The corpus consulted for this map does not contain the Partition Act or the common law of co-ownership, so the entitlement of co-owners to partition by agreement rather than by action is not stated here on statutory authority.
gold_answer_draft.application: The three brothers are the only co-owners and their shares are equal and undisputed, having been fixed by the decree in case No. 345/P; the subject is a single divided allotment of 45 perches. Where all co-owners are ascertained and in agreement, the object the Bank has stated - a divided and defined block for Pramuk - can be reached by a deed of partition instead of a fresh partition action. The steps follow from the provisions above. First, the title should be examined and the Ratnapura Land Registry folio searched, which the notary must in any event do before drawing the deed (Notaries Ordinance s.31(17)(a)); that search will disclose the registration of the earlier partition decree and the Bank's mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share. Secondly, a registered licensed surveyor should survey the 45 perches and prepare a plan blocking it out into three lots of equal value, so that each lot can be described by its particular boundaries and extent as s.31(16)(b) of the Notaries Ordinance and s.13(2) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance require, and so that the plan will stand as evidence if the allotments are later questioned (Survey Act s.13). Thirdly, the deed of partition should be drawn allotting one defined lot to each brother, reciting the plan and carrying a schedule with the description required by s.31(16)(a) of the Notaries Ordinance. Fourthly, all three brothers must execute the deed before a notary with witnesses, since without notarial attestation the deed is of no force (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). Fifthly, the deed must be registered in the Land Registry for the district, because it is an instrument affecting land (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)) and would otherwise be void against a subsequent registered instrument taken for value (s.7(1)); the notary should be instructed and put in funds to attend to registration promptly (Notaries Ordinance s.37). The Bank's position is the open point. Its mortgage is over Pramuk's undivided one-third, and once the shares are converted into divided lots the security no longer answers the description under which it was granted. The prudent course is to have the Bank concur in the deed or to settle the mortgage before execution, but no provision in the corpus consulted determines the effect of a voluntary partition on an existing mortgage of an undivided share, so this should be confirmed on the Mortgage Act and the case law before the advice is finalised. Once each brother holds a divided lot, Anuk may sell his lot, Pramuk may offer his as security for the Bank's loan and build on it, and Dinuk may lease his to the company, each dealing with a defined block rather than an undivided share.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The alternative to a partition action is a voluntary or amicable partition effected by a deed of partition executed by all three brothers. The steps are: examine title and search the Land Registry folio; have a registered licensed surveyor survey and block out the 45 perches into three lots; settle the allotment of the lots among the brothers and deal with the Bank's mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share by obtaining its concurrence or discharging the mortgage; draw the deed of partition with a schedule describing each lot by boundaries and extent and referring to the survey plan; execute it before a notary with witnesses; and register it in the Land Registry for the district. This map is unverified and, because the entitlement to partition by agreement and the effect of the partition on the Bank's mortgage rest on authority outside the frozen statutory corpus, the question is reserved rather than proposed as gold.

answer_claims.claim_text: A deed of partition, being an instrument transferring and extinguishing interests in land, has no force in law unless it is in writing and attested by a notary in the presence of witnesses.
A notary may not attest a deed affecting land unless the deed or a schedule annexed to it carries an accurate and clear description of the land showing its boundaries, extent and situation.

Where the property is a share, the deed must state whether the share is divided or undivided and the fraction it bears to the whole, and a divided share must be clearly and accurately defined by its particular boundaries and extent.

Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search, or cause to be searched, the Land Registry registers to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.

An instrument that purports or operates to create, declare, transfer, release or extinguish any interest in land is an instrument affecting land for the purposes of registration, and a divided portion presented for registration must be defined by its particular boundaries and extent.

An unregistered instrument affecting land is void as against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument, so the deed of partition must be registered.
A notary who has been instructed and put in funds to register a deed he drew or attested commits an offence if he fails to use due diligence in effecting registration.

A plan is receivable in evidence in a Sri Lankan court only if it has been prepared and certified in the manner the Survey Act requires, so the blocking-out survey should be entrusted to a registered licensed surveyor.

The brothers hold equal undivided one-third shares in one divided allotment of 45 perches fixed by the decree in D.C. Ratnapura case No. 345/P, so all co-owners are ascertained and their shares are not in dispute.

Because each brother's share must become a divided share defined by particular boundaries and extent before it can be described in a deed, the 45 perches must first be surveyed and blocked out into three lots by a registered licensed surveyor.
The notary's search of the Ratnapura Land Registry folio will disclose the registration of the earlier partition decree and the Bank's registered mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share.

The deed of partition must then be executed by all three brothers before a notary with witnesses and registered in the Land Registry for the district, failing which it is of no force or is liable to be defeated by a later registered instrument for value.

The effect of the partition on the Bank's mortgage over Pramuk's undivided share is not settled by any provision in the frozen corpus, so the Bank's concurrence should be obtained or the mortgage discharged, and the point confirmed on authority outside the corpus.

The alternative to be advised is a voluntary partition by a notarially executed and registered deed of partition among the three brothers, preceded by a title search and a licensed surveyor's blocking-out plan, after which each brother may sell, mortgage, build on or lease his own defined lot.

The availability of a voluntary partition as an alternative to a partition action rests on the common law of co-ownership and on the Partition Act, neither of which is in the frozen corpus, so the answer cannot be completed on statutory authority alone.

enrichment.original_background:
Anuk de Silva, Pramuk de Silva and Dinuk de Silva are three brothers and they own equal undivided shares of a divided portion of a land in extent of 45 perches as per a Partition Decree in the District Court of Ratnapura in case No. 345/P. Anuk wishes to sell his entitlement of the land. Pramuk wishes to construct a house on his share of the land having mortgaged it to a Bank. Dinuk wants to Lease his share of land to a Company for a commercial purpose. The Bank informed Pramuk that he should have a divided and defined block of land in order to enable them to grant him a loan. Therefore, he informs his brothers that they should file a Partition Action for the division of the property. Anuk has approached you for Legal advice.

Dinuk has requested you to draft an Indenture, of Lease to lease out his block of land after the division of property. The Lessee is OMEGA (Private) Ltd.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Dinuk de Silva is to grant an indenture of lease of his divided block of land to OMEGA (Private) Ltd. The question is how to draft the testimonium clause of that indenture: the clause closing the operative part of the deed, which records that the parties have set their hands to it, in how many parts, at what place and on what date, before the deed passes to the signatures and to the notary's attestation.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of land for a period exceeding one month falls outside the exclusion in the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 for a lease at will or for any period not exceeding one month, and so must be made by writing attested by a notary. That engages the notary's duties under the Notaries Ordinance s.31. Rule (18) obliges the notary to insert in letters in every deed executed before him the day, month and year on which, and the place where, it is executed, so the testimonium must state a place and must spell the date out in words. Rule (12) requires the executants and the witnesses to sign in the presence of the notary and of one another, and rule (8) requires at least two witnesses to subscribe their signatures in letters, so the clause speaks of the parties setting their hands at one place on one date and leads into an execution block with two witness lines. Rules (24) and (26) require the notary to keep a signed protocol and to transmit the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands, so the deed is executed in three parts and the testimonium recites signature hereto and to two others of the same tenor and date as these presents. Because the lessee is a company, Companies Act No. 7 of 2007 s.19(1)(a) governs its signature: an obligation which a natural person would have to make in writing and have notarially attested may be entered into by the company in writing signed under the name of the company by two directors, or by the sole director, or by a person authorised by the articles, or by an appointed attorney, and must then be notarially executed. No common seal is required, the 2007 Act treating a company seal as optional. The wording of the testimonium itself is not statutory; it is settled conveyancing form, and the Notaries Ordinance prescribes a form (Form E, under rule (21)) only for the notary's attestation, a separate clause following the signatures.
gold_answer_draft.application: Dinuk de Silva, the Lessor, executes personally and sets his hand. OMEGA (Private) Ltd, the Lessee, cannot set a hand, so the clause must recite that the company has caused the deed to be signed under its name by two of its directors duly authorised in that behalf, in conformity with s.19(1)(a). The deed will be executed in triplicate, being the original, the duplicate and the protocol, so the parties sign the instrument and two others of the same tenor and date. gold_answer_draft.rule: Priority between competing instruments affecting the same land is decided by the land register and not by the order of execution. Under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) every instrument that creates, charges or encumbers any interest in land is an instrument affecting land, which covers both an Indenture of Lease and a mortgage bond; only a tenancy at will, a tenancy for a month or less, or one determinable on a month's notice is excluded by proviso (xi) to s.8. Section 7(1) then provides that such an instrument, unless duly registered, is void as against a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent instrument which is duly registered. Section 14(2) provides that an instrument is not duly registered unless it is registered in the proper book and folio for the land, and s.27(1) provides that for the purpose of priority the time of presentation in the day book is taken as the time of registration. Section 30(2) allows an intending mortgagee to register a priority notice before the bond is executed, in which case the bond, if registered while the notice is in force, is deemed registered at the time of the notice, and s.30(3) blocks registration of any competing instrument executed by the owner while a notice registered with his written consent is in force. Section 7(2) preserves an exception where the prior registration was obtained by fraud or collusion, and s.7(4) makes clear that registration confers nothing beyond that priority. Under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a) the notary must search the land registry before drawing the bond.
gold_answer_draft.application: The Indenture of Lease creates an interest in the Nugegoda house in favour of Jayantha de Siva and the Mortgage Bond charges the same house, so both fall within s.8(b), provided the lease is for more than a month. The loan is valuable consideration, so the Lending Institution is a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration within s.7(1). Everything therefore turns on the state of the folio for this land, which the notary must ascertain by a search under s.31 rule (17)(a) of the Notaries Ordinance. If the Indenture of Lease has not been registered, the Mortgage Bond, once duly registered in the correct folio under s.14(2), will under s.7(1) render the lease void as against the Lending Institution and the bond will rank first, priority running from the time of presentation under s.27(1). To make that outcome secure against anything Kamal might do in the meantime, the Lending Institution should register a priority notice under s.30 before the bond is executed, so that the bond is deemed registered from the date of the notice and no competing instrument executed by Kamal can be registered while the notice is in force. If, on the other hand, the lease has already been registered, s.7(1) gives Kamal nothing to work with: the lease is duly registered and prior, the later bond cannot displace it, and Kamal cannot honestly promise the Lending Institution first place. Kamal must also be warned that under s.7(2) fraud or collusion in securing the prior registration would defeat the priority so obtained, so concealing the lease from the lender or from the registry is not an option, and that under s.7(4) registration of the bond secures priority and nothing else. The facts do not state the term of the lease, whether the lease has been registered, or whether the bond has yet been executed, so the advice has to be given on both footings.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Who must pay the stamp duty on the Mortgage Bond securing Rs.3,000,000 over the Nugegoda house, to whom it is paid, and by what procedure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 s.4(g) makes a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum affecting property a specified instrument, and s.3(1) charges duty on it. Section 6 provides that, otherwise than in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, stamp duty is payable by the persons it lists, and since no paragraph of s.6 names a bond or mortgage, paragraph (e) applies and the duty falls on the person drawing, making or executing the instrument. Section 8(1) requires the duty to be paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value prior to or at the time of execution, with the value specified on the face of the instrument. Section 8(2) provides that duty on a specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of immovable property may instead be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution, or, where that is impossible for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, within seven days from execution, and that the bank issues a certificate in the prescribed form which is affixed to the instrument. Section 8(3) requires the executant to cancel adhesive stamps at execution by writing his name or initials across each stamp and to perforate any stamp of fifty rupees or more, and s.8(4) deems an instrument bearing uncancelled stamps unstamped to that extent. Section 2 charges the Commissioner-General with the implementation and administration of the Act, and s.10 empowers an Assessor to assess the duty on the person liable and serve a notice to pay where an instrument is not duly stamped. Section 9 sends duty to a Provincial Council only where the instrument is one referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution, and Western Province Financial Statute, No. 6 of 1990 s.37 charges provincial duty on transfers of immovable property, court documents and motor vehicle transfers alone. Under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) a notary must not attest a deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.
gold_answer_draft.application: The Mortgage Bond is a specified instrument under s.4(g). No paragraph of s.6 deals with a bond or mortgage, so paragraph (e) governs and the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the bond, that is Kamal Perera as mortgagor. That allocation is expressly subject to any agreement to the contrary in the opening words of s.6, so if the bond or the loan agreement with the Lending Institution provides otherwise, that agreement prevails; a lending institution's bond ordinarily puts the duty on the borrower, which leaves it with Kamal in any event. Because the bond relates to a mortgage of immovable property, s.8(2) applies and the duty may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at execution, with the bank's certificate of payment in the prescribed form affixed to the instrument; if payment cannot be made by then for reasons beyond Kamal's control it must be made to the prescribed bank within seven days of execution. If adhesive stamps are used instead under s.8(1) they must be affixed to the required value before or at execution, the value must be specified on the face of the bond, Kamal must cancel them at execution under s.8(3) and perforate any stamp of fifty rupees or more, failing which the bond is treated as unstamped to that extent under s.8(4). The house is in Nugegoda, so s.9 and the Western Province Financial Statute have to be considered, but s.37 of that statute does not charge mortgage bonds, so the duty is not a Provincial Council receipt; it is national duty administered by the Commissioner-General under s.2. The notary attesting the bond must not do so unless satisfied under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) that the required stamp duty is provided. If the bond turns out to be insufficiently stamped, an Assessor may under s.10 assess the duty payable by the person liable and serve a notice requiring payment within the time stated.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal Perera, as the person drawing, making and executing the Mortgage Bond, is the person liable for the stamp duty under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.6(e), unless the bond or the loan agreement provides otherwise. The duty is not payable to the Western Provincial Council, because Western Province Financial Statute s.37 does not charge mortgage bonds; it is payable under the national Act, which the Commissioner-General administers. As to procedure, the duty must be met prior to or at the time of execution, either by affixing and cancelling adhesive stamps of the required value with the value stated on the face of the bond, or, as is usual for a mortgage of immovable property, by payment to a prescribed bank whose certificate in the prescribed form is affixed to the bond, with the seven day fallback in s.8(2) where payment beforehand was impossible for reasons beyond his control. The notary will not attest the bond without an assurance that the duty is provided, and an understamped bond exposes Kamal to an assessment and a notice to pay from an Assessor.

answer_claims.claim_text: A bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum of money affecting any property is a specified instrument chargeable with stamp duty under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4(g) read with s.3(1).

Section 6 allocates liability for stamp duty otherwise than in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, so any agreement between the parties on who bears the duty displaces the statutory allocation.
No paragraph of s.6 names a bond or mortgage, so the residual limb in paragraph (e) applies and the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument.
Under s.8(1) the duty must be paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value prior to or at the time of execution, and the value paid must be specified on the face of the instrument.

Under s.8(2) duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at execution, or within seven days of execution where payment by then was impossible for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, and the bank's certificate in the prescribed form is affixed to the instrument.

Adhesive stamps must be cancelled by the executant at the time of execution by writing his name or initials across each stamp, stamps of fifty rupees or more must also be perforated, and stamps not so cancelled leave the instrument unstamped to the extent of their value.

The Act is implemented and administered by the Commissioner-General, and an Assessor who finds an instrument not duly stamped may assess the duty on the person liable and serve a notice requiring payment within a stated time.
A notary must not attest a deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.

Kamal Perera is the person drawing, making and executing the Mortgage Bond as mortgagor, so the duty falls on him under s.6(e) unless the bond or the loan arrangement with the Lending Institution provides otherwise.

Although the house is at Nugegoda in the Western Province, Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges provincial stamp duty only on transfers of immovable property, court documents and motor vehicle transfers, so the duty on this Mortgage Bond is not paid to the Western Provincial Council under s.9 of the 2006 Act.

Because the Mortgage Bond relates to a mortgage of immovable property, the practical route is payment to a prescribed bank before or at execution, with the bank certificate affixed to the bond, rather than adhesive stamps.

Kamal Perera must pay the stamp duty on the Mortgage Bond unless the bond provides otherwise; it is payable under the national Act administered by the Commissioner-General and not to the Western Provincial Council; and it must be paid to a prescribed bank, or by affixing and cancelling adhesive stamps, prior to or at the time of execution, with the seven day fallback in s.8(2), the notary declining to attest until the duty is provided.

Full age for the purposes of the Code's minors chapter is eighteen (s.502), and charge of a minor's property is exercised by a curator certificated by the court (ss.582 and 585). A woman to whom the Thesawalamai applies is subject to Ordinance No. 1 of 1911 in respect of her property wherever situate (s.2), and during marriage she may dispose of immovables only with her husband's written consent (s.6) or under a District Court order dispensing with it (s.8). Property she buys for value during the marriage is her thediatheddam (s.19), and on her husband's death only his thediatheddam is divided, not hers (s.20). On intestacy the surviving spouse takes one-half (Ordinance No. 15 of 1876 s.22) and, subject to that half, the children take the rest equally per capita (ss.23 and 24), the Ordinance governing inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka (ss.20 and 21).

gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876 (s.21), which applies to the estate of a person who dies after the proclamation of the Ordinance and who, if married, married after it (s.20). A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (s.22). Subject to that half, descendants are preferent to all others and all the children take equally per capita (ss.23 and 24). A woman governed by the Thesawalamai needs her husband's written consent only for a disposition made during the marriage (Jaffna Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 1 of 1911 s.6), and on the death of a spouse only the deceased spouse's thediatheddam is divided, the survivor's own acquisition remaining hers (s.20).
