legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three linked steps, one per instance: age plus curatorship for the 2014 deed (Civil Procedure Code ss. 502, 582 and 585); the Thesawalamai application provision plus the consent rule and its District Court alternative for the 2015 deed (Ordinance No. 1 of 1911 ss. 2, 6 and 8); and the testamentary order plus the guardianship requirement for the Executor's Conveyance (Civil Procedure Code ss. 531 and 530). Each instance needs at least two provisions read together.

enrichment.original_background: By a Final Decree dated 3rd September 2006 entered in DC Negambo Partition Action No. 321/P premises No. 3/2 Alwis Town, Hendala depicted as Lot 5 in Plan No. 213 dated 5th March 2006 made by H.S. Weerasena Licensed Surveyor in extent of 36 perches was allotted to one Albert Perera. By Deed of Gift No.675 dated 2nd June 2008 attested by G.N.de Silva Notary Public the said Albert Perera gifted the above Lot 5 in extent of 36 perches to his daughter Kusum Perera. The said Kusum Perera caused the said Lot 5 to be subdivided into. 2 Lots depicted as Lot 5A and 5B (bearing Assessment Nos. 3/2A and 3/2B) in Plan No. 225 dated 3rd June 2009 made by the same surveyor each containing 18 perches and executed a Last will No.980 dated 6th April 2010 attested by G.N.de Silva Notary Public. She died on 23rd May 2012 and her Will was proved in DC Negambo Case No. 456/DTS on 10th March 2013. By the said Last Will she left Lot 5A to her son Gayan Peiris and Lot 5B to her daughter Malika Peiris and an Executors Conveyance was executed by the Executor at the conclusion of the case. In 2014 Gayan Peiris was a minor who was 15 years old and his sister Malika Peiris was 20 years old decided to sell the property to Mrs. Mala Nadaraja and accordingly sold both lots 5A and 5B to her by Deed of Transfer No. 1234 dated 1st August 2014 attested by Alex Perera Notary Public. Mrs. Mala Nadaraja who was governed by the Law of Thesawalamai sold Lot 5A to Nihal & Company by Deed of Transfer 456 dated 3rd February 2015 attested by W.N. de Silva Notary Public .The husband of Mrs. Mala Nadaraja, Moahan Nadaraja was living at that time. After his death Mrs. Mala Nadarja sold lot 5B to Lalith Perera by Deed of Transfer No. 789 dated 5th April 2017 attested by Gamini Peiris Notary Public. The said Lalith Perera died intestate on 2nd March 2018 leaving as his intestate heirs his wife Kamani and two children Hasini and Kushan. The Estate was administered and letters of Administration was issued in DC Colombo Case No. 1579/DTS and an Administrators Conveyance was executed by the Administrator. Kamani was previously married and was having a daughter named Ruvini who was living with her. Kamani gifted her share to all three children.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Three of the instruments in the pedigree could not properly have been executed by the named parties alone. The question is which they are, who else had to be brought in, and what step had to be taken first. This draft is incomplete on the 2014 deed because the general age of majority and the effect of a minor's deed lie outside the corpus.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Full age for the purposes of the Civil Procedure Code's minors chapter is eighteen years (s.502). A person claiming charge of a minor's property must obtain a certificate of curatorship from the court (s.582), which the court grants to the person entitled under a will or deed or to a fit near relative (s.585). Where an heir, legatee or beneficiary in a testamentary action is a minor without a natural guardian, steps must be taken to have a guardian appointed on application to the District Judge heard in Chambers (s.530), the will itself being carried into effect by the order proving it and the grant of probate (s.531). A woman to whom the Thesawalamai applies is subject to Ordinance No. 1 of 1911 in respect of her property wherever situate (s.2), and during marriage may dispose of immovables only with her husband's written consent (s.6); where that consent cannot be had, the District Court may authorise the disposition without it (s.8). All of these dealings are transfers of immovable property that must be notarially executed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2).
gold_answer_draft.application: The first instance is the Executor's Conveyance at the conclusion of DC Negambo Case No. 456/DTS. Last Will No. 980 was proved on 10 March 2013 and Lot 5A was left to Gayan Peiris, who was 15 in 2014 and therefore about 14 in 2013. He was a minor legatee, so a guardian had to be appointed for him in the testamentary case and had to be joined in the conveyance on his behalf. The second instance is Deed of Transfer No. 1234 of 1 August 2014. Malika Peiris, aged 20, could sell Lot 5B in her own right, but Gayan Peiris at 15 could not convey Lot 5A. A curator of his property, holding a certificate of curatorship from the District Court, had to be appointed and joined as an executant on his behalf, with the court's sanction to the sale. The third instance is Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 3 February 2015, by which Mrs Mala Nadaraja, governed by the Thesawalamai, sold Lot 5A to Nihal & Company while her husband Mohan Nadaraja was living. Her own signature was not enough: Mohan Nadaraja had to join the deed and give his written consent, or she had to obtain a District Court order dispensing with it before executing. By contrast Deed of Transfer No. 789 of 5 April 2017 needed no such joinder, because by then she was a widow.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Three instruments required a further party or a prior step: the Executor's Conveyance in DC Negambo Case No. 456/DTS, where a guardian had to be appointed for the minor legatee Gayan Peiris and joined; Deed of Transfer No. 1234 of 1 August 2014, where a certificated curator of Gayan Peiris's property had to be joined as executant with the sanction of the District Court; and Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 3 February 2015, where Mohan Nadaraja had to join and consent in writing, or a District Court order dispensing with his consent had to be obtained. The consequence of the omissions on the first two instruments is not settled by the statutes in this corpus.

answer_claims.claim_text: A person who is to have charge of a minor's property must hold a certificate of curatorship granted by the court, full age being eighteen years for the purposes of the Code's minors chapter.
Where a legatee in a testamentary action is a minor without a natural guardian, a guardian must be appointed on application to the District Judge heard in Chambers.
A married woman subject to the Thesawalamai may dispose of immovable property only with her husband's written consent, or under a District Court order dispensing with that consent.
A guardian had to be appointed for Gayan Peiris, a minor legatee, in DC Negambo Case No. 456/DTS and joined in the Executor's Conveyance of Lot 5A.
A certificated curator of Gayan Peiris's property, and not the 15 year old himself, had to be joined as executant of Deed of Transfer No. 1234 of 1 August 2014 so far as it conveyed Lot 5A.
Mohan Nadaraja had to join Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 3 February 2015 and give his written consent, or a District Court order dispensing with it had to be obtained first.
Deed of Transfer No. 789 of 5 April 2017 required no additional party, Mala Nadaraja being a widow by then.
The three instances are the Executor's Conveyance in DC Negambo Case No. 456/DTS, Deed of Transfer No. 1234 of 1 August 2014 and Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 3 February 2015.

legal_map.block_reason: The Age of Majority Ordinance, which fixes the general age of majority, is not in the frozen corpus; Civil Procedure Code s.502 fixes full age at eighteen only for the purposes of its own chapter. The requirement that a curator obtain the District Court's sanction before alienating a minor's immovable property, and the effect of failing to do so, come from Roman-Dutch common law and judicial authority rather than from any section in this corpus. The second and third instances are fully supported by statute; the first is not. Verifier: the second and third instances are weaker than the map states. Civil Procedure Code s.582 says a claimant may apply for a certificate of curatorship and makes the certificate mandatory only for instituting or defending an action, so no section in this corpus requires a curator to be joined as executant of Deed of Transfer No. 1234; and Jaffna Ordinance s.6 reaches the wife's separate estate, while s.8 supplies a District Court order only in the enumerated cases, none of which is present. Claims CL-M079-Q03-001 and CL-M079-Q03-005 are rejected and the Executor's Conveyance instance under s.530 is the only one that stands on statute alone.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: Whether a deed of gift expressed to be absolute and irrevocable can be revoked, on what ground, by whom, by what process and within what time is answered completely by the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017, ss.2 to 6, read with Registration of Documents Ordinance s.11. The Act does not define gross ingratitude, so whether particular proved conduct crosses that threshold is left to the court on the evidence; the gold answer states that as an open matter rather than deciding it, and the conclusion turns on the statutory route and on the section 3 time bar, both determinate on the enriched facts. On that basis no judicial authority or common-law doctrine is indispensable to the answer given.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a recital in a deed of gift that the gift is absolute and irrevocable prevents the gift from being revoked at all.
If revocation is possible, on what ground, at whose instance and by what mode it may be effected, and whether the donor can revoke by his own act.
Whether the revocation action is open in time, measured both from the execution of the deed and from the date the cause of action arose.
What must accompany the plaint in such an action and what procedure governs it.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Two indispensable steps: section 2 supplies the ground and the exclusive mode of revocation, and section 3 imposes the twin time conditions without which the court cannot entertain the action. The remaining provisions (section 4 lis pendens, section 5 procedure, section 6 definition, Registration of Documents Ordinance s.11) affect how the action is filed and prosecuted, not whether the gift is revocable, so they are not counted.

enrichment.original_background: A Deed of Gift States that it is absolute and irrevocable.
enrichment.enriched_background: By a Deed of Gift bearing No. 2418 dated 12 March 2018, attested by a notary public at Kadawatha, Wimalasena Perera, a retired schoolmaster of Kadawatha, gifted to his nephew Chandana Perera the land and two-storeyed dwelling house called Sirisara Watta, eighteen perches in extent, situated at Kadawatha in the District of Gampaha. The deed was registered in the Gampaha land registry on 3 April 2018. The deed states that it is absolute and irrevocable, and no life interest, fiduciary interest or right of residence was reserved in it. After the gift Wimalasena, who is now seventy-four, continued to live in the house with his nephew's agreement. From February 2019 Chandana stopped supplying the donor with food and medicine, and in the course of a quarrel over the property he assaulted him. On 20 May 2019 he locked the donor out of the house and had the donor's belongings removed to a relative's home, where the donor has lived since. In October 2019 Wimalasena instructs an attorney-at-law that he wishes to have the gift undone. Chandana refuses to join in any cancellation of the deed and denies that he has done anything wrong.

added_facts.fact: The donor is Wimalasena Perera, a retired schoolmaster of Kadawatha; the donee is his nephew Chandana Perera.
added_facts.reason: The question as set names no parties. Section 2 frames the remedy as an action by the donor against the donee, so the scenario needs identified parties in those two roles.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Neutral as to outcome. If the person seeking revocation were someone other than the donor, an heir for example, section 2 would not give that person the action.

added_facts.fact: The subject matter is the land and two-storeyed dwelling house called Sirisara Watta, eighteen perches in extent, at Kadawatha in the District of Gampaha.
added_facts.reason: The question does not say what was gifted. Immovable property in an identified district is needed because the lis pendens application is district-specific.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Neutral as to whether the gift can be revoked. It fixes Gampaha as the district for the lis pendens application; a different district would only change the addressee.

added_facts.fact: The deed bears No. 2418, was executed on 12 March 2018 before a notary public, and was registered in the Gampaha land registry on 3 April 2018.
added_facts.reason: The ten-year limb of the time bar runs from the date of execution, and the addressee of the lis pendens application depends on whether the deed is registered. Neither can be applied without an execution date and a registration status.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. An execution date more than ten years before filing would bar the action outright. An execution date before the 2017 Act would raise a question the corpus cannot answer. If the deed were unregistered, the lis pendens application would go to the Registrar of the district where the land lies rather than the district of registration.

added_facts.fact: From February 2019 the donee stopped supplying the elderly donor with food and medicine, assaulted him during a quarrel over the property, and on 20 May 2019 locked him out of the gifted house and had his belongings removed.
added_facts.reason: Section 2 allows revocation on one ground only. Without pleaded conduct on the donee's part there is nothing capable of amounting to gross ingratitude and the question has no determinate answer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If the donee had done nothing of this kind, no ground under section 2 would exist and the deed could not be revoked at all. Whether this particular conduct is held to be gross ingratitude remains for the court, since the Act does not define the term.

added_facts.fact: The eviction on 20 May 2019 is the latest act complained of, the donor instructs an attorney-at-law in October 2019, and the donee refuses to join in any cancellation of the deed.
added_facts.reason: The second limb of section 3 runs two years from the date the cause of action arose, so the scenario needs a date for that. The donee's refusal removes any consensual cancellation and leaves the statutory action as the only route.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If the last act complained of were more than two years before filing, the court could not entertain the action even though the ten-year limb was satisfied. If the donee agreed to a cancellation, the parties could deal with the matter by a further notarial instrument and no court order would be needed.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a deed of gift which on its face declares the gift to be absolute and irrevocable can nevertheless be revoked; and if it can, on what ground, at whose instance, by what mode, within what time and with what procedural steps.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A statement in the deed that the gift is absolute and irrevocable prevents the donor from undoing the gift by his own act, but it does not put the gift beyond recall. Under the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017, s.2, an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, and only on an order made by a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee. Section 2 is exhaustive both as to the ground and as to the mode, so a unilateral deed of revocation by the donor will not do. Section 3 bars the court from entertaining such an action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose; both limbs must be met. Section 4(1) requires the plaintiff to file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed sought to be revoked is registered or, where it is unregistered, of the district in which the land lies; Registrar of Lands is defined in s.6 by reference to the Registration of Documents Ordinance (Chapter 117), and s.11(6) of that Ordinance treats a duly registered action as pending from the time of registration. Section 5 applies the Civil Procedure Code to the action. The 2017 Act does not define gross ingratitude, so whether proved conduct reaches that standard is for the court on the evidence.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed of 12 March 2018 recites that the gift is absolute and irrevocable, so Wimalasena cannot simply execute an instrument cancelling it, and the donee refuses to join in any cancellation. His only route is an action under s.2 against Chandana. The conduct relied on, withholding food and medicine from an elderly donor, an assault, and finally locking him out of the very house that was gifted, is pleaded as gross ingratitude; whether it is held to amount to gross ingratitude is a matter for the court, because the Act sets no definition. On the time bar in s.3, an action filed in or shortly after October 2019 is about one year and seven months after execution of the deed on 12 March 2018, well inside ten years, and about five months after the cause of action arose on 20 May 2019, well inside two years, so both limbs are satisfied. Because the deed was registered in the Gampaha land registry, the application for registration of lis pendens under s.4(1)(a) is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the Gampaha district, in triplicate and substantially in the form set out in the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and it must be filed in court with the plaint; registration is what protects the donor if Chandana attempts to dispose of the land while the action is pending. The action then proceeds under the Civil Procedure Code by virtue of s.5.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes, the gift can be revoked, but not by the donor's own act and not on any ground he chooses. Notwithstanding the recital that it is absolute and irrevocable, the deed may be revoked only by an order of a competent court, on the single ground of gross ingratitude, in an action filed by the donor against the donee under s.2 of Act No. 5 of 2017. On these facts the action is within both limbs of the s.3 time bar, must be filed with a lis pendens application under s.4 addressed to the Registrar of Lands, Gampaha, and is prosecuted under the Civil Procedure Code under s.5. Whether relief is in fact granted depends on the court accepting that the donee's proved conduct amounts to gross ingratitude, a question the Act leaves open.

answer_claims.claim_text: A recital that a deed of gift is absolute and irrevocable does not make the gift incapable of being revoked; the statute expressly contemplates revocation of an irrevocable deed of gift.
The only statutory ground on which an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked is gross ingratitude.
Revocation can be effected only by an order of a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee, so the donor cannot revoke by a unilateral act of his own.
The court cannot entertain the revocation action unless it is filed both within ten years of the execution of the deed of gift and within two years of the date on which the cause of action arose.

An application for registration of the action as a lis pendens must be filed in court with the plaint, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered or, if it is unregistered, of the district in which the land lies.
A duly registered lis pendens is deemed pending from the time of registration even before summons is served, which is why registration protects the donor while the action is on foot.
The revocation action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code.
Because the donee refuses to join in a cancellation, no consensual undoing of the deed is available and the donor must proceed by the statutory action against the donee.

The donee's alleged conduct, withholding food and medicine from the elderly donor, assaulting him and evicting him from the gifted house, is the conduct relied on as gross ingratitude, and whether it meets that standard is for the court because the Act supplies no definition.

An action filed in or about October 2019 is roughly one year and seven months after the deed was executed on 12 March 2018 and about five months after the cause of action arose on 20 May 2019, so both limbs of the time bar are satisfied.
Since the deed is registered in the Gampaha land registry, the lis pendens application filed with the plaint is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the Gampaha district.

The deed can be revoked despite stating that it is absolute and irrevocable, but only by an order of a competent court on the ground of gross ingratitude in an action by the donor against the donee, filed within both limbs of the time bar, accompanied by a lis pendens application and prosecuted under the Civil Procedure Code.
The donor cannot obtain revocation merely by asserting the ground; the outcome depends on the court being satisfied on the evidence that the donee's proved conduct amounts to gross ingratitude.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990 supplies a complete and self-contained valuation rule. Section 48(1) makes 'value' the base, and the definition of 'value' in section 106 prescribes, for gifted immovable property acquired after 31 March 1977, exactly the two figures the Assessor must form an opinion on and the rule for choosing between them. No judicial authority or common-law doctrine is needed to state how the Assessor arrives at the value, and the facts given (date of acquisition, purchase price, cost of construction, present market value) map directly onto the statutory limbs.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Deed of Gift of land and a house in Kohuwala falls within the Western Provincial Council's stamp duty charge, so that a Provincial Assessor of Revenue values it.
What 'value' the Assessor must ascertain for gifted immovable property, and which limb of the statutory definition applies where the donor acquired the property in March 1978.
How the cost of the house built after acquisition and the present market value of the whole property enter that computation.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps, all inside Statute No. 6 of 1990: (1) section 37 read with the definition of 'Transfer' charges the Deed of Gift; (2) section 48(1) makes the duty base the 'value' of the property conveyed; (3) the definition of 'value' in section 106, reached through the definition of 'gift', supplies paragraph (c) as the operative test. Only these dependencies are counted; the adjudication sections are supporting.

enrichment.original_background: In 1978 March Nimal Perera had purchased a land in extent of 26 Perches situated in Kohuwala for Rs.120,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs. 2,900,000/- He wishes to gift this house and land to his son Aruna and instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift. The present market value of the house and property is Rs.5,700,000/-

gold_answer_draft.issue: How a Provincial Assessor of Revenue attached to the Western Provincial Council arrives at the value of the Kohuwala land and house for stamp duty purposes on the proposed Deed of Gift from Nimal Perera to his son Aruna.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, s.37(a)), and 'Transfer' is defined in s.106 to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable. By s.48(1) the duty is calculated on the 'value' of the property conveyed. 'Value' is defined in s.106. Because a 'gift' is a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth, the gift limbs of that definition apply rather than the ordinary open-market limb. Where the gifted immovable property was acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' requires the Assessor to compare two figures: (i) the price which in his opinion the property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the deed of gift; and (ii) the price which in his opinion the property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument of gift. The value is whichever of the two is lower. Both figures are the Assessor's own opinion, and for that purpose s.63 lets him call for any document or other evidence needed to prove the facts bearing on chargeability and amount, on an adjudication under s.62 which ends in a written determination and an endorsement under s.64.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nimal Perera acquired the 26-perch Kohuwala land in March 1978, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' governs and paragraph (b), which uses a 31 March 1977 base, does not. For limb (i) the Assessor forms an opinion of the open-market price of the property on the date of acquisition in March 1978; the Rs.120,000 paid on the 1978 purchase is the evidence of that price, although the test is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price and not the recited consideration. To that he adds the cost of the improvements made after acquisition and before the deed of gift, namely the Rs.2,900,000 spent on constructing the house, giving Rs.120,000 + Rs.2,900,000 = Rs.3,020,000. For limb (ii) the Assessor forms an opinion of what the land and house together would fetch in the open market on the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the instructions is Rs.5,700,000. He then takes the lower of the two, and Rs.3,020,000 is lower than Rs.5,700,000. In arriving at each figure the Assessor may under s.63 require production of the 1978 deed of purchase, the building plan and the bills, receipts or a quantity surveyor's statement evidencing the Rs.2,900,000 construction cost, and material on current prices in Kohuwala; he is not bound by the parties' own figures, so both limbs remain open until he is satisfied on the evidence. The notary drawing the deed must independently satisfy himself under s.78(2) that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Assessor does not simply take the present market value of Rs.5,700,000. Applying paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' in s.106 of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, he compares the March 1978 open-market price of Rs.120,000 increased by the Rs.2,900,000 cost of constructing the house, that is Rs.3,020,000, with the open-market price at the date of the gift of Rs.5,700,000, and adopts the lower figure. The value of the property for stamp duty on this Deed of Gift is therefore Rs.3,020,000, subject to the Assessor's own opinion of the two open-market prices on the evidence produced to him.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, at the prescribed rate.
A Deed of Gift falls within that charge because 'Transfer' is defined to include a gift.
The duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration recited in the instrument.
A gift is a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth, so the gift limbs of the definition of 'value' apply.

For gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, 'value' is the lower of (i) the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price on the date of acquisition increased by the cost of post-acquisition improvements made before the deed of gift, and (ii) his opinion of the open-market price on the date of the instrument of gift.

Both figures are the opinion of a Provincial Assessor of Revenue appointed under the Statute, and on an adjudication he may require production of documents or other evidence to prove the facts bearing on chargeability and amount.
Because Nimal Perera acquired the Kohuwala land in March 1978, which is after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' applies and not the 31 March 1977 base in paragraph (b).

Under limb (i) the Assessor takes the open-market price at acquisition in March 1978, evidenced by the Rs.120,000 purchase price, and adds the Rs.2,900,000 cost of constructing the house after acquisition, giving Rs.3,020,000.
Under limb (ii) the Assessor takes the open-market price of the land and house at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the instructions is Rs.5,700,000.
The Assessor may call for the 1978 deed of purchase and the bills or receipts evidencing the construction cost before accepting either figure, and is not bound by the parties' own valuation.
The value of the property for stamp duty on this Deed of Gift is Rs.3,020,000, being the lower of Rs.3,020,000 and Rs.5,700,000, and not the present market value of Rs.5,700,000.

block_reason: The rate of stamp duty is not in the corpus. Section 37 of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990 charges duty 'at the prescribed rate' and leaves the rate to be prescribed by regulation under s.77(1)(a) and published in the Gazette (s.76 deals with the description of stamps to be used and with reciprocal exemptions, not with rates). No Western Province stamp duty rate Order or rate schedule in force in October 2019 exists in the frozen corpus, and searches for rate language across the corpus return nothing. The chargeable value of Rs.3,020,000 and the liability of the grantee are supportable from the corpus, but the money amount of duty the question asks for cannot be computed without inventing or recalling a rate, which this task forbids.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The whole chain is statutory: the charge in s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, the base in s.48(1), the definition of 'value' in s.106 and the incidence in s.51(a). No judicial authority or common-law doctrine is required. The obstacle is not the kind of authority needed but that one link, the rate prescribed under s.37, is not present in the frozen corpus.

legal_issues.issue: What amount of stamp duty is payable on the Deed of Gift, applied to the chargeable value of the Kohuwala land and house.
Who is liable to pay that duty on a Deed of Gift.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Four necessary steps: s.37 charge on a transfer of Western Province immovable property, read with the definition of 'Transfer' to catch a gift; s.48(1) making the base the 'value'; paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' in s.106 fixing that value at Rs.3,020,000; and the rate prescribed under s.37, which is the fourth link and is not in the corpus.

enrichment.original_background: In 1978 March Nimal Perera had purchased a land in extent of 26 Perches situated in Kohuwala for Rs.120,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs. 2,900,000/- He wishes to gift this house and land to his son Aruna and instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift. The present market value of the house and property is Rs.5,700,000/-

gold_answer_draft.issue: The amount of stamp duty payable on the Deed of Gift of the Kohuwala land and house from Nimal Perera to his son Aruna, and by whom it is payable.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 37(a) of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990 charges stamp duty on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province 'at the prescribed rate', and expressly allows different rates for different classes of instruments. The base is fixed by s.48(1) as the value of the property conveyed, and for gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977 that value is, under paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' in s.106, the lower of the open-market price at acquisition increased by the cost of post-acquisition improvements and the open-market price at the date of the gift. By s.51(a), unless the deed provides otherwise, the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee. gold_answer_draft.issue: The issue is what document may be presented for registration so that the owner of the Colombo 5 property is told whenever a document affecting that land is presented for registration, to whom that document must be presented, and what legal consequences follow from its registration, including what the owner must then do to have the offending document set aside.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The document is a caveat. Under the Registration of Documents Ordinance s.32(1) any person, called in the Ordinance a caveator, may present for registration a caveat in the prescribed form requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land described in the caveat. The prescribed form is the relevant form in the Second Schedule, which s.50 directs is to be used with such variations as circumstances require. The caveat is presented for registration to the Registrar: s.32(2) obliges the Registrar on receiving a caveat to register it in the same manner as other instruments but to retain the caveat itself. The Registrar meant is a Registrar of Lands, since s.2(2) provides that the business of the land register office and its branch offices is conducted by the Registrar-General of Lands and Registrars of Lands; and because s.32(2) directs registration in the same manner as other instruments, s.14(1) places the caveat in the book allotted to the division in which the land is situated, that is, at the land registry serving the division in which the property lies. What counts as an instrument affecting the land is fixed by s.8, which deems every instrument that purports or operates to create, transfer, charge or extinguish any right, title or interest in land to affect it. The effect of registration is threefold. First, duration: by s.32(3) the caveat is in force for the period specified in it, which cannot exceed the period covered by the fee paid, and the fee item substituted by the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2013 s.5 is charged for each land described in the caveat, for each land registry in which it is registered, and for each period of two years. Second, warning: by s.32(4) the notice to the caveator is in the prescribed form and is sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat, and by s.43(2) the Registrar's endorsement on the duplicate caveat is admissible without proof of his signature or appointment and is prima facie evidence of registration. Third, remedy: by s.32(5), if while the caveat is in force an instrument affecting the land described in it is presented for registration, and the caveator commences an action in a competent court within thirty days from the posting of that notice and proves that the instrument is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by him, fraudulent as against him, or in derogation of his lawful rights, the court may order the instrument rectified or cancelled as necessary to preserve his rights and may order the register corrected. Two limits complete the picture. A caveat does not block registration and is not permanent: under s.33 its registration may be cancelled at the written request of the person who presented it, and a District Court may on the application of any person interested in the property cancel the registration if satisfied that it was or has become unnecessary. By s.34 a person injured by registration of a caveat without reasonable cause, or by unreasonable failure to ask for its cancellation, may recover compensation from the caveator. By s.32(6) the section does not affect any other power a court may possess to order an instrument rectified or cancelled.
gold_answer_draft.application: The property at No. 10, Polhengoda Road, Colombo 5 is land within the Ordinance, registered in a folio in the Colombo land registry, so a caveat describing it can be lodged in the book of the division in which it is situated as s.14(1) requires. Ranjith Wijeratne is a person within s.32(1), and indeed the registered owner, so he plainly may present a caveat; at the October 2019 date the subsection does not confine the right to persons with an interest in the land. The caveat should describe the land, with its boundaries and the volume and folio, and must state the Colombo address he has given, because s.32(4) requires the notice to be posted by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat and he will be out of the country. A transfer purporting to be executed by his brother under the power of attorney revoked in June 2018 would be an instrument that purports to transfer an interest in the land, and so an instrument affecting the land under s.8, which is precisely the event that triggers the notice under s.32(4). Because he expects to be away about two years, and the fee item substituted in 2013 is charged for each two-year period, he should specify a period and pay a fee that keep the caveat in force for the whole of his absence, since s.32(5) operates only while the caveat is in force. If a transfer is then presented, he must act quickly: the thirty days in s.32(5) run from the posting of the notice, not from his receipt of it, and within that period he must commence an action in a competent court and prove the instrument void or voidable by him, fraudulent as against him, or in derogation of his lawful rights, upon which the court may order it cancelled and the register corrected. His apprehension arises from the revoked power of attorney and his brother's conduct, so there is reasonable cause for the caveat and the exposure under s.34 does not arise on these facts; equally, his brother or the bank could apply to the District Court under s.33(2) to cancel the registration if it became unnecessary. It remains open on the facts whether any instrument will in fact be presented, and whether any such instrument would be void or merely voidable is a matter for the evidence in the action.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The document to be presented is a caveat in the prescribed form under s.32(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, presented for registration to the Registrar of Lands of the land registry in whose division the Colombo 5 property is situated, who must register it in the same manner as other instruments and retain the caveat. Its effect is that while it remains in force, for the period specified in it and covered by the fee paid under s.32(3), the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land obliges the Registrar to send notice in the prescribed form by registered letter to the address given in the caveat under s.32(4), and that notice opens a window of thirty days from its posting within which the caveator may sue in a competent court under s.32(5) and, on proof that the instrument is void or voidable by him, fraudulent as against him or in derogation of his lawful rights, obtain an order rectifying or cancelling it and correcting the register. The caveat therefore gives warning and a time-limited right of action; it does not prevent the instrument from being registered, it may be cancelled under s.33, and an unfounded caveat carries the compensation liability in s.34. This states the law as at the matter reference date and does not take account of the later rewriting of s.32.

answer_claims.claim_text: The document that may be presented is a caveat in the prescribed form, and s.32(1) allows any person, thereby called a caveator, to present it for registration requiring to be served with notice of the presentation for registration of any instrument affecting the land described in it.
The prescribed form is a form of the Second Schedule, which is to be used with such variations as circumstances may require and may be altered or added to by regulation.
The caveat is presented for registration to the Registrar, who must on receiving it register it in the same manner as other instruments and must retain the caveat.

The Registrar concerned is a Registrar of Lands conducting the business of the land register office or a branch office, and the caveat belongs in the book allotted to the division in which the land is situated.

A caveat is in force only for the period specified in it, which cannot exceed the period covered by the fee paid, and the caveat fee is charged for each land described, for each land registry and for each period of two years.

Where an instrument affecting the land is presented for registration, the notice to the caveator is in the prescribed form and is sent by registered letter to the address mentioned in the caveat, and the Registrar's endorsement on the duplicate caveat is prima facie evidence of registration.

If the caveator commences an action in a competent court within thirty days from the posting of that notice and proves that the instrument is or was at the time of registration void or voidable by him, fraudulent as against him or in derogation of his lawful rights, the court may order the instrument rectified or cancelled and the register corrected.
The instruments that trigger the notice are those deemed to affect land, namely instruments that purport or operate to create, transfer, charge or extinguish any right, title or interest in land.

Registration of a caveat may be cancelled at the written request of the person who presented it, or by a District Court on the application of any person interested in the property if satisfied that the registration was or has become unnecessary, and the section does not affect any other power of a court to order an instrument rectified or cancelled.

A person injured by the registration of a caveat without reasonable cause, or by unreasonable failure to request its cancellation, may recover compensation from the person who applied for the registration.
The Colombo 5 premises are land registered in a folio of the Colombo land registry, so a caveat describing that land is registrable in the book of the division in which it is situated.
The registered owner is a person entitled to present a caveat under the text in force at the matter date, which imposes no requirement of an interest in the land.

A transfer purporting to be executed under the power of attorney revoked in June 2018 would be an instrument affecting the land, so its presentation for registration while the caveat is in force would oblige the Registrar to post notice to the caveator.

The caveat must state the Colombo address given for service, because the notice is posted to the address mentioned in the caveat and the thirty days run from posting rather than from receipt, which matters for a caveator who is abroad.

Because the absence is expected to last about two years, the period specified in the caveat and the fee paid should cover the whole of that absence, since the remedy operates only while the caveat is in force.

The apprehension arising from the revoked power of attorney and the brother's conduct gives reasonable cause for the caveat, so the compensation exposure for an unfounded caveat does not arise on these facts.
The document to be presented is a caveat in the prescribed form, presented for registration to the Registrar of Lands of the land registry in whose division the Colombo 5 property is situated.

Its effect is that while it is in force the presentation of any instrument affecting the land brings a posted notice to the caveator and opens a thirty-day window in which he may sue and obtain rectification or cancellation of the instrument and correction of the register; it does not prevent registration, it may be cancelled, and an unfounded caveat carries a liability to compensate.
The answer states the law as it stood at the matter reference date and does not apply the later re-enactment of the caveat provisions.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether the notary may tell the testator's children that he has attested a Will executed by their father, and disclose what it contains, while the testator is alive and has given no permission. The issue is whether that knowledge is a secret within the notary's statutory duty of secrecy, and whether either exception to that duty is made out.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31(1) makes it the duty of every notary that he shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The prohibition is general and the two exceptions are the only gateways out of it. That a will attested by a notary falls within this protection is borne out by the way the Ordinance itself handles wills: under s.31(24) a notary's protocol register may record only the number and date of a will or codicil, and under the proviso to s.31(26)(a)(i) the monthly list delivered to the Registrar of Lands likewise carries only the number and date of a will. Breach of rule (1) is not merely unprofessional; the s.31 rules are penally enforced by s.34 of the Ordinance, which makes a notary who disregards rule (1) guilty of an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate and liable to a fine in addition to any civil liability he may incur, although the fine figures in the consolidated text come from a 2022 amendment and were not the figures in force in October 2019.
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that Mr. Wickramaratne had made a Will, and learned its contents, because the Will was executed before him and attested by him on 12 March 2017 and its protocol is in his custody. That is information of which he became possessed in the execution of his office, so s.31(1) is engaged. On the first exception, the employer for this purpose is the testator, the person at whose instance the notary acted, and he is alive and of sound mind; he has given the notary no permission, express or otherwise, to tell his children anything about the Will. The children are not the notary's employer, and holding no power of attorney or other authority from their father they cannot supply the permission on his behalf; their relationship to the testator and their expectation as prospective heirs give them no standing under the rule, and while the testator lives they have no interest in his estate at all. On the second exception, nothing requires the notary to disclose: the children come of their own accord with no court order, summons or other legal process, and no public officer has called for the information. Neither exception being made out, the general prohibition stands. It also applies to the bare fact of attestation and not only to the terms of the Will, since confirming that a named person has made a Will before him would itself divulge something the notary knows only through his office.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. He should decline to confirm or deny whether he has attested a Will for their father and should not disclose its contents; he may properly tell the children that he is bound to keep his client's affairs secret and that they should approach their father. The position is not permanent: if the testator himself expressly permits disclosure, or if a court or some other law requires the notary to disclose, s.31(1) allows him to speak. If he were to divulge the information now, he would expose himself to prosecution under s.34 of the Ordinance in addition to any civil liability.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary must not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.

The Ordinance treats a will attested by a notary as confidential: only the number and date of a will or codicil may be entered in the notary's protocol register, and only the number and date appear in the monthly list of instruments delivered to the Registrar of Lands.

A notary who disregards the duty of secrecy in rule (1) of section 31 is guilty of an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate and liable to a fine, in addition to any civil liability, although the fine figures in the consolidated text were substituted in 2022 and are not the figures that applied in October 2019.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty on an instrument transferring immovable property situated in the Western Province is a provincial charge. Western Province Financial Statute s.37(a) charges duty on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province at the prescribed rate, and allows different rates for different classes of instruments. Section 48(1) requires the duty to be calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and s.106 defines value, for property other than gifted immovable property, as the price the property would have fetched in the open market at the relevant date in the opinion of the Assessor. Section 39 exempts a closed list of instruments, including transfers by or in favour of the Government, and s.51(a) makes the duty on an instrument of transfer payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary. The Statute itself sets no percentage: the rate is prescribed, and s.77(1)(a) empowers the Minister to make regulations for any matter the Statute requires to be prescribed, so the rate is found in a Gazetted regulation rather than in the Statute. The national regime does not apply to this instrument: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4 lists the specified instruments chargeable under s.3 and a deed transferring immovable property is not among them, and s.13 expressly carves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property out of that Act's displacement of the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982.

It is a sale between two private persons, and none of the exemptions in s.39, which turn on Government involvement, court documents or testamentary instruments, covers it, so the charge stands. Under s.48(1) the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and since the whole property is transferred outright, free of mortgage, encumbrance or reservation, that value is the open market price of the property as a whole. Applying the s.106 definition of value, the market value of Rs. 3 million given in the scenario is the base, and the consideration equalling the market value means no question arises of duty being computed on a lower stated price. Under s.51(a), with no agreement to the contrary, the transferee is the person liable to pay. The final step is to apply the prescribed rate in force at the date of execution to the Rs. 3 million base. That rate is fixed by regulation under s.77(1)(a) and published in the Gazette; the regulation is subsidiary legislation and is not in the corpus, so the rate cannot be verified here and the arithmetic cannot be completed on verified statutory text.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The deed of transfer is chargeable with stamp duty under s.37(a) of the Western Province Financial Statute, the duty is to be calculated on the Rs. 3 million market value of the property under s.48(1) read with the definition of value in s.106, and it is payable by the transferee under s.51(a). The question is therefore which instrument fits a title that rests on possession rather than on a grant, and what that instrument can and cannot do for him.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prescription Ordinance s.3 makes ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted possession of land, by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant, enough to establish a claim, whether the possessor is defending or is himself seeking to be quieted in his possession or to establish his claim in any other manner; the possession must be unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce, performance of service or duty, or any other act from which an acknowledgment of a right in another would fairly and naturally be inferred. Prescription Ordinance s.2 extends immovable property to shares and interests in it and to the rights belonging to it. Prescription Ordinance s.15(a) removes the alienable and inalienable rights of the State from the operation of the Ordinance. On the conveyancing side, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) governs dispositive instruments, sale, purchase, transfer, assignment, mortgage and agreements to effect them, and a declaration of a title already acquired is none of these. Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) deems every instrument which purports or operates to declare any right, title or interest in land to be an instrument affecting land, so a purely declaratory deed is registrable. Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1) makes an unregistered instrument void against a subsequent registered instrument taken for value, while s.7(4) provides that registration cures no defect and confers no validity beyond that priority. Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1) requires an accurate and clear description of the land, its boundaries, extent and situation, in the body or in an annexed schedule, and s.14(2) makes registration ineffective unless it is in the proper folio, a new folio being allotted where no instrument affecting the land has been registered before. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (30A) obliges the notary who attests a deed to submit it for registration within thirty days of attestation.

Under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) a transfer presupposes a grantor with a title to give, and here there is none; the client's claim is against the world and derives from his own possession. What the facts do establish is the Prescription Ordinance s.3 case: possession undisturbed and uninterrupted, by the client and by those under whom he claims, adverse to and independent of that of any other, for over thirty years, which is three times the ten year period, and nothing in the facts suggests rent, produce, service or any other acknowledgment of a right in another. The subject is a divided thirty perch allotment of a larger land, which Prescription Ordinance s.2 accommodates. Kapila Fernando who owns the adjacent block of Lot A2 has no access to the main road. After Ananda Senerath purchased Lot A2 he asked him whether he could purchase the right of way over the road reservation marked Lot R1 to go to the main road.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Ananda Senerath, the owner of Lot A2, can sell to Kapila Fernando the right of way over the road reservation Lot R1, so that Kapila Fernando may use it to reach the main road from his own adjoining land.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The corpus yields only part of the rule. A right of way is an interest affecting immovable property, so any purported sale of it would in any event have to be by notarially attested deed (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The decisive proposition, that a praedial servitude is appurtenant to its dominant tenement, cannot be sold apart from that tenement and cannot be enlarged to serve other land, belongs to the Roman-Dutch common law and is not enacted anywhere in the corpus. Municipal Councils Ordinance s.327 states, for the interpretation of that Ordinance only, that servitudes are deemed part of the property to which they appertain or in connexion with which they are enjoyed.
gold_answer_draft.application: The right of way over Lot R1 was granted in favour of Lot A, of which Lot A2 forms part. Kapila Fernando's block is a different land and was never a dominant tenement of that servitude. A sale of the right of way to him would separate the servitude from the land it serves and would extend the burden on Lot R1 to a tenement the servient owner never accepted. Whether that is possible, and what the correct route to access for Kapila Fernando is instead, requires the common law of servitudes, which is outside the corpus.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Reserved. On the common law the expected answer is that Ananda Senerath cannot sell the right of way to Kapila Fernando, because the servitude is appurtenant to Lot A2 and cannot be transferred apart from it, but that proposition cannot be sourced to any provision in the frozen corpus and the question therefore cannot be a statute-only gold item.

answer_claims.claim_text: A servitude is deemed to be part of the property to which it appertains or in connexion with which it is enjoyed, and so is not an independent asset that can be dealt with in isolation.
Kapila Fernando's block is an allotment adjoining Lot A2 and was never part of Lot A, in whose favour the right of way over Lot R1 was granted.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Kapila Fernando, who owns the block adjoining Lot A2, has no access to the main road and holds no servitude over Lot R1, can gain access to his land over the road reservation Lot R1 if Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under the Municipal Councils Ordinance s.37(1)(b), all streets within the Municipality, together with their pavements, stones and materials, are vested in the Municipal Council, save streets specially exempted by the President. A street, for the purposes of that Ordinance, includes any road, lane or passage, whether a thoroughfare or not, over which the public have a right of way (s.327). A street so vested is a public street which the Council is under a duty to maintain and cleanse (s.46(a)); it may be sold, leased or exchanged only after it ceases to be used as a street and with the prior approval of the President (s.50); and the Council may order the removal of any obstruction or encroachment on a street under its control (s.77). Section 65 shows one route by which a road serving private owners is constituted a public road and vested in the Council.
gold_answer_draft.application: If Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council under s.37(1)(b), it is no longer a private road reservation burdened only by servitudes granted to particular lots. It is a street over which, by the definition in s.327, the public have a right of way. Kapila Fernando therefore does not need a grant from Ananda Senerath or from anyone else: he may use Lot R1 as a member of the public to reach the main road from his block. That access is protected in practice, because the Council must maintain the street under s.46(a), cannot dispose of it while it is still used as a street without the President's prior approval under s.50, and can order any obstruction or encroachment on it to be removed under s.77. The scenario does not say how the vesting came about, and s.65 is only one of the possible routes; but the question directs that vesting be assumed, and it is on that assumption that the answer proceeds.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Once Lot R1 is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council it is a public street over which the public have a right of way, so Kapila Fernando can gain access to his allotment over Lot R1 as a member of the public, without purchasing any right of way from Ananda Senerath, and the Council's duties and powers over the street support that access.

answer_claims.claim_text: All streets within a Municipality, other than those specially exempted by the President, together with their pavements, stones and materials, are vested in the Municipal Council.
For the purposes of the Municipal Councils Ordinance a street includes any road, lane or passage, whether a thoroughfare or not, over which the public have a right of way.

A street vested in a Municipal Council is a public street which the Council must maintain and cleanse, and which it may sell, lease or exchange only once the street has ceased to be used as a street and with the prior approval of the President.
The Council may order any person obstructing or encroaching upon a street under its control to remove or abate the obstruction, and may remove it itself if the order is not complied with.

One statutory route by which a road serving private owners becomes vested in the Council is a contract under which the road is constituted a public road and vested in the Council by an appropriate instrument.

On the assumption stated in the question, Lot R1, the road reservation giving access from the lots to the main road, is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council and is therefore a street vested in that Council.

Because a vested street is one over which the public have a right of way, Kapila Fernando may pass over Lot R1 as a member of the public even though he holds no servitude over it and his block was never a dominant tenement of the right of way.
Kapila Fernando can gain access to his allotment over Lot R1 once it is vested in the Kaduwela Municipal Council, and he need not purchase a right of way from Ananda Senerath.
That access is supported by the Council's duty to maintain the street, the restriction on disposing of it while it is still used as a street, and the Council's power to clear obstructions on it.

What duties does he owe in respect of the duplicate: to whom, in what form and by what date it must be delivered or transmitted.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question is what the notary must do with the original of the deed he has attested and with its duplicate, given that he resides and practises at Gangodawila in the Colombo district while the land the deed affects lies at Nuwara Eliya, in a different land registration district.
gold_answer_draft.rule: By rule (20) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance the notary must without delay duly attest the deed executed before him, sign and seal the attestation and state in it the prescribed particulars, among them the number and value of the stamps affixed to the deed and to the duplicate (rule (20)(f)). By rule (24) he must carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of the deed signed by the parties and witnesses to the original, and keep an indexed register of protocols. By rule (26)(a)(i) he must deliver or transmit the duplicate of every deed other than a will or codicil attested by him in a month to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so that it reaches the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of the following month, together with a signed list in duplicate in the prescribed form; on transmission he tenders two lists, one of which the registrar signs and returns, the other being filed and kept with the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.42; Registration of Documents Ordinance s.5(1)). Rule (29) adds a further duty where the deed affects land in a district other than the one in which the attesting notary resides: by the fifteenth day of the month next following execution he must also deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, with a list in duplicate of the deeds relating to lands in that district. The original goes forward for registration, and by section 14(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance an instrument is registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected is situated; an instrument not duly registered is void against a later instrument duly registered for value (s.7(1)). Where the notary has been instructed to register the deed and given a sufficient sum for that purpose, section 37 of the Notaries Ordinance makes it an offence for him to fail to use due diligence in effecting registration. Section 32(1) exempts certain classes of instrument from rules (20), (24) and (26), and section 33 provides that non-observance of a rule of section 31 in a matter of form does not by itself invalidate the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument is a deed of transfer of land in Sri Lanka, executed on 8 March 2019 before this notary alone; it is not a will or codicil and falls within none of the classes exempted by section 32(1), so rules (20), (24), (26) and (29) apply to it in full. On the original, the notary must complete his attestation at once, stating the matters required by rule (20), including the stamps borne by the original and by the duplicate, and must retain the signed protocol under rule (24). On the duplicate, because he resides at Gangodawila, within the Colombo land registration district, rule (26)(a)(i) requires the duplicate to reach the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district on or before 15 April 2019, with the list in duplicate signed by him and two lists tendered to the registrar under section 42. Because the land is at Nuwara Eliya, in a different district, rule (29) is engaged: by the same date, 15 April 2019, he must deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, with a list in duplicate of the deeds he attested relating to lands in that district. As the parties instructed him in writing to register the deed and paid him the registration charges, section 37 obliges him to use due diligence in effecting registration, and section 14(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance means that the original must be presented at the land registry for the Nuwara Eliya division, not at the registry of his own district; delay in registering the original carries the risk under section 7(1) that a later registered instrument taken for value will gain priority.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary's duties divide between the two documents. On the original he must attest it fully and without delay, keep his protocol of it, and, having been instructed and put in funds, use due diligence to have it registered in the land registry of the Nuwara Eliya division where the land lies. On the duplicate he must transmit it, with the lists in duplicate, to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district, the district in which he resides, so that it reaches that registrar by 15 April 2019; and because the land lies in another district he must in addition send to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district, by the same date, a copy of the deed certified by him as correct with a like list. Failure in these duties exposes him to prosecution, but where the default is one of form it does not of itself make the deed invalid.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary must without delay duly attest every deed executed or acknowledged before him, sign and seal that attestation, and state in it the matters set out in rule (20) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, including the number and value of the stamps affixed to the deed and to its duplicate.

He must carefully preserve as his protocol a draft or copy of every deed executed before him, carrying his signature and the signatures of the parties and witnesses to the original, and keep an indexed register of protocols, so that the protocol is a third document distinct from the original and the duplicate (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (24)).

He must deliver or transmit the duplicate of every deed other than a will or codicil attested by him during a month to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, so that it reaches the registrar on or before the fifteenth day of the following month, together with a list in duplicate signed by him in the prescribed form (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (26)(a)(i)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Supported by the text of rule (26)(a)(i); note only that the prescribed form was "Form F" in April 2019 and became "Form F 1" in 2024.

answer_claims.claim_text: When the duplicate is transmitted the notary must tender two lists to the registrar, who signs the lists, returns one to the notary and files and preserves the other with the duplicate among the records of his office, the duplicates being bound into volumes (Notaries Ordinance s.42; Registration of Documents Ordinance s.5(1)).

Where the deed affects land situated in a district other than the district in which the attesting notary resides, he must, besides transmitting the duplicate, deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a copy of the deed certified by him as correct, together with a list in duplicate signed by him, on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the deed was executed (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (29)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Supported by the text of rule (29); the form was "Form F" at the matter date.

answer_claims.claim_text: The original is the instrument that goes forward for registration, and it must be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land affected by it is situated (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1)); an instrument that is not duly registered is void against a later instrument duly registered for value (s.7(1)).
answer_claims.verifier_note: The section 7(1) limb and the registration-in-the-proper-book limb from section 14(1) are supported, but the opening assertion that the original is the instrument that goes forward for registration is contradicted by section 26(2) of the same Ordinance (PROV-M091-901), under which either the original or a duly attested or certified copy may be presented for registration.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary who has received instructions to register a deed drawn or attested by him, and a sum sufficient to meet the expense of registration, commits an offence if he fails to use due diligence in effecting that registration (Notaries Ordinance s.37).

Rules (20), (24) and (26) of section 31 do not apply to the classes of instrument listed in section 32(1) of the Notaries Ordinance, and non-observance of a rule of section 31 in a matter of form does not by itself render the instrument invalid (s.33).
answer_claims.verifier_note: Accurate on its own terms. Note that section 32(1) disapplies rules (20), (23), (24), (25) and (26) only; rule (29) is not among them.

answer_claims.claim_text: This deed of transfer of land in Sri Lanka is neither a will nor a codicil and falls within none of the excluded classes, so rules (20), (24), (26) and (29) apply to it in full.

Because the notary resides at Gangodawila, within the Colombo land registration district, the duplicate of the deed executed in March 2019 must reach the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district on or before 15 April 2019, with the signed list in duplicate and against two lists tendered to the registrar.

Since the parties instructed him to register the deed and put him in funds, he must use due diligence to present the original for registration in the land registry for the division in which the Nuwara Eliya land lies, and not in the registry of his own district.

answer_claims.claim_text: The notary's duties therefore divide between the two documents: on the original, to attest it fully and without delay, to keep his protocol of it, and to have it registered with due diligence in the Nuwara Eliya land registry; on the duplicate, to transmit it to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district by 15 April 2019 with the lists in duplicate, and, because the land lies elsewhere, to send a copy certified by him as correct with a like list to the Registrar of Lands of the Nuwara Eliya district by the same date.
