gold_answer_draft.issue: How, if at all, can the client's last will be lawfully executed when the notary employed to draw it holds a warrant for an area that does not extend to Mount Lavinia, while the testator is bedridden at Mount Lavinia and cannot travel to the notary? Three questions follow: what the statutory mode of executing a will is; whether this notary may attest at the testator's bedside; and what the correct course is if he may not.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A will is valid only if it is in writing and executed in the prescribed manner (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(1)), and the prescribed manner is that the testator signs at the foot or end of the instrument before a notary public and two witnesses who are all present at the same time (s.4(2)). The Notaries Ordinance then regulates the sitting. The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters (s.31 rule (8)); the testator and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he must sign in their presence (rule (12)); he must satisfy himself that the witnesses are of good repute and well acquainted with the testator (rule (9)); where the testator cannot read or asks for the instrument to be read, it must be read over and explained to him, though in the case of a will this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses (rule (11)); he must insert in letters the day, month and year and the place of execution (rule (18)); and he must without delay attest, sign and seal the instrument, stating that the testator and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another (rule (20) and (20)(a)), substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule (rule (21)), keeping the draft or copy as his protocol (rule (24)). Cutting across all of this, a notary shall not authenticate or attest any instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (s.31 rule (22)). The Minister may grant a notary holding a warrant for one judicial zone a fresh warrant for another (s.11). Breach of rule (22) is an offence punishable on summary trial in addition to civil liability (s.34(1)(c)), and although an instrument is not void merely for a notarial failure in a matter of form (s.33), that saving does not cure invalidity arising under another written law. Finally, a beneficial gift to an attesting witness or to that witness's spouse is void as against that person (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11), and the alternative of executing before a District Judge or an authorised Justice of the Peace under the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance s.2 is offered only for instruments required to be executed under s.2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and so is not available for a will.
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the testator must sign before the notary and two witnesses all present together, and because he cannot be moved from his house, the signing must take place at his bedside at Mount Lavinia; there is no statutory route by which the notary can attest from a distance or in stages. That fixes the place of execution outside the area specified in this notary's warrant, and rule (22) forbids him to attest there. He cannot escape the difficulty by recording a place inside his own area, because rule (18) obliges him to insert the true place of execution in letters, and the attestation he must sign under rule (20) records the same. His residence at Battaramulla makes no difference, since it is the area named in the warrant, and not where he lives, that measures his competence to attest; s.9 regulates his residence only through the location of his office. If he nevertheless attests at the bedside he commits an offence under s.34(1)(c), and while s.33 would protect the will from being treated as void for a mere matter of form, the breach is of his territorial competence rather than of form, so the safe course cannot rest on that saving. Two lawful routes remain. Either he applies to the Minister under s.11 for a fresh warrant covering the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, which changes his competence prospectively but not in time for a signing fixed for 15 May 2019, or the will he drew is executed before a notary whose warrant covers that area, such as Mrs. Perera. At that bedside sitting the testator, being alert and able to sign, signs at the foot or end of the will; the two neighbours, who have known him for over twenty years and take nothing under the will, sign as witnesses in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, who then signs in their presence. The daughter and the son should not be used as witnesses even though they are in the house, because a gift to an attesting witness is void as against that witness. The will is read over and explained to the testator, which for a will need not be done in front of the witnesses, and the notary then attests without delay in Form E, stating the true date and place of execution, and preserves the protocol.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The will can be executed, but not by this notary at the testator's bedside. Since the testator cannot travel and the signing must therefore occur at Mount Lavinia, which lies outside the area specified in his warrant, the notary who drew the will is barred by s.31 rule (22) of the Notaries Ordinance from attesting it there and would be criminally liable if he did. The will he has drawn should be executed at the bedside before a notary whose warrant covers the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, with two disinterested witnesses who know the testator, all four present at the same time and signing in one another's presence, followed by a Form E attestation stating the true date and place; alternatively the notary may first obtain a fresh warrant for that area under s.11. Whether Mount Lavinia in truth falls outside a warrant expressed as Colombo depends on the delimitation of judicial zones, which is outside the statutes examined here, so this analysis holds on the facts as stated and remains unverified.

answer_claims.claim_text: A will is valid only if it is in writing and executed in the manner prescribed by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
The prescribed manner is that the testator signs at the foot or end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses who are all present at the same time.

The notary may not attest unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures in letters, and the testator and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, he signing in theirs.
The notary must satisfy himself that the witnesses are of good repute and well acquainted with the testator before accepting them.

Where the instrument must be read over, it must be read and explained in the presence and hearing of the executant, but in the case of a will this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The notary must insert in letters the day, month and year on which and the place where the instrument is executed, must attest it without delay under his signature and seal stating that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule, and must preserve the draft or copy as his protocol.
A notary shall not authenticate or attest any instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.
The Minister may grant a notary who holds a warrant for one judicial zone a fresh warrant authorising him to practise in another judicial zone.

Breach of the territorial rule is an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, and the protection given to instruments defective only in a matter of form does not extend to invalidity arising under another written law.
A beneficial gift under a will to a person who attests its execution, or to that person's spouse, is void so far as concerns that attesting witness or spouse.

Execution before a District Judge or an authorised Justice of the Peace is available only for instruments required to be executed under section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, and so cannot be used for a will.
Because the testator cannot be moved from his house and all four persons must be present together at the signing, the will must be executed at his bedside at Mount Lavinia.
That place lies outside the area specified in the notary's warrant, so he is forbidden to attest the will there.
He cannot avoid that bar by recording a place of execution inside his own area, because he is bound to insert the true place in letters and to record it in his attestation.

His residence at Battaramulla does not enlarge his competence, because it is the area named in the warrant that measures where he may attest, residence being regulated only through the location of his office.

If he attested at the bedside he would commit an offence, and the saving for defects of form would not be a safe answer because the defect would be in his territorial competence rather than in the form of the instrument.

The will he drew can instead be executed at the bedside before a notary whose warrant covers the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, or he may first apply to the Minister for a fresh warrant for that area.

At that sitting the testator, being alert and able to sign, signs at the foot or end, and the two neighbours who have long known him sign as witnesses in letters in his presence and in the presence of one another and of the notary, who then signs in their presence.
The daughter and the son should not be used as attesting witnesses, because the benefits given to them under the will would be void as against them.

The will is read over and explained to the testator, which for a will need not be done in the presence of the witnesses, and the notary then attests without delay in Form E stating the true date and place and preserves the protocol.

The last will can lawfully be executed, but not by the notary who drew it: it must be signed at the testator's bedside before a notary authorised to practise in the area in which Mount Lavinia lies, with two disinterested witnesses, all present at the same time, unless that notary first obtains a fresh warrant for that area.

Whether Mount Lavinia in fact falls outside a warrant expressed as Colombo turns on the delimitation of judicial zones, which is not settled by the statutes examined here, so the conclusion holds on the stated facts and remains unverified.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must a notary licensed to practise in Colombo do before he draws a deed by which his client is to buy a divided fifteen-acre block out of a 212-acre registered rubber estate at Kuruwita in the Ratnapura District: what title investigation the law requires of him, whether the fragmentation control regime applies to the sale of a portion of such an estate, and what other checks and materials he must have in hand before he starts drafting.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a) provides that before any deed affecting an interest in land is drawn by him the notary shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting an interest in the land has been registered. The registers are open to search and certified extracts may be obtained under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42, and the search must be made in the registry for the division in which the land lies (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1)), because an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent registered instrument taken for valuable consideration (s.7(1)). Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33) requires the notary to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property. Rule (16)(a) forbids attestation unless the deed embodies an accurate and clear description showing boundaries, extent and situation, and rule (16)(b) requires a divided share to be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, which calls for a survey plan; a plan is receivable in evidence only if prepared as Survey Act s.13 requires. Under Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.3(1) the transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has been previously obtained by the transferor and the transfer follows any conditions attached to it; by s.25 a rubber estate is one of not less than one hundred acres registered under the Rubber Control Act, and transfer of ownership covers the transfer of such an estate or any portion of it by sale. The application for consent is made in writing by the proprietor to the Chairman of the Board (s.11), no officer of a local authority may approve a blocking out plan of such an estate without the certificate (s.23A(1)), and where a certificate is issued it must be attached to the deed and its number and date recited in the attestation (s.3(4)). Notaries Ordinance s.38(1) obliges the notary to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed; stamp duty is charged on the instrument under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1) and, absent agreement, falls on the person executing it under s.6. Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) prohibits a transfer of title to a foreigner, that is a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka (s.25). Land Reform Law s.3(1) fixes a ceiling of fifty acres of agricultural land other than paddy, and s.5(1) vests the excess in the Commission where a person becomes owner beyond the ceiling. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22) forbids the notary to attest in any area, or in any language, other than that in which he is authorised to practise.
gold_answer_draft.application: Because the estate is 212 acres and registered for rubber control purposes, and the sale is of a portion of it, the transaction is a transfer of ownership of a rubber estate within Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.25, so s.3(1) applies and the notary must first satisfy himself that the vendor has applied to and obtained from the Board a certificate of consent (s.11, s.3(1)); without it the deed he draws would be null and void, and the local authority could not approve a blocking out plan for the fifteen-acre block (s.23A(1)). He must call for Deed No. 4211 of 3 March 1996 and the earlier title deeds (rule (33)) and cause a search of the registers at the Ratnapura Land Registry, the registry for the division in which the land lies (rule (17)(a); Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42 and s.14(1)), obtaining a certified extract of the relevant folio. That search should disclose the 2016 bond in favour of the bank, and since that bond is registered it will take priority (s.7(1)); the notary must therefore require its discharge, or a release of the fifteen acres, to be arranged before the deed is drawn. As the block is a divided portion that has never been surveyed, he must have a plan prepared for it so that the schedule can define it by its particular boundaries and extent (rule (16)(a) and (b); Survey Act s.13). He should verify from the purchaser's identity documents that Wimal is a citizen, so that Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1) does not prohibit the transfer, and check that fifteen acres added to his existing eight acres of coconut land leaves him inside the fifty-acre ceiling in Land Reform Law s.3(1). He must record the true consideration of Rs. 21,000,000 (Notaries Ordinance s.38(1)) and settle with the parties the stamp duty payable on that value and who is to bear it (Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1) and s.6); the rate is fixed by Order and is not stated here. Being licensed for Colombo, he may act although the land is in Ratnapura, but execution must take place within his own area, which the parties' proposal to sign at his Colombo office satisfies (rule (22)).

answer_claims.claim_text: Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land, a notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting an interest in the land has been registered.
The search must be made in the registry for the division in which the land is situated, and the registers may be searched and certified extracts obtained by a person interested or his agent.
The search matters because an instrument that is not duly registered is void against a subsequent duly registered instrument taken for valuable consideration.
The notary must also use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property being transferred.

The transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless the transferor has previously obtained a certificate of consent of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Board and the transfer conforms to any conditions of that consent.

A rubber estate for this purpose is one of not less than one hundred acres registered or deemed registered under the Rubber Control Act, and a transfer of ownership includes the sale of any portion of such an estate.

The certificate of consent is applied for in writing by the proprietor to the Chairman of the Board, must be attached to the deed with its number and date stated by the attesting notary, and without it no officer of a local authority may approve a blocking out plan of such an estate.

The deed must embody an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation, and a divided share must be defined by its own particular boundaries and extent, which requires a survey plan prepared as the Survey Act allows.

The notary must endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration and set it out in the deed, and stamp duty is charged on the instrument and, absent agreement to the contrary, borne by the person executing it.

A transfer of title to a foreigner, meaning a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, is prohibited, and no person may own agricultural land other than paddy in excess of fifty acres, the excess vesting in the Land Reform Commission.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area, or in any language, other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Because the estate is 212 acres and registered for rubber control purposes and the sale is of a portion of it, the transaction is a transfer of ownership of a rubber estate, so the Board's prior certificate of consent must be obtained by the vendor before the deed is drawn.

The notary must call for Deed No. 4211 of 1996 and search the registers at the Ratnapura Land Registry, obtaining a certified extract of the folio, which will disclose the undischarged 2016 bond in favour of the bank; he must require that bond to be discharged or the block released before drafting.
As the fifteen-acre block is a divided and unsurveyed portion, a survey plan must be obtained before drafting so that the schedule can define the block by its particular boundaries and extent.

The notary must verify from identity documents that the purchaser is a citizen of Sri Lanka, and check that fifteen acres added to his existing eight acres of coconut land leaves him within the fifty-acre ceiling.
He must record the true consideration of Rs. 21,000,000, compute the stamp duty on that value and settle who bears it before the deed is engrossed.
Being licensed for Colombo, the notary may act although the land lies in Ratnapura, provided the deed is executed and attested within his own area, which signing at his Colombo office satisfies.

The steps to be taken before drafting are therefore to take instructions and verify identity and citizenship, call for and examine the title deeds, search the Ratnapura Land Registry and obtain a certified extract, clear the registered bond, obtain the Board's certificate of consent, have the block surveyed and the blocking out plan approved, ascertain the true consideration and provide for stamp duty, check the agricultural ceiling, and arrange execution within his own area.
If the Board's certificate of consent is not obtained, the notary should decline to draw the deed, because the transfer would be null and void.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Two things can be stated from the corpus. First, whichever route is chosen, the instrument that carries it must take notarial form and be registered. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 provides that no sale, purchase, transfer, assignment or mortgage of land, and no agreement for effecting any such object or for establishing any security or incumbrance affecting land, is in force or avails in law unless executed and attested in the manner prescribed; Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) brings within the registration Chapter every instrument that creates, limits, assigns, transfers, incumbers, releases or extinguishes any interest in land, which covers a transfer of an undivided share, a deed of partition, a release of a life interest and a mortgage bond alike; and s.7(1) makes an unregistered instrument void against a later instrument taken for value and duly registered. Second, on the apartment Asanka wants to buy, Apartment Ownership Law s.2(a) applies that Law to a building erected on alienated land held as one land parcel and capable of subdivision into parcels; s.9(4) provides that after registration of the condominium plan a condominium parcel with its appurtenant common elements may be held and dealt with in the same manner and form as any land; s.11 ties the share in the common elements to the parcel, so it cannot be dealt with separately; and s.10(1) requires the title to be registered under the Registration of Title Act before the purchaser is entitled to it. What the corpus does not supply is the rule that decides the question actually asked: the effect of the reserved life interest on the sons' powers of alienation, building and mortgage; the rights of a co-owner of an undivided share; and the Partition Law No. 21 of 1977, which governs both an amicable deed of partition and a partition action. Apartment Ownership Law s.23 refers to that Partition Law but the corpus holds none of its text.
gold_answer_draft.application: Asanka can be told what he would be buying if he does acquire a Colombo apartment: a condominium parcel that, once the plan is registered, is dealt with like land, carrying an inseparable share of the common elements, and vesting in him only on registration under the Registration of Title Act. All three can be told that any deed they execute over the Battaramulla land must be notarially attested and promptly registered, and that a deed left unregistered will lose to a later registered deed for value, which is the point their lender will care about. Beyond that the advice cannot be completed on the corpus. Whether Asanka can sell an undivided one-third that is burdened by his father's life interest, and whether a purchaser would take anything of present value, turns on the law of usufruct. Whether Sasanka can build on a specific part of a commonly owned 30 perches before division, and whether a bank would take a mortgage of a bare undivided share subject to a life interest, turns on the law of co-ownership and on lending practice, not on any provision in the corpus; the Mortgage Act interpretation section shows only that an estate, right or interest in or over land is capable of being mortgaged. Whether the obvious practical route, a release of the father's life interest followed by a partition among the three, is available depends on the Partition Law, and whether 30 perches with one house can be split into three lots depends on Urban Development Authority and local authority subdivision rules for Battaramulla. None of that is in the corpus, and the extent of the land makes the point live rather than academic.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The question is reserved as blocked for missing authority. A complete answer requires the Partition Law No. 21 of 1977, the Roman-Dutch law of usufruct and co-ownership, and the subdivision controls applying to Battaramulla, none of which the corpus contains. What can be stated on the corpus, and only as far as it goes, is that any instrument the brothers execute over the land must be notarially attested under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 and registered under Registration of Documents Ordinance ss.7 and 8 to hold its priority, and that an apartment bought by Asanka would give him a condominium parcel dealt with as land under Apartment Ownership Law s.9(4), with an inseparable share of the common elements under s.11, effective on registration under s.10(1).

answer_claims.claim_text: Any transfer of an undivided share, deed of partition, release of a life interest or mortgage bond over the Battaramulla land is a transfer of, or a security affecting, immovable property and has no force in law unless executed and attested in the notarial manner prescribed by the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.

Each of those instruments is an instrument affecting land for the purposes of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, because each creates, limits, assigns, transfers, incumbers, releases or extinguishes an interest in land.

An instrument affecting the land that is not duly registered is void against a party claiming an adverse interest for valuable consideration under a later instrument that is duly registered, so registration is a necessary step whichever route the brothers take.

The Apartment Ownership Law applies to a building erected on alienated land held as one land parcel and capable of being subdivided into parcels, which is the regime that would govern an apartment bought in Colombo.

Once the condominium plan is registered, a condominium parcel together with its appurtenant common elements may be held and dealt with in the same manner and form as any land, and the share in the common elements cannot be disposed of except as appurtenant to the parcel.

A purchaser of a condominium parcel is not entitled to the title, interest or benefit acquired unless it is registered under the Registration of Title Act, so the apartment purchase is completed by registration under that Act rather than under the deeds registration Chapter that governs the Battaramulla land.

If Asanka sells out and buys an apartment in Colombo, what he acquires is a condominium parcel dealt with as land, carrying a share in the common elements that is inseparable from the parcel, and vesting in him on registration.

For mortgage purposes an estate, right or interest in or over land is itself capable of being mortgaged, but this does not establish that a lender would advance a housing loan against Sasanka's undivided share while his father's life interest subsists.

The choice of the most appropriate route cannot be settled on this corpus, because the Partition Law No. 21 of 1977, the law of usufruct governing the reserved life interest and the law of co-ownership governing undivided shares are all outside it, and the Apartment Ownership Law refers to the Partition Law without supplying its text.

What can be advised on the corpus is confined to form and registration for the Battaramulla land and to the nature of the title on the Colombo apartment; the question is therefore reserved for the missing authority.

enrichment.original_background: Lot 3 of the land called Mahatenna in extent of 30 perches in Plan No. 251 dated 5/7/1999 made by A.Samaranayaka Liscensed Surveyor is registered in the Homagama Land Registry under Vol/Folio A 350/25. The owner, sub divided Lot 3 into 2 lots namely Lots 34 and 3B as depicted in Plan No.255 dated 8/12/2000 made by the same Surveyor. He sold Lot 3A to Dininda Perera by Deed No.351 attested by Gamini Herath, Notary Public. Lot 3A was sold at a price of Rupees 7 million but the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council in his opinion of valuation for stamp duty, values the property at Rupees 7.5 million. Dininda Perera constructed a house on Lot 3A and Leased it out to Nimal Fernando for 2 years on a monthly rental of Rs. 75,000/-, He obtained 1 years rent as an advance to set off against 2nd years rent. When the Lease Agreement was submitted for registration the Land Registry informed that it could not be registered because the sub division of Lot 3A is wrongfully registered in the same folio as the original land (Lot 3) is registered namely in Vol/Folio A 350/25.

gold_answer_draft.issue: By what procedure under the Registration of Documents Ordinance can the wrongful registration of the divided Lot 3A in Vol/Folio A 350/25, the folio of the parent Lot 3, be corrected, so that instruments affecting Lot 3A, including the lease to Nimal Fernando, can be duly registered?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1) requires every instrument to be registered in the book allotted to the division in which the land lies and in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner to connect the folios; proviso (a) allows the Registrar, if he thinks fit, to enter an instrument in a new folio with cross references to any previous registration affecting the same land or any part of it. By s.14(2) an instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with s.14. Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General that any error or omission has been made in registering any instrument, s.35(1) requires the Registrar-General to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to it, and to order the error or omission to be corrected; the correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, but does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made. The proviso to s.35(1) allows the Registrar-General to make the same order on proof by any person interested where, by reason of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, that notice cannot be issued. The form of the notice and the manner of the correction are prescribed by regulation under s.49 and by the forms in the Second Schedule under s.50, and by s.2(6) the Registrar-General may himself exercise a Registrar's powers.
gold_answer_draft.application: Lot 3A is a divided and defined portion of Lot 3, carved out by Plan No. 255 of 8/12/2000 and conveyed to Dininda Perera by Deed No. 351. Under s.14(1) the registration of Deed No. 351 should have been carried to a folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of Vol/Folio A 350/25 and connected to it by cross reference, or under proviso (a) to a new folio with cross references; entering it in the parent folio of Lot 3 itself is therefore not registration in accordance with s.14, and by s.14(2) it is not due registration. That is an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of s.35(1), and it is the reason the Land Registry says the lease cannot be registered. The procedure is administrative. A person interested, Dininda Perera as proprietor of Lot 3A or the party who presented the lease, applies in writing to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry, setting out the error and producing the material that shows it: Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251 and Plan No. 255, and a certified extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25. If the error is shown to the Registrar-General's satisfaction, s.35(1) obliges him to issue notice in writing in the prescribed form; because the instrument concerned is a deed, notice goes to the parties to Deed No. 351, that is the vendor and Dininda Perera, and he orders the error to be corrected. If a party cannot be noticed because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the proviso lets the Registrar-General make the order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested. On that order the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, makes the correction in the prescribed manner, carrying the registration of Lot 3A to a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25. By the closing words of s.35(1) the correction does not affect any priority accrued before it is made, so it cannot prejudice interests already ranked in the old folio. Once the folio is corrected the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration in the folio of Lot 3A. If instead the Registrar makes a formal order refusing registration, a separate route exists in s.38(1), an appeal to the Registrar-General within thirty days, but that addresses the refusal and not the folio error.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The error is corrected administratively under the Registration of Documents Ordinance and not by court order. An interested party applies to the Registrar-General of Lands showing the error; on being satisfied, the Registrar-General issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351 and orders the correction under s.35(1); the Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then makes the correction in the prescribed manner by carrying the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25 as s.14(1) requires; and the correction leaves untouched any priority that accrued before it was made. The lease can then be presented for registration in the corrected folio.

answer_claims.claim_text: An instrument affecting land must be registered in the folio in which the first registered instrument affecting the same land is registered, or in another folio bearing a separate number opened in continuation of it, with cross references entered in the prescribed manner.
An instrument is not deemed duly registered unless it is registered in accordance with section 14.

Where an error or omission in registering an instrument is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, he must issue written notice in the prescribed form, in the case of a deed to the parties to the deed, and order the error to be corrected.
The correction is then made by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner and does not affect any priority accrued before the correction is made.

Where notice to a party cannot be issued because of death, legal incapacity or any other sufficient cause, the Registrar-General may make the same correction order on proof to his satisfaction by any person interested.
The prescribed form of the notice and the prescribed manner of correction are fixed by regulation and by the forms in the Second Schedule, not by section 35 itself.

Because Lot 3A is a divided portion of Lot 3 depicted in Plan No. 255, the registration of Deed No. 351 belonged in a separate folio opened in continuation of, and cross referenced to, Vol/Folio A 350/25 rather than in that folio itself.
Registering the sub division of Lot 3A in the parent folio Vol/Folio A 350/25 is therefore an error or omission made in registering an instrument for the purposes of section 35(1).

A person interested, such as Dininda Perera or the party who presented the lease, must first apply to the Registrar-General of Lands through the Homagama Land Registry and show the error to his satisfaction, producing Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251, Plan No. 255 and an extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25.
The Registrar-General, if satisfied, issues notice in the prescribed form to the parties to Deed No. 351, namely the vendor and Dininda Perera, and orders the correction.

The Registrar of Lands, Homagama, then carries the registration of Lot 3A into a separate folio cross referenced to Vol/Folio A 350/25, without disturbing priorities accrued before the correction, after which the lease to Nimal Fernando can be presented again for registration.

The correction is obtained administratively under section 35(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, by application to the Registrar-General, notice in the prescribed form to the parties to the deed, an order to correct, and correction by the Registrar concerned in the prescribed manner, and no court order is required.

Whether the duty is computed on the stated price of Rs. 7,000,000 or on the Rs. 7,500,000 opinion of valuation of the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three linked steps. gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on Deed No. 351, by which Lot 3A at Homagama was transferred to Dininda Perera, where the stated price is Rs. 7,000,000 but the Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council has given an opinion of valuation of Rs. 7,500,000?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, and allows different rates for different classes of instrument. By s.48(1) the duty with which a conveyancing instrument is chargeable is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration expressed in it. Section 106 defines value, for property other than immovable property that is gifted, as the price which in the opinion of the Assessor the property would have fetched in the open market on the relevant date; the same section defines Commissioner as the Provincial Commissioner of Revenue and Assessor as a Provincial Assessor of Revenue. By s.51(a) the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and by s.40(1) it is payable before or at the time of execution. The rate is not stated in the Statute: s.37 refers to the prescribed rate and s.77(1) empowers the Minister to make regulations on any matter the Statute requires to be prescribed. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 expressly leaves instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property outside the provisions of that Act that displace the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982.
gold_answer_draft.application: Lot 3A lies at Homagama and is registered in the Homagama Land Registry, so the land transferred by Deed No. 351 is immovable property situated in the Western Province and the deed is charged under s.37. Under s.48(1) the base of the charge is the value of Lot 3A, and under the s.106 definition that value is the open-market price in the opinion of the revenue officer. The Commissioner of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council has given an opinion of valuation of Rs. 7,500,000, which exceeds the Rs. 7,000,000 at which the lot was sold. The duty is therefore computed on Rs. 7,500,000 and not on the price the parties recorded, and by s.51(a) it falls on Dininda Perera as grantee unless the deed provides otherwise. The remaining element, the rate to be applied to Rs. 7,500,000, is set by regulation under s.77(1) and is not reproduced in any provision available here, so the rupee figure cannot be stated on verified authority. The verifier should also confirm whether the opinion of a Commissioner of Revenue is an opinion of the Assessor for the purposes of the s.106 definition, since that definition names the Assessor.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Deed No. 351 is chargeable with stamp duty under s.37 of the Western Province Financial Statute, computed under s.48(1) on the value of Lot 3A, which by the s.106 definition is the Rs. 7,500,000 open-market valuation rather than the Rs. 7,000,000 price, and payable by Dininda Perera as grantee under s.51(a). The final arithmetic cannot be given: the prescribed rate is fixed by regulation under s.77(1) and no rate schedule exists in the corpus, so this question is recorded as blocked for missing authority rather than answered with a figure.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty at the prescribed rate is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument, the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration stated.
Value means the price which, in the opinion of the revenue officer, the property would have fetched in the open market on the relevant date.
Duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and is payable before or at the time of execution.
The rate is not fixed by the Statute itself; section 37 charges duty at the prescribed rate and the Minister prescribes that rate by regulation.
Transfers of immovable property are carved out of the displacing provisions of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, so the deed is not stamped under that Act.
Lot 3A, registered in the Homagama Land Registry, is immovable property situated in the Western Province, so Deed No. 351 is charged under section 37.
The base of the charge is Rs. 7,500,000, the Commissioner of Revenue's opinion of valuation, and not the Rs. 7,000,000 price at which Lot 3A was sold.
The duty falls on Dininda Perera as grantee under Deed No. 351, absent an agreement to the contrary.

The rate to be applied to Rs. 7,500,000 sits in regulations made under section 77(1) and no such rate schedule is available in the corpus, so the rupee amount cannot be computed on verified authority.
Deed No. 351 is chargeable with provincial stamp duty computed on a value of Rs. 7,500,000 and payable by the grantee, but the calculation is left open for want of the prescribed rate.

legal_map.authority_requirement_reason: The precautions a notary must take about witnesses to a last will are laid down expressly by statute: rules (8), (9), (11), (12), (13), (20) and (24) of section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance, reinforced by section 39 of that Ordinance, together with sections 7, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. Case law would be needed only for the different question whether a particular defect avoids the will, which is not what is asked.

legal_issues.issue: How many witnesses must attest the will and in what form must they subscribe it.
Whom the notary may accept as a witness: what he must satisfy himself about before accepting a person, and who is disqualified by taking a benefit under the will.
In whose presence the testator, the witnesses and the notary must sign, and whether the witnesses must be present when the will is read over.

What the notary must obtain from the witnesses and record about them: the declaration at the foot of the will, their signatures on the protocol, and their full names and residences in the attestation.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary steps, the third crossing enactments. First, the rules that govern the witnesses at the moment of execution: rule (8) on their number and the form of their subscription and rule (12) on the presence in which everyone signs, both owed as duties under the chapeau of section 31. Second, the rule (9) vetting and declaration step, which controls whom the notary may accept before those signatures are taken and whose October 2018 wording has to be recovered from the amending Acts. Third, the step out of the Notaries Ordinance into section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, which disqualifies a beneficiary from attesting; nothing in section 31 says this, so it cannot be reached without the second enactment. Rule (20)(a) and (c) are counted within the earlier steps rather than as a fourth, because they only require the notary to record facts the other rules already oblige him to secure. The supporting provisions add no further necessary link.

enrichment.enriched_background: The Notary knows the testator who wishes to execute a last Will and who is sick and taking treatment warded in a hospital. He is of the opinion that the testator is of sound mind memory and understanding. The testator is Wijesuriya Arachchige Piyasena, aged 74, a retired schoolteacher of No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, who has been warded since 3 October 2018 in Ward 7 of the general hospital at Kandy for treatment of a heart condition. The Notary is Sujeewa Bandara, who is authorised to practise in Sinhala in the judicial zone in which the hospital stands. The Will is written in Sinhala on two sheets and is to be signed at the testator's bedside on 12 October 2018; the testator is literate in Sinhala, can read the Will for himself and can sign his name in letters. By the Will the testator devises his house and land at No. 42, Temple Road, Katugastota, being Lot 1 in Survey Plan No. 3312, to his daughter; bequeaths one undivided half share of a coconut land at Alawatugoda to his nephew Ranjith Kumara; and leaves Rs. 500,000 from his savings account to a neighbour. The two people first offered to the Notary to sign as witnesses are that nephew, Ranjith Kumara, who has come to the ward for the purpose, and Kumudini Silva, a nurse on duty who first met the testator when he was admitted four days earlier and who does not know his occupation or where he lives. Also willing to come to the ward are two neighbours, H. M. Gunapala, a retired postmaster of No. 40, Temple Road, and D. A. Nandawathie of No. 46, Temple Road; each has known the testator for more than twenty years, knows his proper name, his occupation and his residence, takes nothing under the Will, is literate in Sinhala and can sign in letters, and neither is married to anyone who takes under the Will. gold_answer_draft.issue: What precautions must the Notary take with regard to the witnesses when the testator, who is warded in hospital, executes his last Will: how many witnesses are needed, whom he may accept and whom he must refuse, in whose presence the Will and the protocol must be signed, and what he must obtain from the witnesses and state about them in his attestation.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance makes each of its rules a duty of the notary. Rule (8) forbids him to attest any instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters. Rule (9), in the form it bore in October 2018, allowed him to proceed either because he himself knew the executant or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had first to satisfy himself that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their declaration to that effect signed at the foot of the instrument. Rule (12) requires the executant and the witnesses to sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another and the notary to sign in the presence of them all; attesting without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before him at the time of execution is an offence under Notaries Ordinance s.39(c). Rule (13) forbids him to attest an instrument to which he is himself a party. Rule (11) obliges him to read over and explain the instrument where the executant cannot read it or asks for it to be read, but expressly excepts wills and codicils from the requirement that this be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses. Rule (20) requires the attestation to state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another (paragraph (a)), the date and place of execution and the full names of the attesting witnesses and their residences (paragraph (c)), and whether the instrument was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses (paragraph (d)). Rule (24) requires the protocol copy to carry the signatures of the party and the witnesses to the original. Outside the Notaries Ordinance, Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11 makes a beneficial gift utterly null and void so far as concerns an attesting witness, that witness's spouse and anyone claiming under them, though by s.10 the will is not invalidated by an attesting witness's incompetency, and by s.12 and s.13 a charged creditor or a named executor is not disqualified. Section 7 of the same Ordinance requires any alteration made after execution to be executed in the same manner as the will.
gold_answer_draft.application: Two witnesses are needed and each must sign in letters. Of the two people first offered at the ward, the nephew Ranjith Kumara takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will; if he attests it, that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.11), so the Notary must not accept him. The nurse Kumudini Silva met the testator only on his admission four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence. The Notary's own knowledge of the testator satisfies the identification limb of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, so the Will is not exposed on that ground, but she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that the rule contemplates and cannot speak to the particulars the Notary must record under rule (20)(c), so she should not be accepted either. The two neighbours, Gunapala and Nandawathie, meet the conditions: they are two, they are literate in Sinhala and can subscribe in letters as rule (8) requires, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take under the Will. Since the ward allows all of them to remain at the bedside, the Notary should have the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and then sign himself in front of them, as rules (12) and (24) require, which also keeps him clear of s.39(c). He should take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will. Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, rule (11) requires no reading over, and wills are in any event excepted from reading over in the witnesses' presence, but under rule (20)(d) the attestation must record which course was taken, and under rule (20)(a) and (c) it must state that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and give the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of both neighbours. If anything in the Will has to be altered after signing, s.7 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requires the alteration to be executed in the same manner, so the witnesses are needed again.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Notary should use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; choose witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, which the nurse is not and the two neighbours are; satisfy himself that each witness can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' signed declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and set out in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses. This list is drawn from the provisions recorded in this map. Rule (10) of Notaries Ordinance s.31, which was in force in October 2018 and was repealed in 2024, is not reproduced in the corpus, so the possibility of a further witness-related requirement in that rule cannot be excluded from the corpus text.

answer_claims.claim_text: Section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance imposes on every notary a duty strictly to observe the rules set out in that section, so the requirements about witnesses are duties and not matters of practice.
A notary may not attest a will unless at least two witnesses have subscribed their signatures to it in letters, so there must be two witnesses and each must sign his name rather than make a mark.

Under rule (9) as it stood at the matter date the notary could proceed either because he himself knew the person executing the instrument or because at least two of the attesting witnesses knew him, and where he relied on the witnesses he had to satisfy himself before accepting them that they were persons of good repute, well acquainted with the executant and knowing his proper name, occupation and residence, and had to take their signed declaration to that effect at the foot of the instrument.
The testator and both witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in the presence of the testator and of the attesting witnesses.
Attesting a deed without the attesting witnesses having appeared personally before the notary at the time of execution is an offence under section 39 of the Notaries Ordinance.

The attestation must state that the instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and must give the place of execution and the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses.

Where a will gives a beneficial interest to a person who attests it, or to that person's spouse, section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance makes the gift utterly null and void so far as concerns the attesting witness, the spouse and anyone claiming under them, although by section 10 the will itself is not invalidated by the incompetency of an attesting witness.
The notary himself may not be a party to the instrument he attests, so he cannot make up the two witnesses by signing as one of them.
The witnesses to the original will must also sign the protocol copy that the notary preserves.

Where the testator cannot read the will or asks for it to be read, the notary must read and explain it to him, but for wills and codicils this need not be done in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and the attestation must record which course was followed.
Any alteration made to the will after execution has no effect unless it is executed in the same manner as the will itself, which requires the witnesses again.

The nephew who takes an undivided half share of the coconut land under the Will must not be accepted as an attesting witness, because if he attests the Will that bequest becomes null and void so far as he and anyone claiming under him are concerned.

The nurse who met the testator four days earlier and does not know his occupation or his residence is not a witness the Notary can safely accept, because she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance that rule (9) contemplates and cannot supply from her own knowledge the particulars of the testator that the attestation must carry; the Notary's own knowledge of the testator meets the identification limb of rule (9) as it stood in October 2018, but it does not cure her inability to speak to those matters.

The two neighbours are suitable witnesses: there are two of them, each is literate in Sinhala and can subscribe his signature in letters, each has known the testator for over twenty years and knows his proper name, occupation and residence, and neither they nor their spouses take anything under the Will.

Because the ward allows the Notary and both witnesses to remain at the bedside throughout, the Notary can secure that the testator and both neighbours sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another and that he then signs in front of all of them, which also protects him from the offence of attesting without the attesting witnesses appearing personally before him.

Because the testator can read the Sinhala Will himself, the Notary need only record in his attestation that it was read over by the testator, and he must in any event enter in the attestation the date, the hospital ward as the place of execution and the full names and residences of the two neighbours.

The precautions the Notary should take about witnesses are therefore: use two witnesses and no fewer; refuse anyone who takes a benefit under the Will or whose spouse does, and so refuse the nephew; use witnesses of good repute who are well acquainted with the testator and know his proper name, occupation and residence, and so refuse the nurse and use the two neighbours instead; satisfy himself that each can and does subscribe his signature in letters; not act as a witness himself; keep the testator and both witnesses together at the bedside so that all sign the original and the protocol in his presence and in the presence of one another before he signs; take the witnesses' declaration of acquaintance at the foot of the Will; and record in his attestation that all signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, with the date, the place and the full names and residences of both witnesses.

In what words and in whose handwriting must the notary certify the mark of the one brother and the Sinhala signature of the other, and what must the attestation itself state and in what form and language.

legal_map.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps. First, rule (22) fixes English as the language of the deed and of the attestation, which is what makes the Sinhala signature a signature in a language other than that of the notary's warrant. Second, that characterisation, together with the fact that the other brother can only make a mark, brings both limbs of rule (15) into play and, because neither brother can read the English deed, also rule (11) and rule (12) on the manner of execution. Third, rules (20) and (21) require the reading over and the manner of signing established at the second step to be recorded in a signed and sealed attestation substantially in Form E. Only these dependencies are counted; rules (8), (18) and (14) add detail without carrying the chain.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The issue is what instructions the notary, who is licensed to practise in English, must give two brothers executing an English deed of transfer where one of them cannot sign or read in any language and the other signs in Sinhala, and in what words and form he must then certify their respective signatures.
gold_answer_draft.rule: By Notaries Ordinance s.31(22) a notary may not attest a deed in any language other than that in which he is authorised to practise, nor attest a deed drawn in any other language, so an English licence means an English deed and an English attestation. By s.31(11) he may not attest where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the deed, or asks him to read it, unless he has first read it over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that executant and in the presence of the attesting witnesses. By s.31(12) the executants and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence; by s.31(8) at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters, and by s.31(18) the day, month, year and place of execution must be inserted in letters. Section 31(14) requires the full names of executants and witnesses to be ascertained before any signature or mark is made. Section 31(15) governs certification: where a party signs with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorised to practise, the notary must write over the mark or signature, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing; and in the case of a mark he must besides require that person to affix the impression of his left thumb and write over it, at the same time and in the same manner, the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B.". Section 31(20) then requires him without delay to attest the deed, signing and sealing the attestation, and to state in it among other things that the deed was signed by the party and the witnesses in his presence and in the presence of one another, and whether it was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses; and by s.31(21) the attestation must be substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule and must be legibly signed by him in the language in which the deed is written, and also with his usual signature if that differs.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed is drawn in English, which is the language of the notary's licence, so under s.31(22) he may properly draw and attest it. Because neither Ranjith, who cannot read at all, nor Nimal, who reads only Sinhala, can read the English instrument, s.31(11) obliges the notary to read the whole deed over and explain it, or cause it to be explained, in Sinhala in the presence and hearing of both brothers and in the presence of the two attesting witnesses, before anything is signed. He must instruct them that nothing is to be signed until the deed has been fully engrossed and read over, that the two witnesses must be present throughout and must sign their names in letters, and that under s.31(12) both brothers and both witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, after which he will sign himself; he must also ascertain their full names beforehand, as s.31(14) requires, so that the correct names can be written into the certification. Ranjith, who does not know to sign in any language, must be instructed to make his mark on the deed, the duplicate and the protocol, and then to affix the impression of his left thumb. Nimal, who can write, is to sign in Sinhala, which he may do even though the deed and the attestation are in English. Certifying the signatures then follows s.31(15). Over Ranjith's mark the notary must write, in his own handwriting and at the time of execution, the words "This is the mark of Ranjith Weerasinghe", and over the left thumb impression the words "This is the left thumb impression of Ranjith Weerasinghe". Over Nimal's Sinhala signature, which is a signature in a language other than English, he must write in the same way the words "This is the signature of Nimal Weerasinghe". He must insert the date, 12 March 2018, and the place, Gampaha, in letters under s.31(18), and then attest the deed under s.31(20), stating that the brothers and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and that the deed was read over and explained by him to the executants in the presence of the attesting witnesses, and he must sign and seal that attestation, substantially in Form E and legibly signed in English as s.31(21) requires.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The notary should instruct the brothers that the deed will be in English and will be read over and explained to them in full, in the presence of the two attesting witnesses, before execution; that Ranjith is to make his mark and then affix his left thumb impression, and Nimal is to sign in Sinhala; and that both are to do so in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another and of the witnesses, who must sign their own names in letters. He should certify by writing in his own hand, at the time of execution, "This is the mark of Ranjith Weerasinghe" over the mark, "This is the left thumb impression of Ranjith Weerasinghe" over the thumb impression, and "This is the signature of Nimal Weerasinghe" over the Sinhala signature, and by then attesting the deed substantially in Form E, stating that the parties and witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and that the deed was read over and explained in the presence of the attesting witnesses, signing and sealing the attestation in English. One point should be flagged as open: the answer is stated as at the October 2018 session, and the general requirement that every executant of a deed affecting immovable property affix a thumb impression beside his signature dates only from the 2022 amendment, so on these facts Nimal is not required to give a thumb impression.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary may not attest a deed in, or a deed drawn in, any language other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

Where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the deed, or requires the notary to read it, the notary may not attest until he has read it over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that executant and in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The executants and the witnesses must sign in the notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and the notary must sign in their presence; at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters.

Where a party signs with a mark, or with a signature in a language other than that in which the notary is authorised to practise, the notary must write over the mark or signature in his own handwriting and at the time of execution the words "This is the mark (or signature, as the case may be) of A. B.", inserting the name of the person signing.

In the case of a mark the notary must besides require that person to affix the impression of his left thumb and write over it, at the same time and in the same manner, the words "This is the left thumb impression of A. B.".

The notary must without delay attest the deed, sign and seal the attestation, and state in it that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and whether the deed was read over by the executant or read and explained by the notary in the presence of the attesting witnesses.

The attestation must be substantially in Form E of the Second Schedule and must be legibly signed by the notary in the language in which the deed is written, and also with his usual signature if that differs.

The notary must insert the day, month and year and the place of execution in letters and sign the deed, and must ascertain the full names of the executants and witnesses before any signature or mark is made.
answer_claims.verifier_note: The first half (day, month, year and place in letters, and the notary signing the deed) is verified against rule (18); the second half, on ascertaining full names before any signature or mark, rests on PROV-M101-011, whose corpus text is the wording substituted by 31-2022 s.16(7) and is therefore not shown to be the law in October 2018.

answer_claims.claim_text: Because the notary's licence is in English and the deed has been drawn in English, he may lawfully attest this deed, and the attestation must be signed by him in English.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary may tell the adult children of a living testator that he has attested a will executed by their father, and disclose its particulars, when the testator has given no permission and no legal process compels disclosure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) makes it the duty of every notary not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The two exceptions are exhaustive: consent must come from the person who employed him, and the alternative is a legal requirement to disclose, not a moral or family claim. The Ordinance treats a will as peculiarly confidential even in the notary's own compliance duties. Under s.31 rule (24) he must preserve the will as his protocol and keep a register of his instruments, but for wills and codicils only the number and date go into the register; and under the proviso to s.31 rule (26)(a)(i) the duplicate of a will is not sent to the Registrar of Lands, only its number and date appearing in the monthly list. Breach of rule (1) is an offence punishable on summary trial before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability, under s.34(1)(a).
gold_answer_draft.application: The notary learned that Mr. Wickramaratne had executed a will, and learned what it says, because the will was executed before him and he holds the protocol; that is knowledge of which he became possessed in the execution of his office and it falls squarely within s.31 rule (1). His employer for this purpose is the testator, the person at whose instance he attested the instrument, and the testator is alive and has given no permission, express or otherwise, for the matter to be disclosed. The children are not his employer; their expectation of inheriting gives them no present interest in the document, because nothing passes under a will until the testator's death, and no authority from their father is produced. Nor is the second exception engaged: no court has ordered production and no officer entitled under the Ordinance to inspect his records has called for them, so he is not required to do so by law. Confirming even the bare fact that a will exists would divulge the substance of what the testator confided, and the Ordinance's own treatment of wills, which keeps their particulars out of both the notary's register and his return to the Registrar of Lands, tells against any narrower reading. Should the notary answer, he would expose himself to prosecution and civil liability under s.34.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. The notary should not divulge the information. He should decline, politely and without hinting at the answer either way, and tell the children that he is not at liberty to say whether he has attested any instrument for their father and that they must ask their father himself; if the testator authorises disclosure, or if the notary is later required by law to disclose, the position changes, and it changes again on the testator's death, when the will falls to be dealt with in the ordinary way.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
That duty yields only in two cases: where the notary has the express permission of his employer, or where he is required by law to disclose.
A will executed before a notary is preserved by him as his protocol, and only the number and date of a will are entered in the register he is obliged to keep.
In the monthly return a notary makes to the Registrar of Lands, wills and codicils are identified by number and date alone.
A notary who acts in breach of the duty of secrecy commits an offence triable summarily before a Magistrate, in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
The notary's knowledge that the testator executed a will, and of its contents, was acquired in the execution of his office, because the will was executed before him and he holds its protocol.
The testator, and not his children, is the notary's employer for the purposes of the permission exception, and the testator is alive and has given no permission.
The second exception is not engaged either, because no court order and no lawful demand requiring disclosure has been made on the notary.
Confirming that a will exists would itself divulge what the testator confided, and the statutory practice of recording wills by number and date alone tells against a narrower reading of the duty.
The notary should not divulge the information and should decline the children's inquiry, referring them to their father.
If the notary were to answer the inquiry he would expose himself to prosecution and to civil liability.
The position would change if the testator gave express permission, or if the notary were later required by law to disclose.

gold_answer_draft.rule: Intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), the lots being immovable property within s.3. The Ordinance applies here because none of the exclusions in s.2 (Kandyan, Muslim, Thesawalamai) is disclosed, and the s.20 condition is met since every death and marriage in question post-dates the 1876 proclamation. On each intestacy the surviving spouse first takes one-half of the estate (s.22). Subject to that half, the right of inheritance runs in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children take equally per capita and the issue of a deceased child take per stirpes (s.24), and heirs equally near in degree take per capita (s.30). Where descendants fail, the estate goes to the parents (s.25); where both parents have also failed, it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood (s.26). Where the half-siblings are on one side only, s.27 directs that the full siblings take one half of that portion first and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
gold_answer_draft.application: Step 1 - Nimal's holding. Under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 Nimal was allotted 5/12 of lots 6 and 7, and by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998 he bought Aruni's 1/12. At his death he therefore held 5/12 + 1/12 = 6/12, that is a half share of the land. Sunil's 5/12 and Kusum's 1/12 are untouched by the deaths and remain with them. Step 2 - Nimal's intestacy, 23 April 2008. He left his widow Nalini and four children: Achini (by his first wife Malini), Amal, Bimal and Krishni. Nalini takes one-half of his estate under s.22, which is 1/4 of the land. Under ss.23, 24 and 30 the other half, also 1/4 of the land, is shared equally per capita among the four children, giving each child 1/16 of the land. Step 3 - Nalini's intestacy, within a year of April 2008. Her estate is the 1/4 she took from Nimal. Nimal had predeceased her, so there is no surviving spouse to take under s.22, and the whole estate passes to her descendants under ss.23, 24 and 30. Her children are Amal, Bimal and Krishni only; Achini is Nimal's daughter by Malini and is not a descendant of Nalini, so she takes nothing from this estate. Each of the three takes 1/4 divided by 3, that is 1/12 of the land. Immediately after this Amal, Bimal and Krishni each hold 1/16 + 1/12 = 7/48 of the land and Achini holds 1/16. Step 4 - Bimal's death, 4 March 2010, married to Amali and issueless. On the footing that he too died intestate, his estate of 7/48 devolves as follows. Amali takes one-half under s.22, that is 7/96 of the land. The remaining 7/96 must pass down the s.23 order: Bimal left no descendants, and under s.25 it would go to his parents, but both Nimal and Nalini were already dead, so under s.26 it goes to his brothers and sisters of the whole and half blood. Amal and Krishni are of the full blood; Achini is a half-sister on the father's side and there is no half-sibling on the mother's side. Section 27 therefore applies in its final limb: Amal and Krishni first take one half of the 7/96, that is 7/192, in equal shares of 7/384 each, and the other 7/192 is divided per capita among Amal, Krishni and Achini under ss.27 and 30, giving each of them 7/576. So from Bimal's estate Amal takes 7/384 + 7/576 = 35/1152, Krishni takes the same 35/1152, Achini takes 7/576 = 14/1152 and Amali takes 7/96 = 84/1152.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Nimal (holder of 6/12 of lots 6 and 7, being 5/12 under the Final Decree of 1996 plus 1/12 bought from Aruni by Deed No. 346 of 1998) died intestate on 23 April 2008 leaving his widow Nalini and four children, Achini (by his first wife Malini), Amal, Bimal and Krishni; Nalini took one-half of his estate and the four children the other half in equal shares. Nalini then died intestate within a year, and her share passed in equal shares to her own three children Amal, Bimal and Krishni, Achini being excluded as not her descendant. Bimal, married to Amali, then died on 4 March 2010 issueless and, on the footing that he died intestate, his share passed one-half to Amali as surviving spouse and the other half to his siblings, both parents having predeceased him: his full siblings Amal and Krishni taking one half of that portion between them and sharing the remaining half with his paternal half-sister Achini. The present owners of Nimal's half share are therefore Amal, Krishni, Achini and Amali, alongside the original co-owners Sunil and Kusum who are unaffected.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate inheritance to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.21(1), whatever the deceased's domicile, and the divided lots are immovable property within s.3.

The Ordinance's inheritance sections do not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, and apply only to estates of persons dying after the 1876 proclamation who were then unmarried or married after it.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the right of inheritance runs in the order descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals.
Children are preferent to all others in a parent's estate and take equally per capita, and heirs equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes.
Where an intestate leaves no descendants the estate goes to the parents, and where both parents have also failed it goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood.
Where there are half-siblings on one side only, the full brothers and sisters take one half of the sibling portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-siblings.
Nimal held 6/12 (a half share) of lots 6 and 7 at his death: 5/12 under the Final Decree of 21 August 1996 plus the 1/12 bought from Aruni by Deed of Transfer No. 346 of 6 June 1998.
On Nimal's intestate death on 23 April 2008 his widow Nalini took one-half of his estate and his four children Achini, Amal, Bimal and Krishni took the other half in equal shares.

On Nalini's intestate death within a year her share passed wholly to her descendants, namely her three children Amal, Bimal and Krishni in equal shares; Achini, being Nimal's daughter by Malini and not a descendant of Nalini, took nothing from Nalini's estate.

Bimal died on 4 March 2010 married to Amali and issueless, so his descendants failed; both his parents had already died, so no ascendant survived and his estate passed to his collaterals after his widow's half.

Bimal's siblings were his full brother Amal and full sister Krishni and his paternal half-sister Achini, with no half-sibling on the mother's side, so the full siblings took one half of the sibling portion first and shared the other half with Achini.

The pedigree of Nimal's half share is: Nimal, died intestate 23 April 2008, leaving widow Nalini (one-half) and children Achini, Amal, Bimal and Krishni (one-half between them); Nalini, died intestate within a year, leaving her share to Amal, Bimal and Krishni; Bimal, died 4 March 2010 issueless, leaving his share one-half to his widow Amali and one-half to his siblings Amal, Krishni and Achini in the proportions fixed by section 27.
The present owners of the land are Sunil and Kusum, whose original shares are unaffected, together with Amal, Krishni, Achini and Amali as the heirs in Nimal's line.
